title: Filesystem permissions are hardcoded in file storage.
body_text:
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
_x000D_
File permissions for file storage are hardcoded in `sdk/physical/file/file.go`, in lines 239-248._x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
_x000D_
Though I have no problem with the default `0700` permissions for directories and `0600` permissions for files, permissions should be user-configurable.  That way, data in that folder could be backed up with a restricted-permission user that's part of the `vault` group.  Running backup processes using either the `vault` user or the `root` user IMHO give the backup process too much freedom it doesn't need._x000D_
_x000D_
That could be presented as two extra configuration variables inside the `storage` stanza:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
storage "file" {_x000D_
  path = "/path/to/vault/data"_x000D_
  dir_perms = "0750"  # default is 0700_x000D_
  file_perms = "0640" # default is 0600_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Some other application servers use `umask` instead: the bitfield of restricted permissions.  That'd be ok too:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
storage "file" {_x000D_
  path = "/path/to/vault/data"_x000D_
  dir_umask = "0027"  # default is 0077_x000D_
  file_umask = "0137" # default is 0177_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Thank you for Vault,_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Vault SSH CA engine issuing certs with deprecated type ssh-rsa-cert-v01@openssh.com user certificate

Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_

The certificate type is always generated as ssh-rsa-cert-v01@openssh.com. ``` # ssh-keygen -Lf tmpk6pb843_ tmpk6pb843_: Type: ssh-rsa-cert-v01@openssh.com user certificate Public key: RSA-CERT SHA256:hKyRsWm/49TFPj5mISV1jLYErnhacnCLghqTlwFSGZI Signing CA: RSA SHA256:Gw+BOYMg6ZGZWWCOkz28P5qB/IUvmL7to9krSR+dKBs (using rsa-sha2-256) Key ID: "vault-ldap-user-84ac9662125758c1b169bfe3d4c53e3eb604ae785a72708b821a939701521992" Serial: 6124806212823624310 Valid: from 2024-06-27T11:21:27 to 2024-06-27T11:22:57 Principals: user Critical Options: (none) Extensions: permit-port-forwarding permit-pty ``` With FIPS enabled, we cannot use these certs at the client level, much less to connect to a server: ``` # cat /usr/share/crypto-policies/FIPS/openssh.txt Ciphers aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes256-ctr,aes256-cbc,aes128-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-ctr,aes128-cbc MACs hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha1-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256,hmac-sha1,hmac-sha2-512 GSSAPIKeyExchange no KexAlgorithms ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256,diffie-hellman-group14-sha256,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512,diffie-hellman-group18-sha512 PubkeyAcceptedKeyTypes ecdsa-sha2-nistp256,ecdsa-sha2-nistp256-cert-v01@openssh.com,ecdsa-sha2-nistp384,ecdsa-sha2-nistp384-cert-v01@openssh.com,ecdsa-sha2-nistp521,ecdsa-sha2-nistp521-cert-v01@openssh.com,rsa-sha2-256,rsa-sha2-256-cert-v01@openssh.com,rsa-sha2-512,rsa-sha2-512-cert-v01@openssh.com CASignatureAlgorithms ecdsa-sha2-nistp256,ecdsa-sha2-nistp384,ecdsa-sha2-nistp521,rsa-sha2-256,rsa-sha2-512 ```

title: Auto-unseal Recovery Keys should be able to unseal Vault
body_text:
When you configure Vault with Auto-unseal, you get Recovery Keys._x000D_
_x000D_
The name itself makes a strong implication that their purpose is to recover Vault when the auto-unseal is down._x000D_
_x000D_
But actually this turns out to be a false promise - they cannot!_x000D_
_x000D_
Recovery keys are actually only useful to prove to the Vault software that a quorum of administrators are acting together, to authenticate operations which require that._x000D_
_x000D_
This is a pretty common question to come up over on discuss.hashicorp.com._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
I propose that something needs to be done to fix this misleading use of terminology, which has a high risk of causing data loss to users._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
I can imagine three possible ways to proceed:_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
1) Rename "Recovery keys" to "Administrator authentication keys" throughout the product and documentation._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
2) Transition "Recovery keys" to genuinely enable recovery from a lost auto-unseal, by storing a second copy of the key material that is encrypted with the auto-unseal key, encrypted with the recovery key too._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
3) Effectively, both: in a future version of Vault, support a user choice between "Auto-unseal with recovery keys" and "Auto-unseal with administrator authentication keys"._x000D_
_x000D_

title: Standardize namespace across different vault commands (where possible)
body_text:
It was frustrating to discover that when running the command: `vault login ....` the namespace for the token is "token" however when running the command `vault token lookup` the namespace for the token is "id". I think this is a minor nit, and perhaps I'm just not aware of why this would be desirable, however from my point of view it seems like the namespace for a 'token' should be universal, either "token" or "id" (or something else), but _there can be only one_.  _x000D_
_x000D_
top_3_comments_text: VinnyHC: It might help to see that the responses are coming from two different subsystems within Vault, therefore the perspective is different. When issuing the command `vault login` you are being presented with authentication details related to your login; if you inspect the response with the flag `-format=json` you’ll notice the details are part of an `auth` response. Using a field name like `id` here would be confusing as it’s not very specific (i.e. id of what?). When looking up a token using `vault token lookup` you are requesting a particular record from the system; again if you toggle `-format=json`, you’ll notice that the response is in the `data` field; so in this case, `id` can reasonably be assumed as the unique identifier of the record, in this case, a token. It's also worth noting that in order to maintain backward compatibility changing these fields would require a fair bit of effort without much gain. I'm going to close this issue but if you feel that I did not address your concerns please don't hesitate to reopen!

title: PKI: Some CN values are always rejected, even with allow_any_name and pki/sign-verbatim
body_text:
Ran into an issue where I want to generate certificates with multiple `@` signs, which currently seems to be impossible even with `allow_any_name` and `pki/sign-verbatim`. _x000D_
_x000D_
I'm hitting [this error](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/70551bf26c356a25a41945b3195e246237bb1ff0/builtin/logical/pki/cert_util.go#L1055) and the culprit seems to be that the validation [here](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/70551bf26c356a25a41945b3195e246237bb1ff0/builtin/logical/pki/cert_util.go#L272) is being a bit too harsh?

I think the validation could be loosened there if we set all of `allow_any_name=true`, `enforce_hostnames=false`, and `allow_wildcard_certificates=true` in the role. Given that the rest of the checks would otherwise be ignored if all three of those flags are set as such, I think there's an argument to be made about not erring. ~If you want to open a PR, I'd be happy to review it :-) There some [existing test scenarios](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/main/builtin/logical/pki/backend_test.go#L4299-L4505) that could be adapted for validating this case works.~ Sorry, there's more discussion on this than I thought. | addreas: Based on the docs for `allow_any_name` that is what I would expect as well. I think (unless I'm missing something here) in it's current state it is very hard to securely use Vaults OIDC identity provider (ie. it's IDP) to protect an API such as a REST or gRPC endpoint._x000D_
_x000D_
When protecting an endpoint the endpoint will require the caller to use an `access_token`. The `id_token` is not really suited for this purpose. To keep it brief, reasons as to why this is are described in articles such as [ID Token and Access Token: What's the Difference?](https://auth0.com/blog/id-token-access-token-what-is-the-difference/). _x000D_
_x000D_
So that means the endpoint will need to validate the `access_token`. This means the endpoint probably needs to know at least the following things:_x000D_
_x000D_
* Is the token valid now? Has it been revoked?_x000D_
* What is the intended audience of the token? Is this token intended to be used with this specific endpoint?_x000D_
* What is the expiry time of the token? Is this token still valid and how long can we cache certain results?_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
_x000D_
I would like for Vault to offer a OIDC token introspection endpoint ([RFC 7662](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7662)). The token introspection endpoint is an optional part of the OIDC spec but implemented by almost all IDP's (Keycloak, Hydra, etc.). _x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
_x000D_
I've evaluated using the "token lookup" API (since Vault `access_token`'s are actually Vault batch tokens). While that does tell if the token is valid and what the expiry time is there is no way to tell the intended audience of the token. Meaning that if a token gets stolen from service A there is no way for service B to validate if the token is actually valid for service B or only is only valid for service A._x000D_
_x000D_
Vault's OIDC UserInfo endpoint only offers additional information about the identity (name, email, etc.). It does not tell much about the token. At the most it tells if the token is valid when you call the endpoint. But there is no expiry time or intended audience information for example. Which makes sense since that's the job of the token introspection endpoint._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
_x000D_
While a optional piece of the OIDC spec a good chunk of applications will expect the token introspection endpoint to be callable. It will probably be a win for overall compatibility._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
_x000D_
I've also attempted to get some insight in to this via the community forum (see [this post](https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/vault-oidc-identity-provider-access-token-introspection/39733)). However that didn't generate any engagement. Maybe I should have titled it "This one weird Vault OIDC trick has billionaires freaking out" instead 😉.

title: MSSQL - Add support for AlwaysOn Availabilty Groups
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
My org is looking to use mssql database secret engine to dynamically generate sql logins. One major concern we have is that many of our SQL servers are actually AlwaysOn Availabilty Groups for to address HA concerns. One of the flaws with these availability groups is that if you use SQL logins (rather than Windows logins - Active Directory), you have to [manually sync the SIDs across each server](https://www.sqlshack.com/synchronize-logins-between-availability-replicas-in-sql-server-always-on-availability-group/) in the availability group to guarantee that logins will continue to work in the event of a failover. Historically we have always used active directory accounts to skirt around this problem, but with our migration to Vault backed logins, we will need support for login syncing. _x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Ideally we'd be able to specify that a database connection is an AlwaysOn Availability Group. Then the mssql plugin would sync the login across all servers whenever it creates a new login is requested. _x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
I've thought about building something outside of vault to watch our servers and sync logins when they appear, but you need the password to do that and I don't think there is a secure way to get that information to that service. Doing this within the mssql plugin is the only reasonable approach I can think of._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
N/A_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
I would be happy to contribute this feature, I would just like some thoughts on design prior to taking it on. _x000D_

_x000D_

title: PostgreSQL Revocation Statements doesn't allow multiline queries
body_text:
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
PostgreSQL Revocation Statements doesn't allow multiline queries as opposed to creation statements which take into consideration multline queries [by searching for `END` keywords](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/d341378c6353a9e0f776ca024215ea11be8672df/plugins/database/postgresql/postgresql.go#L269). Revocation statement [lacks this logic.](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/f8e907e0deda09a4b4dd7b56d28309ae45de3e75/builtin/logical/postgresql/secret_creds.go#L248)_x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Create any PostgreSQL backend_x000D_
2. For revocation statement use `"DO $$ BEGIN CREATE ROLE \"reassign\"; EXCEPTION WHEN duplicate_object THEN RAISE NOTICE '%, moving to next statement', SQLERRM USING ERRCODE = SQLSTATE; END $$;"`_x000D_
3. See error in vault logs about PostgreSQL syntax error._x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
Revocation statements should consider multiline queries._x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault Server Version (retrieve with `vault status`): 1.10.3_x000D_
* Vault CLI Version (retrieve with `vault version`): 1.10.3_x000D_
* Server Operating System/Architecture: Linux amd64_x000D_

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
As a normal user, without a read capability on `sys/mounts` I cannot list the mounts I have access to through any public API endpoint that I'm aware of._x000D_
_x000D_
There is a UI-specific, internal, API endpoint described here https://www.vaultproject.io/api-docs/system/internal-ui-mounts that does exactly this. So there is clearly a need for this functionality already. The problem with the above endpoint is that it's internal and could change/disappear without prior notice._x000D_
_x000D_
There is a prior issue related to this but I don't think the answer is satisfactory for my particular use case (see discussion on alternatives below): https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/2961_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Make a public endpoint similar to https://www.vaultproject.io/api-docs/system/internal-ui-mounts._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
- Using the internal endpoint above and hoping that it will not break._x000D_
- Adding read capability to `sys/mounts` to all users. This is not an option as that would expose information about existing mounts that the user does not have access to and should perhaps not even be aware of. Even if if it would be OK it would be hard to use as a starting point for exploring the secrets I have access to since, in many of the cases, I'll likely not have access to the actual content of the mount._x000D_

If `template_config` is not present, it would ignore the set `max_retries` value and set retries to 0 (essentially creating an infinite loop of instant retries). top_3_comments_text: cipherboy: @0xArKrant I don't have any specific thoughts for this, but note two things that might help you find next steps: - Vault uses internal, Vault-generate and Vault-replicated TLS certificates to do mTLS between nodes in the cluster on the cluster's port (8201 in your example). This means the TLS handshake error you'll see will occur regardless of whether the consumer-facing `listener` config has TLS enabled or not. - Vault's cluster port is essentially multiplexed and used for many separate protocols. This is done via something called [ALPN](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7301), which states what the _next_ (or underlying) protocol will be, inside of the TLS connection. We use this to choose which set of API handlers to talk to. TLS will err if it can't successfully negotiate the next protocol. Here, from your logs, we see that the leader is attempting to initiate a connection to the failing node, with the next protocol of `raft_storage_v1`. The failure is coming because this target node appears to lack knowledge of the `raft_storage_v1` selected protocol and is thus erring out the TLS connection. Maybe some more context from earlier in the failed node startup might give more context as to why we failed to provision this config? Does this occur only with 1.10.3 or do older versions (say, a 1.9.x series) also have the same error? @ncabatoff Have you seen this before? cipherboy: @0xArKrant I don't have any specific thoughts for this, but note two things that might help you find next steps: - Vault uses internal, Vault-generate and Vault-replicated TLS certificates to do mTLS between nodes in the cluster on the cluster's port (8201 in your example). This means the TLS handshake error you'll see will occur regardless of whether the consumer-facing `listener` config has TLS enabled or not. - Vault's cluster port is essentially multiplexed and used for many separate protocols. This is done via something called [ALPN](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7301), which states what the _next_ (or underlying) protocol will be, inside of the TLS connection. We use this to choose which set of API handlers to talk to. TLS will err if it can't successfully negotiate the next protocol. Here, from your logs, we see that the leader is attempting to initiate a connection to the failing node, with the next protocol of `raft_storage_v1`. The failure is coming because this target node appears to lack knowledge of the `raft_storage_v1` selected protocol and is thus erring out the TLS connection. Maybe some more context from earlier in the failed node startup might give more context as to why we failed to provision this config? Does this occur only with 1.10.3 or do older versions (say, a 1.9.x series) also have the same error? @ncabatoff Have you seen this before? My initial suspicion was wrong port in the config, but the fact that it works and randomly stops working afterwards is weird (with no apparent config changes). title: Concern about change to `ca_chain` behaviour in 1.11.0-rc1 - confusing changelog entry for PR that was not merged, unclear if changes were introduced elsewhere
body_text:
This caught my eye in the 1.11.0-rc1 changelog:_x000D_
_x000D_
secrets/pki: The ca_chain response field within issuing (/pki/issue/:role) and signing APIs will now include the root CA certificate if the mount is aware of it. [https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/pull/15155]_x000D_
_x000D_
It is frustrating that the linked PR contains no explanation for the reason for the change. Also frustrating that actual linked PR was never merged - I guess the changelog has the wrong number?_x000D_
_x000D_
There is a solid technical reason for not including the root CA certificate in `ca_chain` fields. The chain purpose is to build the chain of trust through intermediate CAs. Including root CAs in the chain (i.e. CAs where issuer == subject) has no role in chain building, and just wastes bytes on the network during TLS handshakes._x000D_

This type of reissuance is now possible in Vault 1.11 and thus it makes sense to support building those chains. Finally, note that the `manual_chain` allows you to restrict what gets served on both signing and `/ca_chain` requests. title: New PKI multi-issuer support seems to have made wrong choice about CRL and AIA URLs
body_text:
I've just been reading https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/main/website/content/api-docs/secret/pki.mdx#notice-about-new-multi-issuer-functionality and have come across the following:_x000D_
_x000D_
> Certificate Revocation List (CRL) configuration is common to all issuers,_x000D_
> All authority access URLs are common to all issuers,_x000D_
_x000D_
I am concerned that this is a design error, as a successful forward-rolling CA deployment needs CRL and AIA URLs to be unique for each issuer.
top_3_comments_text: maxb: Now confirmed by reading the code ... these settings need to be per-issuer to properly enable the forward-rolling workflow this was supposed to enable. | cipherboy: Hi @maxb, I think our intent here was to have the default issuer's paths (the existing paths at `/ca`, `/crl` &c) be used for AIA; when the CA rotation is ready, we'd switch the new CA to become default, taking over those paths. These wouldn't be canonical (well, unique) for each issuer (like say, `/issuer/:issuer_uuid/der` would be), but instead be common to the mount. We still encourage as much as possible to have separate, unrelated CAs be separate mount points (and that all issuers in a single mount point really function as a single Authority). I definitely agree generally that per-Issuer AIA selection is necessary though for true multi-issuer support though. We presently consider one mount to be one Authority (common list of serials issued, policies, &c) which hinders this slightly in other regards. I'll bring it up with the team and see what they say. | maxb: Let me type up a more detailed use case to illustrate why the CRL and AIA should never be set to the default/implicit issuer paths, and should always reference a specific issuer: Suppose we are in a renewal situation, transitioning from "ExampleCorp Intermediate CA G1" to "ExampleCorp Intermediate CA G2" (intermediate CAs with differing Common Name and different key material). There is an application with an end-entity certificate issued from G1 deployed. At startup it uses the AIA URL in its own certificate to fetch the intermediate CA that issued its certificate, and serves it to clients in the TLS handshake. (Now, you might say this is a mad design, and just configure the proper chain statically. I would agree. But the mad design of the .NET certificate APIs and .NET Linux runtime steers people to this approach, so I know there are real applications doing this.) For this to work, the AIA URL in the certificate must point **stably** to the specific generation of intermediate used to issue the particular certificate. If the AIA URL points to one which will be dynamically changed to point to a different CA, it will risk causing production breakage of applications relying on it. Now let's consider clients of the above application that are doing CRL checking. They will access the CRL URL embedded in the certificate. It is critical that the CRL URL point to the CRL for the correct CA. If it later dynamically changes to point to a CRL for a different CA, again, it risks breaking production applications which will then fail their revocation checking process. OK then, you might say, this is suboptimal, but you could manage this by doing a coordinated update of the PKI secrets engine configuration, from issuer-specific URLs to G1 endpoints, to issuer-specific URLs to G2 endpoints, at the same time as you change the default issuer. Well, kind of, but in this case you remove the ability to do realistic pre-production testing of the G2 setup. Additionally, not all cases for multiple issuers are a simple cutover from old to new. The PKI secret engine documentation itself proposes a use-case for maintaining a lower-security Vault-backed intermediate and a higher-security HSM-backed intermediate that are concurrently used for issuance, with the choice selected by PKI secret engine role configuration. This case will not be able to function correctly (unless you can do without CRL and AIA entirely) unless the URLs can be configured per issuer.

So I think this behavior would be non-conformant but somewhat expected. This then says, to me, the best approach would be the former (manual aggregation of multiple CRLs into a single entity and distributed accordingly).

CAs that include an https URI in one of these extensions MUST ensure that the server's certificate can be validated without using the information that is pointed to by the URI. Relying parties that choose to validate the server's certificate when obtaining information pointed to by an https URI in the cRLDistributionPoints, authorityInfoAccess, or subjectInfoAccess extensions MUST be prepared for the possibility that this will result in unbounded recursion. ``` This is a "SHOULD NOT", not a "MUST", so there is some leeway there. The second statement with the MUST is more interesting though: if you self-host Vault on a Vault-backed CA and wish to use AIA for its certs, this would violate both conditions, so it definitely is worth thinking about before 1.13 releases... I believe that any client software which enforces the HTTP-ness would be int he wrong based on the above. Do you have examples?
maxb: For myself, I'm satisfied that the main problem I raised this issue about, the mount-global configuration of AIA/CRL URLs, has now been fixed, with the creation of the ability to set AIA/CRL URLs on the `pki/issuer/:issuer_ref` APIs, so I'll go ahead and close this issue now. To respond to your final question - I do not have a concrete example, but I was told that it was an issue for some software in our company. Also, given the RFCs say that CAs SHOULD NOT use https URLs, it seems more than likely some client implementations have decided not to consume what should not be produced :-)

_x000D_
# or using the terraform vault provider:_x000D_
_x000D_
resource "vault_nomad_secret_backend" "nomad" {_x000D_
  backend     = "nomad"_x000D_
  description = "Generate Nomad ACL tokens On-the-Fly"_x000D_
_x000D_
  address = var.nomad_address_x000D_
  token   = nomad_acl_token.vault_secrets_backend.secret_id_x000D_
_x000D_
  # Valid for 6 hours by default_x000D_
  default_lease_ttl_seconds = 21600_x000D_
  max_lease_ttl_seconds     = 21600_x000D_
  max_ttl                   = 21600_x000D_
  ttl                       = 21600_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
2. Create a Nomad secrets backend role with type set to `management`, and read the token:_x000D_
_x000D_
```bash_x000D_
$ vault write nomad/role/role-name type=management_x000D_

_x000D_

_x000D_
resource "vault_nomad_secret_role" "role_name" {_x000D_
  role    = "role_name"_x000D_
  backend = vault_nomad_secret_backend.nomad.backend_x000D_
  type    = "management"_x000D_
}_x000D_

_x000D_

title: Support refresh tokens in Vault's OIDC provider
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently it is possible to retrieve an `access_token` in Vault but not to extend it's lifetime in a OAuth2 / OIDC compatible way. When creating client applications (such as a single page application or IOS / Android app) you don't want the user to have to re-login every day. However creating an access_token with a really long lifetime is often not desirable._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
_x000D_
I would like Vault to support [section 1.5 of the OAuth2 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-1.5), refresh tokens. Allowing me to obtain a new `access_token` (Vault batch token) by using a refresh token. The refresh token is provided to the client at the same time the `access_token` is provided. In Vault's case the refresh token could be used to extend the lifetime of the `access_token` to its `max_ttl`. The `access_token` is allowed to change when it is refreshed (as far as I know). Same goes for the refresh token itself._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
_x000D_
Using the Vault specific API to refresh the token since the OIDC access_token is in essence "juist" a Vault batch token. However that might hurt Vault's OIDC adoption since standard client libraries with support for refresh tokens won't work._x000D_
_x000D_

We currently solve these requirements with other oidc id providers (Dex, Keycloak, Ory) by setting id token expiry to 15 minutes and refresh token max lifetime to 30 days. The upstream identity source (google / github / etc...) are consulted every time the refresh token is used, achieving both requirements. title: Vault agent doesn't survive restarts after using a response-wrapped token in auto auth
body_text:
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
I have a vault agent using approle authentication to fetch a token using a response-wrapped `secret_id` and write it to a file - following the suggestions of the docs. The token I generate via approle has no `ttl` and a `token_period` of 24h, so the vault agent can renew it before it expires indefinitely._x000D_
_x000D_
However, if the VM or service restarts, it doesn't seem to want to use or renew the perfectly valid token it has locally - it tries and fails to re-auth using approle. What's more, it refuses to keep renewing secrets in `template` blocks. The logs show that authentication is failing to unwrap the token again:_x000D_
_x000D_
    error getting path or data from method: error="no known secret ID"_x000D_
_x000D_

_x000D_

Start a vault agent using approle and the following config. Then restart the agent._x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_

_x000D_

      path = "/etc/vault.d/token"_x000D_
    }_x000D_
  }_x000D_

title: Nomad client tokens with multiple Nomad policies based on LDAP groups
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem?**_x000D_
In Nomad, we have one namespace and policies per namespace for each of our projects. _x000D_
Each project has its own LDAP/AD group, and if a users needs access to a project, they get assigned to the corresponding LDAP group._x000D_
_x000D_
This works fine when creating Nomad client tokens using a management token: we combine all policies a user needs (https://learn.hashicorp.com/tutorials/nomad/access-control-tokens?in=nomad/access-control#generate-a-client-token)._x000D_
_x000D_
However, when generating Nomad client tokens with Vault, we cannot dynamically pass the policies, as we have to create Nomad roles which map to Nomad policies in advance (and generate Vault policies in the LDAP plugin which grant read access to those Nomad roles)._x000D_
This is somewhat analogous to the `/auth/token/create` and `/auth/token/create/:role_name` endpoints – the Nomad plugin only offers the latter as `/nomad/creds/:nomad_role`. (If I understand it correctly, this is by design, as Vault restricts access to the respective paths and performs no further checking after that – thus, whoever has access to `/auth/token/create` can potentially create a token for any roles.)_x000D_
_x000D_
What we would love to have is a mechanism to create a Nomad client token which dynamically bundles all (Nomad) roles a user should have access to through their LDAP group membership._x000D_
_x000D_
Here is a rough sketch, as I otherwise get lost with all the different policies, roles and tokens quickly:_x000D_
_x000D_
![VaultNomadTokens](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1836815/176451321-ce0a414d-470d-4f28-83c0-81f8b7746bc3.png)_x000D_
The user authenticates with Vault via AD, gets a Vault token with authorization based on the LDAP groups. Then they want to use that Vault token to request a Nomad client token. They want one for both projects so they do not have to exchange it too often, but since generating all Nomad role combinations doesn't scale for us, there is no such role._x000D_
With Nomad directly, however, it would be possible to issue such a token._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
What we would love to have is a mechanism to create a Nomad client token which dynamically bundles all (Nomad) roles a user should have access to through their LDAP group membership._x000D_
The favorite solution would be to have a single API endpoint a user could query with their Vault token to create a Nomad token._x000D_
_x000D_
(We know that Nomad 1.4 is supposed to have SSO, but we believe this problem is independent from the Authentication mechanism but rather with way Vault's role based access to Nomad works.)_x000D_
_x000D_
It is clear that this is not exactly how Vault's role-based authorization system works, but in this case roles seem to be too inflexible (or at least too inconvenient from our users' perspective)._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
We considered the following possible solutions:_x000D_
_x000D_
***Patch [the logical/nomad plugin](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/main/builtin/logical/nomad/path_creds_create.go)***_x000D_
This would be our preferred solution if it is something Vault can and will provide._x000D_
Otherwise we'd have to try and patch it ourselves and build our custom Vault. _x000D_
I briefly attempted this yesterday but the main hurdle is that I cannot filter the nomad roles for those a requesting client_token is authorized to access. If there is a way to do that, I am more than happy to learn about that and can offer that I/we implement a patch._x000D_
_x000D_
***Custom Vault Plugin***_x000D_
Essentially the same as before, except it would be decoupled from Vault and thus easier to maintain if this is not something which should be part of (upstream) Vault._x000D_
However, has the same problem that I currently didn't find a way to filter the available nomad roles according to the client token authorization._x000D_
_x000D_
***Don't use Vault***_x000D_
We could write our own "self-service" solution with its own Nomad management token and its own mappings from LDAP groups to Nomad policies to create and revoke Nomad client tokens. Potentially, it could use Vault for the LDAP authentication or at least for Authorization using the normal Token mechanism._x000D_
However, we want to avoid writing the whole auth service ourselves, as that always comes with way more security concerns than using an off-the-shelf solution such as Vault._x000D_
_x000D_
***Auto-manage Vault roles***_x000D_
We can imagine to create Nomad roles as they are requested. Again, this would be an additionally service which would consume a Vault-Token, check its Vault policies, read out the authorized Nomad roles, collect the Nomad policies therein, and create a new unique Nomad role with those policies, unless that exists._x000D_
This solution is probably easier to reason about within Vault, but way more complex than the other three._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
We know no other use case right now, but being able to do Nomad authorization based on LDAP groups with the Vault integration to manage the tokens for us seems like a feature others would enjoy, too.
top_3_comments_text: shoeffner: Since we finally were able to switch to OIDC, I can report that this issue can be resolved with Vault as an OIDC provider. While it does not have much flexibility to configure scopes, it works with some caveats: - Only a sparse set of useful properties is available for scopes and those are not really very dynamic: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/oidc-provider#scopes - the [identity.groups prefix used in ACL policies is not available](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/tutorials/policies/policy-templating) for the scopes, barring us from accessing, e.g., identity group metadata (when attempting to edit it, we get an error that "no groups are set", despite the fact that in the same code a couple lines above it looks like the groups must've been set to be able to access `identity.entity.groups.names`) - we would like to, e.g., filter LDAP groups to only contain a specific subset (say, groups with a specific prefix or piece of metadata) - metadata is a map of strings to strings, we were not able to, e.g., assign lists of strings as custom metadata However, the general working gist is: 1. Create policies and/or roles in Nomad 2. Setup the LDAP secret engine 3. Configure [Vault as an OIDC identity provider](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/tutorials/auth-methods/oidc-identity-provider) with a scope which includes the groups: ```hcl resource "vault_identity_oidc_scope" "groups" { name = "groups" description = "The groups scope provides the groups claim using Vault group membership" template = <<-EOF { "groups": {{identity.entity.groups.names}} } EOF } ``` 4. Use Vault as Nomad's OIDC provider and set up an [acl_binding_rule](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/nomad/latest/docs/resources/acl_binding_rule) which adds policies or roles based on the groups. So while this issue is not resolved, using Vault as an OIDC provider circumvents it.

**Describe the bug**_x000D_
Vault returns errors when trying to parse a pem file for the server certificate signing CA._x000D_
_x000D_
I have gotten this error for the use of `VAULT_CACERT` env variable and the `sslrootcert` parameter of the Postgresql storage connection url._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
_x000D_
Case 1:_x000D_
1. Run `VAULT_CACERT=/path/to/vault-ca.pem vault status`_x000D_
2. See error: `failed to read environment: ERROR loading CA File: Couldn't parse PEM in: /path/to/vault-ca.pem`_x000D_
_x000D_
Case 2:_x000D_
1. Set postgresql connection_url to `postgres://{user}:{password}@{db-host:port}/vaultdb?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/path/to/vault-ca.pem&sslcert=/path/to/vault-cert.pem&sslkey=/path/to/vault-key.pem`_x000D_
2. Run `vault server -config=/path/to/config.hcl`_x000D_
3. See error: `Error initializing storage of type postgesql: failed to check for native upsert: pq: couldn't parse pem in sslrootcert`_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
I expected these parameters to make use of the signing CA. Use of `VAULT_CACERT` will work with the Vault server certificate, though this seems like a workaround and not really a solution. Use of the server cert for `sslrootcert` has not worked so far._x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault v1.9.3_x000D_
* RHEL 7_x000D_
_x000D_
Vault server configuration file(s):_x000D_
_x000D_
```hcl_x000D_
storage "postgresql" {_x000D_
    connection_url = "postgres://{user}:{password}@{db-host:port}/vaultdb?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/path/to/vault-ca.pem&sslcert=/path/to/vault-cert.pem&sslkey=/path/to/vault-key.pem"_x000D_
    table = "vault_kv_store"_x000D_
    max_parallel = "128"_x000D_
    ha_enabled = "true"_x000D_
    ha_table = "vault_ha_locks"_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
listener "tcp" {_x000D_
    address = "[::]:8200"_x000D_
    tls_disable= false_x000D_
    tls_cert_file = "/path/to/vault-cert.pem"_x000D_
    tls_key_file = "/path/to/vault-key.pem"_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
plugin_directory = "/etc/vault/plugins"_x000D_
api_addr = "https://{vault-host}:8200"_x000D_
cluster_addr = "https://{vault-host}:8201"_x000D_
ui = true_x000D_
log_level = "trace"_x000D_
disable_mlock = true_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
I came across this issue while attempting to implement mTLS between Vault and Postgresql. I didn't go into to much detail on this here because I was trying to keep this focused on what I thought was the bug._x000D_
_x000D_
If it would be helpful, more details can be found here: https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/configure-vault-postgresql-storage-with-mutual-tls-connection/40809_x000D_
_x000D_
I have also briefly tried Vault v1.10.4, but this was just to see if a newer version would resolve the issue. Most troubleshooting effort has been done with v1.9.3._x000D_

title: [Kubernetes Secret Engine] allow specifying a namespace selector for the allowed namespace in role.
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
When creating a kubernetes secret engine role, one must specify which namespaces should be allowed (https://www.vaultproject.io/api-docs/secret/kubernetes#allowed_kubernetes_namespaces). Namespaces come an go as teams do their work. So, on a very dynamic cluster one would have to constantly update the list of allowed namespaces._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Allow to specify a namespace selector instead of an array of namespaces. This will select a dynamic set of namespaces based on their labels. This is the standard approach in Kubernetes to deal with these issues._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
As of now, because constantly updating the same configuration is untenable, one would probably end up creating a role for each namespace._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
here is an overview of labels and selector: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/_x000D_
here is what a label selector looks like from a API perspective: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.24/#labelselector-v1-meta_x000D_
there are go utility functions to quickly check if an object is selected by an label selector._x000D_
_x000D_
top_3_comments_text: f4z3r: I am quite interested in looking at this. What needs to be achieved in terms of logic seems relatively straight-forward. What I am unsure about is how this can be solved in an elegant way on the secret engine configuration. Currently there is only a string array `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` that can be configured. With the label selector we would need to support a full map, and define what happens if a user defines both the selector and the standard array (or decide to reject this in the validation). Do you already have an idea on how this should ideally look like? | f4z3r: Ok so I will start to implement this. I think I will go with the following principles: - Introduce a new parameter called `allowed_kubernetes_namespace_selector`. - The new parameter behaves similar to `generated_role_rules`, in that it is of type string and one can pass either a YAML or JSON `LabelSelector`. - The two parameters `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` and `allowed_kubernetes_namespace_selector` are mutually exclusive, hence a request setting both should return an error. - The selector (if configured) will be evaluated against a namespace every time a credential for said role is requested. This will involve an additional API call against Kubernetes, as the labels of the namespace for which the credentials are requested are not known to Vault by default (and can change at any time). This has a couple of impacts: - Performance. This should be a relatively minor impact, but the additional API call on credential requests introduces latency. - Permissions. As Vault now needs access to the labels of namespaces, it requires read permissions on namespaces. This is not a critical permission, so it shouldn't be problematic, but documentation will need to be updated. If you have any feedback to this, please let me know. I will start the implementation on the plugin with these principles in mind, but it should not be much work to make changes afterwards. | f4z3r: The more I work on this, the more I have the feeling it might make sense to allow users to set both `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` and `allowed_kubernetes_namespace_selector`, and that it essentially ANDs the values if both are set. This way I would argue that the only illegal configurations would be to set neither, or to only set `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` with an empty array. I feel like this would give the most flexibility to users, does not break backwards-compatibility, and also makes some parts of the code a little cleaner in terms of behaviour (e.g. what happens on an update? Can a user try to "clear" `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` by setting it to an empty array and set `allowed_kubernetes_namespace_selector` instead? These questions quickly make the behaviour a little dodgy if we only allow one of both to be set IMO)

These questions quickly make the behaviour a little dodgy if we only allow one of both to be set IMO)
raffaelespazzoli: I was on PTO. Thanks for picking this up so quickly. I'd have done very similar choices to your, the only thing I'd change is that I'd make the two `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` and `allowed_kubernetes_namespace_selector` mutually exclusive rather than in OR. It's just a matter of style. Because using a namespaces selector allows to essentially set a super-set of conditions relative to what you can do with `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces, one might also consider using only `allowed_kubernetes_namespace_selector` in the API. But it would involve an API change. To offset the performance hit due to the additional call, you can create a cached watcher (as normal operators do) for namespaces. Finally this change could also be propagated to the kube auth engine.
f4z3r: @raffaelespazzoli sure no worries. Regarding the mutual exclusivity, I agree. The issue I encountered was that when updating the configuration, I was unsure how to handle this. For example, I would prohibit setting both parameters on initial creation of the role. Now suppose someone configures the role to use the standard `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces`. After a while he wants to use the selector. How does he clear the value of the allowed namespaces? At the moment an update will allow to merge configurations, such that you can update a single parameter without having to provide all parametera again. I see three options here: 1. We realise that this is an update instead of a create, clear the previously allowed namespaces and set the new selector (instead of throwing an error that both are not allowed) While this is elegant in terms of use, it means that some parameter "clearing" happens implicitely in the background, which I am not a fan of. 2. We force the user to provide both parameters on the update, and the `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` array must be empty. This would be more explicit, but I find it kind of funny to say they are exclusive, yet you have to provide both parameters. 3. Allow to set the selector directly in the `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces`. That way we do not introduce a new parameter and sidestep the two issues above. I am not super sure this is inline with the general "configuration-style" of Vault, and would need to check how this could be validated (to allow yaml or json selectors, and a comma separated list of strings). Let me know what you think. I will check the feasibility of the two first points next week, and see how elegantly this can be solved. For the performance I would leave it like this for now unless it becomes an issue (which I doubt). I don't want to "pre-optimize" the code, and using a watcher would require an additional `list` permission on namespaces, which might be problematic for some users. Regarding the auth method, yes I can have a look at it next week as well. Not yet sure exactly when, but will definitely have the time at some point.
f4z3r: @raffaelespazzoli I thought about this a little more. I believe that in theory option 3 would be the most elegant. This would make the two mutually exclusive, and would be elegant in terms of how the update of the role are handled. However, implementing this would change the typing for the API, and would therefore not be backward compatible with typed clients. Therefore I don't think it makes sense to implement it. The two other options I find not very elegant. Regarding your point: > using a namespaces selector allows to essentially set a super-set of conditions relative to what you can do with `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` while this is true, I don't see why this points to mutual exclusivity. Do you care to explain this a little more? The way I see it, people can: - Set only the `allowed_kubernetes_namespaces` with a list of namespaces or the wildcard. This needs to be preserved in order to avoid a breaking change. - Set only the `allowed_kubernetes_namespace_selector` to have more flexibility, such as in your use case, where the namespaces might be added after the role has been configured. - Set both. While I do see that the use case for setting both is much less prominent than the two others, I think this still makes sense. The reason I think this is mostly because it will map 1 to 1 to how permissions can be provided to the Vault ServiceAccount. Vault might be granted permissions to handle SAs, secrets, etc in namespaces both based on label selectors, and on namespace names at the same time. If we do not allow to set both here in the role, it would mean that we could grant permissions to our Vault on Kubernetes level that cannot be expressed in the role configuration. This would be a little sad to restrict. The only reason I could then think to not allow it, is if it would introduce major complexity. However this is not the case here. Does my reasoning make sense to you? Or do you see this differently?
f4z3r: Regarding the change on the auth engine, I will open an issue that references this on the plugin project, but I will not yet implement it. The auth plugin does not use the standard Kubernetes client, and implementing the namespace label getting will require relatively large changes to the code if we don't want to duplicate too much. I will therefore wait and see what the decision is here, and then implement it once it is clear what way we are going.
raffaelespazzoli: I'm good with the design you are proposing @f4z3r

title: vault template stanza exec object appears to not parse correctly
body_text:
The vault documentation for a template stanza describes the [exec](https://www.vaultproject.io/docs/agent/template#exec) declaration as:_x000D_
```_x000D_
[exec](https://www.vaultproject.io/docs/agent/template#exec) (object: optional) - _x000D_
The exec block executes a command when the template is rendered and the output has changed. _x000D_
The block parameters are command (string slice: required) and timeout (string: optional, defaults to 30s)._x000D_
```_x000D_
For vault `v1.11.0` with consul-template `0.29.0`, the consul template config [docs](https://github.com/hashicorp/consul-template/blob/v0.29.0/docs/configuration.md) show the exec hcl block example as:_x000D_
```_x000D_
template {_x000D_
_x000D_
  # ..._x000D_
_x000D_
  # This is the optional exec block to give a command to be run when the template _x000D_
  # is rendered. The command will only run if the resulting template changes. _x000D_
  # The command must return within 30s (configurable), and it must have a _x000D_
  # successful exit code._x000D_
  # See the Exec section below and the Commands section in the README for more._x000D_
  exec {_x000D_
      command = ["restart", "service", "foo"]_x000D_
      timeout = "30s"_x000D_
  }_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The JSON equivalent (what we are using for config submission to vault-agent) for the exec block should be:_x000D_
```_x000D_
      ..._x000D_
      "exec": [_x000D_
        {_x000D_
          "command": [_x000D_
            "restart",_x000D_
            "service",_x000D_
            "foo"_x000D_
          ],_x000D_
          "timeout": "30s"_x000D_
        }_x000D_
      ],_x000D_
      ..._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
However, this JSON produces the error:_x000D_
```_x000D_
Error loading configuration from $FILE.json: error parsing 'template': 1 error(s) decoding:_x000D_
_x000D_
* 'exec' expected a map, got 'slice'_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
I cannot seem to change the JSON in any manner to get the exec declaration to parse correctly._x000D_
Another user independently reported the same issue in the hashicorp discussion channel [here](https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/ask-vault-agent-templating-error-exec-expected-a-map-got-slice/41074)._x000D_
_x000D_
For now, falling back to use of the deprecated `command` (string) is a workaround._x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
Vault v1.11.0 (ea296ccf58507b25051bc0597379c467046eb2f1), built 2022-06-17T15:48:44Z_x000D_
NixOS, x86_64-linux

title: The forwardedRequestRPCServer should not accept the Echo message from the resurrected server that is declared dead and removed by autopilot
body_text:
<!-- Please reserve GitHub issues for bug reports and feature requests._x000D_

_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
When a dead server has been removed by autopilot, if it comes back for any reason without any change to the data in the storage, it has the record of information of existing leader and unseal information and start sending the Echo request back to the existing leader as if it is still part of the cluster, as I see from the vault status command showing all the cluster information. With the Echo requests, the result seems to be the `vault operator members` shows resurrected server as one of the member but it is actually no longer part of the cluster. This is also inconsistent with the result from `vault operator raft autopilot state` where the server has been removed._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Set up a cluster with 4 nodes of raft backend_x000D_
2. Enable autopilot `vault write sys/storage/raft/autopilot/configuration cleanup_dead_servers=true dead_server_last_contact_threshold=3m min_quorum=3`_x000D_
3. Stop or pause one of the followers_x000D_
4. Monitor until the follower left the cluster, declared dead by autopilot, which would be after 3 minutes as per above configuration._x000D_
5. Check result from `vault operator members` and `vault operator raft autopilot state` will see the output is consistent._x000D_
6. Start or resume the dead follower_x000D_
7. The `vault operator members` will show the resurrected server in the list with status active, the server won't be added to the raft peers. It is still forwarding the request to the existing node, and if the leader change, this server went disappeared from `vault operator members` (looks like it read from peers cache), and the request seems to be forwarded twice to new leader so apparently this zombie node still responding to requests as normal, just does not have data replicated to it as it would have been as a raft peer._x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
I would expect the server won't show up in any command result given the observed information, it should be blocked from request forwarding as well._x000D_
_x000D_
If it should be able to rejoin back as a fresh node in the cluster, it should be able to reset itself and restart the join process automatically as it would probably have known itself that it was dead before after unsealed (maybe the raft/autopilot configuration in the local storage would be able to tell itself, not sure)._x000D_

title: [PKI] Allow deviation from recommended signature algorithms
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
Currently, Vault enforces the signature algorithms to be aligned with the recommendations e.g. from NIST, BSI or Mozilla CA guidelines._x000D_
While that makes sense for the majority of cases, there are some edge cases where it is desirable to deviate from that._x000D_
_x000D_
For example, our scenario is managing Secure-Boot keys for an entire software product line against a specific hardware platform (NXP i.MX8). In our scenario, the Chip only supports up to SHA256 signature algorithms but ECC up to 521 bit curves._x000D_
_x000D_
In vault 1.10.0 there was the possibility to get EC521-with-SHA256 by specifying signature_bits at the pki role, whereas earlier there used to be the possibility to specify signature_bits at the /sign-intermediate endpoint, which then would also use this bit number for issued certificates._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
In my opinion, it would be good to provide a flag or option at the PKI mount path to disable the enforcement of signature algorithms (defaults to false, as it should be for almost everyone). _x000D_
_x000D_
That way, the enforcement would still be in place for most scenarios but we could disable it for advanced use cases with restricted ciphers._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
One alternative in our scenario would be to use scripts with openssl to generate these certs and store them in the KV backend, but that takes the possibility of managing certs and revocations within vault._x000D_

body_text:
Currently, in Golang, as far as I can see, the only way to create an AppRole and specify the `roleId` and `secretId` is via `Logical` calls via the API like so:_x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
vaultClient.Logical().Write("auth/approle/role/concourse", map[string]interface{}{_x000D_
		"backend":                 "approle",_x000D_
		"role_name":               "concourse",_x000D_
		"token_policies":          []string{"concourse"},_x000D_
		"token_no_default_policy": "true",_x000D_
		"bind_secret_id":          "true",_x000D_
		"token_period":            "0",_x000D_
	})_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
And then if we want to change the `role_id` and `secret_id` to be something that we choose we have to do the following._x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
	secret, err := vaultClient.Logical().Write("auth/approle/role/concourse/secret-id", map[string]interface{}{_x000D_
		"secret_id": "secret_id_value",_x000D_
	})_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		log.Fatal(err)_x000D_
	}_x000D_
	secretID := secret.Data["secret_id"].(string)_x000D_
_x000D_
	_, err = vaultClient.Logical().Write("auth/approle/role/concourse/role-id", map[string]interface{}{_x000D_
		"role_id": "role_id_value",_x000D_
	})_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		log.Fatal(err)_x000D_
	}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Can we just have a dedicated method like we do for enabling of the `approle` functionality like so_x000D_
_x000D_

vaultClient.Sys().EnableAuthWithOptions("approle", appRoleOptions)_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Unable to restore backup after seal migration

2. Follow the migration steps identified here: https://support.hashicorp.com/hc/en-us/articles/360002040848-Seal-Migration_x000D_

4. Restart vault_x000D_
5. vault status - identify that vault is sealed, with a shamir key_x000D_
6. Unseal vault using recovery keys - identify that vault is now unsealed, in the same state as 3_x000D_
7. Generate backup using: vault operator raft snapshot save /vault/file/shamir.snap_x000D_
8. Restore shamir.snap to a new Vault, following the SOP: https://learn.hashicorp.com/tutorials/vault/sop-restore_x000D_
9. When attempting to start Vault with the backup restored, notice this error in the logs, and vault immediately stops:_x000D_

title: LoginMFA requires excessive access to OKTA API to function
body_text:
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
When configuring LoginMFA with OKTA, vault is getting a permission denied error when accessing the okta API. We have narrowed the issue down to permission that the LoginMFA code requires on the okta side. The permission allows the API call to delete the user's MFA configuration from the okta service. I suspect that this is a bug with how vault is using the OKTA golang library or with the OKTA golang library itself. If I grant this excessive permission to the token vault used to access the OKTA API vault and LoginMFA will work as expected. Our Enterprise Security Identity team will not allow us to deploy LoginMFA in production as the excessive permission could be used to invalidate users' MFA config for all services they access._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Setup an OKTA developer account with test users (admin user you get by default, test user & API user)_x000D_
2. Config OKTA Authentication > Sign-On Policy to trigger MFA on login by default_x000D_
3. Config OKTA Multifactor > Okta Verify > Enable Push Notification & Disable number challenge (https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/11329)_x000D_
4. Config OKTA Security > Administrators > Roles > Create New role with only "View users and their details" & "View groups and their details"_x000D_
5. Config OKTA Security > Administrators >  create a new user that the API token will be associated with and set the role to the one created above. Also, create a resource set that scopes all test users. Read only admin role._x000D_
6.  Config OKTA Start a separate browser session and login as the new user. (chrome profile or incognito mode)_x000D_
7. Config OKTA Security > API > Tokens > Create Token (while logged in as the new user)_x000D_
8. Config OKTA as the primary OKTA account (not the account used for the token) and set the token user role to the limited one created previously. Security > Administrators > Roles > Admins > Edit the user assignment selecting the new role and resource set previously created. This effectively limits the token to the access granted by the role. _x000D_
9. Config VAULT Setup an auth method like user/pass or okta (we are using okta) _x000D_
10. Config VAULT LoginMFA for use with OKTA _x000D_
```_x000D_
MFA_METHOD_IDS=$(vault write -field method_id identity/mfa/method/okta org_name="$OKTA_ORG" api_token="$OKTA_TOKEN" base_url="$OKTA_BASE_URL" username_format="{{identity.entity.aliases.${OKTA_AUTH_ACCESSOR}.name}}@nachos.com" primary_email=true)_x000D_
vault write identity/mfa/login-enforcement/nachos auth_method_accessors="$OKTA_AUTH_ACCESSOR" mfa_method_ids="$MFA_METHOD_IDS"_x000D_
```_x000D_
11. Login to vault using okta & LoginMFA as the test user_x000D_
```_x000D_
vault login -method okta username=blake_x000D_
```_x000D_
This will result in an error before the MFA push is sent to your authenticator._x000D_
```_x000D_
Asking Vault to perform MFA validation with upstream service. You should receive a push notification in your authenticator app shortly_x000D_
Error making API request._x000D_
_x000D_
URL: PUT https://vault.nachos.com:8200/v1/sys/mfa/validate_x000D_
Code: 403. Errors:_x000D_
_x000D_
* failed to satisfy enforcement nachos. error: 2 errors occurred:_x000D_
	* the API returned an error: You do not have permission to perform the requested action_x000D_
	* login MFA validation failed for methodID: [21516e89-2f78-e4e1-189f-9e0000698539]_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
12. Config OKTA Security > Administrators > Roles > Edit the role and add "Reset users' authenticators" permission. _x000D_
13.  Login to vault using okta & LoginMFA as the test user_x000D_
```_x000D_
vault login -method okta username=blake_x000D_
``` _x000D_
We get the really nice message prompting you to check your authenticator, and then the login succeeds! _x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
Our expectation is that vault would use least privileges when it comes to accessing the OKTA API to do MFA. The "Reset users' authenticators" permission should not be required for this MFA push flow to work. _x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault Server Version (retrieve with `vault status`):  1.11.0_x000D_
* Vault CLI Version (retrieve with `vault version`):  1.11.0_x000D_
* Server Operating System/Architecture: Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS x86_64_x000D_
_x000D_
Vault server configuration file(s):_x000D_
_x000D_
```hcl_x000D_
# Full configuration options can be found at https://www.vaultproject.io/docs/configuration_x000D_
log_level = "trace"_x000D_
log_format = "json"_x000D_
ui = true_x000D_
cluster_name = "nachos"_x000D_
cluster_addr = "http://10.0.0.62:8202"_x000D_
api_addr = "http://10.0.0.62:8200"_x000D_
#mlock = true_x000D_
#disable_mlock = true_x000D_
_x000D_
# HTTPS listener_x000D_
listener "tcp" {_x000D_
  address       = "10.0.0.62:8200"_x000D_
  tls_cert_file = "/opt/vault/tls/tls.crt"_x000D_
  tls_key_file  = "/opt/vault/tls/tls.key"_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
storage "raft" {_x000D_
  path = "/opt/vault/data"_x000D_
  node_id = "nachos"_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
We are blocked from rolling out LoginMFA in production because this excessive permission could be used as a denial of service and remove the authenticator config for any user in our OKTA config.  Related hashicorp support case #75411_x000D_

body_text:

title: RFE: allow signing externally-generated CSRs
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
Vault’s PKI secrets engine currently generates the private key within Vault.  This is less secure than if the private key never leaves the system on which it is generated.  It is also explicitly forbidden by the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Vault’s PKI should support issuing certificates without Vault having ever seen the private key._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
None_x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
This is a blocker for Vault to be used to issue publicly trusted certificates._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here._x000D_

title: RFE: PKI: support requiring attestation of keys
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
The PKI secrets engine supports signing CSRs, but it does not currently allow enforcing that the private key of the CSR was generated on a secure hardware token._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Vault should support verifying an attestation signature that proves that the device itself generated the key pair.  Such attestations are supported by Yubico products, for example._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
None._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
None._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
This would allow ensuring that the issued certificate was securely generated in hardware, as opposed to in software.  This is required for EV code-signing certificates and is useful in other cases as well.
top_3_comments_text: cipherboy: @DemiMarie Is there a standard format for this? I've seen a lot of one-off discussions on how to do this with vendor A or vendor B's products, but I've not really seen an independent standard on this. I think the [CRMF protocol](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4211) does [proof of possession](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4211#section-4) but we don't currently implement that and I don't think CRMF's PoP is sufficient for attestation of key generation. It looks like [this repo](https://github.com/pkic/remote-key-attestation) has a bunch of details of the one-off protocols that people use. | othouvou: @cipherboy there isn't currently a published standard ([PKIX ](https://www.ietf.org/id/draft-ounsworth-pkix-key-attestation-02.html)is draft ATM) but Vault can still provide this functionality in a non-standardized approach, just like other HSM vendors are doing (e.g. https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/attest-key), which is basically a series of checks on underlying manufacturer's HSM certificate and key attributes. It would be good if your product offered this feature since it is required in the publicly trusted PKI world for code and document signing certificates.

title: Forbid revoking Vault’s own certificate
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
If Vault’s own certificate is revoked, one will not be able to communicate with Vault.  If Vault is also the issuer of this certificate, it will be very difficult to recover from this situation._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Vault should refuse to revoke the certificate it is currently using._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
This can be done with ACLs, but that is much more error-prone.  One can also re-issue the certificate by creating a new intermediate, but that is ugly and could be very slow, especially if the root is stored offline.  The most likely recovery technique is to suppress revocation checking, which is insecure._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
See above._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
None
top_3_comments_text: cipherboy: \o hey @DemiMarie, thanks for the suggestion! I'm not sure I agree with this part: > One can also re-issue the certificate by creating a new intermediate, ... Vault presently forbids revocation of issuer certificates within their own mount. You wouldn't accidentally revoke the intermediate, you'd have to do so intentionally by taking its serial to the root mount (or the offline root in this case...). I'm not sure how Vault could prevent this in the offline root case as that's entirely out of our control. For the leaf certificates, while we presently don't have any revocation controls against Vault's own certificates. IMO, leaf certs should be rotated relatively frequently. Revocation is just another trigger for needing rotation, and if you're self-hosting Vault on a Vault-backed CA infra, you're bound to deal with offline (whether by revocation or expiration or some other cause) Vault eventually. Worst case this looks like switching to a localhost-bound non-TLS listener, unsealing, fetching the new cert, and resealing (probably a better discussion for your other ticket :-). But in the specific case of revocation, its typical to be able to override revocation checks on the client. (I don't believe Vault CLI does CRL checks at all but you could be using a custom client). Also, I'm not entirely sure what threat model you'd have wherein the _private key_ of the TLS cert has been compromised, necessitating revocation of the Vault TLS listener cert, but _Vault proper_ hasn't been compromised? Or is this mostly about preventing accidental revocation? While not always strictly the same permissions, it seems likely the cause for necessitating revocation would be host compromise of some sort (but not enough to compromise Vault...? Hmmm....). The latter (full Vault compromise) would trigger say, a seal operation plus taking Vault offline and investigating very carefully -- a much higher risk profile than revoking Vault certs can solve. I think at best this would look like some internal policy constraint being violated (e.g., lacking some internal verification/controls), in which case, why not delay the revocation of the old Vault TLS leaf cert until the new one has been rolled? In general too, we suggest consumers use short-lived TTLs to avoid needing to revoke in all cases but key compromise. title: Allow the user of identity templates in secret/ssh roles `default_user` field
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
_x000D_
We would like to configure an ssh role that issues certificates to entities based on their name by default,_x000D_
_x000D_
i.e. if we have an SSH role configured (using the Vault SSH Role Terraform resource for the sake of example):_x000D_
```_x000D_
resource "vault_ssh_secret_backend_role" "self" {_x000D_
  backend = vault_mount.ssh_client.path_x000D_
  name    = "self"_x000D_
  key_type                = "ca"_x000D_
  allowed_users           = "{{identity.entity.name}}"_x000D_
  allowed_users_template  = "true"_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently they (or the tooling running on their behalf) need to make a call the equivalent of:_x000D_
```_x000D_
vault write ssh/sign/self public_key=@id_rsa.pub valid_principals=ianferguson_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
in order to get a certificate based on their current entity name, in effect requiring the caller to know their entity name and provide it, even though we would like to default to using the entity name if no `valid_principal` field is provided._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Ideally, identity attribute templating could be supported for the `default_user` field the same way it is currently supported for the `allowed_users` field_x000D_
_x000D_
This would allow us to configure out backend role like this:_x000D_
```_x000D_
resource "vault_ssh_secret_backend_role" "self" {_x000D_
  backend = vault_mount.ssh_client.path_x000D_
  name    = "self"_x000D_
  key_type                = "ca"_x000D_
  default_user  = "{{identity.entity.name}}"_x000D_
  default_user_template = "true"_x000D_
  allowed_users           = "{{identity.entity.name}}"_x000D_
  allowed_users_template  = "true"_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
and then have our client side tooling do the equivalent of:_x000D_
```_x000D_
vault write ssh/sign/self public_key=@id_rsa.pub_x000D_
```_x000D_
and receive back an SSH certificate with the entity's name as a principal without needing to do additional network hops to look up the current entity name or guessing configuration in the request parameters_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
- guessing the user's entity name from the `$USER` in their shell (this is not always a 1:1 match or correct)_x000D_
- looking up the current entity's name with a combination of `vault token lookup`+`vault read entity/id/.....` calls. This adds ~2+ additional api calls to Vault, and requires all entity's to have permission to read entity information from the identity backend, which is less ideal_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
_x000D_
This is (tangentially) related to #10946, in that #10946 requires templating support, but this is ultimately only a narrow subset of what the user's in #10946 would like_x000D_
_x000D_
Pull request implementing this can be found here: #16351

title: The transit secrets engine does not support RSA padding scheme pkcs1v15 for encryption.
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
_x000D_
Yes it is. We'd like to use the Vault transit secrets engine to sign and decrypt with an RSA padding scheme of `pkcs1v15` for a usecase where we can't choose an another padding scheme. This is, because we have to work with a given signing and decryption scheme by a standard we have to use for a use case in fintech industry. Vault supports signing with `pkcs1v15` but not for decryption; and also not other operations like encryption._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
_x000D_
We'd like to have the transit engine being able to encrypt and decrypt with the pkcs1v15 RSA padding scheme. Consequently `datakey` and `rewrap` shall provide a padding_scheme parameter too._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
_x000D_
We could implement a plugin, and we already did as a PoC. We believe from a maintenance perspective, to have the option which padding scheme being used for RSA operation is still better. _x000D_
_x000D_
We'll provide a PR, that follows after creating this Issue, that implements the feature including UI support._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
There is none._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
N/A._x000D_

title: UI navigation requesting `GET secrets/config` for kv mount and failing
body_text:
<!-- Please reserve GitHub issues for bug reports and feature requests._x000D_
_x000D_
For questions, the best place to get answers is on our [discussion forum](https://discuss.hashicorp.com/c/vault), as they will get more visibility from experienced users than the issue tracker._x000D_
_x000D_
Please note: We take Vault's security and our users' trust very seriously. If you believe you have found a security issue in Vault, please responsibly disclose by contacting us at security@hashicorp.com. Our PGP key is available at [our security page](https://www.hashicorp.com/security/)._x000D_
_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
Navigation, via the UI, through a KV secrets mount point causes repeated calls to the `secrets/config` endpoint. Three areas of concern here:_x000D_
1. I cannot find documentation describing why read access to the endpoint is necessary (my guess is for displaying max version information?)_x000D_
2. We are correctly failing the permission check (ie the token does not have access to the endpoint), but it is strange we are retrying at (almost) every API request._x000D_
3. The below capture shows that we are querying the resultant-acl API which also does not list the token as having capabilities on `secrets/config`, so it is interesting we are querying it in the first place._x000D_
_x000D_
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10523950/179856107-0e682724-4110-44bf-bfb2-ef33df5b3935.png)_x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Create a KV secrets store with some data (possibly restricted to kv-v2?)_x000D_
2. Create a token with a policy granting list permissions on `secrets/metadata/*` (in order to access it via the UI) -- Important to not include the `secrets/config` read permission_x000D_
3. Navigate the UI, using the generated token._x000D_
_x000D_
Almost every navigation through the KV mount will trigger an API call to `secrets/config` which will 403 due to a lack of permissions. However, this does not seem to impact the UI experience and does not display to the user (check audit logs or network captures as above)_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
I would expect two things here:_x000D_
1. Some documentation saying that this permission is necessary for full/complete user experience in navigating the KV mounts in the UI and describing why the permission is necessary (i.e. what it allows the UI to do for the user). Admittedly, I didn't spend a huge amount of time looking for documentation on this, so it might exist_x000D_
2. Since the UI workflow already appears to be querying `sys/internal/ui/resultant-acl`, I would expect the process attempting to query `secrets/config` to leverage the resultant-acl, see the token does not have permissions, and simply not make the request. I think it would also be acceptable for the `GET secrets/config` to happen once to see/receive the 403 and then have the result cached and not queried again on that mount point._x000D_
_x000D_
The main issue here is that our audit logs contained a number of these requests, all 403'ing, and I would like that not to happen. For our environment, we are fine to simply add read access for `secrets/config` to some our policies, but this was still unexpected behavior and I felt deserved some documentation/discussion._x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault Server Version (retrieve with `vault status`): 1.10.4_x000D_
* Vault CLI Version (retrieve with `vault version`): 1.11.0_x000D_
* Server Operating System/Architecture: Ubuntu 18.04 x86_64 running Vault within a container_x000D_
_x000D_
Vault server configuration file(s): Can provide if needed, but does not seem relevant_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
Add any other context about the problem here._x000D_

Regarding the multiple hits to this endpoint, I agree. We are doing some work on the KV engine for the 1.15 release, which includes how permissions are checked and when.
