But obviously it's not really a _solution_ anyone would like to have; it's just a dirty hack. I guess preferable resolution options would be, from most to least preferable, for the Agent: - implement persistent caching for native OS Agent (Windows/macOS) - add configuration option to automatically revoke my previously retrieved lease(s) for a given secret when 500 response is received from the server - alternative: add configuration option to automatically revoke all my leases when 500 response is received from the server - add lease_id logging under DEBUG level for Agent For the Vault service: - allow granting user permissions to read their leases (per secret or overall) - allow granting user permissions to revoke their leases based on secret name - allow granting user permissions to revoke all their leases

title: Vault Agent does not respect GCP Secrets Engine OAuth2 token TTL, requests new tokens every 5 minutes
body_text:
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
In accordance with the docs, when using the GCP Secrets Engine to generate OAuth2 tokens for service accounts, [the resulting secret is returned without a lease being generated for it](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/gcp#deprecation-of-access-token-leases). Unfortunately, this leads to the Vault Agent giving it the [default treatment for non-leased secrets](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/agent/template#non-renewable-secrets), meaning it will trigger generation of a new token every time `template_config.static_secret_render_interval` passes, which has a default value of 5 minutes, even though the tokens themselves are valid for ~3600 seconds._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Configure Vault Agent to consume OAuth2 tokens from any of the `roleset`, `static-account` or `impersonated-account` endpoints¹_x000D_
2. Let it run for >5 minutes and watch its logs and/or the output files_x000D_
3. Multiple tokens have been issued in less than an hour_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
The secret data returned by the `gcp/*/token` endpoint already includes information about the generated token's lifetime:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
vault read -format json gcp/roleset/some-roleset/token_x000D_
{_x000D_
  "request_id": "b80912cd-ff9e-bdb8-cb12-0bd300d11f12",_x000D_
  "lease_id": "",_x000D_
  "lease_duration": 0,_x000D_
  "renewable": false,_x000D_
  "data": {_x000D_
    "expires_at_seconds": 1680779098,_x000D_
    "token": "XXX",_x000D_
    "token_ttl": 3598_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  "warnings": null_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
One possible course of action would be to make changes to the Vault Agent in order to consume this data and avoid premature requests for new tokens, similar to how [refreshing non-leased secrets is handled in the case of the database Secrets Engine's static roles](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/agent/template#static-roles)._x000D_
_x000D_
Another possible solution would be to rely on the agent's already-present logic for handling secrets with a `rotation_period` field and instead make changes to the `gcp/*/token` endpoints in the GCP Secrets Engine in order to add the necessary fields to the response, which would not only be rather hacky, but also likely require more effort than handling this on the Agent side._x000D_
_x000D_
As a workaround, users can configure the global `template_config.static_secret_render_interval` setting to something larger than 5 and smaller than 60 minutes, *if no other parts in their configuration mandate a different setting*. This workaround could be made more tenable by allowing overrides on the level of individual `template` blocks to, say, re-request and render GCP Secrets Engine OAuth2 tokens in 45 minute intervals while retaining a shorter interval for other secrets/templates._x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault Server Version (retrieve with `vault status`): 1.13.0_x000D_
* Vault CLI Version (retrieve with `vault version`): Vault v1.13.0 (cgo)_x000D_
* Server Operating System/Architecture: Debian 11 (bullseye), amd64_x000D_
_x000D_
Vault server configuration file(s):_x000D_
n/a_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
¹: Example Vault Agent config:_x000D_
_x000D_
```hcl_x000D_
template_config {_x000D_
  static_secret_render_interval = "5m" # <- this can be increased from the default of 5m as a workaround._x000D_
}_x000D_
template {_x000D_
  destination = "/vault/secrets/gcp-oauth-token"_x000D_
  contents = <<-EOF_x000D_
    {{- with secret "gcp/roleset/some-roleset/token" -}}_x000D_
    {{ .Data.token }}_x000D_
    {{- end }}_x000D_
  EOF_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_

title: Create clear guidelines for recovering vault snapshots after loosing KMS key when using auto-unseal mode
body_text:
I'm working on a Vault setup that could be used in production. _x000D_
I would like to use AWS KMS auto-unseal mechanism as a convenient way of managing cluster state, but I also need to have reliant backups to be able to restore Vault's state when anything bad happens._x000D_
_x000D_
I was really terrified, when I realized, that when using auto-unseal, if for some reason KMS data are lost, I will not be able to recover anything from the snapshots._x000D_
_x000D_
The documentation very briefly mentions this fact ( https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/seal#auto-unseal ) and gives a very misleading name to the set of so called "Recovery keys" that are given to the user during Vault's initialization._x000D_
_x000D_
This is really critical issue and I'm surprised that Vault's developers ignore this fact, despite it being raised many times:_x000D_
https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/16294_x000D_
https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/16391_x000D_
https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/11244_x000D_
https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/15490_x000D_
_x000D_
There was some work done on this subject but with no clear information if or when it will be available in the OSS version:_x000D_
https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/pull/18683_x000D_
_x000D_
For me, it seems like a very basic feature, to be able to create reliant backups, independent of the infrastructure._x000D_
_x000D_
I can imagine, that 2 things can be done at this point:_x000D_
_x000D_
Either deploy the solution ( https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/pull/18683 ) in the OSS version._x000D_
_x000D_
Or declare KMS auto-unseal option as an experimental feature that shouldn't be used in production._x000D_
_x000D_
If someone started to use such setup, mislead by the, so called "Recovery keys" name, they can run into big trouble when figuring out, that despite of having regular snapshots and storing the "Recovery keys" in a safe place, they end up in a point that recovery of the data is no longer possible.

Suppose I create a single AES key, import it into a KMS key ring in Project A, and configure Vault to use that key. Later, I export the same raw AES key material, import it into a KMS key ring in Project B, and update Vault’s seal stanza to point at the Project B version of that key. Intuitively it seems like Vault should still be able to unwrap its master key, since the underlying AES bits are identical. Would something like that work? In practice, however, it fails with “INDECIPHERABLE_CIPHERTEXT_FOR_CRYPTOKEY.” The reason is that Vault’s seal blob references the exact KMS resource path (projects/…/cryptoKeys/keyA/cryptoKeyVersions/1) and embeds metadata that KMS uses to decrypt. Even if the raw key material is imported elsewhere, KMS must see the same resource identifier and metadata to unwrap the ciphertext. Simply importing the same AES bits under a different KMS key path doesn’t recreate that metadata, so Vault can’t decrypt its stored envelope. Is that the right thinking? When present, conforming CAs > SHOULD mark this extension as critical. i.e., CA certs must include this, with the possible exception of a root CA. I do not see the subquotes `all types`, `not present`, `not critical` in RFC 5280 so I'm curious where they got that wording from... cipherboy: Regarding the first bullet point, we could and should definitely add a log message here. We cannot err (in general -- we can and do from the config setting) for two reasons: 1. This happens on issuer storage format migration, which would fail all reads of that issuer. 2. If we left this behavior in (allowing CRLUsage when no KU is present), we would fail CRL building entirely for all CAs in a mount. Yes, this is a valid read and matches my understanding. I believe this was communicated in the CL at the time, as it also fixed a bug around CRL issuer name building when we upgraded to a newer Go version (#10550). AFAIK, it is impossible to trigger this behavior with Vault-generated CAs; this behavior would strictly be from an imported CA. We could potentially err on this import on newer versions of Vault, but note that signing is not affected, only CRL generation (including external CRL generation capabilities -- since the key material was already outside of Vault though, you could manually maintain an external CRL without calling into Vault for the signing operation). I think erring on 1.10->1.11+ migration would be a step too far though. Again, subject to the "not clear if clients will reject this CRL due to its apparent issuer lacking CRL Signing KU bits" though.
maxb: > * Why is Vault not surfacing a clearer diagnostic message? Turns out to be because this is a "do this for all issuers" operation, and it is "successfully" building no CRL at all, having reviewed all issuers and determined none of them have CRL signing turned on as a usage. > Regarding the first bullet point, we could and should definitely add a log message here. Thanks to you all for your fast answers and clear analysis of my issue!
cipherboy: @maxb Aha, past me had the same comment on Slack: > Per ITU X.509, I'm going to loosen our crlSigning check: >> keyUsage matches if all of the bits set in the presented value are also set in the key usage extension in the stored attribute value, or if there is no key usage extension in the stored attribute value And then: > Ah I guess it doesn't matter lol: > ``` > * 1 error occurred: > * error building CRLs: unable to build CRL for issuer (f8f04fa1-9d8b-c77e-a227-d390ae652a1e): error creating new CRL: x509: issuer must have the crlSign key usage bit set > ``` Notably, [the latest ITU X.509 specification](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.509-201910-I/en) on printed page 73/pdf page 83 still includes this language. So I think we do have justification to go back to Go and get them to loosen the check.
cipherboy: I've filed https://github.com/golang/go/issues/59669 to discuss this with Go -- we've come up with a workaround (also mentioned in https://github.com/golang/go/issues/49414) that we _could_ assert `KeyUsage` manually on this certificate prior to the CRL generation call. We're still discussing the short-term workarounds we'd like to do in the mean time, however.
cipherboy: @maxb @flassman I've opened a PR which should add the warning infrastructure you talked about above, Max. It was a bit more involved than I was hoping, but its done now so :laughing:

title: OIDC client_tls_cert and key configuration
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
Currently, you cannot use the OIDC authentication provider with an OIDC endpoint that requests a client cert and key. This blocks us_x000D_
from using our OIDC based logins._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
Currently, the LDAP authentication has the configuration options `client_tls_cert` and `client_tls_key`. If those_x000D_
could be added as configuration options to the OIDC authentication method, it would solve the issue._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
We have considered using something like an NGINX sidecar to inject the client cert on its outbound connections but it gets messy and unclean very quickly. Unfortunately, there is no flexibility in the requirement to use the client cert to authenticate the OIDC request._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
There are a number of organizations that use certificates to authenticate client requests. Currently, vault sometimes can deal with these environments and sometimes cant. As OIDC is a standard protocol, and client authentication a common enough requirement, it seems it would provide value to ease OIDC flows._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
The desired flow would be:_x000D_
_x000D_
vault (+vault client cert) -> OIDC source (authenticate client cert, return OIDC well known config)_x000D_
_x000D_

body_text:

_x000D_
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
Vault reorders DNS SAN list when requesting a certificate. Firefox bug [#1757758](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1757758) details how Firefox evaluates SANs in a top-down order and will reject a cert at the first invalid line and Firefox bug [#1196364](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1196364) describes how Firefox rejects wildcard SANs for prefixes not found in the Public Suffix List._x000D_
_x000D_
The workaround then if one wants a certificate signed for non-wildcarded domains and a wildcarded custom TLD is to place the wildcard at or near the bottom of the SAN list after any valid SAN entries that will be used for Firefox. Vault reorders or sorts the list and prevents this from happening._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Generate a certificate via the UI for DNS SANs "`custom.local, *.custom.local`"_x000D_
2. View certificate (`openssl x509 -in cert.crt -text -noout`)_x000D_
3. Observe the SAN list is reordered (`DNS:*.custom.local, DNS:custom.local`)_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
SAN list should be deduplicated without reordering._x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault Server Version (retrieve with `vault status`): 1.12.1_x000D_
* Vault CLI Version (retrieve with `vault version`): N/A_x000D_
* Server Operating System/Architecture: Docker image `hashicorp/vault:1.12.1` on CentOS 7_x000D_

I think this line: https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/3acbeddf7a58915c41310fae41998e4985ca19e5/builtin/logical/pki/cert_util.go#L1146 Could be replaced with a line to `strutil.RemoveDuplicatesStable` but you'll need to duplicate this logic: https://github.com/hashicorp/go-secure-stdlib/blob/c651aeae0c80f35905cf5a275c55e494c0eae09f/strutil/strutil.go#L56-L67 Let me know if you want to file a patch or if you want me to. | cipherboy: @jdloft I think this does have an unintended side-effect though: if a user requested a cert with identifiers in the order `CUSTOM-INVALID, *.example.com`, our sorting today would result in `*.example.com, CUSTOM-INVALID` being issued, which would pass in Firefox for e.g., `mine.example.com`, whereas with the "fixed" new request sorting of `CUSTOM-INVALID, *.example.com` would result in the request failing. (CUSTOM-INVALID meaning an invalid DNS entry or entry that would otherwise fail Firefox's cert parsing). If we do make this change, I think it would have to be 1.14 only, to avoid breaking people for the above reason (though, admittedly you are broken by this behavior) -- this behavior is original to the engine AFAICT. | jdloft: I agree, this is breaking. title: Make raft ha internal tla path configurable
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
We have a vault setup where we run multiple raft ensembles in different regions sharing a single storage backend. Since the raft internal tls certs are stored on the shared storage at a hardcoded path ([core/raft/tls](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/b4a36b4cfb8127557425f1b1124e68510e0f2bbe/vault/raft.go#L33)) it creates a race between the leaders of the different ensembles. Leading to a split-brain where the leaders of the ensembles think the that the tls cert to use is actually incorrect. Which leads to the one of the ensembles losing quorum when a node restarts and requiring multiple hours until cert rotation or operator intervention to fix the issue._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
It would be great if the raft tls path can be made configurable._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
- Scaling down the non leader ensembles using custom scripting. Non trivial amount of operator tooling logic which is error-prone._x000D_
- Sealing the non leader ensemble to avoid TLS cert overwrites. Requires non-trivial operator tooling which is error-prone._x000D_
- Switching to a separate HA storage like MySQL. But this adds an extra dependency and adds cost._x000D_
- Use Consul for HA. We are simply moving the leader election problem from one service to another here._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
- Mainly this would allow Vault to be run in a multi-region setup and provide region failure protection._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
N/A_x000D_

top_3_comments_text: maxb: You are running Vault in HA mode (shown in your `vault status` output) which means you have multiple running instances of the Vault server, communicating amongst themselves, using `etcd` as shared storage (again from the `vault status` output). Only one running instance of Vault can write to the `etcd` storage at a time, as otherwise different nodes could make conflicting updates. To enforce that, each Vault server instance tries to acquire a lock - which is represented as something inside the `etcd` storage, and the one that succeeds knows it can become active. The remaining nodes remain in standby mode, and will forward requests to the active node for processing. So now, your Vault instance is saying "I haven't managed to acquire the lock to allow me to become active, but neither can I see an advertisement from another node, written within the `etcd` storage, to tell me who is currently active, so I can't forward this request!". The next step of debugging is to look at the Vault server error logging, for all nodes, possibly elevating logging levels to DEBUG or TRACE if necessary, to look for evidence explaining why none of the nodes are able to acquire the lock and become active. | miagilepner: Hi, this error means that instance of Vault at http://127.0.0.1:8200 isn't the active node, but the cluster can't find another active node in the cluster. ipaqmaster: Had this issue on a single raft vault node this afternoon while provisioning a new raft-backed Vault cluster. This was before I had provisioned the other two. This single node entered a deadlocked state where it refused to leave standby mode. The other two were indefinitely trying to join the cluster which could never come up. The only consistent thing was `local node not active but active cluster node not found` in the primary cluster member's logs and the message it was giving to the two other vault nodes who were trying to join. The single node did not want to start anymore. Turns out through my configuration tweaking I accidentally set an invalid node_id through typo. It seems that single solo Vault node with everything on it had latched onto a typo `node_id` from /etc/vault.hcl which wasn't valid. But now that Vault had put it into vault.db, it was unable to start the cluster the next service restart. Vault had effectively killed itself by storing the wrong node_id in its cluster node information, expecting a second node who didn't exist. This wrong node_id was visible when grepping for it in vault.db's binary data when it shouldn't be there at all. By luck, the incorrect node_id that Vault's vault.db had latched onto was the same length as the correct node_id for this solo raft-backed vault node. In a last resort to try and avoid starting all over again I: 1. Stopped the vault service 2. Ran `sed -i 's/wrongHostname/rightHostname/g' vault.db` 3. Started vault back up again The single-node cluster came good realising there was no second node to wait for and its own node_id was just missing due to the typo. After unsealing it the other two vault nodes who hadn't been configured yet were able to automatically join the cluster. This is a common problem I run into with vault clusters where even though the correct settings are in /etc/vault.hcl, it's latched onto some other values and will never read those correct settings until the cluster comes up. This also means you can have a working cluster and introduce either bad or NEW settings which break the cluster from the next restart. --------- This may not be the place for additional discussion of this issue... but this is a common problem I run into playing around with vault clusters in both staging and production environments. At this point it's a fear of mine it happens that often. In the case of Vault configuration changes such as: 1. Renaming a vault cluster member's node_id 2. Upgrading a entire vault cluster to HTTPS 3. Renaming all host's in a vault cluster There's a huge bootstrap paradox problem where Vault tries to start its storage cluster _before_ reading /etc/vault.hcl. This means you can enter an invalid node_id and your vault node will come up successfully and only then will it will read that after using its old node_id as per vault.db. It also means if something goes wrong during the bootstrapping of your cluster, say for example a TLS issue which may require you to back out - it's too late. The vault cluster is already configured to use HTTPS and will not read an updated /etc/vault.hcl reversing the change until _after_ the cluster comes up healthily. In my case with this staging cluster I had accidentally set a bad node_id and my single-node cluster came up and then set the invalid node_id. Then I restarted it with the correct node_id in vault.hcl and the other two to-be vault nodes described as retry_join entries. But because of this vault.db hardcoding problem Vault gets stuck in this invalid startup state trying to cluster with a non-existent node instead of just reading /etc/vault.hcl and coming up. This overall issue is very apparent when renaming a vault node or whole cluster of nodes. If the cluster can't come up, it will never read /etc/vault.hcl to update its node_id and peer details so just gets stuck. Given the nature of this problem it also means you can't stop, rename and bring a whole vault cluster back online because every single node will be trying to establish their storage backend connection using their old node_id's and old peer addresses's, which will never work. Even if you keep the old DNS entries to let that be possible, you'll also have to make sure each of their certs have Subject Alternate Names for both the old **and** new addresses without running into SSL errors. And if that vault cluster happens to be the source of your PKI for their certificates, god help you. I've seen a handful of unanswered Vault community threads and github issues about this kind of "Sudden vault cluster startup death for no reason" problem due to the hardcoded database/peer data and I think it's a helpful pointer to let people know a Vault cluster won't read a valid vault.hcl until it successfully starts its existing cluster up with old details first.
maxb: Hi @ipaqmaster, I would agree that the knowledge needed to administer a Raft cluster in failure states is not clearly documented. I have become an expert in this, mainly through experience and reading the source code. I am totally not surprised that changing a node ID would cause the behaviour you observed. Changing a node ID is something that should **never** be done. I have a question for you: why are you specifying the node ID in the first place? If you simply leave it out of the configuration file, Vault will automatically generate a UUID to use as the node ID, and store it as part of the data directory. This completely avoids human error scenarios setting the node ID. As for your emergency binary surgery... there is a supported recovery mechanism for replacing the Raft peer set information at startup. If a file named `peers.json` exists in the data directory at startup, it will be read for replacement Raft peer information, which will be installed into the configuration, after which the `peers.json` file will be deleted. This is how an administrator is intended to recover from serious Raft outage scenarios which prevent the product coming online at all.

miagilepner: When migrating from a seal of the same type, the way we determine if the migration has completed is by trying to decrypt something using both seals and we assume that if the new seal works the migration has already been done and don't do anything. title: External groups are only updated on login or token renew with the correct auth method
body_text:
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
When using external groups, they only get their members updated upon that member using either a login or a token renew with an alias that corresponds to the mount accessor of the external group. Otherwise they stay the same._x000D_
_x000D_
Assuming I have the following setup:_x000D_
- Auth Method for LDAP (e.g. auth_ldap)_x000D_
- Auth Method for JWT (e.g. auth_jwt)_x000D_
- External Group for LDAP (e.g. group_ldap_users)_x000D_
- Internal Group that includes the LDAP group (e.g. group_users) and has an assigned policy (e.g. simple_policy)_x000D_
- Entity for a given user (e.g. johndoe), that has aliases for JWT and LDAP_x000D_
_x000D_
Intention:_x000D_
johndoe is supposed to get permissions depending on his LDAP groups, independent of the auth method used to log in._x000D_
_x000D_
This setup causes two problems:_x000D_
1. Unless johndoe logs in via LDAP, he is never given the permissions to simple_policy, that he is supposed to have. Meaning his JWT auth will not have access to simple_policy either. This is a bit impractical, but still manageable in some cases._x000D_
2. If johndoe has logged in once via LDAP, he gets assigned to the external group group_ldap_users (assuming he is in that group), thus having the permission for simple_policy. Due to the alias mapping, johndoe can now use JWT with the same permissions, as the permissions are granted to his entity. If now someone removes johndoe in the LDAP group, this change **NEVER** gets reflected in Vault, unless johndoe actually logs in via LDAP or renews his token. Assuming he logged in once via LDAP and never again after that, he is now free to still have the access to simple_policy as long as he only uses JWT for auth._x000D_
_x000D_
This issue is just an example and could/should happen in any other scenario with multiple Auth sources that are used to unify entities from different locations._x000D_
_x000D_
From what it looks like, the only locations, where the group memberships get updated, is this method:_x000D_
https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/e55c18ed1299e0d36b88e603fa9f12adaf8e75dc/vault/identity_store_util.go#L2275_x000D_
which is called in this situations_x000D_

https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/e55c18ed1299e0d36b88e603fa9f12adaf8e75dc/vault/expiration.go#L1406_x000D_
_**Login**__x000D_
https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/d7ecfa0b718011e4d66ba292082f82e16f8b398f/vault/request_handling.go#L1544_x000D_
_x000D_

Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Setup a vault instance as described above_x000D_
2. Assign user to LDAP group_x000D_
3. Check that the LDAP group only gets membership updates upon LDAP login, despite usage of an entity with aliases for both auths_x000D_
4. Remove user from LDAP group_x000D_
5. JWT login should still work_x000D_
6. Check that the LDAP group only gets membership updates upon LDAP login, despite usage of an entity with aliases for both auths_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
Either:_x000D_
- on a login / token renew the entity should update **ALL** it's external group memberships_x000D_
- this behavior should be documented and advised against this kind of setup, if this does not make sense._x000D_

title: secrets/gcp: Recommend to use weaker pre-defined role(Service Account Viewer)
body_text:
Currently, it is documented that `secrets/gcp` requires `roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin` to verify the signature signed by the service account if custom roles are not used._x000D_
https://github.com/search?q=org%3Ahashicorp+serviceAccountKeyAdmin&type=code_x000D_
_x000D_
This role is required to grant only two permissions._x000D_
https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/auth/gcp#vault-server-permissions_x000D_
_x000D_
> ```_x000D_
> iam.serviceAccounts.get_x000D_
> iam.serviceAccountKeys.get_x000D_
> ```_x000D_
_x000D_
The Service Account Key Admin is a very powerful role that can do just about anything related to service account keys._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ gcloud iam roles describe roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin_x000D_
description: Create and manage (and rotate) service account keys._x000D_
etag: AA==_x000D_
includedPermissions:_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.create_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.delete_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.disable_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.enable_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.get_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.list_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccounts.get_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccounts.list_x000D_
- resourcemanager.projects.get_x000D_
- resourcemanager.projects.list_x000D_
name: roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin_x000D_
stage: GA_x000D_
title: Service Account Key Admin_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
There is now the weaker, read-only Service Account Viewer. _x000D_
I think it is better to use it._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ gcloud iam roles describe roles/iam.serviceAccountViewer_x000D_
description: Read access to service accounts, metadata, and keys._x000D_
etag: AA==_x000D_
includedPermissions:_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.get_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccountKeys.list_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccounts.get_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccounts.getIamPolicy_x000D_
- iam.serviceAccounts.list_x000D_
- resourcemanager.projects.get_x000D_
- resourcemanager.projects.list_x000D_
name: roles/iam.serviceAccountViewer_x000D_
stage: GA_x000D_
title: View Service Accounts_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
(Only the read-only and trivial `iam.serviceAccounts.getIamPolicy` permission is not included in `roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin`.)

title: misleading error "ldap operation failed: failed to bind as user" when password contains trailing newline
body_text:
**Describe the bug**_x000D_

when passing a password from stdin, it may contain an extra trailing newline. this causes the error `ldap operation failed: failed to bind as user`, which is very misleading. However, the real issue is that it accepted the newline as part of the password._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
_x000D_
> Note: while `echo`/`printf` are used here for ease of reproduction, this applies to anything that could pipe the password to stdin, like a password manager_x000D_
_x000D_

```_x000D_

Error authenticating: Error making API request._x000D_
_x000D_
URL: PUT https://vault.s.voidlinux.org/v1/auth/ldap/login/abby_x000D_
Code: 400. Errors:_x000D_
_x000D_
* ldap operation failed: failed to bind as user_x000D_

this is made clear by using `-output-curl-string`:_x000D_
```_x000D_

```_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
_x000D_
login from stdin works as intended:_x000D_

curl -X PUT -H "X-Vault-Request: true" -d '{"password":"mypassword"}' $VAULT_ADDR/v1/auth/ldap/login/myuser_x000D_
$ printf mypassword | vault login -method=ldap username=myuser password=- _x000D_
Success! You are now authenticated._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Use Transit to verify signatures based solely on an imported public key
body_text:
As a backend developer I wish I could verify tokens' signatures with Vault, for example a JWT, with only a public key supplied. _x000D_
_x000D_
The Transit Engine would import a public key without a private key, and when using the [verify signed data API](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/api-docs/secret/transit#verify-signed-data), it would return if the public key supplied can verify the supplied signature._x000D_
_x000D_
If I am not mistaken, the Veriy Signed Data is currently a mirrored API of the Sign Data, suggesting that Transit imports or creates a private&public keys set, but is not designed for solely import public keys._x000D_
_x000D_
This would help authenticate devices using Trusted Platform Modules, capable of creating their own token based on a embedded private&public keys, where private key is not accessible on purpose._x000D_
_x000D_
Of course, this is easily doable with any crypto library and public keys are easily stored ; but since Vault plays a central role in one's backend security design, it would feel more proper to use Vault in such authentication schema.

_x000D_

```shell_x000D_
vault secrets enable consul_x000D_
vault write consul/config/access address="consul:8501" token="$CONSUL_HTTP_TOKEN" scheme="https" ca_cert=@/path/to/ca-certificate.pem_x000D_
vault write consul/roles/app-role consul_roles="app-role"_x000D_
```_x000D_
2. Run `vault read consul/creds/app-role`_x000D_
3. See error:_x000D_

_x000D_
URL: GET https://vault:8200/v1/consul/creds/app-role_x000D_
Code: 500. Errors:_x000D_
_x000D_

_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
_x000D_
Consul token is generated, with the role `app-role` attached to it. _x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
_x000D_

_x000D_

title: sealHealthTestIntervalNominal
body_text:
Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe._x000D_
Yes, the current setting of sealHealthTestIntervalNominal in Vault is set to 10 minutes, which is too short for some use cases. This results in excessive health checks for an upstream Vault cluster, which can be costly and unnecessary._x000D_
_x000D_
Describe the solution you'd like_x000D_
I would like the ability to configure the sealHealthTestIntervalNominal setting in Vault, so that it can be adjusted to suit different use cases. This would allow users to set a longer interval if desired, reducing the number of health checks and associated costs._x000D_
_x000D_
Describe alternatives you've considered_x000D_
At present, the only alternative is to manually modify the sealHealthTestIntervalNominal variable in the Vault source code. However, this is not ideal as it requires manual intervention and may not be practical for all users._x000D_
_x000D_
Explain any additional use-cases_x000D_
This feature request would be beneficial for any users who have an upstream Vault cluster and need to adjust the health check interval to suit their specific use case. For example, users who are running Vault on premises and have an upstream cluster at GCE may need to set a longer interval to avoid excessive health checks and associated costs._x000D_
_x000D_
Additional context_x000D_
At present, the sealHealthTestIntervalNominal setting in Vault is not configurable, and is set to 10 minutes by default. This results in frequent health checks for an upstream Vault cluster, which can be costly and unnecessary. By making this setting configurable, users would have greater control over the frequency of health checks and associated costs.

(i.e., this isn't a wildcard in the certificate's `common_name` field, we've already trimmed that up, but is instead a glob in the policy to allow say, matching `something.example.com` and `else.example.com` by specifying `*.example.com` in the policy itself). Each of these extensions uses the GeneralName type; one choice in GeneralName is the dNSName field, which is defined as type IA5String. > > ... &c. They seem to use IDNs here, rather than punycode. body_text:
When I input a path on kv2 web ui box like the following:_x000D_
_x000D_
 ccloud/apikey/key1_x000D_
_x000D_
I get redirected to the following url:_x000D_
_x000D_
 https://my-vault.com/ui/vault/secrets/kv2/list/ccloud/apikey/key1_x000D_
 _x000D_
but if I input a shorter path based on the above like the following:_x000D_

_x000D_
I get redirected to the following url with a change from "list" to "show" on the segment before the secret name and a permissions error:_x000D_
_x000D_
 https://my-vault.com/ui/vault/secrets/kv2/show/ccloud/_x000D_
_x000D_
It is true that there is no permissions on a show segment, there is no permission "show", it should actually be a "list" segment._x000D_
Now if I manually change the url from "show" to "list" on the browser it works and there is no permissions error!_x000D_
_x000D_
 https://my-vault.com/ui/vault/secrets/kv2/show/ccloud/ ->  https://my-vault.com/ui/vault/secrets/kv2/list/ccloud/_x000D_
_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Authenticate in Vault Web UI_x000D_
2. Select Secrets tab_x000D_
3. Select KV2 secrets engine_x000D_
4. Input an existing secret on the input box_x000D_
_x000D_
The input box of kv2 should actually use a "list" path segment, not a "show" because that's the name of the permission to see the contents on the path, i.e., "list"!_x000D_
_x000D_
Vault Server version: 1.12.1_x000D_
_x000D_
Policy:_x000D_
_x000D_
path "kv2/" {_x000D_
    capabilities = [ "list" ]_x000D_
}_x000D_
path "kv2/data" {_x000D_
    capabilities = [ "list" ]_x000D_
}_x000D_
path "kv2/data/ccloud/" {_x000D_
    capabilities = [ "list" ]_x000D_
}_x000D_
path "kv2/data/ccloud/*" {_x000D_
    capabilities = [ "list", "read" ]_x000D_
}_x000D_
path "kv2/metadata/ccloud/*" {_x000D_
    capabilities = [ "list" ]_x000D_
}_x000D_
path "kv2/metadata/ccloud/*" {_x000D_
    capabilities = [ "read" ]_x000D_
}
top_3_comments_text: maxb: I think the issue is just that the "secret name" input box currently only supports navigating directly to a secret - and not navigating to a listing of secrets contained in a subpath. --- An aside about the policy you defined above - quite a bit of it is redundant and it can be simplified to this: ``` path "kv2/data/ccloud/*" { capabilities = ["read"] } path "kv2/metadata/ccloud/*" { capabilities = ["list", "read"] } ``` * There is no point granting any access to `kv2/`, that path does not do anything other than return a warning instructing users it is incorrect to call that path (in a KV v2) * There is no point granting `list` access to any path under `kv2/data`, as the `data` subcollection of a KV v2 does not implement `list` operations. * There is no need to separate the grant of `list` and `read` to the `metadata` subcollection into multiple path blocks. Consider also adding: ``` path "kv2/metadata/" { capabilities = ["list"] } ``` unless you are unable to permit your users to see the list of what the top level of `kv2/` contains - with that, you'd be able to just click on `ccloud` rather than using the text entry box. | Monkeychip: @ajfc84 and @maxb thank you both for the comments. _x000D_

_x000D_

context deadline exceeded_x000D_

_x000D_
and I can't see in the proxy it's hitting the database. Connection using `psql` is always successful. _x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
_x000D_
The connection should be verified and I should be able to request credentials via the engine._x000D_
_x000D_

title: sudo/root-protected endpoints are not correctly documented
body_text:
Vault has the concept of a "root protected" or "sudo required" endpoint, where in addition to the regular ACL policies, the `sudo` capability is additionally required._x000D_
_x000D_
The Vault documentation is not very good at reliably telling users which endpoints are root-protected._x000D_
_x000D_
Many root-protected endpoints can be identified via the OpenAPI, which mostly includes an `x-vault-sudo` property on relevant endpoints. However, some root-protected endpoints implement their root protection in ways which are not visible to the OpenAPI generator, causing it too to give misleading information._x000D_
_x000D_
There has recently been some ongoing work to add a table - https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/policies#root-protected-api-endpoints - of all such endpoints to the documentation:_x000D_
_x000D_
* https://hashicorp.atlassian.net/browse/SPE-178_x000D_
* #20650_x000D_
* #20669 _x000D_
_x000D_
I have provided various feedback on the two PRs above, but the preference has been to merge them early making incremental improvements, meaning some of my feedback is in closed PRs even though it hasn't been actioned yet - so I'm creating a new separate issue to more easily keep track of the outstanding documentation defects, over the course of potentially many more PRs._x000D_
_x000D_
---_x000D_
_x000D_
# The `auth/token/create` endpoint family - `auth/token/create`, `auth/token/create-orphan`, `auth/token/create/:role_name`_x000D_
_x000D_
The `auth/token/create` endpoint should be removed from the table. The reason is that the table is headed:_x000D_
_x000D_
> The following paths requires a root token or sudo capability in the policy:_x000D_
_x000D_
but this isn't true for these three endpoints, which are unique - in that they are the only ones in Vault where the APIs can be used by regular tokens, but **additional functionality** is unlocked for root tokens or having sudo capability:_x000D_
_x000D_
Instead, I propose that a separate paragraph be introduced below the table saying:_x000D_
_x000D_
The `auth/token/create`, `auth/token/create-orphan` and `auth/token/create/:role_name` endpoints do not require a root token or sudo capability to use their standard functionality. However, if a root token is used, or sudo capability is granted, these endpoints unlock extra functionality:_x000D_
* Allows creating tokens in child namespaces (Vault Enterprise only)_x000D_
* Allows creating tokens with manually specified IDs_x000D_
* Allows any policies to be attached to the new token, rather than limiting to a subset of the current token's policies_x000D_
* Allows the `no_parent` option to be used to create orphan tokens via the `auth/token/create` endpoint_x000D_
* Allows creating periodic tokens_x000D_
_x000D_
# Root-protected endpoints missing from the current table_x000D_
_x000D_
* `auth/token/revoke-orphan` (POST)_x000D_
* `sys/leases` (GET)_x000D_
* `sys/plugins/catalog/:type` (LIST)_x000D_
_x000D_
Additionally, there are quite a few more root-protected endpoints which have been omitted from the current table because they are deprecated. However, this means that users can come across endpoints in e.g. the OpenAPI spec, in other code, or in `vault path-help` output, which are in fact root-protected, consult the table, and find them missing, and thereby be misled._x000D_
_x000D_
I propose that to cover this eventuality, it would be beneficial to users to include a second table below the main table, mentioning deprecated root-protected endpoints, which are:_x000D_
_x000D_
* `sys/plugins/catalog/:name` (GET, POST, DELETE)_x000D_
* `sys/replication/primary/secondary-token` (POST)_x000D_
* `sys/revoke-force/:prefix` (POST)_x000D_
* `sys/revoke-prefix/:prefix` (POST)_x000D_
_x000D_
or at least mentioning that this possibility exists, if you don't want to enumerate the deprecated endpoints._x000D_
_x000D_
# Odd documentation of `sys/raw` in table_x000D_
_x000D_
I raised this in #20669, but my comment was dismissed._x000D_
_x000D_
Currently:_x000D_
_x000D_
> sys/raw:path | GET, POST, DELETE | Used to access the raw underlying store in Vault_x000D_
> sys/raw:prefix | GET, LIST | Returns a list keys for a given path prefix_x000D_
_x000D_
1) There should be a slash between raw and the colon. That's the normal way to write path parameters in this notation - it shouldn't be missing here._x000D_
_x000D_
2) In my opinion, merge the two rows into one. The only reason they've been separated here is because the existing docs use the path variable :path for some methods, and :prefix for others - but that's just an artefact of the documentation. If you consult the code, or `vault path-help sys/raw/something` output, it's just the one parameter, called path._x000D_
_x000D_
If you choose to reject this, and keep two rows, then at least, the GET method should not be included in the special LIST row, and the super-vague description in the second row "Returns a list keys for a given path prefix" would be better replaced with a copy of the description in the first row.

title: Export of HMAC key returns the wrong values
body_text:
_x000D_
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
The Transit Export endpoint returns erroneous values for HMAC keys. For Vault-generated keys, the Export endpoint returns random 32-byte values (regardless of the requested key size). For imported keys, the Export endpoint returns a blank (empty) key._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Run `vault server -dev -dev-root-token-id root`_x000D_
2. Run this [gist](https://gist.github.com/rzimmerman/5ed32ef75c16d17896e12be9cd11ec14)_x000D_
3. AES keys return the expected value when imported + exported_x000D_
4. HMAC keys that are created are the wrong length (always 32 bytes)_x000D_
5. HMAC keys that are imported do not match the imported key_x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
Per the Gist above, I'd expect the exported key length to match the `key_size` parameter._x000D_
Also, I'd expect the exported HMAC key to match the imported key value. Output on my machine:_x000D_
```_x000D_
> Test create HMAC key of desired length:_x000D_
Key length: 32, expected 64_x000D_
> Test import HMAC key:_x000D_
expected key: 3031323334353637383961626364656630313233343536373839616263646566_x000D_
got:_x000D_
> Test import AES key:_x000D_
expected key: 3031323334353637383961626364656630313233343536373839616263646566_x000D_
got:          3031323334353637383961626364656630313233343536373839616263646566_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
And directly querying the endpoints:_x000D_
```_x000D_
➜  vault read transit/export/hmac-key/hmac-test1_x000D_
Key     Value_x000D_
---     -----_x000D_
keys    map[1:Z4DAJFsjCEVRgyjFFqjVcdrwvPhTuPLYiqqrUEFFK0U=]_x000D_
name    hmac-test1_x000D_
type    hmac_x000D_
➜  vault read transit/export/hmac-key/hmac-test2_x000D_
Key     Value_x000D_
---     -----_x000D_
keys    map[1:]_x000D_
name    hmac-test2_x000D_
type    hmac_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault Server Version (retrieve with `vault status`): 1.13.2_x000D_
* Vault CLI Version (retrieve with `vault version`): Vault v1.13.2 (b9b773f1628260423e6cc9745531fd903cae853f), built 2023-04-25T13:02:50Z (though this happens with github.com/hashicorp/vault-client-go v0.3.2)_x000D_
* Server Operating System/Architecture: MacOS (M1)_x000D_
_x000D_
Vault server configuration file(s): N/A_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
_x000D_
It looks like the Export endpoint is erroneously using the `HMACKey` "supplementary" key for `hmac` key types. This line should probably be returning `key.Key` rather than `key.HMACKey`: https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/1336abddfe58ac4dda6524aa2bd6b099e55700be/builtin/logical/transit/path_export.go#L164-L165_x000D_

title: Add precision in documentation about when the Vault Agent performs renewals with token_period
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
_x000D_
The Vault documentation explains that the Vault Agent renews the Token before the `token_period` is reached. _x000D_
_x000D_
But we have no clear explanation about "exactly" when this renewal is done by the agent. For example if a user configures a `token_period` equals to 6h he does not know if the agent will renew it 1h after or 2h after or 3h after etc._x000D_
_x000D_
For us having this renewal moment information is very important because we have several teams starting Vault Agents in the background (which is a good practice I believe). _x000D_
_x000D_
If our Vault Cluster encounters a critical and "long" incident we would like to prevent all those teams to restart their Vault Agents. There tokens should still be valid (i.e. the `token_period` should be judiciously defined) and during the incident we should be able to let the exponential back-off work until the Vault Cluster is up again._x000D_
_x000D_
Without knowing when the Vault Agent performs its renewals we cannot chose a good `token_period` value and deduce an associated "acceptable" incident duration after which one we'll be required to contact all teams to ask them to completely restart their Vault Agents. _x000D_
_x000D_
We searched in the Vault source code to get the "renewal moment formula" and found this peace of code (https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/262bdc067f7d0db470929039cca38969f1d1c34a/api/lifetime_watcher.go#L380)._x000D_
_x000D_
In the `calculateSleepDuration` function._x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
	// The sleep duration is set to 2/3 of the current lease duration plus_x000D_
	// 1/3 of the current grace period, which adds jitter._x000D_
	return time.Duration(float64(remainingLeaseDuration.Nanoseconds())*2/3 + float64(r.grace.Nanoseconds())/3)_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
So the formula seems to be the following one for a periodic token._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
renewal_moment = 2/3 * token_period + 1/10 * token_period + small_jitter_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
In our case we defined an acceptable incident duration of 2 hours maximum. This one is not aligned with our SLOs but its expected to be long to respond to "extreme" situations and almost never ask all our teams to restart there agents because of a Vault  incident. _x000D_
_x000D_
The result of the formula indicates us that our `token_period` should be equal to ~ 5 hours in this case._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
_x000D_
* **Solution 1** : At least explaining the "renewal moment formula" in the documentation and associated implications about the Vault Agent restarts. _x000D_
* **Solution 2** : Add a parameter in the Vault Agent to change the `2 / 3` in the formula, for example we could define a `token_period` equals to 1h but still want the Agent to renew the tokens each ~ 10 minutes (in this cas we'll use `1 / 6` instead of `1 / 3`). This parameter could be named `renewal_moment_lease_duration_factor` or something like that. This parameter would also allow to lower our `token_period` value which I believed will be better for security._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
_x000D_
Keep the actual behavior and read the source code to know the formula. _x000D_
_x000D_
The downside is that it forces use to have "too long" token periods._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
_x000D_
I do not think about any other use-cases._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
_x000D_
None_x000D_
top_3_comments_text: VioletHynes: Hi there! Thanks for this detailed issue report. I agree that our documentation could maybe be improved in this area, but I worry it won't be as 'exact' as you're hoping for. However, what I don't quite fully understand right now, that I'd like to understand better, is the issue you're having that makes you feel like you need to know the exact renewal time. title: Expiration time option for vault operator generate-root
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
Given that it's [recommended](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/tokens#root-tokens) to revoke root tokens after done using them, it seems weird that `vault operator generate-root` doesn't by default, or even as an option, generate root tokens with a finite TTL. Best practice is to manually revoke them, but it seems a helpful failsafe to be able to specify when creating the token that it should expire in say 15 minutes._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
`vault operator generate-root -init -ttl=1h` should start root token generation, and when the process completes, the issued token would expire after an hour._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
Manual revocation after an hour, which is vulnerable to accidental or intentional failure to revoke the token._x000D_
_x000D_
I see `-wrap-ttl` exists, but I think that's just about response wrapping, not making the root token itself expire._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
This would help root token generation to fail-safe, rather than potentially having a high-value token floating around (also, given #11683 and #11431, it seems harder than one might wish to *find* unexpired root tokens, making leaked root tokens even more risky)._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
I somewhat think that having a default expiry (say, an hour) would make sense, but I suspect that would be too invasive a change. Just having this as an option seems helpful, though.

title: Vault LDAP Auth Method vulnerable to account fuzzing via response.
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ curl -XPOST 'https://vault.localhost.localdomain/v1/auth/ldap/login/fakeUser' -d 'password=fakePassword'_x000D_
{"errors":["ldap operation failed: failed to bind as user"]}_x000D_
```_x000D_
Pretty clear json error text for a failed bind to a user that doesn't exist and a fake password._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ curl -XPOST 'https://vault.localhost.localdomain/v1/auth/ldap/login/realUser' -d 'password=fakePassword'_x000D_
```_x000D_
204 response code with a blank body for a real user account that exists, but the same fake incorrect password. Identifying a valid LDAP account._x000D_
_x000D_
In /ui/ you're given additional error text: `Authentication failed: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'auth')`. I'm guessing the javascript for `/ui/vault/auth` doesn't like receiving the blank body 204 response._x000D_
_x000D_
These responses can be used to scan for valid accounts via a Vault cluster's LDAP authentication endpoint - against whichever OU a Vault cluster is scoped to for it. It's like a `VRFY` command for Vault._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
_x000D_
Because the auth/ endpoint typically deals with unauthenticated remotes Vault shouldn't be handing out any hints. It would be much better that when an Auth Method fails for an unauthenticated remote Vault should just throw something along the lines of `{"errors":["Access Denied"]}` as the error text value - providing no further detail and leaving it to administrators to aid a real staff member if they were actually struggling to gain access._x000D_
_x000D_
In relevant context, the [User Lockout](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/user-lockout) feature exists and is enabled by default with good defaults. Upon discovering a valid user account an attacker would only have a maximum of 5 brute force attempts before the account is locked out for 15 minutes, every 15 minutes. Leaving up to only 480 attempts per day which would be useless for traditional brute force attempts but workable for a sophisticated and targeted attack._x000D_
_x000D_
While this is great for preventing an online compromise and the lockout doesn't impact the existing token session of a user - Being able to disclose accounts like this can be abused for a Denial of Service scenario where an attacker has successfully guessed the username formula of a company and discovered some valid (At least bindable) LDAP accounts. Such an actor would be able to actively prevent those discovered users from reauthenticating after their token expires. But at least the source would be obvious in webserver and reverse proxy logs for a swift firewall drop rule._x000D_
_x000D_
While this would still be possible if an attacker already knows the account names they wish to attack - It would become infeasible to build a list of valid accounts from nothing if Vault's invalid credential response is masked with a blunt "Access Denied" error even on valid username attempts._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
_x000D_
Not many other thoughts. Just don't want Vault to disclose valid ldap user accounts by accident. Having vault be vague about the error reason would be a great improvement but it would also probably be a good idea to sprinkle in some micro-sleeps even for valid account attempts to help prevent attackers guessing valid/invalid users based on the time it takes Vault to respond with the error code._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
_x000D_
* Preventing a vault server from being enumerated for valid ldap accounts via that Auth Method - where an attacker can start brute forcing with no information_x000D_
* Prevent Denial of Service attacks against staff accounts discovered via the above method_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
_x000D_
Another thought - Should Vault's User Lockout feature go for the remote IP address responsible for the lockout rather than potentially locking innocent user accounts?_x000D_
_x000D_
With reverse proxying it would become important to make sure the reverse proxy passes through the correct remote host IP for such a feature to accurately ban an attacker rather than accidentally banning the reverse proxy and locking vault out for everybody.

body_text:

_x000D_

_x000D_
**Describe the bug**_x000D_
When using go api client functions to access vault and perform operations, there are some status codes that should be treated as errors. As an example, reading a non-existing secret yields the same result as getting a temporary redirection status code while redirections are disabled._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
To illustrate the case, find below a test case using the `Read` function. Here I'm using a mock vault server that yields either 404 status code whenever `not-found` is part of the path, 307 when `temporary-redirect`is part of the path or a valid secret in any other case:_x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
package main_test_x000D_
_x000D_
import (_x000D_
    "encoding/json"_x000D_
    "net/http"_x000D_
    "net/http/httptest"_x000D_
    "os"_x000D_
    "strings"_x000D_
    "testing"_x000D_
_x000D_
    "github.com/hashicorp/vault/api"_x000D_
)_x000D_
_x000D_
func newMockVault() *httptest.Server {_x000D_
    return httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(_x000D_
        func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {_x000D_
            switch {_x000D_
            case strings.Contains(r.URL.Path, "temporary-redirect"):_x000D_
                w.Header().Add("Location", r.URL.String())_x000D_
                w.WriteHeader(http.StatusTemporaryRedirect)_x000D_
            case strings.Contains(r.URL.Path, "not-found"):_x000D_
                w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNotFound)_x000D_
            default:_x000D_
                b, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]interface{}{_x000D_
                    "data": map[string]interface{}{_x000D_
                        "key": "value",_x000D_
                    },_x000D_
                })_x000D_
                w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)_x000D_
                w.Write(b)_x000D_
            }_x000D_
        },_x000D_
    ))_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
func newClient(addr string) *api.Client {_x000D_
    cfg := api.DefaultConfig()_x000D_
    cfg.Address = addr_x000D_
_x000D_
    c, err := api.NewClient(cfg)_x000D_
    if err != nil {_x000D_
        panic(err)_x000D_
    }_x000D_
    return c_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
var (_x000D_
    mVault *httptest.Server_x000D_
    client *api.Client_x000D_
)_x000D_
_x000D_
func TestMain(m *testing.M) {_x000D_
    mVault = newMockVault()_x000D_
    client = newClient(mVault.URL)_x000D_
    os.Exit(m.Run())_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
func TestReadOK(t *testing.T) {_x000D_
    s, err := client.Logical().Read("test")_x000D_
    if err != nil {_x000D_
        t.Log("got error", err)_x000D_
        t.FailNow()_x000D_
    }_x000D_
    if s == nil {_x000D_
        t.Log("secret not found")_x000D_
        t.FailNow()_x000D_
    }_x000D_
    t.Log("secret found")_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_

title: When utilizing the PKI secrets engine, allow for the mTLS auth method to pull in the cert details automatically for authentication
body_text:
When a group manages their certificates via Vault PKI Engine(https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/pki)_x000D_
_x000D_
There should be an easy options to allow for the mTLS auth method to use the certificates stored in the PKI engine for authentication. In the current state, the certificate has to be generated, and then manually moved over to the mTLS auth options. This makes it harder to automate and redundant while increasing the odds of the certificates not matching_x000D_
https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/auth/cert_x000D_
top_3_comments_text: cipherboy: @Esity Sadly I'm not sure this is a feasible approach. Vault lacks an inter-plugin communication method and its unlikely we'll see such any time soon as it would be a significant investment both from a security/design perspective but also from an implementation perspective. Even with such cross-mount (and potentially, cross-cluster) mechanisms, you'd still need to indicate to cert auth which issuers it should trust/validate against, which is little different than the current mechanism (other than ensuring the value gets copied over correctly). Cert auth method should not be used with individual leaf certificates, but instead used with root/intermediate CAs in the mount. Using something like TFVP could perhaps solve this issue, by ensuring proper construction of cert auth method from Vault PKI CAs. n.b.: the wording here: > the certificate has to be generated, and then manually moved over to the mTLS auth options. makes me think that perhaps leaf certs are being directly trusted in Cert auth method, which I'd strongly caution against as a best practice. | heatherezell: With @cipherboy's notes here, I'm going to go ahead and close this issue now. title: Support CLI aliases
body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**_x000D_
I frequently would like to get the metadata attached to tokens. Currently this process involves running `vault list auth/token/accessors`, and then `vault token lookup -accessor {accessor}` on each of those token accessors._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe the solution you'd like**_x000D_
If there was a way to create CLI aliases so that I could fine-tune this behavior to my specific use case it would be great._x000D_
_x000D_
**Describe alternatives you've considered**_x000D_
I could create a separate alias in my shell (i.e. `alias vault-find-token='vault blahblah command here'`), but having it as an alias under the `vault` command itself would be much cleaner._x000D_
_x000D_
**Explain any additional use-cases**_x000D_
The GitHub CLI [supports this behavior](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_alias), so it definitely seems like it can work well._x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
N/A

I am, of course, aware that both `git` and `gh` have built in alias support, with people enthusiastic about both... but both of those are implemented differently, making two more different ways to do aliases on top of what the shell already provides. If every program that provided subcommands jumped on this trend, each putting their own personal spin on how they thought the feature should work, it would be seriously chaotic for users. There's an elegant simplicity to just letting the shell take care of this, I think. | hwittenborn: I've thought about this a bit since I made this issue initially, I guess I just forgot to make a comment. title: PKI Secret Engine auto-tidy
body_text:
The wrong concept was used from the beginning, it needs to be redone._x000D_
_x000D_
`PKI Secret Engine documentation for auto-tidy_x000D_
(https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/api-docs/secret/pki#configure-automatic-tidy)_x000D_
 has a parameter interval_duration_x000D_
(https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/api-docs/secret/pki#interval_duration)._x000D_
This needs to explicitly call out the default value to be 12 hours._x000D_
`_x000D_
_x000D_
`[interval_duration](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/api-docs/secret/pki#interval_duration) (string: "") - Specifies the duration between automatic tidy operations; note that this is from the end of one operation to the start of the next so the time of the operation itself does not need to be considered.`_x000D_
_x000D_
Since the next cleaning starts at an interval_duration after the end of the previous one, over time, its start will be shifted, and will be released during business hours when the Vault is already loaded with users._x000D_
_x000D_
With a significant number of PKI certificates stored, the Vault heavily loads the backend storage with read operations and uses much more than usual (x10) RAM for indexing or checking them._x000D_
_x000D_
Therefore, for these tasks, the approach as in the cron is more optimal._x000D_
Need to specify the day and time to start cleaning, for example, on Friday at 11pm, and then cleaning will go on all weekend, without interfering with the main work and going faster because there is no load or it is much less from users._x000D_
And add a check that if the cleaning is already in progress (there can be a lot of certificates, they missed the previous cleaning or something else), then do not start a new one.
top_3_comments_text: cipherboy: @ser6iy This is indeed an issue, and a bit of a hard problem... Presently, PKI tidies are expensive for a couple of reasons: 1. (RAM) There can be many certificates stored within a mount. Paginated lists, a desired future enhancement to Vault, could help here (as we wouldn't store all certificates in memory), but so could things like using `no_store=true`, avoiding the need to tidy (most) certificates. Obviously this doesn't jive with ACME (which requires `no_store=false` on roles) and is unavoidable in other operational scenarios. 2. (Storage/Compute) They read+parse each certificate/ACME object/revocation entry and check if it has (presently) expired. Things like `pause_duration` help here, by decreasing the number of certs processed in a given interval. Using a different data structure could limit our search to more-likely-to-be-tidied certificates (e.g., maintaining another mapping by expiration) -- and perhaps help with the storage related cases in the best-case (many different expiration times). We also have some customers run a huge number (3k+) PKI mounts, with lots of stored certificates per mount, making PKI tidies not only expensive in the local sense (of a mount), but in the global, cluster-resource expensive sense as well. While a cron based scheduling is desirable for some, with this large number of mounts, if _all_ of these PKI mounts tidied at exactly the same time, it would definitely overwhelm the cluster. By using `interval_duration`, one gets some natural variability (based on when the last tidy concluded, which is influenced by how long the tidy took), and so there's a chance for all 3k+ tidies not to be running simultaneously. The design too was in part influenced by the data we had available and an ease of simplicity: if the existing tidy has finished very recently, you're unlikely to want to schedule one right away. _If_ there are not a huge number of certificates in the mount (and thus, not starving the Vault cluster for memory), then (IMO) `pause_duration` _should_ be sufficient to box the resource consumption into a sufficiently small window that regular issuance and revocation succeed just fine. Running such a resource-bound tidy automatically (regardless of when) has far more benefits than having precise scheduling. But obviously this is not true globally, and there's definitely value in cron-like scheduling as well. Additionally, each mount _type_ today has its own tidy operation with its own semantics. PKI's is one of the more complicated, and hence the introduction of an automated, cancel-able tidy, but Transform has one, AppRole has another, &c. Here, IMO, we really need a Vault-wide tidy interface (\o hence the Core tag) that standardizes perhaps both mechanisms (interval-based and time-of-day-based) tidy running, that allows mutual-exclusion, perhaps time-boxed execution (to prevent tidy from continuing past some duration), and a standard UX to configure & enable tidies, regardless of the underlying mount type. Note that this statement: > And add a check that if the cleaning is already in progress (there can be a lot of certificates, they missed the previous cleaning or something else), then do not start a new one. already occurs under the existing design. | ser6iy: @cipherboy Yes, you are right, both schedulers for cleaning have their advantages in use, it would be ideal to have both types in the functionality and the ability to select them in the config. I hope this will be taken into implementation. Thanks for your detailed answer.

**Describe the bug**_x000D_
_x000D_
Trying to start a Vault cluster with a vault.hcl which specifies to use Raft - fails. This is a result of the strict vault.service file currently in the main branch preventing write access to /var/lib/vault even when following current deployment steps on the website._x000D_
_x000D_
**To Reproduce**_x000D_
Steps to reproduce the behavior:_x000D_
1. Install Vault_x000D_
2. Make a vault.hcl which uses a relative Raft storage path as per the documentation._x000D_
3. Service fails to start as it cannot write its vault.db file._x000D_
_x000D_
**Expected behavior**_x000D_
The service to start._x000D_
_x000D_
This is possible with `su - vault -s /bin/bash -c 'vault server -config=/etc/vault.hcl'` which works around the vault.service strictness._x000D_
_x000D_
**Environment:**_x000D_
* Vault Server Version (retrieve with `vault status`): <During initial setup>_x000D_
* Vault CLI Version (retrieve with `vault version`): Vault v1.13.2 (cgo)_x000D_
* Server Operating System/Architecture: Archlinux_x000D_
_x000D_
Vault server configuration file(s):_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
storage "raft" {_x000D_
  path    = "./data"_x000D_
  node_id = "vault01"_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
**Additional context**_x000D_
Add any other context about the problem here._x000D_
_x000D_
Before this issue I also submitted a downstream bug report https://bugs.archlinux.org/task/78742 where it were confirmed the package uses the provided vault.service file from vault.
top_3_comments_text: maxb: This is not an upstream issue, but an error in the Arch packaging. The HashiCorp package uses different directories for the `vault` user home directory, and the data directory. In this configuration, `ProtectHome=read-only` is valid. The Arch package assigns `/var/lib/vault` as both the home directory and the data directory, making `ProtectHome=read-only` now a problem - but only because of Arch's decision to use the same directory for both roles. | ipaqmaster: Thanks for the clarification Max | maxb: Also, a factual correction: > https://bugs.archlinux.org/task/78742 where it were confirmed the package uses the provided vault.service file from vault. No, what they actually said (emphasis mine) was: > the upstream provided .service file [1] (which we are **not** using...yet)
all_comments_text:
maxb: This is not an upstream issue, but an error in the Arch packaging. The HashiCorp package uses different directories for the `vault` user home directory, and the data directory. In this configuration, `ProtectHome=read-only` is valid. The Arch package assigns `/var/lib/vault` as both the home directory and the data directory, making `ProtectHome=read-only` now a problem - but only because of Arch's decision to use the same directory for both roles.
ipaqmaster: Thanks for the clarification Max
maxb: Also, a factual correction: > https://bugs.archlinux.org/task/78742 where it were confirmed the package uses the provided vault.service file from vault. No, what they actually said (emphasis mine) was: > the upstream provided .service file [1] (which we are **not** using...yet)
maxb: Also, a couple of suggestions about your Vault configuration, which are not related to the problem you experienced, just things I noticed in reading it: > path = "./data" I would discourage using a relative path here. It is better to use an absolute path, to insulate yourself from an unplanned change to the current directory of the Vault server process. > node_id = "vault01" I would discourage manually specifying Raft node IDs. Leave it unset so that the Vault process generates a random UUID and stores it on disk in the data directory, and that way you'll never have to worry about accidentally configuring a conflict, which could seriously impact cluster operations.
ipaqmaster: Personally the setup I'm using right now is using full paths. My example above was trying to follow the documentation on the hashicorp developers subdomain as closely as possible (Which also exhibits the issue). I understand relative complicates things especially in this situation. > https://bugs.archlinux.org/task/78742 where it were confirmed the package uses the provided vault.service file from vault. My bad. Busy day.
hashworks: I'm the maintainer of the Arch vault package. > The Arch package assigns /var/lib/vault as both the home directory and the data directory, making ProtectHome=read-only now a problem - but only because of Arch's decision to use the same directory for both roles. This is not correct - see the [systemd documentation](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.exec.html#ProtectSystem=) on ProtectSystem=full and ProtectHome=read-only: > ProtectSystem= > Takes a boolean argument or the special values "full" or "strict". If true, mounts the /usr/ and the boot loader directories (/boot and /efi) read-only for processes invoked by this unit. If set to "full", the /etc/ directory is mounted read-only, too. > ProtectHome= > Takes a boolean argument or the special values "read-only" or "tmpfs". If true, the directories /home/, /root, and /run/user are made inaccessible and empty for processes invoked by this unit. If set to "read-only", the three directories are made read-only instead. This means the only directories the Arch Linux vault systemd unit can't write to are /usr, /boot, /efi, /etc, /home, /root and /run/user. The vault home directory /var/lib/vault is still writable. ProtectHome is NOT specific to the user home directory. > Service fails to start as it cannot write its vault.db file. My guess is that the service fails because the directory does not exist, vault will not create it: ``` Error initializing storage of type raft: open /var/lib/vault/data/node-id: no such file or directory ``` If you create `/var/lib/vault/data` it might complain about permissions, so make sure it is owned by the vault user. ``` Error initializing storage of type raft: open /var/lib/vault/data/node-id: permission denied ``` With the current Arch Package and the following config and an existing directory with correct permissions the raft database is created correctly: ``` ui = true # EDIT: "backend" is not a valid config option, see the comment of maxb below. # backend "file" { # path = "/var/lib/vault" # } cluster_addr = "http://127.0.0.1:8201" api_addr = "http://127.0.0.1:8200" storage "raft" { path = "/var/lib/vault/data" } listener "tcp" { tls_disable = 1 } ``` ![image](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/assets/2362091/dbf3b66c-eb27-48aa-bb23-042afabb1037) ``` $ tree /var/lib/vault /var/lib/vault └── data ├── node-id ├── raft │ ├── raft.db │ └── snapshots └── vault.db 4 directories, 3 files ```
hashworks: > the upstream provided .service file [1] (which we are not using...yet) I've [adjusted the package](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/packaging/packages/vault/-/commit/5007691691d6fb722aa8e78e89e067956fc8cee4) to use the systemd unit file provided by vault, so we can avoid future confusion about this.
ipaqmaster: Much appreciated. I understand your above comment clearly too.
maxb: > This is not correct - see the [systemd documentation](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.exec.html#ProtectSystem=) on ProtectSystem=full and ProtectHome=read-only: > > > Oops. That's my bad for assuming `ProtectHome` would apply to the actual home directory, and trusting that the original report of this being a permissions problem was true. I guess I should be more sceptical and demand actual error messages be copy/pasted, as a matter of course. A separate matter: In the example configuration shown above: > backend "file" { > path = "/var/lib/vault" > } This part is not valid Vault configuration, being ignored since `backend` is not a known block name for Vault server configuration.
hashworks: > This part is not valid Vault configuration, being ignored since backend is not a known block name for Vault server configuration. Correct, my bad. Not sure where it came from.
