title: Sign/verify OCI image layout
body_text:
### What is the areas you would like to add the new feature to?

Notation CLI

### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Currently, to sign container images, users need to push the container images in the remote registry first. What will happen if the remote registry is already compromised? The container images can be tampered with by the attacker before signing. The signed container images could contain malicious code that users are not aware of since the signature can be validated as normal.

### What solution do you propose?

The proposal is to sign the container images before pushing them to the remote registry. The container image on local disk is in the form of OCI image layout. OCI image layout is defined in [OCI image spec](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/v1.1.0-rc2/image-layout.md), which is a directory structure that contains files and folders. _x000D_
_x000D_
Introducing new experiences of signing local OCI images and offline verification_x000D_
_x000D_
Scenario 1: Sign local OCI images, push to the remote registry, and verify OCI images in the registry_x000D_
- Publisher: Build an OCI image and save it on the local disk as OCI image layout_x000D_
- Publisher: Notation signs the local OCI image, and stores the signatures locally_x000D_
- Publisher: Push the local OCI image together with the signatures to a remote registry_x000D_
- Consumer: Notation verifies OCI images as current experience_x000D_
_x000D_
Scenario 2: Offline verification_x000D_
- Publisher: Build an OCI image and save it on the local disk as OCI image layout_x000D_
- Publisher: Notation signs the local OCI image, and stores the signatures locally_x000D_
- Publisher: Copy the local OCI images together with the signatures to other local filesystems_x000D_
- Consumer: Notation verifies the local OCI image against the local signatures_x000D_
_x000D_


### What alternatives have you considered?

No other alternatives so far.

### Any additional context?

_No response_

title: Support experimental feature
body_text:
### What is the areas you would like to add the new feature to?_x000D_
_x000D_
Notation CLI_x000D_
_x000D_
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
Experimental features for CLI commands refer to functionality that are not yet part of the base version of a CLI tool but can be accessed by enabling the appropriate options. The purpose of using experimental features is to enable users to try out new functionality or improvements, and to provide feedback for further development or refinement. It can also help identify issues or bugs that may not have been caught during testing. They may not work as expected and are not recommended for use in production or critical systems._x000D_
_x000D_
### What solution do you propose?_x000D_
_x000D_
The proposal is to use environment variable to enable experimental features for Notation CLI. The proposed name is `NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL`. _x000D_
_x000D_
**What is default behavior?**_x000D_
By default, the experimental features are disabled. The related CLI command flags are not shown to users from Notation CLI help command. _x000D_
_x000D_
**How to enable experimental features?**_x000D_
To enable experimental features, users set `NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL_CLI` in their environment, for example `export NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL_CLI=1`. _x000D_
_x000D_
**What will happen after experimental features are enabled?**_x000D_
The CLI flags related to experimental features are shown to users and marked as `[Experimental]` in the description in the help document. _x000D_
When using experimental features, the CLI output should warn the users that these are experimental features, like `Caution: This feature is experimental and may not be fully tested or completed and may be deprecated. Report any issues to "https://github/notaryproject/notation` for further improvement."_x000D_
_x000D_
**How do users know there are experimental features and how to use them?**_x000D_
The release note or readme.md should give users guidance on how to enable/disable experimental features, other documents are also required to explain to the users on how to use experimental features._x000D_
_x000D_
### What alternatives have you considered?_x000D_
_x000D_
Another alternative is that by default the experimental features are visible to users, but in order to use them, user need to set the corresponding environment variable._x000D_

title: Improve the error msg for OCI v1.0 registries or registries that don't support deletion API
body_text:
### What is the areas you experience the issue in?_x000D_
_x000D_
Notation CLI_x000D_
_x000D_
### What is not working as expected?_x000D_
_x000D_
When using Notation CLI to sign an artifact in OCI v1.0 compliant registries such as GHCR or registries that [don't support deletion API](https://github.com/docker/hub-feedback/issues/1759) (e.g. Docker Hub), Notation will return an unexpected error message and may mislead or confuse users. It happens when signing an artifact for the second time._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
### What did you expect to happen?_x000D_
_x000D_
Improve the error message to be more descriptive and user-friendly, and tell users about the right result exactly. Giving an example: Successfully signed `<registry>/<repository>@<digest>`. Please note that Notation can't delete the referrers index since this is an OCI v1.0 compliant registry or the deletion API is disabled by the registry._x000D_
_x000D_
### How can we reproduce it?_x000D_
_x000D_
We have a user who signed a sample image in GHCR. It returned the following error message when this user signed the same image for the second time:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ notation sign --signature-format cose --key $REMOTE_KEY_NAME ghcr.io/demo-user/python@sha256:xxxx_x000D_
Error: failed to push signature to registry with error: failed to push manifest: failed to delete dangling referrers index sha256:xxx for referrers tag sha256-1ba1561: DELETE "https://ghcr.io/v2/demo-user/python/manifests/sha256:e1b7d6": response status code 405: unsupported: The operation is unsupported._x000D_
```_x000D_
It may confuse users why this signing behavior failed due to an old referrers index manifest deletion failure. From an end user's point of view, the user is left with the impression that the signing failed. Now the user is left wondering why this happened and if she/he doesn't know the internals of OCI registries she/he may think the issue is with Notation.  _x000D_
_x000D_
In fact, the signing is successful and the signature has been attached to the image but it doesn't tell users the right result unless users view the referenced signatures using `notation list` as below._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
ghcr.io/demo-user/python@sha256:xxxx_x000D_
└── application/vnd.cncf.notary.signature_x000D_
    ├── sha256:85f65b60a6e260d52ba5f8d556d444320b92c2ac140ec8d4944dbd8b03deb18c_x000D_
    └── sha256:96130e5a5e314ef90e56e24559e48065d2889c39661b9b3a944e6862e1e51c0a_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
### Describe your environment_x000D_
_x000D_
Ubuntu 20.08_x000D_
_x000D_
### What is the version of your Notation CLI or Notation Library?_x000D_
_x000D_
Notation CLI v1.0.0-RC.3

title: Introduce an experimental flag to enable backward compatibility with OCI registries
body_text:
### What is the areas you would like to add the new feature to?_x000D_
_x000D_
Notation CLI_x000D_
_x000D_
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
We have a Notation user who recently encountered a problem that not being able to view the signature after signing an artifact stored in Google Artifact Registry._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ notation ls us-west1-docker.pkg.dev/xyz/test/net-monitor:v1_x000D_
…_x000D_
failed to decode response: invalid character '<' looking for beginning of value_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
It works well when using `oras discover` with a [compatibility flag](https://github.com/oras-project/oras/blob/main/docs/proposals/compatibility-mode.md#configure-compatibility-with-oci-registry-using-a-flag---distribution-spec) `--distribution-spec`. _x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ oras discover us-west1-docker.pkg.dev/xyz/test/net-monitor:v1-o tree --distribution-spec v1.1-referrers-tag_x000D_
_x000D_
us-west1-docker.pkg.dev/xyz/test/net-monitor@sha256:123456_x000D_
└── application/vnd.cncf.notary.signature_x000D_
    └── sha256:123456_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
 _x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
### What solution do you propose?_x000D_
_x000D_
We may need to introduce an experimental flag like `--compatibility oci-v1.0` to `notation ls` to enable maximum backward compatibility with OCI v1.0 compliant registries, which is similar to ORAS [--distribution-spec](https://github.com/oras-project/oras/blob/main/docs/proposals/compatibility-mode.md#configure-compatibility-with-oci-registry-using-a-flag---distribution-spec). _x000D_
_x000D_
It will help Notation users to view the signatures associated with an artifact, regardless of whether the registry complies with the OCI Spec v1.0 or v1.1 or supports Referrers API. _x000D_
_x000D_
In a similar case, ORAS uses `--distribution-spec <spec version>-<api>-<option>` to configure the backward compatibility with the registry. I think this format might be complicated for Notation users if we just copy it. _x000D_
_x000D_
If you have an idea about the flag name, please comment below. _x000D_
_x000D_

title: Support clean up the source key and certificate generated by Notation
body_text:
### What is the areas you would like to add the new feature to?_x000D_
_x000D_
Notation CLI_x000D_
_x000D_
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
`notation key delete` can only remove the key from the signing key list and `notation cert delete` can only remove the self-signed certificate from the trust store. This is by design since Notation doesn't support signing with [local keys](https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/issues/539) and managing local keys. _x000D_
_x000D_
Per discussion in https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/pull/606#discussion_r1154664392 and another issue #604 , users want to delete the source key and certificate generated by `notation cert generate-test` in a convenient way.  _x000D_
_x000D_
### What solution do you propose?_x000D_
_x000D_
Providing a flag `--cleanup` to `notation cert generate-test` to allow users to delete the specified source key and certificate generated by `notation cert generate-test`. This flag is only used to delete the test key and self-signed certificate. The keys and certificates that are not generated by Notation will not be able to be deleted with this flag. _x000D_
_x000D_
For example, delete a source key and cert generated by `notation cert generate-test "wabbit-networks.io"`:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ notation cert generate-test --cleanup wabbit-networks.io_x000D_
Deleted <key_name> and <cert_name> _x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
### What alternatives have you considered?_x000D_
_x000D_
N/A_x000D_
_x000D_
### Any additional context?_x000D_
_x000D_
_No response_

title: `notation policy init` command is necessary for user experiences
body_text:
### What is the areas you would like to add the new feature to?

Notation CLI

### Is your feature request related to a problem?

In version 1.0.0-rc.4, `notation policy` only supports `import` and `show`.  Thus, to use notation CLI for artifact verification, a beginner has to follow the workflow below:_x000D_
1. Search for an example of notation trust policy either from specs or online docs._x000D_
2. Create a trust policy file, copy and paste the example they found from step 1 into it._x000D_
3. Change the values of the trust policy based on user's needs._x000D_
4. Call `notation policy import <path-of-the-file-from-step3>` to actually configure Notation trust policy. Errors are highly possible because steps 1~3 are completed manually by the user._x000D_
5. Set up trust store based on trust policy with `notation cert add`._x000D_
6.  Finally start doing verification with `notation verify`._x000D_
_x000D_
The workflow above is not user friendly and error prone. IMO, learning cost for a new user of Notation is too high.

### What solution do you propose?

Introduce `notation policy init` command. The command should prompt step by step with detailed descriptions on each field of the trust policy and ask users to type in values accordingly. On success, the command gathers answers from the user and configure Notation's trust policy within a single command._x000D_
For example,_x000D_
```_x000D_
provide "name" of your trust policy statement [Required]: <user-input>_x000D_
provide "registryScopes" of your trust policy statement, it is an array of fully qualified repository URIs of the artifacts, valid examples "["registry.hello-world.io/software/hello-world"]", "["*"]" [Required]: <user-input>_x000D_
..._x000D_
```_x000D_
Now, the workflow for a beginner using Notation verification becomes:_x000D_
1. Call `notation policy init`_x000D_
2. Call `notation cert add`_x000D_
3. Call `notation verify`

### What alternatives have you considered?

An alternative could be:_x000D_
`notation policy init` creates a default trustpolicy.json for the user. _x000D_
If the user needs a more formal trust policy configuration, then they could do `notation policy show`, change trust policy fields, and `notation policy import` to update the default trustpolicy.json.

### Any additional context?

_No response_

title: Mark feature "support OCI Referrer API" as experimental feature
body_text:
### What is the areas you experience the issue in?

Notation CLI

### What is not working as expected?

Currently [Referrer API](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/v1.1.0-rc1/spec.md#listing-referrers) is by default verified by Notation since `v1.0.0-rc.4`. For example, when using `notation sign`, if registries support referrer API, notation will not use an image index pushed to a tag described by the [referrers tag schema](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/main/spec.md#referrers-tag-schema). Since OCI spec 1.1 (including both image spec and distribution spec) is not officially released yet, support of Referrer API could lead to breaking changes or portability issue after Notation v1 is released. On the other hand, users may be confused that sometimes image index is pushed, sometimes not, which is an issue of consistency.

### What did you expect to happen?

Mark feature "support OCI Referrer API" as experimental feature, and document it properly. Users can use experimental features only after env variable `NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL=1` is set. _x000D_
The default behavior of Notation is always using an image index pushed to a tag described by the [referrers tag schema](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/v1.1.0-rc2/spec.md#referrers-tag-schema). If users set env variable `NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL=1`, Notation will check the support of OCI referrer API first, if registries support Referrer API, then notation will not push image index; if registries don't support Referrer API, notation will push image index as the default behavior. _x000D_


### How can we reproduce it?

N/A

WSL

Notation `v1.0.0-rc.4`

`notation sign` has a flag `--signature-manifest` to sign an artifact and store the signature using OCI artifact manifest. This flag is defined in [notation sign](https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/blob/main/specs/commandline/sign.md#experimental-sign-an-artifact-and-store-the-signature-using-oci-artifact-manifest)._x000D_
_x000D_
[image-spec v1.1.0-rc.3](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/releases/tag/v1.1.0-rc.3) removed OCI artifact manifest. This is a breaking change that we need to rethink when delivering a stable Notation v1.0.0._x000D_

Still thinking

title: feat: Print out the signature digest when sign an artifact
body_text:
### What is the areas you would like to add the new feature to?

Notation CLI

### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Notation does not print out the digest of the generated signature artifact when signing an OCI artifact using `notation sign` . In this case, users are not able to find the signature generated from the last step if there are multiple signatures associated with the signed OCI artifact.

```
$ notation sign $IMAGE
Successfully signed localhost:5001/net-monitor@sha256:073b75987e95b89f187a89809f08a32033972bb63cda279db8a9ca16b7ff555a
```

```
$ notation ls $IMAGE
localhost:5001/net-monitor@sha256:073b75987e95b89f187a89809f08a32033972bb63cda279db8a9ca16b7ff555a
└── application/vnd.cncf.notary.v2.signature
    └── sha256:ba3a68a28648ba18c51a479145fca60d96b43dc96c6ab22f412c89ac56a9038b
    └── sha256:22f412c89ac56a90385fca60d96b43dc96c6abbba3a68a28648ba18c51a47914
```

### What solution do you propose?

I think we could only print out the signature digest and remove the signed artifact digest from the output as below. The artifact digest is known and immutable when using `notation sign` so we may not need to print out it.

title: Make Notation as a background process

### Is your feature request related to a problem?

One of the challenges we face in our enterprise scenarios is signing and verifying numerous artifacts from various container registries. This can become a CPU intensive operation when we run multiple Notation CLI commands in parallel._x000D_
_x000D_
This problem stems from the fact that each CLI command creates a new process, which consumes a significant amount of CPU and memory resources._x000D_


### What solution do you propose?

My suggestion is to create a Notation service executable that can run as a background process and listen to a network port._x000D_
_x000D_
The caller can use http-based IPC to request signing and validating operations on artifacts._x000D_
_x000D_
This approach will reduce resource consumption, as there will be only one process handling all sign and verify requests.

One possible solution is to package the Notation CLI executable on the host machine and invoke the CLI command from our service._x000D_
_x000D_
However, this solution has a scalability issue. According to my benchmark, it can consume all the CPU resources of the host machine when there are more than 50 notation sign and verify operations. Therefore, it is not suitable for handling a large number of artifacts.

title: Support system wide installation and usage of Notation
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
As a system administrator I want to install and configure notation in system wide directory(aka central place) and allow all other users to run it._x000D_
_x000D_
As a system administrator, I want to perform a system-wide installation and configuration of Notation, thereby enabling all users to execute it seamlessly._x000D_
_x000D_
### What solution do you propose?_x000D_
_x000D_
There can be multiple ways to support this, as a starting point, we may explore the option of supporting a configuration file(`config.json`) located in a predefined system-wide directory. Notation can then check for the presence of this configuration file to determine the location of the required plugins and configurations._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
### What alternatives have you considered?_x000D_
1. Install Notation to a system-wide directory._x000D_
2. Install the plugin and create trust-store trust policy and other config files in the system-wide directory using the specified [directory-structure](https://notaryproject.dev/docs/concepts/directory-structure/)._x000D_
3. Now, each user can set XDG_CONFIG_HOME to the directory created in step 2 and start using notation._x000D_

title: Add support for multiple trust policies
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

There is a use case that can allow verification performed by an admission controller in a multi-tenant cluster, where we have two teams with the same image reference deployed in different namespaces using different signatures and trust policies._x000D_
_x000D_


### What solution do you propose?

Adding support for passing trust policies when verifying._x000D_
_x000D_
### Solution_x000D_
_x000D_
What we are doing right now in our use case is_x000D_
1. Replace notation verifier with notation verifier factory_x000D_
2. Notation verifier factory is a collection of verifiers, every verifier is created for each trust policy in the notation directory_x000D_
3. All notation verifiers are refreshed every time there is a change in trust policy or trust stores._x000D_
4. To specify what trust policy to use, one can pass trustpolicy in the request or set DEFAULT_TRUST_POLICY env in the deployment._x000D_
_x000D_
It would be great if we can do something similar internally instead of externally_x000D_
1. We can have a `trustpolicies.json` that will have the locations of all trust policies names and locations and have a default._x000D_
2. Instead of keeping track of one Trust Document, we can have a factory that will return either the default trust document or the right trust document based on the request.

### What alternatives have you considered?

We are doing something similar at the verifier level, but having this at a lower level would be great

### Any additional context?

_No response_

title: Sign local container images before they are pushed to registries
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
### Background_x000D_
_x000D_
Nowadays, in order to sign container images, users must first push the images to a registry. However, registries are not within the trust boundary of Notation, as outlined in the [threat model](https://github.com/notaryproject/specifications/blob/v1.0.0/threatmodels/notation-threatmodel.md). If a registry is compromised, attackers can tamper with container images during the short period between when they are pushed to the registry and when they are signed by users. From the perspective of image consumers, the image can be verified against the signature successfully, but it may still be malicious. This is a serious security issue that cannot be easily detected._x000D_
_x000D_
Notation supports an experimental feature that allows users to [sign a local image in OCI layout format](https://notaryproject.dev/docs/how-to/oci-image-layout/). However, this is not how most users build their container images. Most users build container images using Docker Engine, including Docker CLI and `dockerd` as the daemon. The container images built on a local machine are not in the format of OCI layout; instead, they are in Docker’s own format. Docker Engine also supports `containerd` as the daemon, and the image built on a local machine is in the format of OCI layout with minor differences. However, supporting `containerd` is not yet a stable feature._x000D_
_x000D_
### Scenario_x000D_
_x000D_
A software engineer wants to sign local container images built by `docker build` before pushing images to a registry. Verification of the image should be the same workflow for signing and verifying images stored in OCI complaint registry._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
### What solution do you propose?_x000D_
_x000D_
`docker save` command can save a local image into a tar file, however, it is in the format of docker own, not OCI layout or other standard format. The tar file is not the one that `docker push` command pushes to the registry. So, if we sign local images created by `docker save` command, the digest is different from digest of manifest of the image that is pushed to the container registry. To sign tar file created by `docker save`, and verify it before `docker load`, I would suggest considering feature [sign and verify arbitrary file](https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/issues/741)._x000D_
_x000D_
My proposal is to create an official docker plugin to generate an OCI descriptor and sign the descriptor.  Here is the experience._x000D_
_x000D_
1. Built a container image using command `docker build/buildx`_x000D_
    `docker build -t localhost:5001/net-monitor:v1 https://github.com/wabbit-networks/net-monitor.git#main`_x000D_
1. List the container images on local machine to confirm the image was built_x000D_
    `docker images`_x000D_
1. Run docker plugin named `descriptor` to generate a OCI descriptor for the container image. _x000D_
   `docker descriptor generate localhost:5001/net-monitor:v1` -o net-monitor.json_x000D_
1. Sign the descriptor_x000D_
   `notation sign --descriptor net-monitor.json --output-signature digest.sig`_x000D_
1. Push the local container image to an OCI compliant registry_x000D_
   `docker push localhost:5001/net-monitor:v1`_x000D_
1. Push the signature_x000D_
   `notation push digest.sig localhost:5001/net-monitor:v1`_x000D_
1. List the signature to confirm it is existing and associated with the image_x000D_
   `notation list`_x000D_
_x000D_
### What alternatives have you considered?_x000D_
_x000D_
Use a tool to convert local docker images to an OCI layout, and then sign the OCI layout as the experimental feature._x000D_
_x000D_
### Any additional context?_x000D_
_x000D_
_No response_

title: Check validity of applicable TP and TS before fetching signatures from registry.
labels: bug, error message, help wanted, perf
body_text:
**Context:** https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/pull/771#issuecomment-1731705600_x000D_
Currently signature verification process in Notation, involves fetching the signature and subsequently validating the trust store's vakidity. However, this method has the following concerns:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. The error messages provided to users in case of verification failure are not very user-friendly.  (Refer to the link above for examples)_x000D_
2. If either the Trust Store (TS) or Trust Policy (TP) is malformed, signature validation will always fail. This renders the fetching and validation of signatures unnecessary. Essentially, we're advocating for fast fail._x000D_
_x000D_
**Ambiguous Specification**_x000D_
Presently, there exists specifications that introduces a conflicting requirement. In one instance, we state that before commencing signature verification, both the TS and TP should be valid, while in other, this is not explicitly emphasized._x000D_
* https://github.com/notaryproject/specifications/blob/v1.0.0/specs/trust-store-trust-policy.md#signature-verification_x000D_
* https://github.com/notaryproject/specifications/blob/v1.0.0/specs/signing-and-verification-workflow.md#verification-prerequisites_x000D_
_x000D_
**Recommended  Solution**_x000D_
1. Amend the [specification](https://github.com/notaryproject/specifications/blob/v1.0.0/specs/signing-and-verification-workflow.md#verification-prerequisites) to state: "User has configured a valid trust store and trust policy."_x000D_
2. Make a code change to validate the relevant TS and TP before obtaining the signature. Here, 'relevant' refers to the TP and TS identified for a specific scope.

title: Support Time-stamping
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
Signature validation will fail if signing key/certificates are expired. In this case, signers need to rotate the key/certificates in time and re-sign container images using new key/certificates. The lifetime of a signature is limited by the lifetime of a corresponding signing key/certificate._x000D_
_x000D_
### What solution do you propose?_x000D_
_x000D_
Time-stamping (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3161) extends the trust of signature beyond the validity period of a certificate, thus signers do not need to regularly re-sign images before certificates are expired. RFC 3161 said that Time-stamping helps establish whether the image was signed before or after the certificate was compromised. However, in the real world, the compromised time is not the time of certificate revocation. The compromised time is not determined. So, the proposal is to not use Time-stamping for revocation scenarios._x000D_
_x000D_
### What alternatives have you considered?_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently Notation does not support Time-stamping, so signers need to regularly rotate the key/certificates in time and re-sign container images using new key/certificates. However, this process requires signers to establish a re-sign workflow, which leads to usability problems and waste of resources._x000D_
_x000D_
### Any additional context?_x000D_
_x000D_
There is an [existing issue](https://github.com/notaryproject/roadmap/issues/59) in roadmap repo, however this repo is not in active mode.

And from verification point of view, there is no need to mark "default", since a verifier wants to verify images signed with different keys, it is unusual to have a "default" certificate verifying images signed with a default signing key. In other cases, a verifier can only configure trust store without the need of adding signing keys. @yizha1 Thanks. FeynmanZhou has answered my question.

title: Support FIPS 140 validated crypto module(s)
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) requires that any cryptographic functions (e.g. hashing) utilize cryptographic modules validated and listed by NIST under https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-module-validation-program/validated-modules/search/all

### What solution do you propose?

1. The crypto provider (https://pkg.go.dev/crypto) must offer this feature.  Working with this provider to determine what compilation/import flags (if any) are required to explicitly leverage FIPS validated modules is therefore the first step._x000D_
2. Depending on whether a variant build/flag of https://pkg.go.dev/crypto is required, CLI/tool vendors may support a command line flag such as `--fips-mode true` which engages the appropriate version of https://pkg.go.dev/crypto.  However if the providers of https://pkg.go.dev/crypto can attest that their library is fully FIPS 140 validated and can supply the https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-module-validation-program/validated-modules/search/all Certificate #, then no such flag is required.

### What alternatives have you considered?

Utilize an OpenSSL go library that utilizes FIPS validated modules, or build OpenSSL for go using a version of OpenSSL that is FIPS validated (3.0.9 as of this writing) https://www.openssl.org/source/_x000D_
_x000D_
![image](https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/assets/31080393/612c5266-04eb-495f-bc1b-258e7dbb1576)_x000D_


### Any additional context?

The following Cloud Service Providers reference the Notary Project as their recommended method for signing containers.  Any US Federal customer of these providers must therefore meet the FIPS compliance requirement described above. _x000D_
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tutorial-sign-build-push_x000D_
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-signing.html

title: Support using signing key from GitHub Encrypted Secret
body_text:
Signing an image with Notation GitHub Actions relies on a vendor-specific plugin such as [AWS Signer plugin for Notation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/signer/latest/developerguide/Welcome.html), [Azure Key Vault for Notation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tutorial-sign-build-push), [HashiCorp Vault plugin](https://github.com/notaryproject/notation-hashicorp-vault/pulls).. This is a production solution for users to keep the private signing keys secure enough._x000D_
_x000D_
However, OSS project maintainers come from different vendors and might not be reluctant to use a vendor-specific plugin in their GHA workflow and release process._x000D_
_x000D_
In addition, when users get started with Notation GitHub Actions, they might have some limited access or are unavailable to use a KMS. Instead, they may want to load a private key from the GitHub Encrypted Secret for convenience. _x000D_
_x000D_
There was a discussion and related feature request in the [Slack channel](https://cloud-native.slack.com/archives/CQUH8U287/p1689187088295789). _x000D_
_x000D_
Signing with a private key loaded from the GitHub secret could be helpful in this scenario. But we need to investigate whether the GitHub encrypted secret is secure enough to store private keys._x000D_
_x000D_
To make the Notation GHA signing experience easier, I would suggest supporting signing with a private key loaded from GitHub Encrypted Secret. _x000D_
_x000D_
This will make Notation be a good solution to secure open-source project. Open-source project maintainers can easily sign their release binary assets in their release workflow with Notation GitHub Actions.

```_x000D_

title: Check whether the detached signature file meets the OpenSSF Scorecard check criteria or not
body_text:
### What is not working as expected?

CNCF provides a tool Clomonitor to run OpenSSF Security Best Practice checks on CNCF projects. There is a signing related check that has not been passed in the security check items. See https://clomonitor.io/projects/cncf/notary#notation_security._x000D_
_x000D_
According to [OpenSSF Scorecard signing check criteria](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/main/docs/checks.md#signed-releases), only these signature file formats `*.asc (pgp), *.sig, *.sign, *.sigstore, [*.intoto.jsonl](https://slsa.dev/)` could be detected by OpenSSF Scorecard check tool. _x000D_
_x000D_
![image](https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/assets/40452856/63822e18-20f6-4a26-9c0e-b89faf9ee451)_x000D_
_x000D_
According to our current design and [spec](https://github.com/notaryproject/specifications/blob/main/specs/signing-and-verification-workflow.md#signing-steps-1), Notation blog signing generates the signatures using `.sig.jws` and `.sig.cose` file format. We need to check whether these detached signature file meets the OpenSSF Scorecard check criteria or not. 

### What did you expect to happen?

OpenSSF Security Best Practice check on the signing part should be passed after the Notation release assets are signed by Notation. Notary Project signature file should meet the OpenSSF Scorecard  [OpenSSF Scorecard signing check criteria](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/main/docs/checks.md#signed-releases).

See https://clomonitor.io/projects/cncf/notary#notation_security.

N/A

v1.1.1

title: Add more logs for timestamp validation
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
When using the `notation verify` command to validate a signature with timestamp validation enabled, the signature verification succeeds even if the signing certificate has expired, provided the signature was generated before the certificate’s expiry. This behavior is expected. However, the verbose log output is not informative, as shown below:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
INFO Performing timestamp verification..._x000D_
INFO TSA identity is: ***_x000D_
Successfully verified signature for ***_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
### What solution do you propose?_x000D_
_x000D_
The current log indicates that timestamp validation is enabled and is now validating the timestamp:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
INFO Performing timestamp verification..._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Subsequently, the log shows the TSA identity:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
INFO TSA identity is: ***_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
It is proposed to enhance the log output to provide more detailed information about the timestamp verification process. For example, the log should indicate whether each certificate in the certificate chain has expired or not._x000D_
_x000D_
Examples for valid certificates:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
INFO Performing timestamp verification..._x000D_
INFO The certificate <Subject of Leaf> is still valid and will expire on <Time>._x000D_
INFO The certificate <Subject of Intermediate> is still valid and will expire on <Time>._x000D_
INFO The certificate <Subject of Root> is still valid and will expire on <Time>._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Examples for an expired leaf certificate:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
INFO Performing timestamp verification..._x000D_
WARN The certificate <Subject of Leaf> has expired. It expired on <Time>._x000D_
INFO The certificate <Subject of Intermediate> is still valid and will expire on <Time>._x000D_
INFO The certificate <Subject of Root> is still valid and will expire on <Time>._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Additionally, we can make it more clear about what TSA identity is_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
INFO The subject of TSA leaf/signing certificate is: ***_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
### What alternatives have you considered?_x000D_
_x000D_
There could be other information printed out for timestamp validation. Any suggestions are welcome._x000D_
_x000D_
### Any additional context?_x000D_
_x000D_
Notation v1.2.0-beta.1

title: Attestations
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?_x000D_
_x000D_
### Description_x000D_
_x000D_
An attestation is a cryptographically signed collection of claims related to one or more software artifacts. According to [SLSA](https://slsa.dev/attestation-model), an attestation consists of authenticated statements about a software artifact or a collection of software artifacts. Examples include signed provenance files or signed SBOM files for container images. Attestations are crucial for ensuring the security and trustworthiness of the software supply chain. _x000D_
_x000D_
Attestations are typically involved in the processes of creating attestations for software artifacts and verifying them before using the corresponding software artifacts. For instance, users generate SBOM attestations for container images in CI/CD pipelines and verify these attestations at admission control before deploying the container images on K8s clusters._x000D_
_x000D_
[In-toto attestations](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation) are popular in the cloud-native ecosystem as part of the in-toto framework, which is designed to secure the integrity of software supply chains. You can find [existing vetted predicates](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/tree/main/spec/predicates#vetted-predicates). Below are some examples of their adoption:_x000D_
_x000D_
- [GitHub artifact attestations](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/using-artifact-attestations/using-artifact-attestations-to-establish-provenance-for-builds)_x000D_
- [SLSA attestations](https://slsa.dev/attestation-model)_x000D_
_x000D_
To adopt in-toto attestations, the following open issues should be considered by the Notary Project community:_x000D_
- Unsupported Envelope Type: In-toto attestations utilize the [DSSE envelope](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/blob/v1.1.0/spec/v1/envelope.md) and do not support the Notary Project signature envelopes such as JWS/COSE._x000D_
- Performance concern: Since the attestation includes the payload, large payload sizes (e.g., an SBOM for a Windows image, which could be hundreds of megabytes) can lead to performance issues during attestation download and verification. _x000D_
_x000D_
### Request_x000D_
_x000D_
This issue requests the Notary Project to identify scenarios, create specifications, and provide reference implementations for attestations, including:_x000D_
- Scenarios for using attestations throughout the cloud-native secure supply chain._x000D_
- Notary Project specification of the attestation format and storage in OCI-compliant registries._x000D_
- Notary Project specification of workflows for creating and verifying attestations._x000D_
- Reference implementation (Notation) of Notary Project attestation specifications including CLI specifications_x000D_
- Integration of Notary Project attestation tooling into popular CI/CD pipelines._x000D_
_x000D_
Your comments are welcome._x000D_

title: Support extending trust store with Linux kernel keyrings
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Modern Linux-based systems use the [kernel keyrings](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/keyrings.7.html) (part of a broader [kernel service](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.0/security/keys/core.html)) to determine what keys are trusted by the system._x000D_
_x000D_
Among other things, this allows the owner of a system and the owner of the OS image to both contribute keys to the trust store. Inability to use the kernel keyring means that any changes to the trust store need to be reflected in the policy, typically on disk.

### What solution do you propose?

Externalize or extend the trust store to use certificates in the kernel keyring, possibly when instructed to do so via a trust policy or an environment variable.

### What alternatives have you considered?

The alternative seems to be for a userspace process to walk over the kernel keyrings, perform export operations, reconstruct a trust policy and populate the trust store, which results in duplication, need to synchronize lifecycle events, and more userspace code which increases the attack surface._x000D_
_x000D_
For example, the [AKV plugin](https://github.com/Azure/notation-azure-kv/blob/main/docs/self-signed-workflow.md#:~:text=Add%20the%20certificate%20to%20your%20trust%20store%20and%20the%20trustpolicy.json%20to%20Notation%20configuration%20directory%3A) calls for an `az keyvault certificate show ...` followed by a `notation cert add`. This is the specific step I'm suggesting we can get rid of by a trust policy potentially indicating it's acceptable for `notation` to use the kernel keyring as an extended trust store._x000D_
_x000D_
I read the documentation on [plugins](https://github.com/notaryproject/specifications/blob/v1.0.0/specs/plugin-extensibility.md) which appears to focus on extending signing mechanisms, not on externalizing trust stores.

### Any additional context?

_No response_

I think this is a valid ask. If I understand correctly, the request is for the Notary Project trust store to be enhanced to read certificates from the OS system trust store. OS system owners can manage certificates in the system trust store. As a result, normal users won’t need to configure the Notary Project trust store themselves; they would only need to specify which trust store to use in the trust policy and define the trust identities. | JeyJeyGao: I have a concern that the notation trust store contains the root certificate that the user trusted specifically for notation verification. However, the system store may contain certificates for other purposes, and other apps may mistakenly add or delete certificates from the system store. Therefore, implicitly using those certificates may not work as expected. Is it possible to do `notation cert add --from-keyrings <certificate-name>` ? By doing this, we allow the user to use a certificate from the system store by explicitly selecting the certificate. Also, we don’t need to change the notation trust store to fit both Linux and Windows certificate stores. | bureado: There are many certificate stores in Linux. Some are in userspace, others are in kernel space, and they all have various ways to access them. Kernel keyrings such as `builtin_trusted_keys`, `machine` or `platform`, only allow new keys to be added if you rebuild the kernel or show presence in a machine reboot. Having a key in one of those keyrings mean you can install kernel modules. All of those things are at a higher privilege level than Notation, containerd or anything else. I'm suggesting a feature that doesn't require `notation cert add`. I shouldn't need to write a certificate to the Notation trust store that is already stored elsewhere in the system, and rather should be able to have just a pointer. This pointer can be to a single certificate (less ideal) or the entire store. Yes, there should be a way for the trust policy owner to indicate which stores are allowed (or, for example, an environment variable that, instructs notation to only use the trusted kernel keyrings)

title: Support COSE Hash Envelope for Blob COSE signature
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

The current [Blob COSE signature](https://github.com/notaryproject/specifications/blob/main/specs/signature-envelope-cose.md#cose-payload) uses a JSON format payload, which requires an additional JSON decoder to process the signature payload. This approach is not optimal, especially for low-power devices, as it reduces efficiency and undermines the goal of using COSE signatures.

An ongoing IETF proposal describes enhancements to COSE detached signatures. You can find the proposal here: [COSE Hash Envelope Draft](https://cose-wg.github.io/draft-ietf-cose-hash-envelope/draft-ietf-cose-hash-envelope.html). Once the IETF proposal is approved, the Notary Project will no longer align with the industry standard, resulting in potential interoperability and compatibility challenges. 

### What solution do you propose?

In the IETF proposal, new parameters such as `media type` and `hash algorithm` are added to the protected header. The payload parameter contains the hash value of the blob content. Below is a table showing how the parameters and headers in the COSE Hash Envelope can represent the parameters defined in the Notary Project Blob signature payload:

| Notary Project Blob siganture payload parameter |  COSE Hash Envelope                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| `mediatype`                                                             | `protected.media_type`                   |  
| `digest`                                                                    | `payload` and `protected.hash_alg` |
| `size`                                                                        |    NA                                                |
| `annotations`                                                           |    NA                                                |

The COSE Hash Envelope does not include a size parameter. While it is theoretically possible for different content sizes to produce the same hash value, this is extremely unlikely with modern cryptographic hash functions like SHA-256, which are designed to make collisions highly improbable. So, it is acceptable without `size` parameter.

Regarding the `annotations` field, it is optional, and the scenarios for blobs to use these annotations are unclear. If needed in the future, a Notary-specific CoseHeaderValue can be registered with the IETF to store additional Notary-specific information.

This issue proposes that the Notary Project Blob COSE signature adopt the COSE Hash Envelope as the default signature format. The benefits include:

- **IETF Standard**: Ensures interoperability and compatibility.
- **Optimized for COSE**: Removes the use of JSON payloads, making it more efficient, especially for low-power device scenarios.

Since the IETF proposal is still in draft form, an alpha/beta version of both specifications and implementations can be released initially. Once the IETF draft is approved, the implementation can be stabilized.

### What alternatives have you considered?

No

### Any additional context?

_No response_

title: Support signing and verifying multi-platform images
body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

As multi-platform images are getting more and more popular, Notation should consider a way to support signing and verifying a multi-platform image. 

Multi-platform images are often published as OCI image indexes or Docker manifest list, containing references to platform-specific images. Currently, Notation CLI primarily focuses on signing and verifying a single image, but this approach has limitations:

- If only the image index is signed, a compromised platform-specific image may go undetected while the signature remains valid.
- If only platform-specific images are signed, the integrity of the image index is not assured.

Supporting signing and verification for both the image index and platform-specific images will enhance security and integrity in multi-platform deployments.

## Use cases

- Docker Official Images
Example: docker.io/library/nginx provides multi-platform support for different CPU architectures.
Verifying signatures before pulling images in production environments prevents supply chain attacks.

- Kubernetes Official Images
Example: k8s.gcr.io/kube-apiserver supports multiple architectures such as AMD64, ARM64, and PPC64LE.
Signing ensures that all platform-specific images are verified before deployment in Kubernetes clusters.

- Other CNCF project images
Example: `ghcr.io/ratify-project/ratify:v1.4.0` and `ghcr.io/oras-project/oras:v1.3.0-beta.2` provide multiple architectures. For ratify image signed by `notation, you can find that only the multi-platform image (index) of the ratify image has been signed but all platform-specific images are not yet. See the [query result](https://artifact-explorer.azurewebsites.net/artifact?image=ghcr.io/ratify-project/ratify:v1.4.0)

Here are a few users asked for this feature:
- https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/issues/1080
- https://github.com/notaryproject/notation/issues/18
- https://github.com/ratify-project/ratify/issues/2157

### What solution do you propose?

- Signing Multi-Platform Images: Provide an option in Notation CLI to recursively sign a multi-platform image (index) along with its platform-specific images.
- Verification of Multi-Platform Images:
    - Ensure that verification can check signatures for both the image index and its referenced images.
    - Introduce trust policy to enforce required signatures on either the index, platform images, or both.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/57862438-ec0a-4006-a974-313c69d43ec6)

### What alternatives have you considered?

Signing only the image index: Leaves individual platform images unverified.
Signing only platform-specific images: Leaves the index open to manipulation.
Allowing configurable policy to choose signing strategy: Could provide flexibility for different security models.



### Any additional context?

**Open question**: Should this feature allow selective signing of only the index or specific platform images? For example, users may want to sign a patched image and its index if there is a single-arch vulnerable image in a multi-platform image.

title: GQ signature support
body_text:
Currently, an OpenPubkey token contains the original signature from the OIDC provider. This arguably means that it isn't safe to share the OpenPubkey token, as the token could be used to impersonate the subject to a service that doesn't check the audience claim, or to trick an OpenPubkey client to issue a token for the subject._x000D_
_x000D_
We can create a GQ signature to prove that we have the original OIDC provider's signature. This can be verified using the original OIDC signing payload (`header || '.' || payload`) and the OIDC provider's public key. This works because GQ signature private keys are equivalent to RSA signatures._x000D_
_x000D_
The GQ signature can be published in place of the OIDC provider's signature in an OpenPubkey token._x000D_
_x000D_

body_text: As OpenPubkey tokens are JWS, we need to have a way of identifying the signature as being a GQ signature. The `alg` will be set to `RS256`  because the protected headers are fixed, so we will need to add an unprotected header to flag this.

title: Cryptography review and remediation
body_text:
As noted in https://github.com/bastionzero/openpubkey/pull/3 our GQ signature implementation uses golang's bigint library which is known to be leak information via a [timing side-channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Side-channel_attack). Before going 1.0 with this code base we need perform a review and remediation of cryptography used in this project. _x000D_
_x000D_
At minimum this should consist of:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. **Constant time operations tests:** Unittests verifying constant time of sensitive cryptographic operations, such as GQ signature generation and user key pair generation, see #56_x000D_
3. **A review of cryptographic dependencies:** Check that the cryptographic libraries we depend on are making the right choices and are protecting against threats such as ECDSA nonce reuse._x000D_
4. **A review of our implementation of GQ signatures:** this should including documenting and understanding the implications of any differences between our implementation and  [ISO/IEC 14888-2:2008](https://www.iso.org/standard/44227.html)._x000D_
5. **Lifecycle and protection of secrets:** Ensuring that sensitive cryptographic secrets are zerod/deleted when no longer in use and that they do not persist after they are needed. For instance with GQ signatures, we should delete the RSA signature immediately after the GQ signature is constructed. We should carefully consider the lifecycle of our ephemeral keypairs, currently we just write them to disk, see #47, #51, #52, #53 _x000D_
_x000D_
Suggestions to grow this list are welcome. When we get closer to 1.0, many of the items on list will be broken out into separate tickets.

GQ Signature flagging
body_text:
Reading through https://github.com/bastionzero/openpubkey/pull/14 I had the following thoughts I wanted record about possible ways to flag that a signature if GQ Signature._x000D_
_x000D_
Consider the following two approaches:_x000D_
_x000D_
The unsigned header flag approach_x000D_
====_x000D_
_x000D_
We flag that a OP RSA signature has been replaced by a GQ Signature by adding a unsigned header field: `"sig_type": "oidc_gq"` Lets call _x000D_
_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
	"payload": "payload",_x000D_
	"signatures": [{_x000D_
		"protected": {"alg":"ES256","rz":"5","upk":{"crv":"P-256","kty":"EC","x":"RI","y":"Hk"}},_x000D_
		"header": {_x000D_
			"sig_type": "cic"_x000D_
		},_x000D_
		"signature": "user signature"_x000D_
	}, {_x000D_
		"protected": {"alg":"RS256","kid":"6f7254101f56e41cf35c9926de84a2d552b4c6f1","typ":"JWT"},_x000D_
		"header": {_x000D_
			"sig_type": "oidc_gq"_x000D_
		},_x000D_
		"signature": "GQ signature"_x000D_
	}]_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
The altered protected header approach_x000D_
====_x000D_
_x000D_
Alternatively we could alter the protected header changing the `alg` field to `GQ256` and then signing the altered protected header and payload with the GQ signature. A verifier would then reconstruct the message the OP signed with RSA by changing the algorithm field back. It would look like:_x000D_
_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
	"payload": "payload",_x000D_
	"signatures": [{_x000D_
		"protected": {"alg":"ES256","rz":"5","upk":{"crv":"P-256","kty":"EC","x":"RI","y":"Hk"}},_x000D_
		"header": {_x000D_
			"sig_type": "cic"_x000D_
		},_x000D_
		"signature": "user signature"_x000D_
	}, {_x000D_
		"protected": {"alg":"GQ256","kid":"6","typ":"JWT"},_x000D_
		"signature": "GQ signature"_x000D_
	}]_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Comparison_x000D_
====_x000D_
_x000D_
**The unsigned header flag approach**_x000D_
_x000D_
**Pros:**_x000D_
* Results in a simpler implementation of the the verifier and the signer._x000D_
* None of the values which are signed by OP are altered or reserialized._x000D_
_x000D_
**Cons:**_x000D_
* Standard OIDC validators don't know about GQ signatures or the `sig_type` header so they will likely attempt to verify the GQ signature as if it was a very large RSA signature resulting in a hard to debug failure._x000D_
* Uses an unsigned header, which means we have to worry about what happens if someone alters this header. Ideally there is no content which is not covered by a signature. This is a minor con._x000D_
_x000D_
**The altered protected header approach**_x000D_
_x000D_
**Pros:**_x000D_
* Standard OIDC validators will see that the `alg` is set to algorithm they don't support and fail gracefully producing a meaningful error message: Signature algorithm `GQ256` is unsupported._x000D_
* If we want to standardize GQ signatures in JWS as `alg` is the standard way of flagging the signing algorithm_x000D_
_x000D_
**Cons:**_x000D_
* Likely a source of bugs and a pain point for implementors as signed message content is very fragile. Changing the protected header requires serializing and deserializing it. Different JSON libraries make minor changes to whitespace or the ordering of keys that result in signatures not verifying. These signature verification issues can creep in both when generating the GQ signature and when verifying it, as they both involve deserializing the protected header, making a change and then serializing it again._x000D_
_x000D_
We could bypass this con by storing the base64 encoding of the OPs signature in the protected header. That seems a little abusive toward the JWS standard._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_

EthanHeilman: > I think it would be fine to simply move the claim signature type claim to the protected headers on cosigner signatures. At the moment the unprotected header is called sig_type but we might want something shorter. One option would be to get rid of `sig_type` altogether and just inferring if a signature is OIDC, CIC or COS based on the protected header parameters. * OIDC signature - If no `upk` or `iss` claim in protected header. * CIC signature - If `upk` in protected header. * COS Signature - If `iss` in protected header. If we did want to move the sig_type into the protected header, I would propose the using the `typ` (type) [JOSE](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml) header introduced in [RFC-7515 JSON Web Signature (JWS)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515.html#section-4.1.9) and [RFC-7519 JSON Web Token (JWT)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519#section-5.1) in place of `sig_type`. The beauty of this approach is that the OP's OIDC signature should already have `typ=JWT.` Technically the JWT RFC says, "Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL", but I've yet to see any OIDC Provider that does not set `typ=JWT` in the protected header of their signature. I just checked and Google, Azure, and Github Actions all specify `typ=JWT.` Even if an OP did not set `typ=JWT` in the protected header, we could infer a signature was the OIDC signature because either `typ=JWT` or no `typ` was set in the protected header. * OIDC signature - If `typ=JWT` or no `typ` set * CIC signature - if `typ=CIC` * COS signature - if `typ=COS` The only downside to this approach is that technically the `typ` header is intended to describe the media type of the payload. Instead we would be using it in a slightly off-label manner. The JWS RFC does not fully think through how typ should be used when there are multiple signatures and I think using typ in this fashion for typing signatures is reasonable and fits with the spirit if not the letter of the JWS RFC. [RFC-7515 JSON Web Signature (JWS) Section 4.1.9](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515.html#section-4.1.9) > The "typ" (type) Header Parameter is used by JWS applications to declare the media type [[IANA.MediaTypes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515.html#ref-IANA.MediaTypes)] of this complete JWS. This is intended for use by the application when more than one kind of object could be present in an application data structure that can contain a JWS; the application can use this value to disambiguate among the different kinds of objects that might be present. It will typically not be used by applications when the kind of object is already known. This parameter is ignored by JWS implementations; any processing of this parameter is performed by the JWS application. Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL. [..] [RFC-7519 JSON Web Token (JWT) Section 5.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519#section-5.1) > The "typ" (type) Header Parameter defined by [[JWS](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519#ref-JWS)] and [[JWE](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519#ref-JWE)] is used by JWT applications to declare the media type [[IANA.MediaTypes](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519#ref-IANA.MediaTypes)] of this complete JWT. This is intended for use by the JWT application when values that are not JWTs could also be present in an application data structure that can contain a JWT object; the application can use this value to disambiguate among the different kinds of objects that might be present. It will typically not be used by applications when it is already known that the object is a JWT. This parameter is ignored by JWT implementations; any processing of this parameter is performed by the JWT application. If present, it is RECOMMENDED that its value be "JWT" to indicate that this object is a JWT. While media type names are not case sensitive, it is RECOMMENDED that "JWT" always be spelled using uppercase characters for compatibility with legacy implementations. Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL.
jonnystoten: This sounds good, I've updated #66 to use this approach. Another option would have been `cty` (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515.html#section-4.1.10) but it is indeed nice that the OIDC tokens already have `typ` set to `JWT`.
EthanHeilman: > Another option would have been cty @jonnystoten Oh, that is interesting. If I am reading the RFC correctly the cty only covers the "secured content" which means it doesn't refer to other signatures?
jonnystoten: I think it means it describes the payload field only, but (like with `typ`) it doesn't cover what it means to have different values in different signature headers.

title: Nonce isn't checked on validation
body_text:
We don't actually check that the nonce is a hash of the CIC when verifying a PK token. The check currently reads the nonce from the PK and then checks that the PK token contains the same nonce, and of course this will always be true. We should instead construct it from the CIC._x000D_
_x000D_
We have a function to compute the nonce hash already which is used to get the nonce when signing, but it suffers from the same JSON key order issue mentioned at the end of #15 - I haven't checked but wouldn't be surprised if the nonces we're generating aren't actually hashes of the CIC protected headers. We should instead hash the exact bytes that are going into the JWS. This might mean that we need to do some more manual signing of the JWS rather than leaning on the jws library.

title: Make code less panicky
body_text: There are lots of calls to `panic` and `logrus.Fatalf` which can crash the calling program. We should instead make sure we're returning errors in most of these cases. (There may be good reasons to panic in a truly exceptional situation.)

title: PK Token Compact Representation
body_text:
[RFC-7515: JWS (JSON Web Signatures)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515.html) specifies two serialization formats for JWS: JSON and Compact._x000D_
```_x000D_
Two closely related serializations for JWSs are defined.  The JWS_x000D_
Compact Serialization is a compact, URL-safe representation intended_x000D_
for space-constrained environments such as HTTP Authorization headers_x000D_
and URI query parameters.  The JWS JSON Serialization represents JWSs_x000D_
as JSON objects and enables multiple signatures and/or MACs to be_x000D_
applied to the same content._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
[RFC-7515: Section 7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515.html#section-7.1) defines the Compact Serialization format as:_x000D_
```_x000D_
7.1  JWS Compact Serialization_x000D_
_x000D_
   The JWS Compact Serialization represents digitally signed or MACed_x000D_
   content as a compact, URL-safe string.  This string is:_x000D_
_x000D_
      BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)) || '.' ||_x000D_
      BASE64URL(JWS Payload) || '.' ||_x000D_
      BASE64URL(JWS Signature)_x000D_
_x000D_
   Only one signature/MAC is supported by the JWS Compact Serialization_x000D_
   and it provides no syntax to represent a JWS Unprotected Header_x000D_
   value._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Note that this means the JWS Compact Serialization only supports one signature. This prevents us from using it as-is for PK Tokens as our PK Tokens are JWS with more than one signature._x000D_
_x000D_
While the JWS JSON Serialization supports multiple signatures and thus can easily support our PK Tokens the RFC says: `This representation is neither optimized for compactness nor URL-safe.`_x000D_
_x000D_
It would be useful for OpenPubkey to have a compact, URL-safe serialization. I am proposing the following format for JWS Compact Serialization format._x000D_
_x000D_
## JWS Compact Serialization for multiple signatures_x000D_
_x000D_
(JWS Protected Header1,Signature1) through (JWS Protected HeaderN,SignatureN) _x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
      BASE64URL(JWS Payload) || ':' ||_x000D_
      BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header1)) || ':' ||_x000D_

title: OpenPubkey single use signatures support
body_text:
DOI (Docker Official Images) using OpenPubkey extends OpenPubkey with the notion of single use signatures. This provides the security property that even if the signing key was compromised it can not be used or abused to sign another image._x000D_
_x000D_
To accomplish this Docker exploits the flexibility of the CIC and specifies an extra claim in CIC which commits to the hash of the data to be signed using the claim 'att'._x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
func (sv *opkSignerVerifier) Sign(ctx context.Context, data []byte) ([]byte, error) {_x000D_
	hash := s256(data) // SHA-256_x000D_
	hashHex := hex.EncodeToString(hash)_x000D_
_x000D_
	tokSigner, err := pktoken.NewSigner("", "ES256", true, map[string]any{"att": hashHex})"_x000D_
```_x000D_
https://github.com/openpubkey/signed-attestation/blob/main/opk.go#L24_x000D_
_x000D_
This results in `CIC` which is `{'rz': crypto.random(), 'upk': <publickey>, 'alg': 'EC256', 'sig': SHA-256(dokcerImage)}`_x000D_
_x000D_
This single use signature feature is generic. We should consider if we want to support this as part of OpenPubkey itself.

title: PK Token Properties
body_text:
I want to have a discussion about what our goals are with the PK Token because it impacts data structures which are always nice to get as right as possible, as soon as possible. _x000D_
_x000D_
I propose that the PK Token should have the following three properties:_x000D_
_x000D_
**Property 1**: The PK Token does not require any outside information in order to verify itself_x000D_
- This isn't to say that external code shouldn't verify certain claims or parameters. For example, it would still be best practices to check that the issuer claim or a key algorithm match expected values, but a PK Token would only use its own values for verification._x000D_
_x000D_
**Property 2**: A valid PK Token should have, at a minimum:_x000D_
- A single oidc provider signature whether that be in the form of rsa or gq (or other!)_x000D_
- A single user signature over the same payload including client instance claims headers_x000D_
_x000D_
**Property 3**: The PK Token supports any number of cosigners_x000D_
- A PK Token can have zero or more cosigners without violating **Property 1**
top_3_comments_text: jonnystoten: Apologies for the late comment! **Property 1**: I _think_ this is fine but this stuff is tricky. I was worried that not requiring alg be checked against an externally provided value could be dangerous, but I think we're OK because we require use of JWK, so the alg in the JWK must match the alg in the JWS. Does that make sense? **Property 2**: You mean we require one OP signature but we allow more than one and we require one user signature but we allow more than one, right? It would be strange to have multiple OP signatures I think, is there a use case for that? Multiple user signatures makes sense if you want to bind multiple keys. **Property 3**: Makes sense to me! | lgmugnier: > Property 1: I think this is fine but this stuff is tricky. I was worried that not requiring alg be checked against an externally provided value could be dangerous, but I think we're OK because we require use of JWK, so the alg in the JWK must match the alg in the JWS. Does that make sense? The emphasis I want to make with this property is the division of responsibilities. To your point, the internal pktoken validation might check that the JWK's algorithm is the same as the `alg` claim, that makes it "internally valid". But there is this second set of responsibilities like doing that external check on whether the value of the `alg` claim is acceptable. For example, if `alg` was "None" that's technically an accepted value so the pktoken would still _internally_ verify, but that would be bad if that were the case so it may not be _externally_ valid. What I really want to accomplish with this property is to force this idea that you can validate the pk token anywhere, for the most part, like other json web things. Sure, you might not check whether it was issued by "google" instead of "evil.co" or whether the signing algorithm is "None", but if a pk token lands in your lap, you can validate it. So, from a technical stance what I'm saying is that I want to put the bulk of the formatting and signature verification code into the pk token object itself, have something like `(p *PKToken) Verify() error`, and other entities like the client, verifier, provider, cosigner, etc. can do additional, unique checks e.g. that fields match expected values or fall within certain parameters. > Property 2: You mean we require one OP signature but we allow more than one and we require one user signature but we allow more than one, right? It would be strange to have multiple OP signatures I think, is there a use case for that? Multiple user signatures makes sense if you want to bind multiple keys. I wanted to boil the pk token down to it's most minimally viable parts. I avoided making claims about "one or more" and keeping it "exactly one of" because, to your point, that might make sense for cic but not really for op but who knows what use cases people might have down the line. We can always add to the properties, if you want to say something about "one or more". The way I have translated this (surreptitiously) into code already is in how I've defined the "New" function: ```golang func New(idToken []byte, cicToken []byte, isGQ bool) (*PKToken, error) ``` If we lock down direct access to the object even further (as I'd like to) then this relationship becomes clear: the only way to create a new pktoken is minimally with both an op and a cic signature. | EthanHeilman: Only one OP per PK Token I see an iron requirement due to the fact that a PK Token can only contain a sub issued by a single OP. I do worry that Property 2 could be read as excluding refresh tokens. Since there would now be two OP signatures per PK Token. I don't believe this is the intent of Property 2. I'm mostly aligned on Property 2 & 3, I want to discuss Property 1 in this comment and think through why we might want to verify PK Tokens outside of the PK Token struct. ### Option 1: Supply allowlist config struct at verification time, the allowlist would not be saved inside the PK Token and would need to be resupplied each time verify is called ```golang err = pkt.Verify(cxt, &Allowlist{ AllowedProviders: []oidc.OpenIdProvider{opGoogle, ...}, AllowedCosigners: []cos.CosignerProvider{mfaCosigner, ...}, }) ``` **Pros:** 1. The parameters in Verify to enforce that an allowlist is specified. It is clear what verification rules are being applied. This is nice developer UX. 2. Easy to try more than one Allowlist for the usecase, I want googleOp for this cosigner, but if that fails try githubOp without a cosigner. 3. Stateless **Cons:** 1. Allowlist needs to be available to whatever function calls verify each time verify is called. 2. Statelessness prevents caching results from verification ### Option 2: Supply Allowlist to PK Token and store it as part of the pkt object. ```golang pkt.AddAllowlist(&Allowlist{ AllowedProviders: []oidc.OpenIdProvider{opGoogle, ...}, AllowedCosigners: []cos.CosignerProvider{mfaCosigner, ...}, }) err = pkt.Verify(ctx) ``` **Pros:** 1. You can cache verification results in the PK Token itself and track the validity of a PK Token in the PK Token struct. **Cons:** 1. Does not use the parameters in Verify to enforce that an allowlist is specified, e.g., someone could call pkt.Verify(ctx) without first adding an allowlist. 2. PK Token now has verification metadata which is not derived from deserialization a json PK Token. ### Option 3: A PK Token verifier struct: ```golang allowlist := &Allowlist{ AllowedProviders: []oidc.OpenIdProvider{opGoogle, ...}, AllowedCosigners: []cos.CosignerProvider{mfaCosigner, ...}, } verPkt := pktokenverifier.New(ctx, allowlist) err = verPkt.Verify(pkt) ``` **Pros:** 1. Very flexible: Lets developers bring their own validators without needing access to the internals of our package. 2. Verification changes can happen independently from PK Token interface, can add new public key logs without changing provider interface. 3. You can cache verification results and PK Token validity in the PKtokenVerifier itself. 4. Enforce the creation of allowlists in the parameters to the PKTokenVerifier constructor 5. No verification meta data stored in PK Token, PK Token is now just deserialization of the PK Token and helper methods **Cons:** 1. Verification lives outside of the PK Token ### Edit: Cyclical dependencies The issue I run into whenever moving verification out of the client is that the providers and cosignerProviders live in the client and the client also needs to call verify. This creates a cyclical dependency, client depends on verifier package, verifier package depends on client package. I could solve this problem by creating a provider and cosigner interface in the verifier package. I'm not a fan of this approach because if we created interfaces for the verifier we would have two interfaces for same struct. A change to that interface would then require changing all the structs that depend on it and now another interface. It works, but it addresses the symptom not the underlying issue. A better approach which addresses the underlying issue would be to break providers out into their own package `providers` which is imported by both `client` and `verifier`. The `verifier` could live inside the `pktoken` package, but I like how currently the `pktoken` package doesn't have dependencies on the providers. It provides a nice separation.

title: Management of sensitive data in memory
body_text:
Derived from #11 _x000D_
>**Lifecycle and protection of secrets:** Ensuring that sensitive cryptographic secrets are zerod/deleted when no longer in use and that they do not persist after they are needed. For instance with GQ signatures, we should delete the RSA signature immediately after the GQ signature is constructed. We should carefully consider the lifecycle of our ephemeral keypairs, currently we just write them to disk._x000D_
_x000D_
Potential ways to address this:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Avoid using strings and instead use byte slices whenever handling sensitive data_x000D_
  a. Strings are immutable in Go and difficult to wipe_x000D_
2. Use the [memguard](https://github.com/awnumar/memguard) package with `LockedBuffers` or `Enclave` objects to handle sensitive data and use the built in data scrubbing methods_x000D_
  a. This prevents sensitive data from being swapped to disk or leaked through core dumps and ensures it is cleaned up properly_x000D_
3. Minimize the lifetime of sensitive data in memory by scrubbing immediately after the data is no longer needed _x000D_
