title: GHA Runner VM Entropy for Key Generation
body_text: # Problem #_x000D_ _x000D_ The `Sign()` method generates ephemeral keys for signing attestations shown here:_x000D_ https://github.com/openpubkey/signed-attestation/blob/f64048341ecd651ed894f094ab70213d20ee6bbb/opk.go#L30-L33_x000D_ _x000D_ Using `GenKeyPair()` in `utils`:_x000D_ https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/f662c2ce7ecfd68427be19374409a927b8898223/util/files.go#L100-L109_x000D_ _x000D_ Depending upon the system on which this is running, the entropy available (and sources it is derived from) may not be very high quality. The quality of the entropy source is important in determining how secure the resulting signatures are by ensuring that we are generating unpredictable private keys._x000D_ _x000D_ A planned use-case is running this as a GitHub Action (GHA). [GHAs run on Virtual Machines](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/understanding-github-actions#the-components-of-github-actions). Typically, VMs are poor sources of entropy and are very deterministic unless effort is made to provision them with a quality entropy source._x000D_ _x000D_ There are several [mitigating factors](#user-content-mitigating-factors) for key compromise built into the solution. Although, identifying the entropy source for GHA runners and improving it if needed, is another mitigating factor for preventing key compromise._x000D_ _x000D_ ## Entropy source for GHA runners_x000D_ _x000D_ It appears that the ubuntu VM images have been updated to include `haveged` https://github.com/actions/runner-images/issues/672. Unsure if that is the latest change w.r.t. entropy sources in GHA VMs._x000D_ _x000D_ >haveged is a daemon — derived from [the HAVEGE algorithm](http://www.irisa.fr/caps/projects/hipsor/) — designed to help (the kernel) gather entropy from more sources (than the kernel itself does). It is common to install it on physical hosts to gather entropy faster from their entropy-rich environment. However, it is not recommended to use it in virtual machines, since the very reasons that make them prone to entropy starvation will hinder, if not defeat, HAVEGE (or the quality — randomness — of the entropy it will gather)._x000D_ _x000D_ ## Testing the VM configuration_x000D_ _x000D_ A lot of sources point to this [writeup](https://security.stackexchange.com/a/34552) about `HAVAGE` (the algorithm that `haveged` is based on). It discusses how it uses the [rdtsc](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Stamp_Counter) (x86 processor time stamp counter with sub-nanosecond precision) as a source of entropy. _x000D_ _x000D_ They highlight three possible VM configurations for how `rdtsc` is implemented:_x000D_ >For a virtual machine system, there are three choices with regards to this instruction:_x000D_ > 1. Let the instruction go to the hardware directly._x000D_ > 2. Trap the instruction and emulate it._x000D_ > 3. Disable the instruction altogether._x000D_ _x000D_ I created a GHA action to run the example code to gain some insight into how the GHA VMs might be configured for `rdtsc` and good news! It appears that the `rdtsc` instruction is configured to go directly to the host hardware. Which is the best possible option of the three configurations._x000D_ _x000D_ See the action run here https://github.com/mrjoelkamp/gha-vm-rdtsc-test/actions/runs/6720417160/job/18264356488_x000D_ Looking for a value between 10 - 100._x000D_ result:_x000D_ ```bash_x000D_ average : 34.859_x000D_ ```_x000D_ _x000D_ This result determines whether the GHA VMs are configured to use the host's `rdtsc` derived from hardware as opposed to being emulated or not available. If it failed (and the entropy was emulated or hardcoded) that could be a major issue._x000D_ _x000D_ What it doesn't answer, is whether it is appropriate to use the GHA VM's entropy source (`haveged`) for RNG when generating cryptographic key material. We also assume that the GHA VM will continue to provide an environment where we can securely generate key material and perform cryptographic operations in._x000D_ _x000D_ # Solution #_x000D_ _x000D_ In addition to the current Go based KDF and crypto library, I recommend that OpenPubKey support cloud provider KMS solutions for cryptographic functions (AWS, GCP, Azure, Hashicorp, etc.). A lot of these systems are backed by Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) with high entropy RNG. _x000D_ _x000D_ For example:_x000D_ > AWS KMS key generation is performed on the AWS KMS HSMs. The HSMs implement a hybrid random number generator that uses the [NIST SP800-90A Deterministic Random Bit Generator (DRBG) CTR_DRBG using AES-256](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-90Ar1.pdf). It is seeded with a nondeterministic random bit generator with 384-bits of entropy and updated with additional entropy to provide prediction resistance on every call for cryptographic material._x000D_ _x000D_ There are many other added benefits to supporting external KMS solutions as well:_x000D_ - Controlled execution environment that is optimized for cryptographic operations_x000D_ - Runtime access to private keys not accessible by software interface_x000D_ _x000D_ # Mitigating Factors #_x000D_ _x000D_ ## Ephemeral Key Lifetime_x000D_ If the system only trusts the ephemeral keys to sign data in a short time frame, the compromise of the private ephemeral may be of little significance. Although, depending on how deterministic the RNG is, an attacker could potentially determine the private key ahead of ephemeral key generation with significant statistical probability._x000D_ _x000D_ ## Transparency Log_x000D_ Including a Transparency Log to store signatures that could be monitored by publishers to determine if an actor forged a signature using a compromised key and generated a signature outside of their control. Although, this countermeasure would be reactive as opposed to preventative and requires active monitoring and alerting._x000D_ _x000D_ ## Layered Signing_x000D_ The OPK One Time Signature could also mitigate this issue by providing a hash of the image in the payload that is signed by the Identity Provider. If an image was modified and signed by someone who had compromised a user signing key, the hash comparison would fail for the modified image. This requires that the verification client implement this check._x000D_

title: sensitive data in `math/big` package
body_text:
Identified in #48 _x000D_
_x000D_
GQ signing uses the `math/big` library for big integer math, specifically the modulus inverting function:_x000D_
https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/69500f1bd4de345649e5bf2773d87cf418dac177/gq/sign.go#L95-L104_x000D_
_x000D_
Sensitive data (OIDC provider signature) is copied into memory within the `big.Int` type as part of the `SetBytes()` method. Unfortunately, the `bit.Int Bytes()` method copies the underlying data to a new byte slice. So there is no way to wipe the data from this object once it is copied in.

title: sensitive data in `lestrrat-go/jwx` package
body_text:
Identified in #48 _x000D_
_x000D_
The `pktoken` package in `pktoken.go` uses the `"github.com/lestrrat-go/jwx/v2/jws"` package as introduced in https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/pull/45. _x000D_
_x000D_
The OIDC provider signature is stored in the `PKToken` struct in the `Op` field as a `jws.Signature` type:_x000D_
https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/463f605d392dea081d445e9cef95f65dcd662cfe/pktoken/pktoken.go#L28-L35_x000D_
_x000D_
The `Signature` type stores the byte slice containing the signature data and is not directly exposed making it not possible to implement `LockedBuffer` at this level. But we can wipe the value from memory using the `memguard.WipeBytes()` method like so:_x000D_
https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/463f605d392dea081d445e9cef95f65dcd662cfe/client/client.go#L88-L90_x000D_
_x000D_
Although, this won't provide the same data safety features we would get if implemented as a `LockedBuffer`. We could gain a bit more control over the memory management by reverting back to `[]byte` for PK token signatures (and refactoring them to `LockedBuffer`) but a discussion around that should occur before proceeding.

title: GQ package uses math/big
body_text:
The GQ package uses `math/big` for its implementation which is not safe for cryptographic use:_x000D_
_x000D_
> Note that methods may leak the Int's value through timing side-channels. Because of this and because of the scope and complexity of the implementation, Int is not well-suited to implement cryptographic operations. The standard library avoids exposing non-trivial Int methods to attacker-controlled inputs and the determination of whether a bug in math/big is considered a security vulnerability might depend on the impact on the standard library._x000D_
_x000D_
I had a look at what how the crypto/rsa package deals with this and found that there's an [internal `bigmod` package](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/internal/bigmod) which is used instead of `math/big`. Interestingly, this has only been the case since Go 1.20 as detailed [on Filippo Valsorda's blog](https://words.filippo.io/dispatches/go-1-21-plan/). This `bigmod` package would be the ideal package to use instead of `math/big`, but as it's internal we cannot import it. Filippo maintains a re-exported copy of the internal library at https://github.com/FiloSottile/bigmod so that could be the easiest thing to use.

body_text:
The OPK paper discusses an method for the client instance authenticating to the MFA cosigner called "POP Auth". title: How do we deal with missing/non-unique `kid` on JWKS endpoint?
body_text: In implementing a ledger for OIDC public key, we've found that according to spec, the `kid` is only mandatory if there is more than one key on the JWKS endpoint, and only needs to be unique for each HTTP response on that endpoint. `kid` is obviously super important when trying to lookup the public key given an OPK. I was wondering if adding a hash of the OP public key to the OPK header would solve this? Any other ideas?
top_3_comments_text: kipz: Relevant thread in slack: https://openssf.slack.com/archives/C060S7FHA3E/p1700039887986919 | EthanHeilman: My current thoughts are that we use the JTK ( JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint) from [RFC-7638 JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7638.html) standard to encode the OP's public key and than either include the JTK as an unprotected header or as part of the CIC protected header. I've gone back and forth several times. I am leaning toward always including the jkt as part of the OP unprotected header. My notes follow. ## Encodings and key name Before we look at where to put them. I want to examine some options for how to encode the hash of the OP public key: `JKT ( JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint) from [RFC-7638 JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7638.html) is standardizes how to hash and represent a JWK such as the ones used in OpenID Connect JWKS URIs. * While early versions of the drafts references a JOSE header field with the `jkt` this is not in the latest version of the standard and `jkt` is not registered at the IANA protocol registry for[ JOSE Headers (JSON Web Signature and Encryption Header Parameters) ](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml#web-signature-encryption-header-parameters). * However `jkt` is registered in the IANA protocol registry for[ JWK (JSON Web Keys) under JWT Confirmation Methods](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jwt/jwt.xhtml#claims) as JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint. [RFC 9449 OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html#name-jwk-thumbprint-confirmation) shows `jkt` being used as a JWT claim. ```json { "sub":"someone@example.com", "iss":"https://server.example.com", "nbf":1562262611, "exp":1562266216, "cnf": { "jkt":"0ZcOCORZNYy-DWpqq30jZyJGHTN0d2HglBV3uiguA4I" } } ``` JWS does have a JOSE header field specifically for that purpose called: (X.509 Certificate SHA-256 Thumbprint). ["x5t#S256"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515#section-4.1.8) (X.509 Certificate SHA-256 Thumbprint)) > The "x5t#S256" (X.509 certificate SHA-256 thumbprint) Header Parameter is a base64url-encoded SHA-256 thumbprint (a.k.a. digest) of the DER encoding of the X.509 certificate [RFC5280] corresponding to the key used to digitally sign the JWS. Note that certificate thumbprints are also sometimes known as certificate fingerprints. Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL. However OPs may not always provide X.509 DER encodings of their public keys and I am concerned with introducing the complexity of serializing a JWK at an JWKS URI to a X.509 DER encoding. It is unclear what the canonical form of JWK to X.509 serialization is since x509s have fields that don't depend on the JWKs. I would suggest using the `jkt` key and encoding the OPs public key according to RFC-7638 JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint. ## Where to put the hash? The nicest solution would be to put the OP (OpenID Provider) public key in the CIC commitment in the nonce that the user's client sends to the OP. Unfortunately that won't work because the user's client doesn't know what public key the OP will use to sign their ID Token until the OP returns the ID Token to the user. Let's look consider the various options: ### Store JKT in unsigned header of the OP **Pros:** 1. It is simple, and it works 2. Since it is unsigned, it can be added at any point by any party and parties that don't care about `jtk` can discard it without breaking signature verification. 3. The use of jkt here very clearly refers to the OP's public key. **Cons:** 1. It introduces unsigned headers which have repeatedly been misused by implementers and resulted in a number of security vulnerabilities. 2. Someone could prove the OP signature is incorrect by adding an bad jtk to the unprotected header. This could cause problems for systems that verify a signature, certificate once and then cache that outcome as they would conclude the PK Token is invalid and then reject it when it shows up without the bad jtk. 3. Parties can discard it without breaking signature verification. Potentially breaking long term verification without realizing it. 4. It would be nice to only have protected headers in PK Tokens so we never have to think about unsigned fields. ### Store JKT as an extended claim in Protected header of the CIC After getting the ID Token, the user's client would add the jtk to the protected header of the CIC. **Pros:** 1. Covered by the CIC signature. 2. This can be a standard part of PK Token creation to address issues where an misconfigured OP reuses a kid. **Cons:** 1. It break the rule the CIC commitment in the nonce is always the same as the protected header of the CIC and thus is always committed to in the nonce. This is not a technical limitation, but just would be an exception to how we treat the values in the CIC. 2. It isn't clear that jkt refers to the OPs public key. One might assume that since it is in CIC protected header next to the user's public key, that it is the thumbprint of the user's public key. ### Store JKT an additional signature in the PK Token After getting the ID Token, the user would sign and add two signatures to the PK Token. The first signature would be the CIC. The second signature would be the CICA (CIC After) which includes claims made after the ID Token is issued. This could be refreshed ID Tokens, signed select disclosures or any other claims a user's client may wish to make after the original ID Token issuance. **Pros:** 1. Works and is fairly clear. **Cons:** 1. Adds another signature, increasing the size of the PK Token. 2. Parties can discard it without breaking signature verification. Potentially breaking long term verification without realizing it. 3. Feels inconsistent to have this extra signature which only shows up because the OP doesn't have a kid. | jonnystoten: I'm in favor of "Store JKT in unsigned header of the OP". I don't think the cons are very strong for that option.

title: OIDC ID Token refresh in client
body_text:
When available the OpenPubkey client should support the ability to use a refresh token to request an refreshed ID Token. This refreshed ID Token will be stored in an unprotected header of the ID Token._x000D_
_x000D_
1. If refresh token returned from OP, client must save this refresh token,_x000D_
2. If refresh called on client, client must make a refresh call to the OP and save the refreshed ID Token_x000D_

title: Add Allowlist match function to OP providers
body_text:
We currently (as of PR #86) do not handle the case where the same provider (OP) is specified twice in an allowlist with different audiences. That is same providers sharing the same Issuer but having separate audience claims. Instead it will match on the first provider with the correct issuer and then verify using that provider._x000D_
_x000D_
The reason we check for matches rather than just verifying is to avoid blindly downloading a JWKS URI based on the issuer (iss) claim of an ID Token. Instead we check that the issuer is correct and then run verification. _x000D_
_x000D_
The ideal way to solve this problem is to add a function to the (OP) Provider interface called something like `Matches(idt IDToken) (bool)` and let each provider determine how decides if an ID Token belongs to it.

title: Cosigner Versioning
body_text:
Changes to the Cosiginer protocol and APIs are likely to present backwards compatibility problems. To address this we should:_x000D_
_x000D_
Put the supported Cosigner protocol versions in the well-known configuration URI of the cosigner. Using the URL pattern like: https://<cosigner>/.well-known/openpubkey-configuration_x000D_
_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
"issuer":"https://<cosigner>",_x000D_
"jwks_uri":"https://<cosigner>/.well-known/jwks.json",_x000D_
"cosigner_versions_supported": ["1", "2", "4"],_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Then the client can determine if any of the cosigner versions it supports match any of the cosigner versions supported by the cosigner server. If no match is found, the client outputs a meaningful error._x000D_
_x000D_
The client species the cosigner version it wants via the URI path it uses to access the API. For instance `https://<cosigner>/<cosigner-version>/initAuthURI?...`.

title: Design for Gitlab CI support
body_text:
As discussed in [Issue 26: Add GitLab CI signing example](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/issues/26) the approach used to sign software artifacts in github can not be used with gitlab because the gitlab workload can not specify the aud (audience) claim. Instead an aud claim is hardcoded in the workload configuration YAML. In this issue we propose the following design for gitlab and other settings where there is no client specified nonce or audience field._x000D_
_x000D_
## Generating a PK Token in Gitlab_x000D_
_x000D_
To generate a PK Token:_x000D_
1. The workload creates a key pair, (upk, usk), and requests an ID Token from the OP (gitlab)._x000D_
2. On receiving the ID Token from gitlab, the workload: generates the CIC (upk, alg, nonce), signs the CIC and ID token under the GQ signature._x000D_
3. The workload then immediate deletes the OPs RSA signature on the ID Token._x000D_
_x000D_
The CIC is included as part of the GQ protected header of the ID Token. Thus, when the GQ signature signs the new protected header, it also commits to the CIC. As is currently done with GQ signatures, the original protected header of the ID Token is base64 encoded and included in the protected header signed by the GQ signature._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
payload: {_x000D_
  "iss": "gitlab.example.com",_x000D_
  "aud": "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN:1234567890",_x000D_
  ..._x000D_
} _x000D_
signatures: [_x000D_
  {"protected": {"typ": "JWT", "alg": "GQ256", "kid":  Base64(origProtected), _x000D_
  "cic": SHA3_256(upk=alice-pubkey, alg=ES256, rz=crypto.Rand()),_x000D_
  "signature": GQSIGN(RSA-sig, (payload, signatures[0].protected))`_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  {"protected": {"upk": alice-pubkey, "alg": "EC256", "rz": <rz>},_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(alice-signkey, (payload, signatures[1].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
## Verifying a Gitlab PK Token_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Check the aud claim is prefixed with "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" and that the rest of the aud claim matches the expected aud claim._x000D_
2. Check that CIC signature verifies,_x000D_
3. Check that the CIC protected header values are committed to in the cic claim in protected header of GQ signature and that the GQ signature verifies for gitlabs public key._x000D_
_x000D_
## Security_x000D_
_x000D_
If configured correctly, this is approach offers the same security as the approach used with github. However this approach does introduce a  security risk of misconfiguration not present in the github case. If a GQ signature is not used and an attacker learns the ID Token, the attacker can compute the GQ signature from the RSA signature and insert their own public key. _x000D_
_x000D_
We mitigate the risk of this occurring by:_x000D_
_x000D_
* Requiring that PK Tokens that use the GQ signature to attest to the CIC must have "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" prefixed in the audience and that they are not considered valid PK Tokens otherwise. This also prevents attacks in which a gitlab ID Token not intended for use as a PK Token is replayed as a PK Token. Note that this rule does not apply to other types of PK Tokens._x000D_
* Ensuring that OpenPubkey clients always enforces the deletion of the RSA signature and only generates GQ signature PK Tokens for gitlab._x000D_
_x000D_
We argue that this sort of misconfiguration is very unlikely because outside of OpenPubkey, ID Tokens are treated as highly sensitive authentication secrets and within OpenPubkey we prevent this misconfiguration. Someone must configure their gitlab to put "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" in the aud claim, not use the OpenPubkey protocol and then must expose the ID token to an attacker. We can not prevent people from writing their own insecure protocols._x000D_
_x000D_
## Cosigner (Optional)_x000D_
We propose a security enhancement that adds a cosigner to remove the gitlab OP as a single point of compromise. It also provides additional protection against replay attacks, however we consider this protection to be unnecessary given the other safeguards above._x000D_
_x000D_
The aud claim can be postfixed by a commitment to a public key, `cpk`, whose corresponding signing key, `csk`, configured in gitlabs secret manager. This signing key can be used by the workload to sign the CIC in addition to the GQ signature._x000D_
_x000D_
Since this signing key's public key is committed to in the aud claim in the ID Token, an ID Token even with a aud claim prefixed with "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" and the RSA signature is no longer sufficient to attest to the CIC._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
payload: {_x000D_
  "iss": "gitlab.example.com",_x000D_
  "aud": "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-CPK"+SHA3_256(cpk),_x000D_
  ..._x000D_
} _x000D_
signatures: [_x000D_
  {"protected": {"typ": "JWT", "alg": "GQ256", "kid":  Base64(origProtected), _x000D_
  "cic": SHA3_256(upk=alice-pubkey, alg=ES256, rz=crypto.Rand()),_x000D_
  "signature": GQSIGN(RSA-sig, (payload, signatures[0].protected))`_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  {"protected": {"upk": alice-pubkey, "alg": "EC256", "rz": <rz>},_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(alice-signkey, (payload, signatures[1].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  {"protected": {"cospk": cosigner-pubkey, "alg": "EC256"_x000D_
  "cic": SHA3_256(upk=alice-pubkey, alg=ES256, rz=crypto.Rand()),_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(cosigner-signkey, (payload, signatures[2].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Any OpenPubkey verifier configured to expect this audience claim can check this cosigner signature. This removes the gitlab OP as a single point of compromise. This approach can be adapted to JWKS URIs, but changing the aud claim to use be "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-CPK"+Cosigner-JWKS-URI_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Proposed zklogin JWS
body_text:
As zkLogin was inspired by OpenPubkey to use the nonce in the ID Token to commit to the user's public key upk it is worth examining if OpenPubkey can employ zkLogin zero knowledge proofs to provide anonymous or private PK Tokens. This issue examines the feasibility, benefits and disadvantages of using zkLogin proofs in OpenPubkey._x000D_
_x000D_
[zkLogin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.11735) is a protocol for using zero knowledge proofs to add privacy to OIDC._x000D_
Given an ID token idt and public key upk it creates a zero knowledge proof, pi, which proves knowledge of the ID Token and commits to certain claims in the ID Token._x000D_
_x000D_
Using Google as the example OP [the format of a ID Token payload using a zkLogin nonce](https://docs.sui.io/concepts/cryptography/zklogin#notations) is:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
payload: {_x000D_
  "iss": "https://accounts.google.com",_x000D_
  "aud": "[REDACTED_GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID]",_x000D_
  "sub": "123456789010",_x000D_
  "email": "alice@acme.co",_x000D_
  "nonce": 'Base64(Poseidon_BN254(upk, max_epoch, rz)'_x000D_
  ..._x000D_
} _x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The format of the nonce is very similar to that of OpenPubkey. The main differences are:_x000D_
* The ZKP friendly hash function Poseidon_BN254 is used instead of SHA3_256. _x000D_
* An expiration time of the token is specified using max_epoch, i.e., the maximum epoch beyond which the token should not be accepted_x000D_
* The algorithm of user's public key is specified in the nonce as a [1 byte flag](https://docs.sui.io/concepts/cryptography/transaction-auth/signatures) to the user's public key upk. The public key that includes the flag in this way is called an extended public key._x000D_
_x000D_
The zkLogin proof commits to the user's [address ](https://docs.sui.io/concepts/cryptography/zklogin#address-definition) which is computed as: _x000D_
`addr = Blake2b_256(flag, iss, addr_seed)` _x000D_
where _x000D_
`addr_seed = Poseidon_BN254(claimkey, idT.[claimkey], idT.aud, Poseidon_BN254(user_salt))` _x000D_
_x000D_
If the claimkey was "email" then it would be _x000D_
`addr_seed = Poseidon_BN254(email, idT.email, idT.aud, Poseidon_BN254(user_salt))`._x000D_
_x000D_
The addr serves as a pseudonymous identity with the `user_salt` blinding the identifier. If you don't know the `user_salt`, you can't determine the email. The user knows the `user_salt`. This allows them to selectively reveal the identity claim in the ID Token. zkLogin generally assumes user's want anonymity so they don't reveal the `user_salt` and they just use the `addr` as their identity._x000D_
_x000D_
This allows users to interact in public using pseudonym, but then privately interact using their true name identifiers._x000D_
_x000D_
zkLogin assumes the following is public:_x000D_
* Iss (issuer)_x000D_
* Aud (audience)_x000D_
* Addr and Addr_Seed_x000D_
* extended public key_x000D_
_x000D_
zkLogin assumes the following is private:_x000D_
* user identity claim (email, sub)_x000D_
* user_salt_x000D_
_x000D_
## Proposed OpenPubkey zkLogin PK Format_x000D_
_x000D_
Below is a proposal for how to structure a OpenPubkey PK Token using the objects in zkLogin. This PK Token does  not reveal any identity claims about the user, sub, email are all protected._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
payload: {_x000D_
  "iss": "https://accounts.google.com",_x000D_
  "aud": "[REDACTED_GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID]",_x000D_
  "nonce": 'Base64(Poseidon_BN254(upk-ext, max_epoch, rz)'_x000D_
} _x000D_
signatures: [_x000D_
  {"protected": {"typ": "ZWT", "alg": "...", "kid": "1234...",  "addr": 'addr_seed'},_x000D_
  "signature": ZKP(idt, salt)`_x000D_
  },_x000D_
 {"protected": {"typ": "ZIC", "upk-ext": alice-pubkey, "alg": "EC256",  "rz": crypto.Rand(), max_epoch": exp, },_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(alice-signkey, (payload, signatures[1].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
* The ZWT signature enables the verification of the claims in the payload via the zkp. The allows the verification of the proof of knowledge of an ID Token with the fields supplied in the payload (iss, aud, etc..). Note that for privacy, the payload no longer contains all the fields in the original ID Token._x000D_
* The ZIC signature allows the opening of the nonce commitment, revealing the user's public key. This is very similar to your standard CIC signature._x000D_
_x000D_
We now consider the case where a user wishes expose one of their identity claims, email_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
payload: {_x000D_
  "iss": "https://accounts.google.com",_x000D_
  "aud": "[REDACTED_GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID]",_x000D_
  "nonce": 'Base64(Poseidon_BN254(upk, max_epoch, rz)'_x000D_
} _x000D_
signatures: [_x000D_
  {"protected": {"typ": "ZWT", "alg": "...", "kid": "1234...",  "addr": 'addr', "claimKey": "email" "claimValue": "alice@acme.co", "user_salt": 'user_salt'},_x000D_
  "signature": ZKP(idt, salt)`_x000D_
  },_x000D_
 {"protected": {"typ": "ZIC", "upk": alice-pubkey, "alg": "EC256",  "rz": crypto.Rand(), max_epoch": exp, },_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(alice-signkey, (payload, signatures[1].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
]_x000D_
```_x000D_
Since user_salt is revealed, we can now open the addr_seed and check claimKey and claimValue. We use email in this example but other claims can be used as well._x000D_
_x000D_
## Open Questions_x000D_
_x000D_
* Can this easily be adapted to the fields in github or gitlab? Is it even needed?_x000D_
* Can multiple claims be revealed atomically without altering ZKP used in zkLogin?

title: Proposal: Remove memguard
body_text:
I'd like to propose that we remove memguard from OpenPubkey._x000D_
_x000D_
Some background to why we added memguard can be found in the original issues #11 and #47. The PR that added it is #48. I added [a comment to that PR](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/pull/48#issuecomment-1803552330) with some thoughts which I can expand on here._x000D_
_x000D_
I think there are three issues with the implementation:_x000D_
_x000D_
## Lack of complete protection_x000D_
_x000D_
Memguard does two things for us:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Provides a function to wipe byte slices, which we can use to remove secrets from memory._x000D_
2. Provides a LockedBuffer type which prevents the contents in memory being swapped to disk._x000D_
_x000D_
I think the wiping byte slices is a reasonable idea, but the LockedBuffer is more problematic. If we need to pass the underlying bytes from a LockedBuffer to a library function (in the stdlib or a dependency) and that function copies the bytes, we lose the protection that the LockedBuffer is giving us. This kind of thing is very difficult to keep track of - any upgrade to a dependency or the stdlib could introduce some copying without us noticing unless we're auditing the code. For the stdlib this is even more difficult because the version of Go that an application using OpenPubkey is built with determines the version of the stdlib._x000D_
_x000D_
Some places where this happens are documented in #51, #52, and #53. This may not be exhaustive!_x000D_
_x000D_
I think at the end of the day, Go isn't really suited to this sort of manual memory management._x000D_
_x000D_
## Leaky abstraction_x000D_
_x000D_
The way memguard needs to be used means that the OIDC client interface needs to know about memguard, which is slightly cumbersome for implementers._x000D_
_x000D_
This isn't the end of the world, and I do think that this added complexity of the implementation could be worth it if the result was totally bulletproof, but as it doesn't fully prevent secrets being swapped etc, I don't think the juice is worth the squeeze._x000D_
_x000D_
## Issues debugging_x000D_
_x000D_
I've also ran into issues debugging the code with VS Code which I think is down to https://github.com/awnumar/memguard/issues/150._x000D_
_x000D_
# Other things to note_x000D_
_x000D_
This would be a breaking change as memguard forms part of the public-facing interface as noted above. We should make a decision on whether to do this before we release v1.0._x000D_
_x000D_
/cc @mrjoelkamp @EthanHeilman
top_3_comments_text: EthanHeilman: I think about our use of memguard LockedBuffers as consisting of two things: * LockedBuffers in the client * LockedBuffers in the GQ signature library ## LockedBuffers in the client and provider In the client and provider we used a LockedBuffer to protect the ID Token RSA signature when we are computing a GQ signature. This use of LockedBuffer in the client is not a useful as we would like it: * It adds a small but real complexity to implementing new OpenID Providers, * It is only needed for the GQ Signature setting, there is no security need for ID Tokens we don't want to transform into GQ signatures. * Since the ID Token's RSA signature is sent over the wire, lots of code handles it before it is placed in a LockedBuffer it does not provide complete protection. Github which the current OP where the LockedBuffer helps security has the ID Token read by http.Client-->json.Marshall and then is placed in the LockedBuffer. I do believe in the github setting, the LockedBuffer does provide a real improvement in security, as it makes it less likely that our code will leak the ID Token RSA signature. title: The relationship between OPs and PK Tokens
body_text:
I wanted to write up an issue on this because while we in OpenPubkey have discussed the nature of the relationship between OP (OpenID Providers) and PK Tokens there isn't much written down._x000D_
_x000D_
## PK Token Issuance/Validity and OpenID Providers/OIDC Clients_x000D_
_x000D_
One can not meaningfully ask if a PK Token is valid by itself. The question validity must always been  understood in reference to both a OpenID Provider and an OIDC Client._x000D_
_x000D_
Some examples:_x000D_
* With the Google OP,  the PK Token is only valid if the OIDC Client ID specified in the aud (audience) claim in the ID Token matches the expected value. Additionally within the context of the Google OP we must check that the CIC is committed to in the nonce claim in the ID Token. _x000D_
* Contrast this with the Github OP where there is no set aud (audience) claim to match against in the ID Token as the CIC is committed to in the nonce, but Github PK Token must be GQ signatures. _x000D_
*  The proposed Gitlab OP implementation has a set prefix in the aud claim which must match the expected value. Unlike GoogleOP or the Github OP, the CIC isn't committed to directly in the ID Token at all but committed to by the GQ Signature itself. https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/issues/100_x000D_
_x000D_
For things like zkLogin we can use the architectural existence of providers clients (OPs) provides an excellent point to transform SNARK based ID Tokens into PK Tokens. The makes expiration of the PK Token depend on the provider client implementation.  https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/issues/101_x000D_
_x000D_
## PK Token usage and OpenID Providers/OIDC Clients_x000D_
_x000D_
Beyond just validity, using a PK Token depends on the OP. _x000D_
_x000D_
* GoogleOP always has an email claim._x000D_
* AzureOP (currently not added) does not have an email claim (although it sometimes does). Instead the email can be looked up from Microsoft using the sub claim. _x000D_
* GithubOP doesn't always have an email claim._x000D_
* zkLoginOP may or may not have an email claim but to read the email, the user must reveal a value opening the email commitment._x000D_
_x000D_
The following pattern fits this relationship well:_x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
googlePkt, err := GoogleOP.Verify(pkt)_x000D_
if googlePkt.email == "alice@gmail.com" {_x000D_
..._x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
Since we know that Google PK Tokens always have email addresses, if we cast PK Tokens to the subtypes of PK Tokens based on the OP we can let have compile time type checking of PK Token claims._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Check RSA Public Key verifies RSA signature when generating GQ Signature
body_text:
Currently we don't check the RSA Public Key is correct when generating a GQ Signature. If you accidentally supply the wrong Public Key you get the hard to diagnose error message "error creating GQ signature: input overflows the modulus."_x000D_
_x000D_
Benefits:_x000D_
* We can improve error handling by just check the RSA Public Key is correct and return a more meaningful error message._x000D_
* Sometimes GQ will succeed in generating a signature for the wrong RSA Public Key. It should not, this is a bug._x000D_
_x000D_
This behavior was noticed will writing PR #122 but was the bug was not introduced in that PR_x000D_
_x000D_
## Replication_x000D_
_x000D_
95% of the time this will trigger the bug and throw the error: "input overflows the modulus"_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {_x000D_
	oidcPrivKey1, err := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)_x000D_
	require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
	oidcPrivKey2, err := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)_x000D_
	require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
	require.NotEqual(t, oidcPrivKey1, oidcPrivKey2)_x000D_
_x000D_
	idToken, err := createOIDCToken(oidcPrivKey1, "test")_x000D_
	require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
	signerVerifier, err := NewSignerVerifier(&oidcPrivKey2.PublicKey, 256)_x000D_
	require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
	gq, err := signerVerifier.SignJWT(idToken)_x000D_
	require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
	require.Nil(t, gq)_x000D_
}_x000D_
```

title: Thoughts on how to handle the OP PublicKey function on OpenIdProvider
body_text:
Currently the OpenIdProvider has the following PublicKey function: _x000D_
`PublicKey(ctx context.Context, headers jws.Headers) (crypto.PublicKey, error)`_x000D_
_x000D_
This works for now but doesn't provide the extensibility and features the project will need in the future. More specifically:_x000D_
_x000D_
The return value doesn't provide everything we need_x000D_
* It returns `crypto.PublicKey` without the full JWK. There are fields in the JWK the caller may wish to inspect. If we ever want to support non-RSA OP keys we will want the alg at minimum._x000D_
* On the return it does not provide information about where the PublicKey came from. Consider using this function with historic OP JWKS logs. You may wish to know when the JWKS was saved, is it currently on the repo? did an JWKS oracle attest to it? Etc..._x000D_
_x000D_
It takes jws.header as the single selection criteria where this header is the protected header or public header of ID Token. This is done to allow the function to look up keys by both kid and jtk. Additionally it allows PublicKey to detect that a protected header is a GQ protected header and that it needs to decode the kid to find the original header and original kid._x000D_
_x000D_
The downsides of taking a jws.header:_x000D_
* It exposes the jwx libraries jws.header object. This makes switching libraries difficult and requires that people implementing to this interface use jwx. We are slowly moving away from jwx objects being externally exposed_x000D_
* While it is extensible, you can always add keys to the jws.header, it is clear that you can or should do that. I would prefer something that makes clear exactly what fields can be used to filter PublicKeys on a provider._x000D_

title: ProviderVerifier Interface should be OpenIdProvider Interface without RequestTokens
body_text:
The current ProviderVerifier interface _x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
type ProviderVerifier interface {_x000D_
	// Returns the OpenID provider issuer as seen in ID token e.g. "https://accounts.google.com"_x000D_
	Issuer() string_x000D_
	VerifyProvider(ctx context.Context, pkt *pktoken.PKToken) error_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
and OpenIdProvider interface is:_x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
type OpenIdProvider interface {_x000D_
	RequestTokens(ctx context.Context, cic *clientinstance.Claims) ([]byte, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByKeyId(ctx context.Context, keyID string) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByJTK(ctx context.Context, jtk string) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByToken(ctx context.Context, token []byte) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	Verifier() verifier.ProviderVerifier_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Ideally ProviderVerifier is just a strict subset of OpenIdProvider such that_x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
type OpenIdProvider interface {_x000D_
	RequestTokens(ctx context.Context, cic *clientinstance.Claims) ([]byte, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByKeyId(ctx context.Context, keyID string) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByJTK(ctx context.Context, jtk string) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByToken(ctx context.Context, token []byte) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	Issuer() string_x000D_
	VerifyProvider(ctx context.Context, pkt *pktoken.PKToken) error_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
and _x000D_
```go_x000D_
type ProviderVerifier interface {_x000D_
	PublicKeyByKeyId(ctx context.Context, keyID string) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByJTK(ctx context.Context, jtk string) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	PublicKeyByToken(ctx context.Context, token []byte) (*discover.PublicKeyRecord, error)_x000D_
	Issuer() string_x000D_
	VerifyProvider(ctx context.Context, pkt *pktoken.PKToken) error_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This has two advantages:_x000D_
* It allows ProviderVerifier to share OP Public Key look ups with OpenIdProvider for better code reuse._x000D_
* Reduces the chance that issuer is sit differently in the verifier than in the provider_x000D_
* Easier to think about OpenIdProvider would just be ProviderVerifier + RequestTokens

title: ProviderVerifier and CosignerVerifier look up JWKS by pktoken issuer rather than issuer of the verifier
body_text:
ProviderVerifier and CosignerVerifier both use the issuer set in the PK Token to look up the JWKS. This is dangerous because the PK Token is untrusted._x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/733122b92f282ac5a27a730d474e44960caaee6e/verifier/providerverifier.go#L200-L208_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/733122b92f282ac5a27a730d474e44960caaee6e/verifier/cosignerverifier.go#L64-L72_x000D_
_x000D_
Instead ProviderVerifier and CosignerVerifier should check the issuer set in the ProviderVerifier and CosignerVerifier matches the PK Token and only perform the lookup if they match._x000D_
_x000D_
Security Impact_x000D_
====_x000D_
_x000D_
Verify.VerifyPKToken checks the issuer matches before calling ProviderVerifier and CosignerVerifier. This prevents this bug from having a security impact as currently used. However we should not rely on the behavior of Verify.VerifyPKToken. ProviderVerifier and CosignerVerifier should be secure if used independently.

title: Add support for CAC (Common Access Card) X.509 Cards
body_text:
## What is a CAC_x000D_
[CAC (Common Access Card) is a widely used authentication mechanism](https://www.cac.mil/common-access-card/) that includes [a user's key pair and a PKI certification attesting to the user's identity and their public key on a physical card](https://www.cac.mil/common-access-card/cac-security/). It is basically an X.509 client cert on a card.  These are also called [PIV (Personal Identity Verification) cards.](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/piv)_x000D_
_x000D_
![image](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/assets/274814/0630cc56-15bd-4776-8247-e86ebf2d4f5e)_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
## Not just for the military_x000D_
_x000D_
While typically issued to members of the US Government, especially US Military. I've been told the underlying infrastructure and devices are available to the public. For instance you can buy a CAC compatible card read [on amazon for 15 dollars](https://www.amazon.com/HID-OMNIKEY-R31210320-01-Smart-Reader/dp/B06XY2XLWF) and you buy a CAC compatible [PKI Contract ISO 7816-4 card](https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/#iso:std:iso-iec:7816:-4:ed-4:v1:en) and put your own X.509 client cert on them._x000D_
 _x000D_
## Why?_x000D_
 _x000D_
CAC and open OpenPubkey share the same security philosophy and pair well together. They both seek to bind a user's public key to a user's identity._x000D_
_x000D_
Why use OpenPubkey at all if you have a CAC? _x000D_
_x000D_
* OpenPubkey uses ephemeral keys, rotated frequently, that sign in process memory. _x000D_
* This allows very fast signatures since they can be computed outside of the a smart card, but with a very limited exposure window. Enabling the CAC to support protocols that require very frequent signing (10s to 1000s of signatures a second)._x000D_
* The use of ephemeral keys that are authorized by the CAC but not stored in the CAC, allows for wider protocol support. For instance OpenPubkey would allow the use of quantum resistant signatures for message authentication and encryption with a CAC without requiring that the CAC support these algoriths,_x000D_
* The OP attestation of identity claims in a PK Token provides additional security beyond the CAC and the CAC provides additional security beyond the OP attestation of identity claims. The security of both authentication systems is increase by joining them _x000D_
_x000D_
## Potential Uses_x000D_
_x000D_
I am still coming up to speed on CAC. These are preliminary ideas._x000D_
_x000D_
1. **CAC as Cosigner:** Use a CAC as a cosigner. Rather than reaching out to a remote cosigner, instead have a local cosigner which uses the CAC to cosign the PK Token. Any verifier capable of verifying the CAC's certificate on the PK Token, can reject PK Tokens not cosigned with a CAC identity matching the identity in the ID Token._x000D_
2. **CAC as MFA Device:** Use CAC as an MFA credential to the cosigner. For usecases were verifiers may not be able to verify the CAC, we can use the CAC as simply a second factor. A CAC is this setting is basically just a webauthn device._x000D_
3. **CAC as OP :** The CAC could be used to self-issue the ID Token, where the CAC functions as the OP. This is safe todo because the CAC is a certificate. The advantages of this approach:_x000D_
    1. **OpenPubkey as a compatibility layer for CAC:** Anything that supports OpenPubkey or JWS (JSON Web Signatures) can make use of a CAC as the secure element. _x000D_
    2. **Make CAC's privacy preserving:**  For instance as discussed in 101#, we can support zkLogin PK Tokens. This allows people to use a CAC to authenticate while only revealing the identity claims they wish to reveal. For instance: "I am older than 25" or "I am authorized to use this computer and the encryption of my identity is 0x1234..., it can be decrypted by the auditors decryption key"._x000D_
    3. **Use CAC + OpenPubkey as a cheap hardware wallet** Using a CAC to issue an ID Token and then using ZKPs to make that ID Token private would enable CACs to function as privacy preserving cheap hardware wallets on SUI, ETH or other blockchains._x000D_
4. **Smuggle PK Tokens in CAC Authentications:** CAC is [supported in some ssh clients](https://www.idmanagement.gov/implement/scl-ssh/). We should look into how we might package a PK Token into an ssh CAC auth request._x000D_
_x000D_

title: Should we change `clientinstance.Claims` to support ZKP Commitments
body_text:
In pktoken/clientinstance/claims.go we have the struct that we use for representing the CIC (Client Instance Claims). _x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
// Client Instance Claims, referred also as "cic" in the OpenPubKey paper_x000D_
type Claims struct {_x000D_
	publicKey jwk.Key_x000D_
_x000D_
	// Claims are stored in the protected header portion of JWS signature_x000D_
	protected map[string]any_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
The issue is that maps and jwk.Key representations are unordered. We rely on the fact that our JSON Marshaller alphabetically sorts maps and jwk.Keys so that the hash is the same each time. This hash is as the commitment, a.k.a., the cicHash._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
// Returns a hash of all client instance claims which includes a random value_x000D_
func (c *Claims) Hash() ([]byte, error) {_x000D_
	buf, err := json.Marshal(c.protected)_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		return nil, err_x000D_
	}_x000D_
_x000D_
	return util.B64SHA3_256(buf), nil_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This presents three problems: (1.) Incompatibilities between implementations due to map, jwk and JSON ordering, (2). string encoding incompatibilities, (3). issues supporting ZKP friendly commitments._x000D_
_x000D_
The incompatibility issues are fairly straight forward so I won't go into detail here. Let's instead look at the ZKP friendly commitments using zkLogin commitments as the example. See previous discussion on supporting zkLogin: https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/issues/101_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
## ZKP Friendly Commitments (zkLogin)_x000D_
_x000D_
zkLogin commits to the CIC using a Base64 encoding of a Poseidon hash. _x000D_
`"nonce": 'Base64(Poseidon_BN254(upk, max_epoch, rz)`_x000D_
more exactly:_x000D_
`nonce = Base64(Poseidon_BN254([bigint(upk) / 2^128,  bigint(upk) % 2^128, exp, rz]).to_bytes()[len - 20..])` where exp is the expiration and rz is the randomness._x000D_
_x000D_
Given a cic supplied to a zkLogin provider in `RequestTokens(ctx context.Context, cic *clientinstance.Claims)` and when receiving a cic from `VerifyProvider(ctx context.Context, idt []byte) (*clientinstance.Claims, error)` can we support zkLogin?_x000D_
_x000D_
**Let's work through this:** _x000D_
_x000D_
When zkLogin provider receives the CIC:_x000D_
* it extracts upk, rz  from the CIC provided_x000D_
* it can check the alg in the CIC and throw an error if the alg is not supported by the commitment scheme (zkLogin only supports one alg)_x000D_
* it can check the typ (type) in the CIC and throw an error if the typ is not unexpected_x000D_
* the exp (expiration) can be computed by the provider from the current time + expiration length set in the providers configuration (rounding zeros to avoid a privacy leak)._x000D_
* if there are additional claims in the CIC that the provider doesn't expect, the provider throws an error_x000D_
_x000D_
The provider then commits to upk, rz, exp_x000D_
_x000D_
When zkLogin provider verifies and ID Token and CIC:_x000D_
* it can check the alg in the CIC and throws an error if the alg is not supported by the commitment scheme (zkLogin only supports one alg)._x000D_
* if the exp is too old, it throws an error._x000D_
* it can check the typ (type) in the CIC and throw an error if the typ is not unexpected_x000D_
* it extracts bigint(upk), rz  from the CIC provided and then infers the exp from configuration. Using these values it reconstructs the commitment._x000D_
_x000D_
### Differences between zkLogin providers and other providers_x000D_
_x000D_
Unlike other providers, zkp providers don't commit to all the values in the CIC, instead values like alg, typ are specified in the provider configure and rejected on both generation and verification if they don't match the configured values._x000D_
_x000D_
Additionally the provider adds the exp (expiration) to the commitment, but the exp isn't specified in the CIC._x000D_
_x000D_
## Conclusion_x000D_
_x000D_
Supplying clientinstance.Claims to the provider is good enough. If we want to enforce order on CIC claims, we can add that later as a requirement to providers.

title: Compact Representation Format for PK Tokens
body_text:
This issue proposes a Compact representation for PK Tokens. The goals of such a format are:_x000D_
* Must avoid multiple base64 encodes to result minimal size, that is a compact representation,_x000D_
* Must handle including JKT of OP public key, if one exists_x000D_
* Must handle refreshed ID Tokens_x000D_
* Must not include unsigned values_x000D_
_x000D_
## Proposed Format_x000D_
Our compact representation format for PK Token:_x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
Base64(payload)+":"+Base64(OP protected)+":"+Base64(OP sig)+":"+Base64(CIC Protected)+":"+Base6464(CIC Sig)_x000D_
```_x000D_
If we wish to include a refreshed ID Token, we add it to the back using the JWT compact representation: _x000D_
```golang_x000D_
Base64(refreshed-protected)+"."+Base64(refreshed-payload)+"."+Base64(refreshed-sig)_x000D_
```_x000D_
and get (newlines added for clarity):_x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
Base64(payload)+":"_x000D_
+Base64(OP protected)+":"+Base64(OP sig)+":"_x000D_
+Base64(CIC protected)+":"+Base64(CIC sig)+"."_x000D_
+Base64(refreshed-protected)+"."+Base64(refreshed-payload)+"."+Base64(refreshed-sig)_x000D_
```_x000D_
By protected, we denote the protected header that is paired with a particular signature._x000D_
_x000D_
The order of protected header, signature pairs doesn't matter since the `typ` claim in each protected allows anyone to determine the type of protected header: is it a OP, CIC or COS protected header and signature. _x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
The above example only shows the OP and CIC protected headers and signatures, but this compact format supports an unlimited number of protected header and signature pairs._x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
Base64(payload)+":"_x000D_
+Base64(protected_1)+":"+Base64(sig_1)+":"_x000D_
+Base64(protected_2)+":"+Base64(sig_2)+":"_x000D_
+Base64(protected_3)+":"+Base64(sig_3)+":"_x000D_
// ..._x000D_
+Base64(protected_N)+":"+Base64(sig_N)+"."_x000D_
+Base64(refreshed-protected)+"."+Base64(refreshed-payload)+"."+Base64(refreshed-sig)_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
## Parsing_x000D_
_x000D_
This compact representation is intended to be easy to parse._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
compact_PKT, compact_RIDT.protected, compact_RIDT.payload, compact_RIDT.sig=Split(".", compact_PKT)_x000D_
_x000D_
parts=Split(":", compact_PKT)_x000D_
compact_PKT.payload=parts[0]_x000D_
compact_PKT.OP.protected=parts[1]_x000D_
compact_PKT.OP.sig=parts[2]_x000D_
compact_PKT.CIC.protected=parts[3]_x000D_
compact_PKT.CIC.sig=parts[4]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
## The JKT field_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently we include the jkt (JSON Key Thumbprint) field as a public header as discussed in [How do we deal with missing/non-unique kid on JWKS endpoint?](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/issues/61). Since public headers are not signed, it will not be included in the compact representation. To include it we add a new rule to the CIC construction: CIC claims that start with underscores (`_`) are not included in the CIC commitment. Thus, if a user wants to include the JKT in the Compact representation, they can do so by putting it the CIC protected header as "_jkt" and then sign it._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
  {"protected": {"upk": alice-pubkey, "alg": "EC256", "rz": crypto.Rand(), "typ": "CIC", "_jkt": "0ZcOCORZNYy-DWpqq30jZyJGHTN0d2HglBV3uiguA4I"},_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(alice-signkey, (payload, signatures[1].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_

We could easily just add the jtk to the new GQ protected header. The downside to this approach is that it only works for GQ signed PK Tokens. Maybe that is ok.

title: Should client return PK Tokens by reference or value?
body_text:
It can be confusing to reason about PK Tokens if they are passed by reference as it can change under us. Nothing really surprising here, but we should think if we want to pass by value to increase safety and make the code easier to reason able._x000D_
_x000D_
Pass by reference:_x000D_
`func (o *OpkClient) Auth(ctx context.Context, opts ...AuthOpts) (*pktoken.PKToken, error)`_x000D_
_x000D_
Pass by value_x000D_
`func (o *OpkClient) Auth(ctx context.Context, opts ...AuthOpts) (pktoken.PKToken, error)`_x000D_
_x000D_
Since some of the struct variables as also references, we would probably want to change them to pass by reference or no longer expose them and use Getters and Setters to manage them. Pass by value would be a fairly big breaking change so if we want to make it, we should make it now._x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
type PKToken struct {_x000D_
	raw []byte // the original, raw representation of the object_x000D_
_x000D_
	Payload []byte     // decoded payload_x000D_
	Op      *Signature // Provider Signature_x000D_
	Cic     *Signature // Client Signature_x000D_
	Cos     *Signature // Cosigner Signature_x000D_
_x000D_
	// We keep the tokens around as  unmarshalled values can no longer be verified_x000D_
	OpToken  []byte // Base64 encoded ID Token signed by the OP_x000D_
	CicToken []byte // Base64 encoded Token signed by the Client_x000D_
	CosToken []byte // Base64 encoded Token signed by the Cosigner_x000D_
_x000D_
	// FreshIDToken is the refreshed ID Token. It has a different payload from_x000D_
	// other tokens and must be handled separately._x000D_
	// It is only used for POP Authentication_x000D_
	FreshIDToken []byte // Base64 encoded Refreshed ID Token_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
## Feedback_x000D_
_x000D_
### Pass by value (Yea)_x000D_
_x000D_
1. "As a proponent of functional programming, I personally I favour pass-by-value for the reasons you mention. I detested hidden mutable state. IMO, it should be up to the computers to optimise things, not programmers "_x000D_
_x000D_
### Pass by value (Nay)_x000D_
1. "One downside to pass by value is that the return values cannot be nil, which might break some of the error handling and may be an odd design pattern for Go"_x000D_
2. Pass by reference but deep copy the reference, gets you everything pass by value gets you but involves minimal changes_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
## History_x000D_
I ran into this issue while writing following test._x000D_
_x000D_
This code will result in pkt1 being the same as pkt2 despite pkt1 originally not having a refreshed ID Token. This is because pkt1 and pkt2 point to the same object_x000D_
```go_x000D_
pkt1, err := c.Auth(context.Background())_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
pkt2, err := c.Refresh(context.Background())_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
pkt1Com, err := pkt1.Compact()_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
pkt2Com, err := pkt2.Compact()_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
require.NotEqual(t, string(pkt1Com), string(pkt2Com))_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
If we get the compact representation before calling refresh the test passes_x000D_
```go_x000D_
pkt1, err := c.Auth(context.Background())_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
pkt1Com, err := pkt1.Compact()_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
pkt2, err := c.Refresh(context.Background())_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
_x000D_
pkt2Com, err := pkt2.Compact()_x000D_
require.NoError(t, err)_x000D_
require.NotEqual(t, string(pkt1Com), string(pkt2Com))_x000D_
```

title: We should use algorithm from public key rather than alg from token in verification
body_text:
In the code below, we use the alg set in the ID Token to verify the ID Token. This does not present a security risk because we also check it is the expected algorithm and for GQ256 we need to do this. However we should check that public key in `pubKeyRecord.PublicKey` is RS256. _x000D_
_x000D_
```go_x000D_
	algStr := idt.GetSignature().GetProtectedClaims().Alg_x000D_
	if algStr == "" {_x000D_
		return fmt.Errorf("provider algorithm type missing")_x000D_
	}_x000D_
	alg := jwa.SignatureAlgorithm(algStr)_x000D_
	if alg != gq.GQ256 && v.options.GQOnly {_x000D_
		return fmt.Errorf("non-GQ signatures are not supported")_x000D_
	}_x000D_
_x000D_
	switch alg {_x000D_
	case gq.GQ256:_x000D_
		if err := v.verifyGQSig(ctx, idt); err != nil {_x000D_
			return fmt.Errorf("error verifying OP GQ signature on PK Token: %w", err)_x000D_
		}_x000D_
	case jwa.RS256:_x000D_
		pubKeyRecord, err := v.providerPublicKey(ctx, idToken)_x000D_
		if err != nil {_x000D_
			return fmt.Errorf("failed to get OP public key: %w", err)_x000D_
		}_x000D_
		alg := jwa.SignatureAlgorithm(algStr)_x000D_
		if _, err := jws.Verify(idToken, jws.WithKey(alg, pubKeyRecord.PublicKey)); err != nil {_x000D_
			return err_x000D_
		}_x000D_
	}_x000D_
```

title: Notes on the SSH3 plugin system
body_text:
The SSH3 authentication plugin system was introduced in https://github.com/francoismichel/ssh3/pull/135_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
SSH3 uses init to enable a plugin to register itself as an server or client side auth plugin._x000D_
_x000D_
- Client side auth plugin is how the client adds its authentication to a request_x000D_
- Server side auth plugin is how the server checks the authentication the client added (server side auth is not how the server authenticates itself to the client)_x000D_
_x000D_
## How SSH3 authenticates with ssh keys_x000D_
_x000D_
![SSH3-privkey-auth](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/assets/274814/9bec55c6-bd20-4252-b080-35686b56fb0c)_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
Should be a fairly simple to add since the existing plugin uses ssh keys. SSH3 creates a JWT called token:_x000D_
```go_x000D_
token := jwt.NewWithClaims(signingMethod, jwt.MapClaims{_x000D_
  "iss":       username,_x000D_
  "iat":       jwt.NewNumericDate(time.Now()),_x000D_
  "exp":       jwt.NewNumericDate(time.Now().Add(10 * time.Second)),_x000D_
  "sub":       "ssh3",_x000D_
  "aud":       "unused",_x000D_
  "client_id": fmt.Sprintf("ssh3-%s", username),_x000D_
  "jti":       b64ConvID,_x000D_
})_x000D_
signedString, err := token.SignedString(key)_x000D_
```_x000D_
where key is the ssh key and b64ConvID is the conversation id. They then set the JWT as the HTTP  Authorization header. As the conversation id is unpredictable and set by the server this JWT acts as a POP (Proof of Possession) of the ssh key._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
## How to add OpenPubkey as a plugin_x000D_
_x000D_
![SSH3-openpubkey-auth](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/assets/274814/d7dbbc5c-e3a1-412d-b8ef-c87bb7c3ad8b)_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
We can almost completely reuse this pattern in OpenPubkey._x000D_
_x000D_
Create JWT that includes PK Token and is signed with user's signing key._x000D_
_x000D_
The main unknown is how to determine which identity and OpenID Providers to trust. This is likely already solved in SSH3 as it supports OIDC. I just need to figure out how SSH3 does this.

title: Fulcio Attestation of Githab OP JWK
body_text:
Assume Fulcio includes the workflow-SHA1 from the Github ID Token in the x509 it generates. _x000D_
_x000D_
- This implies Fulcio checked the signature of the ID Token and that it verified against the GitHub OP JWK._x000D_
- This implies that the GitHub Action ran successfully and the workflow-SHA1 in the x509 commits to the code that ran in the GitHub Action._x000D_
_x000D_
Consider a GitHub Action which:_x000D_
1. Hardcodes the current Github OP JWKS in its code. The workflow-SHA1 must commit to the current Github OP JWKS._x000D_
2. And this GitHub Action simply checks that the GitHub OP JWKS hardcoded into it matches the GitHub OP JWKS as the JWKS URI._x000D_
_x000D_
A ID Token for such GitHub Action will only be issues by Github if the hardcoded JWKS matches the real JWKS at the JWKS URI. Thus if Fulcio issues an x509 for this ID Token, we know that the workflow-SHA1 represents a successful execution of this comparison and that we can extract the hardcoded JWKS from the workflow-SHA1._x000D_
_x000D_
Thus, Fulcio+Rekor can function as a JWKS oracle for past GitHub OP public keys.

title: OPK SSH should detect OpenSSH version
body_text:
OPK only works with `OpenSSH v. 8.1 or greater` . The OPK SSH cli should detect if it is being asked to verify on a server with versions less than 8.1 and produce a warning._x000D_
_x000D_
OpenSSH used to impose a 4096-octet limit on the string buffers available to the percent_expand function. In October 2019 as part of the 8.1 release, that limit was removed. If you exceeded this amount it would fail with `fatal: percent_expand: string too long`_x000D_
_x000D_
The OPK SSH verifier when called by by OpenSSH server using the command `./opkssh ver ...` should determine the version of OpenSSH server  calling it and then log this information to the openpubkey log using `log(fmt.Sprint("OpenPubkey SSH requires OpenSSH v. 8.1 or greater"))`_x000D_
_x000D_
The path into `./opkssh ver ...` can be found in:https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/main/examples/ssh/opkssh/cli.go#L68_x000D_
_x000D_

title: GQ library should support RSA exponents other than 2^16+1 safely
body_text:
The GQ library uses the security parameter to compute the value $t$, which is the number of challenge responses we need to make to reach the soundness needed by the security parameter. The library makes the assumption that the RSA exponent is always 1 larger than a factor of 8. This is the case when $E=65537$ since $65537=2^16+1$ so $65537-1$ is exactly two bytes. However for values like $E=3$ we only get $50.7$ bits of soundness when $256$ bits of soundness is desired.

```golang
func NewSignerVerifier(publicKey *rsa.PublicKey, securityParameter int) (SignerVerifier, error) {
	n, v, nBytes, vBytes, err := parsePublicKey(publicKey)
	t := securityParameter / (vBytes * 8)
```
https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/main/gq/gq.go#L136C2-L136C39

When $E=65537$ $vBytes=2$ and $t=16$. Since  $E=65537$ gives us $2^{16}$ soundness per challenge response, since $2^{16 \times 16} = 2^{256}$ we have $256$ soundness. However for $E=3$ $vBytes=1$ and $t=32$, but $E=3$ gives us only $3$ soundness and this is a problem because $3^{32} \approx 2^{50.71}$.

Thus currently the library is unsafe to use RSA public keys in which the exponent E is not $65537$. This shouldn't be difficult to fix. This issue is to track this bug so that we remember to fix it.

title: Document Azure email claim issue
body_text:
There used to be an issuer where azure let people specify any email in their ID Tokens. This presents an issue if we use email as an identifier and use Azure as an OPKSSH OpenID Provider.


> According to the document https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/migrate-off-email-claim-authorization?source=recommendations, mutable claims such as email in tokens can be insecure if they are mistakenly used as a unique identifier for an account. To avoid unexpected security incidents, Microsoft has changed the default to not include such claims in tokens as of June 2023. With this change, email claims are no longer included in ID tokens unless they are verified by the domain owner.
> 
> An email is considered domain owner verified if:
> 
> The domain belongs to the tenant where the user account resides and the tenant administrator has verified the domain
> The email is from a Microsoft account (MSA)
> The email is from a Google account
> The email was used to authenticate using the one-time passcode (OTP) flow


See also:
- [microsoft ID token claims reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/id-token-claims-reference)
- [Migrate away from using email claims for user identification or authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/migrate-off-email-claim-authorization?source=recommendations)
- [Secure applications and APIs by validating claims](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/claims-validation)

title: Key management improvements on the client and SSH agent support
body_text:
Right now `opkssh login` writes the extracted private key file to `~/.ssh/id_ecdsa` or `~/.ssh/id_dsa` with the comment `openpubkey` such that it can be picked up by the OpenSSH client.

You cannot rely on the `id_dsa` filename being read by the client in newer version. The `id_dsa` filename is normally used for DSA signature algorithms. The code to recognize this filename could optionally be disabled since OpenSSH 9.7p1 (2024-03-11) via https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/commit/4e838120a759d187b036036610402cbda33f3203. It was removed by default since [OpenSSH 9.8p1 (2024-07-01)](https://www.openssh.com/releasenotes.html#9.8p1), and will be completely removed "early 2025".

Key files eventually expire and are presumably specific to a specific OpenID Provider, so if you are logging into two different servers using different policies, the file will be continously overwritten by two competing `opkssh login` invocations.

Potential solutions:
- Rely on the `IdentityFile` OpenSSH client option in `~/.ssh/config` to configure a custom location of the file. Users can also use `ssh -i /path/to/private-key` to pass an extra key. While you could set the option in `/etc/ssh/ssh_config` or `/etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/*.conf` ([Debian (2020)](https://salsa.debian.org/ssh-team/openssh/-/commit/1d24b89769d822139b42c5fe1d3182db67665687), [Arch Linux (2023)](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/packaging/packages/openssh/-/commit/dd1004979e221b1d0894ec635c9848e6d433937f), etc.), that file is only in use when `~/.ssh/config` does not exist. So you might have to patch `~/.ssh/config` too.
- Add private keys to an SSH agent. Advantages:
  * SSH agent forwarding (`ssh -A`) makes it possible to SSH to a trusted server, and continue authenticating to other SSH servers. Useful if you trust the first server and want to use Git over SSH for example.
  * No private key material is written to the filesystem, so there is nothing to clean up.
  * An expiry time ensures that stale keys are automatically removed from the agent. See `ssh-add -t 86400`
  * Applications using libssh (like Wireshark's [sshdump](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/man-pages/sshdump.html)) can also use the agent.
  * Sandboxed applications using Flatpak can also [use SSH agent forwarding](https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/issues/1438) without exposing all of their private key files in `~/.ssh/` to an application.

title: Use an unprivileged user on the SSH server for opkssh verify
body_text:
In the [README](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/main/opkssh/README.md) and the [installation script](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/c28020447a4f6cdaeee96c42702fa57c305580db/opkssh/scripts/install-linux.sh#L71), you run the tool as root user. This opens up an attack vector and contradicts the recommendation "to use a dedicated user that has no other role on the host than running authorized keys commands".

It appears that the SSH server only needs:
- The ability to execute the `opkssh verify` command. Typically in `/usr/local/bin/opkssh`, it does not not belong in `/etc/` (#271)
- `opkssh verify` needs read-only access to `/etc/ssh/auth_id` and`/etc/ssh/providers`

Proposed solution:
- Create a new dedicated system user and group, `opkssh`
- Restrict file permissions such that the `opkssh` group has readonly access.
- Adjust the SSHD config to use the new `opkssh` user instead of `root`.

These instructions should be sufficient to achieve that (minus the `sshd_config` change):
```sh
useradd --system --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --no-create-home --homedir /nonexistent opkssh
install -dm755 /etc/opk
install -m640 -g opkssh /dev/null /etc/opkssh/providers
install -m640 -g opkssh /dev/null /etc/opkssh/auth_id
````

title: Document the importance of order of operations in verifying a PK Token
body_text:
To prevent enumeration attacks and reflection attacks it is very important to verify a PK Token in the following order:

(1). First check if the issuer matches an approved issuer and audience, this prevents a malicious party from putting random websites in the issuer field and tricking the verifier into making web requests to those sites. This does introduce a timing channel where an attacker could determine the allowed OP (OpenID Provider) by noticing when that the verifier fails early because the OP issuer doesn't match. However which OPs are allowed is generally considered public. For instance webapps show the approved OP on the login screen and OPs typically don't make an effort to hide this information.

(2). Second check after downloading the OP's public key, verify the signatures in the PK Token.

(3). Finally, if the signature check passes, check if the policy for the identity in the PK Token allows the request action to occur.

Consider the risk if we checked policy first. It would be obvious if the identity was allowed because of the timing difference of the signature check. If we check the signature before policy:
- The attacker must have a valid PK Token for an approved issuer and audience. This eliminates most attacks.
- The attacker does learn they don't have access for that identity, but timing channel or not, an attacker with valid credentials can always determine if policy allows an action by simply trying the action. If it fails, policy disallows it, if it succeeds, policy allows it.

title: Why is id token used instead of access token?
body_text:
## Background

I'm completely new to OpenPubkey.

I've read the following sections of [the spec](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/296.pdf):

- Abstract

- 1 Introduction

- 3 The OpenPubkey Protocol

    - 3.1 Creating a PK Token

    - 3.2 Verifying a PK Token

## Question

I may be wrong, but as far as I know, access tokens should be used to protect APIs, resources, etc. while id token should be used only client-side and should never be sent to servers. (Intuitive explanation of this may be "it is overkill to send `address` claim of id token only to access APIs, resources, etc.)

[DPoP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449), for example, adds proof-of-possession mechanism to access tokens.

Now I have a few elementary questions:

- Why does OPK try to protect id tokens instead of access tokens?

- To which parties (servers) does the spec assume PK tokens are sent? (I assumed API servers, resource servers, etc., but my assumption was incorrect in the first place?)
top_3_comments_text: your-diary: Reading [the `README.md` of this repository](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/blob/main/README.md) and [a Docker blog](https://www.docker.com/blog/signing-docker-official-images-using-openpubkey/), I think I understand the motivation of OpenPubkey. I still don't understand `Abstract` and `1 Introduction` of [the paper](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/296.pdf) though; I don't tell how the chapters of the paper are directly related to the two documents above: The abstract of the paper says > This allows OpenPubkey to upgrade OpenID Connect from Bearer Authentication to Proof-of-Possession and `1 Introduction` defines "Bearer Authentication" as > The audience checks the OP’s signature on the ID Token, then grants the user access to the account corresponding to the identity attested by the ID Token. This form of authentication is called Bearer Authentication. To me, this looks like the "protect APIs, resources, etc." usecase mentioned in the OP, and at least unrelated to public keys. --- As for the > send address claim of id token problem in the OP, `OIDC ID tokens can contain personal information` section of the Docker blog above also mentions that, but with no general solution provided. (Maybe I should understand OpenPubkey as a very practical and easy-to-adopt solution given that OIDC is already prevalent and thus, by design, not an ideal-world purpose-tailored solution?) | EthanHeilman: Thanks for these questions > I may be wrong, but as far as I know, access tokens should be used to protect APIs, resources, etc. while id token should be used only client-side and should never be sent to servers. Both Access Tokens and ID Tokens are intended to be sent to servers, APIs, resources. The traditional difference is that Access Tokens were opaque, that is, just a random string. The API would receive the Access Token need to query an API at the service that issued the Access Token to determine say the email address of the user. ID Tokens are much more simple, they contain all the information themselves, so any API that receives them doesn't need to make an additional API request. > Why does OPK try to protect id tokens instead of access tokens? OPK uses ID Token instead of Access Tokens, because ID Tokens contain email addresses and OpenPubkey has a trick for including a public key in an ID Token. title: Token validity problems with WithIssuedAtOffset
body_text:
OIDCs providing short expiration times (1m) can cause opkssh to fail the token validation as expired.

opkssh looks out for out of sync clients by skewing issuedAt validation of the received token by 1 minute using WithIssuedAtOffset. With this it makes sure that the client does not receive a token that is not valid yet.
This can have the opposite effect if the expiration time defined by the OIDC is too short (1m). The client will fail with "token expired".

The underlying problem is, that WithIssuedAtOffset does not only skew the tokens issuedAt time, but instead skews the system time the token is compared against. With this all time based checks are affected by the offset.

This behavior is part of the validation in the zitadel/oicd module.

As agreed in the Community Meeting on 2025.04.16 this could be corrected by removing/suppressing checks on iat and exp on the client side entirely.

Relates to: #294

title: redirectURI does not work with anything besides localhost
body_text:
## Description

When using `redirect_uri` in the config file with anything besides localhost causes standard_provider.go to fail.

## How to reproduce

*Disclaimer*: The only way I know how to reproduce this for now is with opkssh client. By the way, this started as a discussion in opkssh project here: https://github.com/openpubkey/opkssh/discussions/227

Create a `config.yml` configuration:

```yaml
default_provider: keycloak

providers:
  - alias: keycloak
    issuer: https://keycloak.mydomain.org/auth/realms/myrealm
    client_id: opkssh-client
    scopes: openid profile email groups
    redirect_uris:
      - http://myserver.mydomain.org/login-callback
```

Download and install latest opkssh client.

```shell
curl -L https://github.com/openpubkey/opkssh/releases/latest/download/opkssh-linux-amd64 -o ~/opkssh; chmod +x ~/opkssh
```

Run the client with the `config.yml` file.

```shell
~/opkssh login --config-path ./config.yml 
```

## Current Behavior

The client show the following error:

```log
2025/06/19 16:14:26 Error executing login command: error logging in: error requesting OIDC tokens from OpenID Provider: redirectURI must be localhost, redirectURI was myserver.mydomain.org
Error: error logging in: error requesting OIDC tokens from OpenID Provider: redirectURI must be localhost, redirectURI was  myserver.ryax.io
```

## Expected Behavior

Should accept connections on localhost but generate the login redirectURI to the correct location.

## Leads

I created a branch where I tried simply to remove the condition that checks for the correct redirectURI and made it listen on localhost, for me the problem is that redirectURI should not be the same address used to listen on. 
https://github.com/RyaxTech/openpubkey/blob/pedrovelho-patch-1/providers/utils.go#L50
