**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, cosign is not able to leverage the existing trust established by container runtime engines such as Docker or Containerd against private registries signed with an internally-trusted certificate authority. For example, although pulls might be successful from such a registry either signing or verifying will inevitably throw an error:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
$ step certificate inspect https://harbor2.zoller.com --roots /etc/docker/certs.d/harbor2.zoller.com/ca.crt --short_x000D_
X.509v3 TLS Certificate (RSA 2048) [Serial: 1583...5751]_x000D_
  Subject:     harbor2.zoller.com_x000D_
               harbor2_x000D_
               hostname_x000D_
  Issuer:      ZollerCA_x000D_
  Valid from:  2020-06-24T13:23:17Z_x000D_
          to:  2022-06-24T13:23:17Z_x000D_
_x000D_
$ docker pull harbor2.zoller.com/library/alpine:3.12.1_x000D_
3.12.1: Pulling from library/alpine_x000D_
188c0c94c7c5: Pull complete_x000D_
Digest: sha256:d7342993700f8cd7aba8496c2d0e57be0666e80b4c441925fc6f9361fa81d10e_x000D_
Status: Downloaded newer image for harbor2.zoller.com/library/alpine:3.12.1_x000D_
harbor2.zoller.com/library/alpine:3.12.1_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
$ ./cosign verify --key cosign.pub harbor2.zoller.com/library/alpine:3.12.1_x000D_
Error: Get "https://harbor2.zoller.com/v2/": x509: certificate signed by unknown authority_x000D_
main.go:48: error during command execution: Get "https://harbor2.zoller.com/v2/": x509: certificate signed by unknown authority_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
While it is possible to set the environment variable `SSL_CERT_FILE` with the path to the signing CA (as suggested in [this Slack thread](https://sigstore.slack.com/archives/C01PZKDL4DP/p1636232865192300)), this is problematic especially for external tools (ex., Kyverno) which leverage cosign as there may be no equivalent ability for this to be done._x000D_
_x000D_
If cosign is not able to leverage the trust already established by these mainstream container engines, it may be helpful if there were a flag which could be set along with a path to a CA certificate to establish this trust, for example `--ca-cert`. Alternatively, the use of the `--allow-insecure-registry` flag would need to be used which isn't ideal or the aforementioned environment variable.

title: Secrets should not be stored in the git repository
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently the secret key used to sign the binaries for a release is stored in `.github/workflows/cosign.key`. This allows a bad agent access to the key and could be used to brute force the password or attempt to recover the password through other means. Once the password is recovered any malicious binary could be replaced and the signature could be regenerated to make it appear that the malicious binary is valid. _x000D_
_x000D_
The secret key **should not be** committed to the repository. The contents of the file should created as a secret in the repository settings and then reconstituted as a file during the signing process. Once the signing process is complete the file should be destroyed to prevent the secret from remaining on any of the runner machines. _x000D_
_x000D_
Since the key has the potential of being compromised, it is necessary to generate a new key pair to use for all future releases. It would also be advisable to rebuild, resign and re-release all binaries from a reasonable point in time (I would say from the v1.0.0 release)._x000D_

title: Machine-Readable output for a few cosign subcommands
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Under certain circumstances it might make sense to provide machine-readable output for a few cosign subcommands._x000D_
It could be useful to provide information about the used certificate when verifying a blob or OCI image in JSON for further consumption._x000D_
_x000D_
I am especially thinking about the Issuer and the URI fields in the certificate. These two fields could establish some sort of trust for end users._x000D_
_x000D_
Let's assume we have a Linux package maintainer. A project X builds source tarballs with Github Actions and signs them. These source tarballs are then released on their website and on Github._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
The Linux package maintainer only checks the website, downloads a tampered source tarball and valid signature, but when checking the issuer and the URI field the Linux maintainer would know that something is wrong._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
This not real cosign output depicts the problem:_x000D_
_x000D_
Project X located at github.com/projectX/projectX creates a new tarball and signature. The related certificate has the following URI and Issuer:_x000D_
```_x000D_
URI: https://github.com/ProjectX/ProjectX/.github/workflows/goreleaser.yml@refs/tags/v0.3.1_x000D_
Issuer:  https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
Later, a malicious actor hacks into Project X's Webservice and uploads their own malicious version of the service with a valid signature:_x000D_
```_x000D_
URI: https://github.com/MaliciousActor/ProjectX/.github/workflows/goreleaser.yml@refs/tags/v0.3.1_x000D_
Issuer:  https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
The Linux maintainer could check for the URI and the Issuer and if the URI does not match https://github.com/ProjectX/ProjectX/_x000D_
the Linux maintainer would be alerted in the package build process._x000D_
_x000D_
For this feature it would be nice to have JSON readable output from cosign. I thought about something like this:_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ cosign verify-blob /tmp/PROJECTX.tar.gz --signature /tmp/PROJECTX.tar.gz.sig --format json_x000D_
```_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
    "CertificateTrusted": "True",_x000D_
    "Email": [],_x000D_
    "URI": ["https://github.com/PROJECTX/PROJECTX/.github/workflows/goreleaser.yml@refs/tags/v0.3.1"]_x000D_
    "Issuer": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",_x000D_
    "Verified": "True"_x000D_
    "TLog": {_x000D_
        "UUID": "228527476f82c59641e27b8fb9b32f5fadbe47cf42c544ea97dc798490c4c14e",_x000D_
        "Index": 853327,_x000D_
    }_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
More Information we could embed into the JSON:_x000D_
_x000D_
* Fulcio Root CA ID?_x000D_
* Rekor Instance URI?_x000D_

title: dx: revise the `--upload` and add `--output-signature` flags
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
From the [discussion we had here](https://github.com/imjasonh/kontain.me/pull/64#discussion_r749370886) with @imjasonh and @developer-guy, dropping the idea here, so we do not forget!_x000D_
_x000D_
**~--upload~ --skip-upload**_x000D_
_x000D_
We currently use the `--upload=false` [flag](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_sign.md#options) to decide whether to upload the signature, `true` by default. Since passing `true` does not change the current logic, I think it had better to rename this flag something like: `--skip-upload`._x000D_
_x000D_
**--output-signature**_x000D_
_x000D_
If we are working with the pull-through cache/mirror repositories, we probably want to skip the upload stage and export the signature to a specified file by defining an `--output-signature`._x000D_

title: `cosign download sbom` for multi-arch images
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
This came up developing: https://github.com/google/ko/pull/506_x000D_
_x000D_
Basically what we're doing in `ko` with multi-arch builds is producing an SBOM attached to each image.  However, `cosign download sbom` only does a shallow look, and reports that there are no SBOMs._x000D_
_x000D_
I think that we should first check the index, but if nothing is found (or maybe regardless) walk the child images looking for additional SBOMs.  This should be trivial to do by wrapping what we have in `walk.SignedEntity` to collect things recursively._x000D_
_x000D_

title: Keyless verification using custom OIDC scopes and claims
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
The [keyless](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/KEYLESS.md) flow currently uses the OIDC `email` claim as the Subject in the generated certificate. _x000D_
_x000D_
This is great, but does not allow writing policies like:_x000D_
- signed by a user with an `admin` role_x000D_
- signed by a member of the `code-review` group_x000D_
- etc._x000D_
_x000D_
A possible way to enable such policy checks would be to add support for [custom OIDC scopes](https://developer.okta.com/blog/2017/07/25/oidc-primer-part-1#whats-a-scope). _x000D_
_x000D_
For example, here is a possible implementation of the `sign` command:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
 cosign sign $IMAGE --oidc-scopes "groups, roles" _x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
(...not sure if `scopes` or `claims` is the appropriate term to use above.)_x000D_
_x000D_
Cosign can add the custom scopes in the OIDC request and add all returned claims as [Subject Alternative Names](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-4.2.1.6) in the certificate. _x000D_
_x000D_
The Cosign verify command can add verification support via SANs as follows:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
cosign verify $IMAGE --subjectAltName "roles:admin, groups: admin, owners"_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Higher level policies can then leverage this, to allow checks like, `reviewed by at least 2 members of the owners group`._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
Also see slack discussion at: https://sigstore.slack.com/archives/C01PZKDL4DP/p1636548948221800

title: Documenting pitfalls of registry usage in `cosign policy init` and `cosign policy sign`
body_text:
### Background_x000D_
_x000D_
`cosign policy init` allows users to define a policy around how many signatures and from whom should be considered necessary to consider an artifact as "trustworthy" -- e.g., two or more of [`alice`, `bob`, `carla`] must sign the policy before the signed thing is okay to run in prod. This policy is stored in a content-addressed blob in the registry, referenced by a manifest with a mutable tag._x000D_
_x000D_
`cosign policy sign` allows a user to add their signature to the list -- e.g., `alice` has signed the policy, and now only one of `bob` or `carla` needs to sign for the artifact to be used in prod. It does this by reading the policy config blob, adding the new signature details, and writing it back, referenced by the same original mutable tag._x000D_
_x000D_
### Problem_x000D_
_x000D_
Because the policy (who can sign, how many are needed) and the signatures (who has signed so far) are stored in the same blob in the same repository in the same registry, all of `alice`, `bob` and `carla` must have push access to the registry. Other users might have access, either because they're other contributors to the project (e.g., `dave`) or an attacker who's merely gained push access to the registry (`ernest`). In this example, even though his signature isn't necessary to meet the threshold of the policy, `dave` can run `cosign policy sign`, or even just perform registry operations to modify the policy that's referenced by the mutable tag, to add their signatures._x000D_
_x000D_
Because the policy config and the signatures are in the same object in the registry, any user that can contribute their signature can _also_ modify the policy config, either to change the set of required maintainers (now [`alice`, `bob`, `dave`]) or lower the threshold of require maintainers. This means an attacker with push access to the repo can change the policy from "two or more of [`alice`, `bob`, `carla`] must sign" to "one of [`ernest`] must sign; here's `ernest`'s signature😈 ". In theory they could also change the `threshold` to `0`, effectively disabling the policy, regardless of who's signed so far. They could also remove other maintainers' signatures._x000D_
_x000D_
Without registry push audit logs, it would be impossible to know whether this policy was changed, if those pushes aren't also published to Rekor (which presumably a malicious actor just wouldn't do)_x000D_
_x000D_
### Proposal _x000D_
_x000D_
We should document these pitfalls, and recommend some safeguards against these scenarios:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Clients verifying policies should lookup changes to the policy in Rekor, and fail if the latest version seen by Rekor is not the same as the current policy in the registry -- this guards against untracked modifications to the policy in the registry, and keeps Rekor as a transparent source of truth about the history of the policy._x000D_
2. Clients verifying policies should lookup changes to the policy in Rekor, and fail* if any change modified the policy config, and didn't just add a signature -- that is, all versions of the policy seen by Rekor have the same `signed` section._x000D_
    - *We might _want_ to let users change their policy over time -- e.g., "oh whoops I forgot `dave` should also be allowed to sign; sorry `dave`" -- how can a verifying client detect in general whether the policy edit was not malicious? Was adding `dave` malicious? 🤷 _x000D_
_x000D_
Thoughts? Is there anything else I'm missing? Where's the best place to document this?_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Messaging around key storage
body_text:
I think we should evaluate our messaging around key storage and encourage users away from questionable practises such as storing long term private keys in secrets / on disc and alike. We should instead start to pivot towards recommending folks use Keyless or a KMS, HSM etc._x000D_
_x000D_
Looking at the [github blog yesterday](https://github.blog/2021-12-06-safeguard-container-signing-capability-actions/#so-how-does-container-signing-with-github-actions-work), the first example outlined storing a private key (with no passphrase) in a SECRET. In many ways sigstore was started to address this sort of situation, and keyless was / is the killer feature to address the hazards with key management and the risks of key compromise of long term keys._x000D_
_x000D_
No fingers being pointed here, we are still a young project in the greater scheme of things,  but as keyless starts to make its first steps out of experimental, I recommend we amend documentation to carry warnings about the possible risks of storing private keys in such manner and when we can, encourage & educate developers / users onto a different and perhaps safer path._x000D_
_x000D_

title: Specify and implement on-disk "verification bundle" format
body_text:
Right now we stash a bunch of information for verifying signatures (fixed-key and keyless) in OCI images. This includes fields like:_x000D_
_x000D_
* the signature itself_x000D_
* the signed payload_x000D_
* the certificate (and chain)_x000D_
* the transparency log index/uuid/inclusion proof_x000D_
* a signed timestamp_x000D_
_x000D_
Full info is here: https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/specs/SIGNATURE_SPEC.md_x000D_
_x000D_
This works great for OCI stuff (`cosign sign`) but doesn't really work for blobs. Right now users that sign blobs have to keep track of all of these things on their own._x000D_
_x000D_
We should try to standardize a single "bundle" for all of this stuff on disk. It could be as simple as just the JSON info we stick into OCI, but there might be better options. JSON is a necessary prereq for working with OCI so relying on it there isn't a big deal, but for blobs maybe we could avoid a JSON dependency with something simpler._x000D_
_x000D_
The overall flow could be something like:_x000D_
_x000D_
`cosign sign-blob <blob> > bundle.sig`_x000D_
_x000D_
`cosign verify-blob <blob> --bundle bundle.sig`_x000D_
_x000D_
Where this would contain enough information for a keyless verification and offline transparency log lookup._x000D_
_x000D_
cc @luhring

title: The `upload` flag of `cosign initialize` is not used
body_text:
`cosign initialize` has an `upload` flag which is supposed to set a threshold of root key signers and has default value 3. Currently this value is not used in any way because we always take the root threshold of the local repo and use this number to update from the remote one._x000D_
I propose to change the name of the flag from `upload` to `threshold` and use it to override the root threshold when updating from the remote TUF repo. I believe this was the original intent of this flag.

title: Enforce image signing on AWS ECS
body_text:
We have a requirement to enforce image signing on AWS ECR. Any AWS service that tries to run a container should be prevented from doing so if the image does not pass signature verification. All of our container run on ECS. Per [the suggestion on issue 383](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/383#issuecomment-865957513), I'm trying to run a program that listens for ECS events, verifies the image signature, and kills the container if verification fails. I've been trying to prototype this on Lambda, but I've run into two problems that I believe are deal breakers for using Lambda for this:_x000D_
_x000D_
- The only way I could figure to run Cosign on Lambda was in a Docker container Lambda, which begs the question, what verifies the signature of the container that the Lambda runs?_x000D_
- I've found no way to run Docker-in-Docker on a Lambda container, meaning the Lambda can't do `docker login <ecr-repo>` and Cosign can't access the image._x000D_
_x000D_
A similar solution I thought of is to run Cosign as a Go package inside a Go lambda. That would still present the problem of how to authenticate the Lambda to ECR. I'm not sure it's possible to run Cosign as a package in Go. Even if it is, no one in the company is a Go developer, and we're not keen to maintain a lone Go function for this purpose. That said, I wouldn't reject the solution out of hand if there was one._x000D_
I'm wondering if anyone in the Cosign community has seen image signing enforced on ECS done with Cosign before, and what the architecture looked like. Mainly I'm thinking about where to run the program that will run `cosign verify`, and how it listens for events.

Tools like `kaniko` have support for writing the published digest to a file to support results in systems like Tekton._x000D_

We then also need every tool to start adding support for emitting / augmenting these files, so we'd also need kaniko, ko, buildpacks, ... to support adding emitted image digests to this file.
sudo-bmitch: > > we need the media type to avoid CVE-2021-41190. > > Really only if the manifest referenced by digest doesn't include one, which I'd wager the vast majority of images/indices (still using docker media types) do, no? For the vast majority of images, yes. I'm thinking of possible malicious intents. Perhaps a security check is run to validate the image before signing it (maybe not a vulnerability scan since those change over time, but some kind of static compliance check), and it only sees the image descriptor and checks that. The attacker then uses that signature to deploy the index with a malicious image to prod on a different registry. My thought for the OCI Layout is that it makes a nice way to pass an image between steps in a CI pipeline, only pushing to the registry near the end of the pipeline when your ready to deploy, rather than the beginning while you're still validating the result. It will probably be a while before the tooling gets to that point, but I'm pushing for baby steps in that direction (while updating my own tooling for the same reasons).

**Description**_x000D_

_(this is related to https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1232)__x000D_

Suppose I want to author policy that requires two of my five approvers to have signed attestations about a new release before it can be admitted to production.  We need something like #1232 to assess who is making the claim (for keyless, for keys who knows?)._x000D_
_x000D_

_x000D_
type Input []AttestationPayload_x000D_
_x000D_
type AttestationPayload {_x000D_
    // ID holds information about the identity that signed this claim._x000D_
    ID Identity `json:"id"`_x000D_
_x000D_
    // Claim holds the in-toto statement that the identity above is claiming to be true._x000D_
    Claim Statement `json:"claim"`_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
type Identity struct {_x000D_
    // Key holds the PEM encoded public key that was used to verify the attestation._x000D_
    // This is populated if an explicit key was provided for verification._x000D_
    Key []byte `json:"key,omitempty"`_x000D_
_x000D_
    // Fulcio holds the root URL (key?) that was used for verification_x000D_
    // This is populated for "keyless" verification._x000D_

_x000D_
    // Issuer holds the URL of the OIDC issuer that verified the signatory's identity._x000D_
    // This is populated for "keyless" verification._x000D_
    Issuer string `json:"iss,omitempty"`_x000D_
_x000D_
    // Subject holds the subject identifier that was encoded into the certificate._x000D_
    // This is populated for "keyless" verification._x000D_
    Subject string `json:"sub,omitempty"`_x000D_
_x000D_
    // TODO: encode extensions in here as well._x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_

title: Add GitLab Support for Ambient Credential Detection
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
There are some environment variables provided by GitLab to the runner environment which we can use to authenticate._x000D_
_x000D_
```shell_x000D_
_x000D_
CI_JOB_JWT: A RS256 JSON web token to authenticate with third party systems that support JWT authentication, for example HashiCorp’s Vault._x000D_
_x000D_
CI_JOB_JWT_V2: alpha: A newly formatted RS256 JSON web token to increase compatibility. Similar to CI_JOB_JWT, except the issuer (iss) claim is changed from gitlab.com to https://gitlab.com, sub has changed from job_id to a string that contains the project path, and an aud claim is added. Format is subject to change._x000D_
_x000D_
CI_JOB_TOKEN: A token to authenticate with certain API endpoints. The token is valid as long as the job is running._x000D_
```_x000D_
👉 https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/variables/predefined_variables.html _x000D_
_x000D_
cc: @dlorenc @dentrax @orhun
top_3_comments_text: dlorenc: There's some discussion over here: https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/issues/243 The tokens are currently missing an audience so we can't use them directly. It sounds like that might be in progress though! | mattmoor: Yeah, we should NOT do this before the public Fulcio supports gitlab via `--identity-token`, otherwise it'll create annoying failure modes. | marshall007: If possible, I think using `CI_JOB_TOKEN` is probably the best medium-term approach. If Fulcio is passed our `CI_JOB_TOKEN` it can make an API call to `GET <gitlab-server-url>/api/v4/job` to tretrieve the job definition for the given token. See docs: https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/api/jobs.html#get-job-tokens-job One desirable property of the `CI_JOB_TOKEN` is that we automatically revoke its access as soon as the job is terminated. Its access is also limited to API endpoints that are specifically relevant to the CI job it is created for. I understand this is still not as ideal as crafting a JWT with a specific `aud` claim, just noting that we have some other mechanisms in play that limit the replay-ability of `CI_JOB_TOKEN`s. --- I'm pushing on adding support for custom `aud` claims in `CI_JOB_JWT_V2`, but it's going to take some time as it will involve extending our CI job YAML definitions and deprecating some old behavior (both user-facing and potentially breaking changes). title: Consider one-to-one mapping of an invocation to scan result
body_text:
The recent addition of the [`COSIGN_VULN_ATTESTATION_SPEC`](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/3dd690ea18cd65adbcea2e9ae9686cbb4b2ee428/specs/COSIGN_VULN_ATTESTATION_SPEC.md) supports storing multiple scan results originating from a single invocation. I think it would be more intuitive if we encouraged folks to map a single invocation to a single scan result._x000D_
_x000D_
This would not only make it easier to construct the payload, but easier to write and evaluate policy against as well. I think we should discourage concatenating the outputs from multiple scans in a single invocation. Doing so would be inconsistent with what `invocation` is intended to represent as far as I can tell._x000D_
_x000D_
Constructing separate vulnerability attestations for different types of scanners makes it easier to write a process that evaluates one or more policies against them. For example, you would download a single, named vulnerability attestation and have some guarantee (or at least a reasonable expectation) that it will contain a result set of a particular schema._x000D_
_x000D_
Slack thread for reference: https://sigstore.slack.com/archives/C01PZKDL4DP/p1640878335099100

title: Improve TUF expiration tests
body_text:
#1270 was a short term fix to handle expired TUF metadata, but we should improve this. I think it'll take a patch in go-tuf to make it easier to test._x000D_
_x000D_
We want to verify the following configurations in cosign:_x000D_
_x000D_
* the embedded TUF metadata is expired_x000D_
* the embedded TUF metadata is not expired_x000D_
_x000D_
This requires modifying local TUF state and the clock. We could do this by dynamically generating TUF metadata with different timestamps, or by changing the local clock time to be before/after the embedded one expires. _x000D_
_x000D_
This function is exposed for "monkey-patching" in go-tuf, but it's not granular enough unfortunately: https://github.com/theupdateframework/go-tuf/blob/master/verify/verify.go#L68_x000D_
_x000D_
If we force this to be "expired", then it will **always** return true. We could use this to force our embedded roots to expire, but then it also blows up when fetching the updated ones from the remote store. I think we need to modify this to instead support patching the "time.Now()" call, which is inside of the time.Until call. Then we could jump into the future or past.

title: Log verification for expired targets
body_text:
**Overview**_x000D_
_x000D_
This is a tracking issue for supporting verification for expired/rotated targets. @asraa and I will be working on this._x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, cosign assumes the latest TUF metadata can be used to validate signatures. As the Fulcio CA certificate will expire, we will have to rotate that target at some point. This will cause cosign to not be able to validate the signatures that chain up to the expired CA certificate, since the TUF metadata will contain a different certificate. _x000D_
_x000D_
We propose bundling a pointer to the metadata used when generating the signature. We will do this by including the snapshot or timestamp JSON in the signature bundle. Cosign will use this to find versioned TUF metadata. _x000D_
_x000D_
[Design doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jIE44Fw7CVr0dLLwK9pYgNCIkzdCCeIUVuwgr0HRa8E/edit#)_x000D_
_x000D_
**Tasks**_x000D_
_x000D_
For cosign:_x000D_
_x000D_
- [x] Add current snapshot/timestamp.json to an entry’s bundle_x000D_
- [ ] Add verification by pulling the referenced versioned x.targets.json and x.root.json_x000D_
- [ ] Cache previous x.targets.json files and expired Fulcio certificates_x000D_
_x000D_
There are a few tasks for the [Sigstore TUF repo](https://github.com/sigstore/root-signing/)._x000D_
_x000D_
- [ ] Enable consistent snapshots in Sigstore root_x000D_
- [ ] Add versioned targets.json and complete list of targets to Sigstore’s TUF root (and synced to GCS bucket)_x000D_
- [ ] Generate snapshot/timestamp more frequently_x000D_
_x000D_
top_3_comments_text: asraa: Some more thoughts to make the experience of expired target verification along with BYO TUF root: - [ ] we may want to change the sigstore TUF root to pull in directories of targets rather than hard-coded target names (e.g. add all targets in a path `fulcio/**` to the trusted root pool rather than pull in a hardcoded target name `fulcio_v1.crt.pem`). this would reduce friction between any target version names and BYO TUF people | haydentherapper: A few other things we'll need to consider: * I need to update `cosign attest` to store the timestamp too, this should be a simple change. * How does this work with offline verification when you provide a locally saved bundle? We'll have to look in the cache of saved targets and fail if the target that's referenced in the timestamp is missing. * `cosign sign-blob` is a little trickier, since it only outputs a signature. Priya is working on saving a local bundle, which will include the timestamp which we can use. For online verification, maybe we provide the timestamp with the signature? Or maybe we deprecate returning only the signature and return the bundle? | haydentherapper: As I was implementing verification using the TUF timestamp, I ran into an issue. As a reminder, the verification flow is roughly: 1. Read the timestamp from an annotation on the OCI image 2. Using the timestamp, fetch the versioned snapshot 3. Using the snapshot, fetch the versioned root (N) and targets 4. Verify the root by walking the chain from 1.root.json to N.root.json 5. Verify the timestamp, snapshot and targets 6. Use the old targets to verify the OCI image The TUF spec no longer requires that the root metadata be included with the snapshot. Recently, [go-tuf](https://github.com/theupdateframework/go-tuf/pull/198) removed including root.json in the snapshot. This means step (3) is not possible, because there will be no reference to a versioned root. This leaves us a few options: * Keep generating snapshots that contain the root, ignoring the spec. I am concerned this option will cause issues in the future. * Attempt verification using all root metadata that could be valid when the signature was generated. This sounds like an overly complex solution. A bit too wide of a cast net. * Implement another solution we had proposed, storing all targets. See the [design doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jIE44Fw7CVr0dLLwK9pYgNCIkzdCCeIUVuwgr0HRa8E/edit#bookmark=id.fluccoq2av4f) for more details. To summarize, this solution is far simpler. On verification, we will simply load all targets from the target metadata. For the verification of the signature, we will load all Fulcio certs into the root pool. We will have something similar for bundle verification using the Rekor public keys. We'll keep track in custom TUF metadata of which target is active, and use that to inform users when they're verifying a signature using old targets. The main trade-off is that the targets metadata will grow over time. If we want to cap its size, we will need to decide on how long we'll keep old targets around. This can be decided later though, as we aren't frequently rotating targets. This also simplifies the revocation story. To mark a target as revoked, we simply remove it from the set of targets, which is aligned with how TUF expects revocation to occur. @asraa and I do think there's still value in tracking revocation somehow, through a TUF delegation - I have a separate doc discussing this in more detail that I'll circulate shortly. @dlorenc @bobcallaway - Y'all reviewed the original proposal, lemme know if you have any concerns with this other approach.

body_text:

title: TUF: Support option to reference mirror during verification/signing
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, `cosign initialize` is the only way to update BYO TUF metadata. If the TUF metadata is out of date on verification/signing, then cosign will fetch the updated TUF metadata from the [hosted GCS bucket](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/pkg/cosign/tuf/client.go#L61)._x000D_

One option would be to move `mirror` and `root` to global flags, so that these could be used with any `cosign` command. The TUF client would need to be refactored to look for these flags when updating TUF metadata._x000D_
_x000D_
#1288 improves UX for this issue, so that the flag values don't have to be passed with each invocation._x000D_

title: The port for the OIDC callback listener cannot be specified
body_text:
`cosign` is starting a callback listener on localhost which receives the code from the OIDC issuer. The problem is that it uses a random free port, see [here](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/blob/main/pkg/oauthflow/interactive.go#L138). So there is no way to know the exact redirect URL in advance for the OIDC dance. This is a problem because some (most?) OIDC issuers require a white list of callback URLs to be configured in advance otherwise they won't work. One example is Auth0 where I can put `http://localhost:<port>` as callback URL if I know the port number in advance._x000D_
_x000D_
So I propose adding a new command line argument (e.g. `--oidc-callback-port`) which specifies the port number of the callback listener. By default it will be 0 which means a random free port on localhost (current behavior). Let me know if this sounds reasonable and I will start working on PRs for the sigstore library and cosign.

title: Add DSSE support to verify-attestation
body_text:
## Description_x000D_
_x000D_
As described in [chains issue #329](https://github.com/tektoncd/chains/issues/329), when the signature(s) get stored as a taskrun annotation, it is represented using the [dsse envelope format](https://github.com/secure-systems-lab/dsse/blob/master/protocol.md). For example:_x000D_
_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
  "payloadType": "application/vnd.in-toto+json",_x000D_
  "payload": "",_x000D_
  "signatures": [_x000D_
    {_x000D_
      "keyid": "SHA256:kCuGI6EgqjVnVlFV8kvkUAq47XK6BiNLFC/yTZztHxk",_x000D_
      "sig": "MEQCIA4D7s3f4yHcF9Jxm0QV+m+RGV1wR+6QN+yKwl5qzSiBAiAlPAB5iKrwKOyyCZrejs/f6Ps3biuImCHcQSBJSH23uQ=="_x000D_
    }_x000D_
  ]_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently there is no way to use `cosign` to verify the payload against the signature(s). _x000D_
_x000D_
It would be nice to be able to run something like:_x000D_
_x000D_
```bash_x000D_
cosign verify-attestation --key k8s://tekton-chains/signing-secrets ./dsse-signature_x000D_
```_x000D_

Let me know if I am missing something or if there is another way. | rgreinho: More details here on what I am trying to achieve. First of all, I started by setting up tekton and chains following the tutorial we wrote here: https://github.com/thesecuresoftwarefactory/ssf/blob/main/examples/buildpacks/dual-storage-backend.md. So writing a little piece of code I got my DSSE verifier CLI. I put the code in (cosign/cmd/example/dsse.go): ```go package main import ( "crypto" "encoding/json" "fmt" "log" "os" ssldsse "github.com/secure-systems-lab/go-securesystemslib/dsse" sigs "github.com/sigstore/cosign/pkg/signature" "github.com/sigstore/cosign/pkg/types" "github.com/sigstore/sigstore/pkg/signature" "github.com/sigstore/sigstore/pkg/signature/dsse" ) func main() { // Load the public key. pubKey, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1]) if err != nil { panic(err) } verifier, err := sigs.LoadPublicKeyRaw([]byte(pubKey), crypto.SHA256) if err != nil { panic(err) } // Load the DSSE. enveloppe, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[2]) if err != nil { panic(err) } // Verify the DSSE. VerifyDSSE(verifier, []byte(enveloppe)) } func VerifyDSSE(verifier signature.Verifier, signature []byte) error { env := ssldsse.Envelope{} if err := json.Unmarshal(signature, &env); err != nil { return err } if env.PayloadType != types.IntotoPayloadType { return fmt.Errorf("invalid payloadType %s on envelope. Expected %s", env.PayloadType, types.IntotoPayloadType) } dssev, err := ssldsse.NewEnvelopeVerifier(&dsse.VerifierAdapter{SignatureVerifier: verifier}) if err != nil { return err } acceptedKeys, err := dssev.Verify(&env) for _, acceptedKey := range acceptedKeys { log.Printf("Payload verified by: %s", acceptedKey.Sig) } return err } ``` Which outputs: ``` ❯ go run cmd/example/dsse.go ./cosign.pub ./dsse.sig 2022/01/21 09:50:34 Payload verified by: {SHA256:evuxKnXdpLJ5zS0oLi/y+nBkWcJUGemMPU8CjyETres MEUCIQDBmE1ZRFjUVic1hzukesJlmMFG1JqWWhcthnhawTeBNQIga3J9/WKsNlSZaySnl8V360bc2S8dIln2/qo186EfjHA=} ``` So now, it would be great if this feature was part of cosign. If I can get some pointers, I would be more than happy to implement it. Like I said initially it would be nice to include this in the `verify-attestation` command, which currently only verifies OCI images, but if there is another command where this would make more sense, I am all ears.

I made a graphviz to try to help here: ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1714486/150449672-cb24ef38-7766-4d35-8adc-89ea75811d6a.png) Does that help? We do use ECDSA P256, with the sha256 hash algorithm by default. For the PEM-encoding, this blog post explains it a bit: https://smallstep.com/blog/everything-pki/ In short, a public key pem file is: * A public key is represented in ASN.1, and encoded into a DER bytestream * base64 encoded into a string, with some basic line wrapping * Wrapped in a header `-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----` and footer `-----END PUBLIC KEY-----` Here's an example: ``` -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- MFkwEwYHKoZIzj0CAQYIKoZIzj0DAQcDQgAEm7o4k/Hef3rGKxe0zl90u5qlidna LhtjVlqQEAlLKSFTDC1yB8uzsCJeG0S6wwCcXOTQ1T+f29FuLP0MY8Zlgg== -----END PUBLIC KEY----- ``` To decode this, you'd do the reverse process: * parse the pem "block", which strips the header and footer and base64 decodes the inner bytes. * Decode the der bytes into an asn1 object, and unmarshal that to a PKIX type. * The PKIX type contains an algorithm (ed25519, ecdsa-p256, RSA, etc.) and the raw public key bytes which can be used for verification. Does that help?

title: Azure Container Registry authentication
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Hi!_x000D_
_x000D_
As always, thank you for the great work you are doing with cosign and sigstore. :1st_place_medal: _x000D_
_x000D_
There seems to be a bug with how cosign authenticates with Azure Container Registry:_x000D_
```shell_x000D_
./cosign verify --k8s-keychain --key azurekms://sigstore.vault.azure.net/sigstore myregistry.azurecr.io/mycontainer:dev_x000D_
ERRO[0000] Error parsing the serverURL                   error="docker-credential-ecr-login can only be used with Amazon Elastic Container Registry." serverURL=acrlabscsg.azurecr.io/aad-oidc-identity_x000D_
Error: GET https://myregistry.azurecr.io/oauth2/token?scope=repository%3Amycontainer%3Apull&service=myregistry.azurecr.io: UNAUTHORIZED: authentication required, visit https://aka.ms/acr/authorization for more information._x000D_
main.go:46: error during command execution: GET https://myregistry.azurecr.io/oauth2/token?scope=repository%3Amycontainer%3Apull&service=myregistry.azurecr.io: UNAUTHORIZED: authentication required, visit https://aka.ms/acr/authorization for more information._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
After spending some time troubleshooting this, it seems to be related to two bugs in upstream packages. These are packages used by `go-containerregistry`. I'll document it here but we'll most likely need to fix the bugs upstream to get it working correctly with cosign._x000D_
_x000D_
**Bug 1**_x000D_
The authentication helper for Azure Container Registry doesn't parse the URL correctly, meaning it's not stripping the path and query from the URL that it receives and then tries to issue a token using it which will fail._x000D_
_x000D_
Reference for the method: https://github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env/blob/fe33c00cee21eacc9fc67b6492b2c0cbe08b8bbe/pkg/credhelper/helper.go#L67_x000D_
_x000D_
If we look at the same Elastic Container Registry (AWS) helper, we can clearly see them extracting information before passing it to their other functions: https://github.com/awslabs/amazon-ecr-credential-helper/blob/69c85dc22db6511932bbf119e1a0cc5c90c69a7f/ecr-login/ecr.go#L46_x000D_
_x000D_
Issue: https://github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env/issues/3_x000D_
PR: https://github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env/pull/4_x000D_
_x000D_
**Bug 2**_x000D_
The helper wrapper being used for Azure Container Registry in `go-containerregistry` is returning a username and password, where the username is `<token>`._x000D_
_x000D_
If we read the comment in their code, it says that OAuth will be used if username is set to `<token>` - but this only applies if we have an `IdentityToken` instead of a `Password` which is what the helper wrapper returns._x000D_
_x000D_
We can clearly see when using ACR locally it's using IdentityToken: (~/.docker/config.json)_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
        "auths": {_x000D_
                "myregistry.azurecr.io": {_x000D_
                        "auth": "MDAwMDAwMDAtMDAwMC0wMDAwLTAwMDAtMDAwMDAwMDAwMDAwOg==",_x000D_
                        "identitytoken": "eyI...In0"_x000D_
                }_x000D_
        }_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
I'm not sure what the best solution here is, I've tested with using my own helper wrapper that returns IdentityToken instead of password and it works as expected._x000D_
_x000D_
Reference for the IdentityToken check: https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/blob/86ab60664adc985dec1a8ab30af5cddf3c610db3/pkg/v1/remote/transport/bearer.go#L138-L142_x000D_
_x000D_
Reference for the helper wrapper not setting IdentityToken: https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/blob/86ab60664adc985dec1a8ab30af5cddf3c610db3/pkg/authn/keychain.go#L161_x000D_
_x000D_
Issue: https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/issues/1255_x000D_
PR: https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/pull/1256_x000D_
_x000D_
**Next steps**_x000D_
_x000D_
I'm mainly creating this issue here to make sure others testing cosign can see it and to gather my thoughts after digging deep into this rabbit hole. If anyone sees any clear signs of insanity from my side, please point it out and tell me where I'm screwing up. :100: _x000D_
_x000D_
I'll be creating issues and PRs in the other repositories and linking them here.

title: VAULT KMS signing and verification broken after rotating a key in vault
body_text:
The Vault transit engine has a fundamental feature for rotating keys (https://www.vaultproject.io/docs/secrets/transit), therefore each digest returned from vault has a prefix identifying the version of the used key. For example **vault:v3:XXXXXXX** links version 3 of the key. The version of course is important for the verification._x000D_
_x000D_
Detailed analysis:_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/blob/245ddc285f5a25d3b2e1e87dd5f19b0bf7e942f3/pkg/signature/kms/hashivault/client.go_x000D_
_x000D_
> func vaultDecode(data interface{}) ([]byte, error) _x000D_
_x000D_
removes the "vault:vN" prefix from the digest and _x000D_
_x000D_
> func (h hashivaultClient) verify(sig, digest []byte, alg crypto.Hash) error _x000D_
_x000D_
Adds a predefined prefix to the secret. _x000D_
_x000D_
Possible solution: _x000D_
Do not remove and add the prefix again, simply store the whole secret returned from vault.

Right now the default behavior of Cosign is to sign using the latest key and always validate using version 1, even if that version is no longer valid in Vault. Leaving aside the above discussion for a minute, my "bandaid" suggestion would be that if the key version hasn't been overridden anywhere, cosign attempts to [query the key details from Vault](https://www.vaultproject.io/api-docs/secret/transit#read-key). This would return the range of valid keys, and it could try all of them in order. Return early on the first success, otherwise return a failure. This requires that the VAULT_TOKEN grants access to read the key details, but I don't think that's entirely unreasonable. I have a related suggestion about improving how Connoisseur authenticates to Vault to keep a token current, but I think that probably belongs in a separate issue

So when you use Cosign, the signature would mention which version of the key was used to sign. I strongly prefer (2), but I can see the argument for (1), especially because it might be a while before (2) is ready. I would be willing to merge a PR to do (1). My steps for reproducing the issue are as follows: ```shell # start vault server in separate shell vault server -dev -dev-root-token-id root -dev-listen-address 0.0.0.0:8200 # login to vault and enable transit export VAULT_ADDR='http://0.0.0.0:8200' export VAULT_TOKEN=root vault secrets enable transit # create the transit key cosign generate-key-pair --kms hashivault://cosign-keys vault read transit/keys/cosign-keys # create a blob cat >blob.txt <<EOF Some random stuff. title: Improve the way PKCE is determined/disable check

**Description**_x000D_

I would like to use `cosign` in `keyless mode` with a custom token issuer - i.e Azure_x000D_

_x000D_
I understand that PKCE is recommended and will be enforced in oauth 2.1 but i see this being an issue with multiple Identities and was wondering if we could either provide a flag to disable the PKCE check? Open to other ideas and discussions._x000D_

**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
For example, conftest has the ability to share Rego policies[^1] over OCI registries which means that users can pull or push rego policies to OCI registries, which we can do the same for CUE basically. ```shell_x000D_
cosign verify-attestation -policy devopps/cue-policies:latest $image_x000D_
_x000D_
cosign verify-attestation -policy devopps/opa-policies:latest $image_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
[^1]: https://www.conftest.dev/sharing/_x000D_

luhring: >ideas welcome! Here's one idea for what a flow might look like for the MVP. The user copies a command from a project README and runs it. ``` console $ sget https://my.site/install.sh | sh ``` ### Here's what sget does #### 1. Retrieve the HTTP resource `sget` acts as an HTTP client to download the resource (and follows a normal TLS validation process when using HTTPS, just like `curl` does). #### 2. Verify retrieved bytes Before sending any bytes to stdout, we verify the bytes we just retrieved. To do this, we: 1. Calculate the digest of the bytes we downloaded. 2. Search Rekor _by digest_ for matching signature records. 3. The bytes are considered valid if one or more signatures matched in Rekor can be verified given who the user trusts (more on this in a bit). #### 3. Output verified bytes Send the entire payload to stdout, such that the user can pipe those bytes to a command like `sh` as needed. ### Who does the user trust? IMHO, this is the hardest and most important piece of the user experience. I don't fully understand the TUF-like system that was proposed earlier, and I don't think we should expose something like TUF to users under normal circumstances (if ever), but I do like the idea of using OIDC IDs (e.g. `dan.luhring@anchore.com`) as a way for the user to specify trusted identities. I'm wondering if we need some kind of local state on the user's machine that specifies the identities that the user trusts. I'm not sure what/who these identities should be, and how they should be represented. Maybe we can prompt the user for trusting new identities as we encounter them (e.g. exit non-zero, with an error message like "You don't trust the signer; if you want to start trusting them, run command X."). If we're going for mass adoption, I think we should avoid anything too esoteric or difficult to use. ### Benefits of this approach There's very little work for project maintainers to do: sign your artifact (e.g. shell script), such that the signature is sent to Rekor. No other HTTP resources besides the artifact (e.g. shell script) need to exist on the remote server. And there's even less for the user to do: just run `sget`. After the MVP, we can add more configurability to how verification works.

I think there's still some questions to sort out, but I think that's roughly along the lines of something we'd need for this to work for arbitrary URLs, especially when the maintainers might not have done anything to enable better assurances for `sget` users specifically. > I'm wondering if we need some kind of local state on the user's machine that specifies the identities that the user trusts. This seems unavoidable, basically. Do we need some separation of globally trusted identities and per-site trusted identities? I might trust anything Luke has signed, but might only trust something Dan signs in the context of Dan's site. Or is trust a globally binary state? I'm not sure. In the absence of trusted identities, can we show a warning like "NNN users have marked this as trustworthy, here are a handful of them: `a@foo.com`, `b@bar.com`, etc." -- this would tell us that the file has already been widely fetched and marked as okay, by users willing to attach their username to it. It's still spammable by bad actors, but sampling those can help prevent that, if all the sampled identities seem sketchy or share a spammy domain. Both of these require some flow for prompting users to note their trust of the artifact, which might also be challenging. Once you `sget | sh`, how can we prompt the user to tell us that they should put their username into Rekor to vouch for the artifact? `sget` could block, show the fetched contents, and prompt for an approval before piping to stdout, but that's a bit of a speedbump if you just want to get to the `| sh` part. And it won't work for all in a headless CI mode. > There's very little work for project maintainers to do: sign your artifact (e.g. shell script), such that the signature is sent to Rekor. No other HTTP resources besides the artifact (e.g. shell script) need to exist on the remote server. I think nailing this will be crucial to adoption, especially early on while `sget` has not established its value to consumers or maintainers. Once folks are getting value from `sget` with no effort on the part of the maintainers, it's easier to convince them that it's worth adding their signatures and policies to make it even more valuable.
luhring: I've been thinking a lot about Jason's comment above. This trust thing is a fascinating problem! >Do we need some separation of globally trusted identities and per-site trusted identities? I might trust anything Luke has signed, but might only trust something Dan signs in the context of Dan's site. I definitely see value in this distinction (it reminds me vaguely of SSH config: "here are my trust settings for _any_ host, here are my settings for _host X_, etc."). I think something like this would be good to include. I'm wondering if it should be in the MVP or not. >In the absence of trusted identities, can we show a warning like "NNN users have marked this as trustworthy, here are a handful of them: a@foo.com, b@bar.com, etc." -- this would tell us that the file has already been widely fetched and marked as okay, by users willing to attach their username to it. I love this! ❤️ It adds a social component to the world of OSS software installation. It reminds me a bit of GitHub stars. "Oh, I see _Dan Lorenc_ trusts this thing? Okay yeah, I'm willing to trust it, too." **Tangent:** It might be neat to have a web UI to showcase this, maybe sourcing data from Rekor, to make things more grokkable for the average user. I'm envisioning a way to browse signed things (e.g. scripts) (indexed by digest and/or content URL). And for each thing, you can see how many identities have signed it, and for each identity, some context about who they are (thanks to OIDC). Maybe you can also see each person's list of things they trust. If I'm getting too web-of-trust-y, call me out! 😃 --- I think it would be helpful if, when `sget`-retrievable things are **signed**, the URL gets included in the signature payload (maybe as an annotation?). This could help the user verify that the resource author intended for a given resource to be what's provided by a **specific URL**. For example, without this in place, the following would be possible: - `sget https://my.site/v1/install.sh` -> bytes for v1's script -> signed by the correct identity -> valid (this is expected ✅ ) - `sget https://my.site/v2/install.sh` -> bytes for v1's script -> signed by the correct identity -> valid (oh no! 😱 ) (In other words, this could help prevent "rollback" and "indefinite freeze" attacks [described on the TUF site](https://theupdateframework.io/security/).) If the signature payload included the intended URL, `sget` could further verify that the provided URL matches the URL `sget` was given by the user. Also, users may want `sget` to have the option to explicitly skip this additional validation. Perhaps the user **_knows_** that they're fetching content from a mirror/proxy/etc., and they wouldn't expect the URL to be known at time of signing, so they're willing to accept losing this validation. --- Another thought, for later on: I've been thinking about the ["requirements"](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/technotes/tn2206/_index.html#//apple_ref/doc/uid/DTS40007919-CH1-TNTAG4) concept in Apple's code signing system. This might relate to the claims/annotations feature in Cosign (although I'm still learning about this feature). This is a way for the software publisher to specify additional constraints for the verifying client to check, in addition to the raw signature being verified successfully. These "requirements" can be things like "the root cert should be Apple's root CA", or "the signing cert should be _X_", etc. Down the road, I could see these making sense as optional flags to `sget`, especially since `sget` commands are probably just copy-and-pasted 99% of the time. For example, a project's README.md might show this command: ``` $ sget https://my.site/install.sh --required-signer="jason@hall.com,dan@lorenc.com,luke@hinds.com" | sh ``` This would serve to narrow the scope of what signatures are considered valid. If `sget` determines the signature is otherwise valid, but none of the signers listed in the command are the identity attached to the signature, validation would fail. This wouldn't protect against attacks on the README content. But it might be a nice, simple mechanism for "trusting the right thing for this particular installation". The other advantage is that it could provide a secure approach to a **stateless user environment**, provided the `sget` client _does_ trust whatever root CA was used for the signatures (e.g. Fulcio).
dlorenc: > First, come up with a plan that answers the questions: > > * what language should `sget-new` be written in? (Rust vs Go, or something else) > > * _why_ is that language the right choice, practically speaking? > * what does `sget-new` need to do to be considered ready for release into the wild? > > * not "fully functional", just MVP > * it needs to do _something_ more than just fetch, we have `curl` for that today > * who wants to work on this, and where? sigstore/sget exists, modulo language question above. These sound like a good set of questions to answer tomorrow in the call. I'll suggest we do it in a bit different of an order: * Who is going to use `sget-new`, and what are they going to use it for? * What are the commands/flags/surface the tool should have to support that? * What are the different ways it should support fetching contents? Just one system/protocol, or should we support as many as possible? * How will trust/key management be handled? NOTE: This one is really hard so instead I'd suggest that we just reuse cosign's approach: fixed keys, keyless signatures with an identity, or full, custom TUF pinned back up to the sigstore TUF root. We can hand-wave this for now and figure it out later, without designing a new way to define and establish trust. Then: - Who wants to work on this, and what is the best language/repo for it to live in?
lukehinds: I really recommend that before delving into questions such as how will the UX play out, what language, flags etc, we first define and outline what is the current and projected scope of sget-go. Otherwise you risk misunderstandings coming up later on.

title: Improve handling of tlog interaction when `--upload=false`
body_text:
Currently, when `COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1` is set, content is always published to rekor. However, when `--upload=false`, it should be possible to not only support storing image signatures and certificates locally, but the necessary details to avoid needing to communicate with rekor._x000D_
_x000D_
## Assumptions:_x000D_
* `COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1` set_x000D_
_x000D_
## Discussion:_x000D_
* Support is needed to avoid uploading to tlog when `--upload=false` is set_x000D_
* Verification always assumes that content is stored in the tlog. Verification will fail if content is not available._x000D_
* `sign-blob` contains the functionality to store a bundle to disk through the `--bundle` flag. Feature should also be implemented in `sign`. When verifying, bundle can either be provided from disk or from rekor to avoid communication if needed_x000D_

title: cosign attest --replace fails to create attestations on random.Image() generated images
body_text:
While implementing the unit test for #1366, I discovered that `cosign attest --replace` silently fails to create any attestations on images created by [go-containerregistry's `random.Image()`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/google/go-containerregistry/pkg/v1/random#Image). That PR added a failing `TestAttestationReplace()` test which is currently skipped because the replace option doesn't create any attestations._x000D_
_x000D_
This can be reproduced outside the unit tests like this (using the v1.5.0 release binary):_x000D_
```bash_x000D_
>random.go <<EOF_x000D_
package main_x000D_
_x000D_
import (_x000D_
	"context"_x000D_
	"log"_x000D_
_x000D_
	"github.com/google/go-containerregistry/pkg/authn"_x000D_
	"github.com/google/go-containerregistry/pkg/name"_x000D_
	"github.com/google/go-containerregistry/pkg/v1/random"_x000D_
	"github.com/google/go-containerregistry/pkg/v1/remote"_x000D_
)_x000D_
_x000D_
func main() {_x000D_
	n := "localhost:5000/x/y"_x000D_
_x000D_
	ref, err := name.ParseReference(n, name.WeakValidation)_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		log.Fatal(err)_x000D_
	}_x000D_
	img, err := random.Image(512, 5)_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		log.Fatal(err)_x000D_
	}_x000D_
_x000D_
	regClientOpts := registryClientOpts(context.Background())_x000D_
_x000D_
	if err := remote.Write(ref, img, regClientOpts...); err != nil {_x000D_
		log.Fatal(err)_x000D_
	}_x000D_
}_x000D_
_x000D_
func registryClientOpts(ctx context.Context) []remote.Option {_x000D_
	return []remote.Option{_x000D_
		remote.WithAuthFromKeychain(authn.DefaultKeychain),_x000D_
		remote.WithContext(ctx),_x000D_
	}_x000D_
}_x000D_
EOF_x000D_
# Create an image localhost:5000/x/y using random.Image()_x000D_
go run random.go_x000D_
# The --replace option silently fails to create any attestations on images created by random.Image()_x000D_
cosign attest --replace --predicate predicate.json localhost:5000/x/y --key cosign.key_x000D_
# The following command shows no attestations exist_x000D_
cosign download attestation "localhost:5000/x/y"_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The `cosign attest --replace` option works fine on other images. I tested using images copied from Docker Hub using skopeo, and was able to create and replace attestations.

title: Clarifying questions re: cosign vulnerability attestation spec
body_text:
Hi! I saw @developer-guy open https://github.com/anchore/grype/issues/614. I think vulnerability scan attestations are a great idea, and I've been catching up on what exists already via these places so far:_x000D_
_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/specs/COSIGN_VULN_ATTESTATION_SPEC.md_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/442_x000D_
- https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/58_x000D_
_x000D_
Before starting to apply this spec in a real implementation, I have a few questions that would help me better understanding how to use it._x000D_
_x000D_
(ALSO: I should apologize for _just now_ asking these questions and not weighing in earlier in the issue and PR discussions. Sorry about that! 🙇 )_x000D_
_x000D_
1. The `invocation` object is shown in the spec but its fields aren't documented below like the other parts of the spec. I don't understand the role that `invocation` is intended to play in vuln scanning workflows. I believe @dlorenc [suggested](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/58#issuecomment-896218417) that we drop this object. Can it be removed from the spec? And if not, could we document the intent of this data in the spec?_x000D_
_x000D_
2. I was following the conversation [here](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/58#issuecomment-904600218), and it looks like there's an intention to use the statement's `predicateType` field to specify not only this Cosign spec but also the type of the "wrapped" data that goes into the `result` object. Is that true? If so, could the spec example be updated to show how this relationship should work? (i.e. can we include a bit more of the in-toto statement than just the predicate itself?)_x000D_
_x000D_
3. It looks like this specification features Trivy consistently throughout the document. (And it looks like the example attestation isn't using a wrapped _standard_, it's using Trivy's own JSON format.) Is this intentional?_x000D_
_x000D_
4. Is `result` the right name for a field that wraps an entire scan output from another spec? I'm thinking this term might be overloaded. Those specs tend to include data that's a **superset** of "results", and then `result` tends to be an actual field _within_ the specification (i.e. to specify the vulnerability _matches_)._x000D_
_x000D_
5. The data contained in `scanner` seems to always be included in other specifications (e.g. see [SARIF](https://github.com/oasis-tcs/sarif-spec/blob/master/Documents/CommitteeSpecifications/2.1.0/sarif-schema-2.1.0.json#L2897-L2923), [CycloneDX](https://github.com/CycloneDX/specification/blob/1.4/schema/bom-1.4.schema.json#L166-L202)). Is this redundant?_x000D_
_x000D_
6. The `metadata` section shows the start and finish times for the scan. Two thoughts on this: a) this tends to be provided in the vulnerability standard spec (e.g. see [SARIF](https://github.com/oasis-tcs/sarif-spec/blob/master/Documents/CommitteeSpecifications/2.1.0/sarif-schema-2.1.0.json#L1138-L1148), [CycloneDX](https://github.com/CycloneDX/specification/blob/1.4/schema/bom-1.4.schema.json#L116-L121)), and b) (which may be moot), usually the time of the scan is relatively less important than other time-based factors. What matters most in a vulnerability scan are the inputs that are required to reproduce the same results: the vulnerability dataset, the list of discovered software (ideally an SBOM), and the scan tool itself. It can be misleading to promote "scan time" (especially when coupled with a "finish time") to consumers making a policy decision, because a later scan run doesn't necessarily imply that the scan was done in light of more recent vulnerability data, as some would assume._x000D_
_x000D_
Thanks for the help!

But here is an example: > > ```json > "predicateType": "https://sigstore.dev/v1/VulnerabilityScanResult+sarif" > "predicateType": "https://sigstore.dev/v1/VulnerabilityScanResult+json" > ``` +1 to documenting how to use this field for wrapping vulnerability scan data in this particular attestation spec. 👏 But the examples of `...+sarif` and `...+json` don't quite clear it up for me. From what I understand, all in-toto predicate data should ideally be JSON, and so we shouldn't need to specify "JSON" in `predicateType` URIs. Addressing this would also obviate my next question, which is "what data structure is actually described by `"https://sigstore.dev/v1/VulnerabilityScanResult+json"`?". ## Demonstrating the spec w/ a Trivy-specific format (question 3) >The only real "standard" we saw around this was SARIF, which isn't widely supported enough for me to feel comfortable requiring. I think it's important that we use an open standard for the wrapped data format for this spec (i.e. not a format specific to a single vulnerability scanning tool). I'd suggest using either SARIF or CycloneDX for the examples in this spec. If neither of these meet the requirements for an open standard, let's follow up so I can understand the reqs a bit better! ## Naming the field for scanner output (question 4) >>Is result the right name for a field that wraps an entire scan output from another spec? I'm thinking this term might be overloaded. Those specs tend to include data that's a superset of "results", and then result tends to be an actual field within the specification (i.e. to specify the vulnerability matches). > > Naming is hard! Any other suggestions? I'm not picky :) Agreed 😄 If this field is contextualized by its parent field `scanner`, maybe something like "output", resulting in `.scanner.output`? This name is unlikely to be used in the spec that the scanner is outputting. >Since result is an arbitrary `interface{}` type, i'm not sure how results fits in this case, it sounds like list of interfaces `[]interface{}` to me. I don't think we should make this field have a slice type. I think we leave it as a completely arbitrary type, which can be strongly inferred using the "wrapped type" described in `predicateType`. ## Redundancy of `scanner` section (question 5) > >The data contained in scanner seems to always be included in other specifications (e.g. see [SARIF](https://github.com/oasis-tcs/sarif-spec/blob/master/Documents/CommitteeSpecifications/2.1.0/sarif-schema-2.1.0.json#L2897-L2923), [CycloneDX](https://github.com/CycloneDX/specification/blob/1.4/schema/bom-1.4.schema.json#L166-L202)). Is this redundant? > > I kind of like having this at the top level since it would make it easier to write policy against consistently, without needing to know where to look in different places. But I'm not too opinionated here. After thinking about this more I agree, @dlorenc. I like the idea of policy (and queries) for attestations being achievable for certain situations without needing to delve into the wrapped data. The `db` section might be an exception to this, since these data values seem to require an understanding of the underlying tool — but certainly up for discussion. ## The `metadata` section (question 6) > >What matters most in a vulnerability scan are the inputs that are required to reproduce the same results: the vulnerability dataset, the list of discovered software (ideally an SBOM), and the scan tool itself. It can be misleading to promote "scan time" (especially when coupled with a "finish time") to consumers making a policy decision, because a later scan run doesn't necessarily imply that the scan was done in light of more recent vulnerability data, as some would assume. > > Strongly agree with you. We thought that times might be useful for some tracing and estimating scan durations. It would be great to extend and add some more important fields in metadata spec. What kind of information would be much useful to see in this case? Any spec model you want to propose? Why is it important for consumers of this data to trace and estimate scan duration? What impact would this have on downstream policy? Re: adding more fields, I'd lean toward @dlorenc's thinking on **question 5**. If we want to have a section of this spec specifically motivated by high-level policy evaluation outside of the wrapped scan data, perhaps we just have one section for this (not two: `scanner` and `metadata`). I could see a case for "scan time" being one of the fields, but like I mention above, we'd need to be careful when describing the intended use of this field. If we're considering more fields to pull out from existing vulnerability scan specifications, I'd suggestion perusing the SARIF and CycloneDX vulnerability scan specs. ## Overall thinking A recurring suggestion I saw in https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/58 that I never saw applied was to map out a realistic story of how consumers might use these vulnerability attestations in a real security workflow. I think if we did this, that'd really help to motivate which fields are generally useful and which ones aren't needed after all. Thanks for everyone's thoughts so far! I'm looking forward to the end state of this discussion. ❤️
jessesanford: I am interested in if the predicateType field was ever overloaded to include wrapped type? It looks like it was agreed that using the "+" syntax was not necessary and that "/" would be used instead here: https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/58#issuecomment-904600218 however in the above comment by @Dentrax https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1381#issuecomment-1055459832 "+" is mentioned again. Also the current version of the spec no wrapped type is mentioned in the predicate type URI at all: "cosign.sigstore.dev/attestation/vuln/v1" https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/specs/COSIGN_VULN_ATTESTATION_SPEC.md Is this decision still in flight?

title: Plan for Reference Types Work!
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
The reference types work is off and running now in OCI, and we should start to think through how we'll adopt it here in cosign._x000D_
_x000D_
Assuming the work completes, gets adopted by registries, and meets all the use cases required by cosign, we still have a few choices to make!_x000D_
_x000D_
* When do we add support, and how? Do we need to wait for all registries to support it, or can we do a transition with a fallback option?_x000D_
* How would a fallback work? Could we always check the new location and fall back to the old one? Should we always check both?_x000D_
* How about writes? Always push to the new location first, then fallback to the old one?_x000D_
* Should we just make it a config option?_x000D_
_x000D_
I think as soon as there's a workable draft spec merged in https://github.com/opencontainers/wg-reference-types, we should create a dev branch here in cosign to let people try it out, without us needing to answer the fallback questions right away. Maybe a "cosign-oci-ref" build or something that only works with the new APIs._x000D_
_x000D_
We could also publish and run a ttl.sh-like ephemeral registry that supports the new API as it gets developed, to let people try it out against a real endpoint without requiring them to run something locally.

title: Can URL output by sign-blob be public?
body_text:
If one were to run the following setup via pubic CI, would that pose a security risk? Would it be bad if anyone could see the OAuth URL?_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/FUN.md#level-11
top_3_comments_text: dlorenc: cc @bobcallaway | bobcallaway: In general, I don't think it poses a security risk (but would opt to hide it by default): (a) it is unlikely that this would even work because it would require you to fully automate the browser (and subsequent HTTP traffic) within the CI process to complete the OAuth2 dance to get the ID token (b) only other processes on the same CI runner would have access to post to the loopback address where the `redirect_uri` is pointed, so even if someone did read the value of `state` they wouldn't be able to replay it without having access to the runner (c) in addition, the `code_challenge` value is held in memory of the `cosign` process and if you can reverse a SHA256 hash to a value then we have bigger problems in the industry :/ So net: I think its a good question but I personally don't believe it poses a risk.

title: Return multiple rekor entries if looked up during verify-blob
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
In verify-blob with the transparency log enabled, we'll attempt to look up an entry in the log using the search API. This will return the latest signature/cert found for a blob, which may not be the one the user actually is looking for. We should consider improving this UX if multiple entries are found. The relevant codepath is here:_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/78fb2dc6bcf078fbff5ec14ce5a3a7d5f7c789b6/pkg/cosign/tlog.go#L183_x000D_
_x000D_
In general we'll also need to better explain the guarantees of the search API. The results returned from it are generally considered "best-effort" and are not guaranteed to be comprehensive. Every result in that API is valid - but the API does not necessarily return every result.
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: This *behavior* was fixed in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1673 . We could still explain better what's going on; I'll send a quick PR for that. | znewman01: Oh actually https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1673 *does* add a message clarifying the guarantees. It does so *only* when relevant: that is, the search API *didn't* find a corresponding signature. This can be closed.

title: enhance reproducibility by passing additional ldflags
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
According to the talk on the [Slack](https://sigstore.slack.com/archives/C01D0PA9QKF/p1644605730298959) channel, thanks to @Foxboron:_x000D_
_x000D_
> Generally speaking; go and build flags is a rabbit hole since Go is unable to parse cli flags and env flags correctly. There is also a difference between hardening flags (PIE and RELRO) and reproducible builds flags. Setting trimpath and unsetting buildid is enough._x000D_
> https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Go_package_guidelines_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Extract more certificate-extensions for validation
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
Prerequisite for kyverno/kyverno#3216_x000D_
_x000D_
In the `signature` package there are functions to extract the issuer (`CertIssuerExtension`) and subject (`CertSubject`) from a generated certificate. In sigstore/fulcio#306 I implemented several extensions (https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/blob/main/docs/oid-info.md) extracted from GitHub OIDC claims._x000D_
_x000D_
I suggest to add the ability to read those extensions too with additional functions (or a generic function which receives the name as parameter) to make it possible for kyverno to validate this values too with a policy._x000D_
_x000D_
I would be happy to make a PR for that if desired. 😉

title: Import key-pair to GCP KMS
body_text:
Hello,_x000D_
_x000D_
I have generated a key-pair using `./cosign-darwin-amd64 generate-key-pair` i used it to sign several container images._x000D_
And now i want to import the key-pair into GCPKMS to store it securely. _x000D_
_x000D_
Since i already used it to sign images i do not want to regenerate a key-pair with `--kms gcpkms://...` option._x000D_
_x000D_
When i tried to upload the signature in GCP using gcloud i got the following error : _x000D_
```_x000D_
gcloud kms keys versions import \_x000D_
  --import-job test \_x000D_
  --location global \_x000D_
  --keyring g3s \_x000D_
  --key test \_x000D_
  --algorithm ec-sign-p256-sha256 \_x000D_
  --target-key-file cosign.key_x000D_
ERROR: (gcloud.kms.keys.versions.import) INVALID_ARGUMENT: Wrapped ECDSA key has invalid length of 664._x000D_
``` _x000D_
_x000D_
Is there a way to import an already generated key inside KMS ?_x000D_
_x000D_
Thanks_x000D_
_x000D_
top_3_comments_text: dlorenc: Hey! I'm not sure there is a way to do that today - the cosign generated keys are stored encrypted in a format that GCP won't natively know how to decrypt (a nacl/secretbox). It would probably be pretty straightforward to put together a small go program to do the decryption, but I'm not sure it would make sense to add to cosign directly. If you're interested in the go program approach I can provide a quick sample to get you started! | jp-gouin: Hi @dlorenc thanks for your answers ! yes please , i would like to try the go approach This could be part of a toolbox project near cosign | huberts90: @dlorenc I would really appreciate if you could share the Go program. I tried to incorporate the code from [LoadPrivateKey](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/pkg/cosign/keys.go#L210-L226), for some reason it fails inside `secretbox.Open`. cc @jp-gouin

title: Better non-OCI registry handling
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_

_x000D_
We should improve this experience by either_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Returning a clear and actionable error message like "Looks like your container registry isn't OCI compliant. Try setting COSIGN_DOCKER_MEDIA_TYPES=1 and trying again" or_x000D_
2. Detecting this automatically and just setting docker media types ourselves_x000D_

title: Sanitize cosign's dependency tree
body_text:
### Problem_x000D_
_x000D_
Cosign's module dependencies are pretty heavy._x000D_
_x000D_
Its [go.mod](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/f005e25466c3b6954546b718ce3a56d0efd6ec2b/go.mod) currently transitively depends on k8s.io/client-go, the AWS SDK, the Azure SDK, a GCP cloud storage API client, Docker internals, fsnotify, OpenTelemetry, a Kubernetes controller framework, a GitHub API client, cuelang, and many more._x000D_
_x000D_
This can make it difficult to consume for clients that don't want all that functionality, and may just want to sign some bytes using a key, push the resulting image to an OCI registry, and upload data to Rekor with certs via Fulcio._x000D_
_x000D_
For example, `sget`, which does relatively little compared to `cosign` -- it verifies signatures on an image and fetches a blob -- has a [go.mod file that's 280 lines](https://github.com/sigstore/sget/blob/b2bf5a609ad32c8f8aa1cfe5995681932ce17f2b/go.mod), producing a 72 MB binary 🏋️ ._x000D_
_x000D_
Large dependency trees lead to larger built binaries (see above), larger attack surfaces, longer and more fragile builds, and (most interesting to me personally as a maintainer!) more toil for maintainers to update dependencies and sift through security alerts for those vulnerabilities._x000D_
_x000D_
### Possible Solutions_x000D_
_x000D_
- Moving more dependencies into sigstore/sigstore (https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/issues/81), and taking that opportunity to reconsider if any dependencies can be replaced by lighter-weight alternatives_x000D_
- Taking better advantage of Go interfaces, especially for KMS services, and moving implementations of those interfaces into separate Go modules or separate repositories_x000D_
- Splitting the cosigned webhook into a separate Go module from the `cosign` CLI, possibly even moving it to a separate repo_x000D_
_x000D_
The `cosign` CLI would likely not get any smaller as a result of this work -- it still naturally depends on all the KMSes, K8s, cloud SDKs -- but other clients that want to do `cosign`-like things (signing, and especially verifying) wouldn't need to._x000D_
_x000D_
cc @luhring @jonjohnsonjr
