woodruffw: (Another tiny nit is that "subject" is a little bit overloaded between X.509 and OIDC, which is why I suggested "identity" as the cross-cutting thing between X.509 SANs and OIDC identities. But ultimately I don't think it matters, as long as we're consistent!)
haydentherapper: This has some up before - https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1313 There's some questions around how best to represent a subject. I haven't given a lot of thought to the UX side of this, but from a security perspective, I want to make sure it's hard to specify the wrong matching identity.
haydentherapper: `cert-san` reveals unnecessary details of X.509 in my opinion, where the subject is in the certificate is just an implementation detail. We need to consider that the subject may not be an email either, it could be a SPIFFE ID, it could be a GitHub/GitLab/CI identity. I'm somewhat leaning towards preferring separate flags for different identity types. There's also the question, to come back to the previous discussion, of what represents an identity. Is an identity the pairing of subject and issuer (i think yes)?
woodruffw: Yeah, I agree re: `--cert-san` -- if for whatever reason the SAN extension ceases to be sufficient in the future, users shouldn't have to be aware of that. And yeah, I think this is all predicated on a final decision about what an identity really *is* in Sigstore 🙂 -- I've been treating it as *just* the OIDC subject/SAN without regard for the OIDC issuer (given that we trust all IdPs currently), but @znewman01 has raised excellent points about IdPs being unable to prevent bad practices by users (like old, insecure credentials on forgotten accounts). If we'd like to punt on that to move this forward, I think `--cert-subject` probably best encompasses what we're trying to model here. (My 0.02c on design: I'd personally prefer a single `--cert-subject` flag with a discriminant/variant syntax, but that's a very weak preference due to how we use `click` in `sigstore-python`).
woodruffw: As a motivating example: here's something I'd expect a Python end-user to want to do, to verify that some package was signed by **at least one** trusted identity: ```bash $ sigstore verify \ --certificate foo.crt \ --signature foo.sig \ --cert-identity owner1@example.com \ --cert-identity owner2@example.com \ foo.tar.gz ``` Or, for example, trusting maintainers *or* one of their publishing workflows: ```bash $ sigstore verify \ --certificate foo.crt \ --signature foo.sig \ --cert-identity owner1@example.com \ --cert-identity owner2@example.com \ --cert-identity github:foo/bar \ foo.tar.gz ``` (Where `github:` is a psuedo-type that expands to something like `uri:https://github.com/foo/bar/...`) That latter one is a little further afield, but maybe something aspirational?
znewman01: Whew, long (but interesting) thread! I see 3-ish related problems in the above discussion: 1. Clarify the `--cert-*` family of flags. 2. Provide a syntax for resolving strings to identities (or perhaps identity *predicates*). 3. Provide policies about identity verification. I think @woodruffw's proposal w/r/t (1) is a good idea: we should add a `--cert-identity` flag. However, it's somewhat blocked on (2), which is blocked on "figure out everything about identity in Sigstore." (We *could* very carefully define a future-proof syntax for `--cert-identity` but I worry that it might prematurely limit us in solving (2) for real.) One way to deal with this in the near term is to focus on (3): force the users to specify explicit verification policies (using, e.g., CUE). This has a few advantages: - it's *really* explicit, and there's no risk of typing a string that checks something *other* than what I intended (as in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1871 ) - we can "lint" policies ("did you really mean to omit the OIDC provider?") - it allows predicates over arbitrary certificate attributes (as in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1313) - it allows for unambiguous combinations of subpredicates (AND vs. OR---it's not obvious to me that passing `--cert-identity` multiple times should mean OR) - easy to line up behavior between cosign and policy-controller - buys us time to figure out the "sugar" in (1) and (2) The chief disadvantage to my mind is that the UX is substantially worse for simple cases. The other is that docs in this area are a little light; see [Cosign Generic Predicate Specification](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/specs/COSIGN_PREDICATE_SPEC.md) and [Sigstore Docs > Cosign > In-Toto Attestations](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/attestation).
jku: > `--cert-identity github:foo/bar \ ` > (Where github: is a psuedo-type that expands to something like uri:https://github.com/foo/bar/...) Just to be sure we're on the same page: The "github identity" is the **workflow that was executed**, not the specific GitHub project. I'm pretty sure I could create project of my own, and use the sigstore-python workflow to build my projects sources. To actually verify the project build in a useful way we are going to need access to more or less custom X509 extensions: in Github case it's the (I believe sigstore reserved) 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.*. Whether exposing these semi-custom extensions values as github-specific options to the CLI tools makes sense is unclear... but they absolutely need to be available if we want to verify GitHub builds. I just wanted to make the context clear: defining "identity" is not enough make builds usefully verifiable, access to the other extensions is 100% required. As my 2c, I'm not sure adding a service-specific "github:" as a special value in the CLI interface makes sense: you are still going to have to include 95% of the URI in the argument, why not just use a generic "URI:" prefix -- essentially follow the openssl text output here?
woodruffw: > Just to be sure we're on the same page: The "github identity" is the workflow that was executed, not the specific GitHub project. Yep, that was meant to be shorthand for this: ``` https://github.com/foo/bar/.github/workflows/workflow.yml@refs/something ``` > I'm pretty sure I could create project of my own, and use the sigstore-python workflow to build my projects sources. How would you do this? I'm not saying it's impossible, just that I wasn't aware that you could -- my understanding is/was that you could only run a repository's workflow by triggering one of the workflow's own events, not an event on your own repository. You can always trigger the "same" workflow in a fork of course, but then the org name will vary.
jku: > my understanding is/was that you could only run a repository's workflow by triggering one of the workflow's own events, not an event on your own repository I think you're entirely correct and I was confused. the SAN does seem to identify the project for the reasons you state (but does not promise much about the workflow or source content since the ref they use is a tag and not a hash)
woodruffw: > I think you're entirely correct and I was confused. the SAN does seem to identify the project for the reasons you state (but does not promise much about the workflow or source content since the ref they use is a tag and not a hash) Yep...there's another extension (`1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.3`) that contains the SHA hash for the symbolic ref, which we'll also probably want a flag for. Hashes via a CLI are not the best thing in terms of UX, but in terms of integrity guarantees (for a user who absolutely can't trust symbolic refs) I suppose we can't do much better 🙂

title: Cosign, Spire, and Attestation failures
body_text:
Cosign attest should have flags for what identity is for signing attestation and another for the registry. _x000D_
_x000D_
If you use spire, cosign can not upload to the registry with the spire x509 SVID. It would be beneficial if we could instruct cosign explicitly via flag to use providers for specific tasks. _x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
Environment_x000D_
_x000D_
Fulcio - helm chart version 0.3.0_x000D_
Rekor - helm chart version 0.2.11_x000D_
Tekton Pipelines - v0.2.3  _x000D_
Tekton Chains - v0.8.0_x000D_
Spire - `gcr.io/spiffe-io/spire-server@sha256:fbf64ed15687c1a5141b52d46d2b9082837fd286af16fbf670d155d0ec5e3dd3 #v1.2.0`_x000D_
Cosign - `gcr.io/projectsigstore/cosign:v1.9.0`_x000D_
GKE - _x000D_
``` k version_x000D_
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"24", GitVersion:"v1.24.0", GitCommit:"4ce5a8954017644c5420bae81d72b09b735c21f0", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-05-03T13:36:49Z", GoVersion:"go1.18.1", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/arm64"}_x000D_
Kustomize Version: v4.5.4_x000D_
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"21", GitVersion:"v1.21.11-gke.900", GitCommit:"20da4c21b3a6b1a56ff6ad5ecb7dee013aaf1b83", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-03-30T09:37:00Z", GoVersion:"go1.16.15b7", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The tekton task uses the KSA and GSA that has access to GCR registry, this works fine. If we were to mount the Spire socket, the same KSA is registered with Spire, the GCR upload fails. _x000D_
_x000D_
```yaml_x000D_

kind: Task_x000D_

    type: string_x000D_
    description: container image name_x000D_
  - name: COSIGN_REPOSITORY_x000D_
    type: string_x000D_
    description: OCI repository for cosign to push sbom attestation too_x000D_
    default: ""_x000D_

title: verify: rekor public key should be obtained from the custom instance define via --rekor-url
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
When using `cosign verify` with a custom `--rekor-url` value,  I realized the rekor public key is not taken from the custom instance. The rekor public key is always obtained from the `rekor.sigstore.dev` endpoint. _x000D_
_x000D_
I believe `cosign verify` should always use the public key obtained from the endpoint defined via `rekor-url` for our custom rekor instance. Nowadays it only works if you set the environment variable `SIGSTORE_REKOR_PUBLIC_KEY` with the public key from your rekor instance.
top_3_comments_text: asraa: Hi! Yes this is true. This is because ideally you should be pinning your trust for the ecosystem components out of band, which is why you probably should curl the pem from the custom rekor-url and use SIGSTORE_REKOR_PUBLIC_KEY | hectorj2f: @asraa But that is what I'd assume it should be automatically done (in the cosign code) when providing a specific rekor-url flag, so I don't need to provide the rekor-url and set the env variable. | hectorj2f: We also realized that any restart of the rekor instance changed the public key value, so that looks like one more reason to get the public key from the specified instance when set.
all_comments_text:
asraa: Hi! Yes this is true. This is because ideally you should be pinning your trust for the ecosystem components out of band, which is why you probably should curl the pem from the custom rekor-url and use SIGSTORE_REKOR_PUBLIC_KEY
hectorj2f: @asraa But that is what I'd assume it should be automatically done (in the cosign code) when providing a specific rekor-url flag, so I don't need to provide the rekor-url and set the env variable.
hectorj2f: We also realized that any restart of the rekor instance changed the public key value, so that looks like one more reason to get the public key from the specified instance when set.
asraa: Hey Hector! Maybe I could clarify documentation for the flag -- this is where the client should be talking to for the log information, but trusted that log would mean that you have no out of band trust pinned in the client. Otherwise, there would be no need to verify any signature from Rekor.
asraa: > We also realized that any restart of the rekor instance changed the public key value, so that looks like one more reason to get the public key from the specified instance l when set. A rekor server deployment can also be specified with a particular signer, that'll avoid a creation of an in-memory key pair: https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/blob/ed585a3385f9d6447f886d6948554e261288bc6a/config/rekor.yaml#L59
haydentherapper: A couple more thoughts: We should avoid pulling the key directly from the log because it opens us up to various attacks. This could include man in the middle, where an attacker injects their own key material and inclusion proofs and signed tree heads. Pinning a key out of band would make this detectable. Much like with PKI where you pin a root certificate that you trust, you need to start the trust root somewhere for an inclusion proof. If we ask the log for its key before verifying, a signature is pretty much unnecessary. The `SIGSTORE_REKOR_PUBLIC_KEY` flag was meant for testing. Users for Cosign should get the trusted verification material from TUF. I'd like to take the stance that TUF is the only way to use Cosign as a CLI (Cosign as a library is a different story, it's up to the users of those libraries how they want to inject key material).
asraa: Closing in favor of documenting the out of band one https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2122 Eventually we will remove this. See https://github.com/sigstore/scaffolding/issues/211 Scaffolding is WIP to create a TUF server, people should use scaffolding, create their own custom TUF repo, OR use SIGSTORE_REKOR_PUBLIC_KEY in worst case scenario
hectorj2f: Awesome! Thanks @asraa

title: copy: introduce new `--sbom-only`, `--att-only` flags
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, we only have `--sig-only` flag to copy only image signature. I thought it would be nice to have also `--sbom-only` for copy _SBOM_ and `--sbom-only` for copy _ATT_._x000D_
_x000D_
But using both these flags in the same time might be mutually exclusive since flags have `-only` suffix means _do not copy anything but only .._._x000D_
_x000D_
UX design:_x000D_
_x000D_
```bash_x000D_
# 1. mutually exclusive, throw an error_x000D_
$ cosign copy --sbom-only --sig-only --att-only <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
_x000D_
# 2. remove -only suffix to do both operations in the same time_x000D_
# this would also mean: _also copy the image itself_, but actually does not_x000D_
$ cosign copy --sbom --sig --att <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
_x000D_
# 3. if user want to copy sig, sbom and att, have to run the followings_x000D_
$ cosign copy --sig-only <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
$ cosign copy --sbom-only <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
$ cosign copy --att-only <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
_x000D_
# 4. introduce a new --copy-only flag that accept custom string array_x000D_
# no need to call cosign twice_x000D_
$ cosign copy --copy-only=sbom,sign,att,etc <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
_x000D_
# 5. happiest path_x000D_
$ cosign copy --sig-only <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
$ cosign copy --sbom-only <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
$ cosign copy --att-only <SRC> <DST>_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_

This means that if a [replication rule](https://goharbor.io/docs/2.5.0/administration/configuring-replication/create-replication-rules/) applies to a signed artifact, Harbor will apply the replication rule to the signature in the same way it applies it to the signed artifact._x000D_

You will be able to see the relationship between the two artifacts in the target Harbor interface, in the same way that you do in the source registry._x000D_

When replicating from Harbor to another target registry type, the target registry will not manage the link between the signed artifact and any associated signatures. You will see the subject manifest and signatures as coordinating artifacts under the same repository.

title: dockerfile-verify: inline certificate verification options
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
In `cosign dockerfile verify`, verification options like `--certificate` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer` are passed as command-line arguments._x000D_
This leaves the user burdened with mapping certificate criteria to images externally, and for multi-stage builds invoking `cosign verify dockerfile` multiple times._x000D_
_x000D_
I propose allowing the `options.CertVerifyOptions` to be encoded within comments of the Dockerfile:_x000D_
```dockerfile_x000D_
# cosign-verify: certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" enforce-sct=true_x000D_
FROM gcr.io/test/image:v1_x000D_
_x000D_
# cosign-verify: certificate-oidc-issuer=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com certificate-github-workflow-repository=thepwagner/my-cool-repo certificate-github-workflow-name=release.yaml_x000D_
FROM gcr.io/test/image:v1_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The implementation would parse any comments preceding a `FROM` statement and support the same options as the CLI, expressed as key-value pairs. Values specified at the command line would  overwrite those derived from comments._x000D_
_x000D_
Naively the `VerifyDockerfileCommand` could invoke the embedded `VerifyCommand` multiple times with each unique `options.CertVerifyOptions` discovered. Grouping by unique options would mean users not using the comments are unaffected._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
Does anyone else want this?_x000D_
Does it belong in `cosign`, or should it be a separate tool?_x000D_
_x000D_
### Related_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1626 (I _really_ want `certificate-github-workflow-repository` and `certificate-github-workflow-name` 😍 )_x000D_

```_x000D_

title: Discourage signing references to images that aren't digests
body_text:
If you run `cosign sign container.registry.io/foo:tag`, then you're vulnerable to:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Race conditions, where `:tag` changed. Immutable tags help with this, but it's hard for cosign to know whether a registry's tags are immutable._x000D_
2. Funny business, where the registry itself changes the image._x000D_
_x000D_
It's much more meaningful to sign the *digests*, which are immutable._x000D_
_x000D_
In Slack discusssion, @imjasonh writes:_x000D_
_x000D_
> I think we could just recommend signing by digest more, maybe show some warning about signing by tag, or requiring confirmation?_x000D_
_x000D_
I think this is a good idea.

mtrmac: > Discourage signing references to images that aren't digests FWIW, as the original author of the c/image “simple signing” payload format, I think this should be exactly the opposite: discourage signing digest references. Or, to be more precise, the signing operation must _point_ at an image by digest[1] — but the signed payload should name the image, in `critical.identity.docker-reference`, using _both_ a repo name and a tag_, not just a repo (like Cosign currently does), and not replacing the tag in that field with a digest. --- First, a technical note: the signature payload, both as originally specified and as created by `cosign sign`, _already contains_ a separate digest field: https://github.com/containers/image/blob/main/docs/containers-signature.5.md#criticalimagedocker-manifest-digest . So putting a digest in the other field, `critical.identity.docker-reference`, is at best redundant. Actually, Cosign enforces that the `docker-manifest-digest` value matches the image, in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/0081e1a11299e294f2e030a4889f62a774c5bd69/pkg/cosign/verifiers.go#L44 ; it does AFACS does nothing with a digest value in `critical.identity.docker-reference`, so putting a digest in the `identity` field would be not just redundant, but possibly also misleading. --- Now, as to the main reason: There are basically two reasons to sign an image: nonrepudiation (for which just the pair of `critical.image.docker-manifest-digest` + a signature by the expected key is sufficient, and doesn’t matter for this argument), and end-to-end integrity in an untrusted environment (using third-party or untrusted registries, mirrors, caches). One of the ways an untrusted transport can attack users is to substitute different “legitimate” images, correctly and intentionally signed by the intended author — causing the user to use a different image than the one that was intended. For example, a malicious registry might, when asked for `app:10.2`, serve `app:10.0-prerelease.1` instead, which has known vulnerabilities. The self-contained and isolated nature of container images makes this kind of attack fairly likely to work, in that the victim might be able to run the substituted image without noticing any obvious breakage. The protection against this should be effortless, based only on existing data. Users are unlikely to carry around an extra version number around, in addition to the minimal required deployment configuration (e.g. a k8s Pod spec), and users can not be reasonably expected to actively do an extra step (and to never forget) in order not to be vulnerable AFAICS, about the only practical UI for this is to match the deployment instruction (image name in `podman pull $image` / k8s `pod.spec.containers[].image`), which already expresses users’ intent, against a name inside the signature. Anything else could work technically but is unlikely to be used. And that’s why the `critical.identity.docker-reference` field exists in “simple signing” at all, and why signature enforcement in the “simple signing” format requires that the whole name:tag of the users’ image request matches this field inside the signature (with configurable exceptions, mapping and the like). System administrators can then configure a system-wide `policy.json` configuration with the keys expected to sign various images, and users can ideally just use `podman pull` without worrying about signature enforcement or configurations or transport integrity at all — just like they rely on the automatic matching “subject” field of certificates used in TLS to protect HTTPS connections, without having to worry about substitution attacks. Now, Cosign might or might not share the view that this kind of protection against substitution attacks is important, or practical enough to enforce; so Cosign might or might not decide to enforce name:tag verification by default. But I’d very much like for `cosign sign` to create signatures that allow this kind of name:tag matching to be done. --- The end-user UI for `cosign sign` could then be something like ```sh cosign sign --digest sha256:… registry.example.com/namespace/name:tag ``` where the `--digest sha256:…` option ensures that the correct image is signed, and the `registry.example.com/namespace/name:tag` argument both specifies what image to sign, and what value to put into `critical.identity.docker-reference`. The above is the basic use case; some users may require more control, with ```sh cosign sign --digest sha256:… --sign-identity registry.example.com/production-namespace/name:released-tag \ registry-staging.example.com/staging-namespace/name:released-tag-staging ``` to decouple the signed identity from the physical location of the image that is being signed --- [1] (which is best exposed by not _having_ a separate signing operation, but by integrating signing into a `podman push`-like operation directly, but that’s a whole another matter)
ianlewis: > For example, a malicious registry might, when asked for `app:10.2`, serve `app:10.0-prerelease.1` instead, which has known vulnerabilities. The self-contained and isolated nature of container images makes this kind of attack fairly likely to work, in that the victim might be able to run the substituted image without noticing any obvious breakage. Yes. I think the argument was more that a malicious (or even a non-malicious) registry or user could simply change the `10.2` tag to a different digest after the original push, but it basically results in the same thing you're describing. > The end-user UI for `cosign sign` could then be something like > > ```shell > cosign sign --digest sha256:… registry.example.com/namespace/name:tag > ``` > > where the `--digest sha256:…` option ensures that the correct image is signed, and the `registry.example.com/namespace/name:tag` argument both specifies what image to sign, and what value to put into `critical.identity.docker-reference`. I think that's fine. The spirit of this issue is more around verifying the digest and was perhaps just making the assumption about the UI. For example, if this solution is adopted a warning could be printed to users encouraging them to use the `--digest` option.

title: support remote signing via reproducible builds
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
Have cosign on the developers machine run the same build, creating a signature locally and then sending the signature to the remote in machine, where it is checked and applied. (See also https://www.qubes-os.org/doc/split-gpg/ for something similar in concept.)_x000D_
Besides allowing signing on an untrusted machine while still retaining security, this makes it possible to independently verify the process without relying on the signature._x000D_
_x000D_
I have seen people using cosign with fulcio to sign builds in e.g. GitHub Actions. This would support signing in a GitHub action while affording better security.
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: Overall, I agree with you that reproducible builds and software signatures go well together! Is your argument something like the following? - Some people are having GitHub Actions sign with private keys stored as GitHub Secrets. - This is bad for a couple of reasons: - GitHub Actions can now sign anything it wants. So if (1) GitHub is compromised, or (2, more likely) the GitHub actions configuration changes, we could have signatures of evil builds. - That private key had to be generated somewhere else, and so it might have leaked as it was uploaded to GitHub. - Instead, we should have developers build + sign locally, and then send that signature to GitHub Actions - GitHub Actions publishes the secret *only if* it got the same result. Then, the overall effect is: *both* GitHub CI *and* the developer need to cooperate to publish an artifact. I think this is a good goal, and agree that reproducible builds help with this. However, to me, it sounds more straightforward to have GitHub Actions sign the artifact as well, and then clients can check that there are signatures from *both* the developer and CI. Do you agree that the effect would be similar? (If you're worried about accidentally publishing artifacts without appropriate signatures, you can have distinct CI jobs for (1) build+sign and (2) publish release, with the latter gated on the same threshold of signatures.) But I think things get even better with [keyless signatures](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/dad7d3f1892a9c00c0bf5bd09eefe1a4ad13218d/KEYLESS.md). Then, we can do the following: - I, the developer, build and sign my artifact using a key I only hold locally. - From the public source, GitHub CI builds a (bit-for-bit identical) artifact, and signs using a Sigstore signature based on the [GitHub Actions OIDC identity](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect). - Now, as a client, I can check that I have a signature from *both* the developer *and* GitHub CI. - Bonus points for using [in-toto](https://in-toto.io/) to manage this threshold. It's capable of expressing things like: "I need a claim that the artifact with hash X was built from commit Y using build process Z, signed by (GitHub CI AND (developer A OR developer B))" --------------------------------------- Another question: I don't see why this is a cosign feature. The reproducibility check would look something like: ``` $ gcc -o a.out main.c $ [get the signature from the dev] $ cosign verify-blob --signature user-sig.sig --key user-key.pub $ [publish a.out as usual] ``` The tricky part lies in "get the signature from the user". How would cosign implement this feature? It seems to me easier to have the developer provide the signature as a build input when they kick off the release process. ------------------------------------------------ Curious to hear your thoughts! | JanZerebecki: Yes, my argument was somewhat like that. Important details in my scenario are that they are 1) using Github Web UI to do merges (not git merge and push) and tags 2) do not use commit signing 3) already use what cosign calls keyless mode. So (3) makes it different, but your criticism of your scenario applies equally to mine as the entity in control of the commit signing key used for Web UI actions, any secret in the CI, and the OIDC endpoint are the same. ### Simplifying while slightly improving security Both a secret key in the CI or OIDC can help with associating the target project and branch of a merge or target project and tag name. However for software projects released from git with tags that are machine comparable versions, we do not need to differentiate the project/repo if the user is differentiated. Because the source branch and user are already included in the signed commit or tag created by the back end of the Web UI, we can write the public key identifier, hash of user, and tag hash to rekor. If rekor were to implement a solution to split view and availability, that would give us without any additional authentication even better security. We can do better than (3) with reproducible builds and authenticating the input via the signature created by (1). This as a side effect made the process easier on the person making the release. The CI can ensure this by doing the build twice. ### Aside on keys We could improve the security quite a bit by making git sign commits and tags by default. It would create a key on first invocation without any user input. This would remove all the friction, that GPG singing commits usually involves. Github has no key rotation in place for the GPG key the Web UI uses to sign. (Same for their SSH host key.) And they only use one secret across all involved servers. I have not checked the details of OIDC, does it mandate something like key rotation chained with signatures and allow offline verification after the fact? To get short lived keys we can use something like is done in Decentralised IDentifieres to chain key rotations and do that automatically during signing if x time went by. For developers with multiple machines, we can offer cross signing. For recovery we can store a chained recovery use once key in their mailbox/dropbox/etc or use a passphrase to derive a key or use social recovery with a quorum. Maybe FIDO2 keys can be directly incorporated into such a scheme, to allow offline verifiable 2fa, or as the sole secret storage. To not rely only on the secrecy of the private key we can use keys whose policy is to only make signatures that are published to rekor. If we want to bind keys to Github identities, we can use something like what Keybase or https://github.com/wiktor-k/openpgp-proofs does. We can define who owns a repo based on these keys in the repo itself, e.g. in a file named `.gittrust`. And have git verify by default if this is present in the default branch. But this aside is not integral to this feature request. ### Strengthen the source To avoid the centralized single point of failure, any maintainers from the project could then confirm the rekor entry based on their local git repo by something like `cd /path/repo && cosign confirm tag-name`. 3rd parties could review it with something like https://github.com/crev-dev/crev and store a reference to the review in rekor. ### Strengthen the binary Anyone can run a rebuilder like https://github.com/in-toto/rebuilderd that follows the repo and/or the entries for the repo in rekor, reproduces the build and sends the signed attestation to rekor. Github CI could be one of those. ### Tying it together I'm a bit unsure about this one as I'm not familiar with some of the parts affected. We can combine the above two and a) satisfy legacy systems with just one signature that can not do any multi signature policy and not query rekor (otherwise we could just do with the above and a policy on how to verify from rekor and possibly gate the CI publish on a threshold appearing in rekor) and b) make sure the CI doesn't release without maintainer confirmation by: 1) In the Github Action send intent to sign with the intoto meta data which is enough to reproduce the build to rekor (this is so the developer doesn't accidentally sign something which was not tested to at least be reproducible by two runs) 2) wait for signature from next step to appear in rekor and then transplant it to the binary 3a) (this overlaps with what https://github.com/in-toto/rebuilderd does) on the developers machine trigger a build, receive the intoto meta data, check that it matches the input the developer provided (e.g. same git commit or tag provided locally), check that the build result is the same, 3b) sign it, send signature to rekor. Using rekor here as the transport is just an example, it could as well be a git branch, that the CI can only append to. ### Make secure easy I have the hunch that for good UI cosign should itself call whatever (in-toto-verify?) is needed to reproduce based on the in-toto recipe derived from local git which the CI also uses, as manual steps lead to things being non-reproducible. | znewman01: I'd like to check that I'm understanding your proposal: GitHub merge commits are signed by GitHub, *not* maintainers, so if we check (1) that a commit is signed, and (2) a build is done by GitHub CI, (1) isn't giving us a whole lot of assurance (single-point-of-failure, no tie to maintainer identity). But we like the GitHub workflow; how do we get the security assurance of signed commits without giving that up? We can have maintainers add extra signatures after-the-fact, after reproducing the build from their local checkout. I think there are a bunch of good ideas here, but it's a little difficult to understand what concretely needs to get done. Perhaps the best thing to do would be to build a *separate* tool? Or maybe this is a feature-request for the in-toto tooling itself? Some alternatives here include [Guix's approach](https://programming-journal.org/2023/7/1/), which doesn't quite work in a GitHub-centric workflow but is interesting enough that I'll include it.

We can do better than (3) with reproducible builds and authenticating the input via the signature created by (1). This as a side effect made the process easier on the person making the release. The CI can ensure this by doing the build twice. ### Aside on keys We could improve the security quite a bit by making git sign commits and tags by default. It would create a key on first invocation without any user input. This would remove all the friction, that GPG singing commits usually involves. Github has no key rotation in place for the GPG key the Web UI uses to sign. (Same for their SSH host key.) And they only use one secret across all involved servers. I have not checked the details of OIDC, does it mandate something like key rotation chained with signatures and allow offline verification after the fact? To get short lived keys we can use something like is done in Decentralised IDentifieres to chain key rotations and do that automatically during signing if x time went by. For developers with multiple machines, we can offer cross signing. For recovery we can store a chained recovery use once key in their mailbox/dropbox/etc or use a passphrase to derive a key or use social recovery with a quorum. Maybe FIDO2 keys can be directly incorporated into such a scheme, to allow offline verifiable 2fa, or as the sole secret storage. To not rely only on the secrecy of the private key we can use keys whose policy is to only make signatures that are published to rekor. If we want to bind keys to Github identities, we can use something like what Keybase or https://github.com/wiktor-k/openpgp-proofs does. We can define who owns a repo based on these keys in the repo itself, e.g. in a file named `.gittrust`. And have git verify by default if this is present in the default branch. But this aside is not integral to this feature request. ### Strengthen the source To avoid the centralized single point of failure, any maintainers from the project could then confirm the rekor entry based on their local git repo by something like `cd /path/repo && cosign confirm tag-name`. 3rd parties could review it with something like https://github.com/crev-dev/crev and store a reference to the review in rekor. ### Strengthen the binary Anyone can run a rebuilder like https://github.com/in-toto/rebuilderd that follows the repo and/or the entries for the repo in rekor, reproduces the build and sends the signed attestation to rekor. Github CI could be one of those. ### Tying it together I'm a bit unsure about this one as I'm not familiar with some of the parts affected. We can combine the above two and a) satisfy legacy systems with just one signature that can not do any multi signature policy and not query rekor (otherwise we could just do with the above and a policy on how to verify from rekor and possibly gate the CI publish on a threshold appearing in rekor) and b) make sure the CI doesn't release without maintainer confirmation by: 1) In the Github Action send intent to sign with the intoto meta data which is enough to reproduce the build to rekor (this is so the developer doesn't accidentally sign something which was not tested to at least be reproducible by two runs) 2) wait for signature from next step to appear in rekor and then transplant it to the binary 3a) (this overlaps with what https://github.com/in-toto/rebuilderd does) on the developers machine trigger a build, receive the intoto meta data, check that it matches the input the developer provided (e.g. same git commit or tag provided locally), check that the build result is the same, 3b) sign it, send signature to rekor. Using rekor here as the transport is just an example, it could as well be a git branch, that the CI can only append to. ### Make secure easy I have the hunch that for good UI cosign should itself call whatever (in-toto-verify?) is needed to reproduce based on the in-toto recipe derived from local git which the CI also uses, as manual steps lead to things being non-reproducible.

title: `attach attestation` should support Attestation Bundles
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Users may have multiple attestations that they want to attach to a given image.  `cosign download attestation` supports downloading all the attestations for a given image, but `cosign attach attestation` doesn't support uploading multiple attestations._x000D_
_x000D_
It would be nice if `attach attestation` supported [in-toto Attestation Bundles](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/blob/main/spec/bundle.md)_x000D_
_x000D_
This could probably be added fairly easily with [some small modifications here](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/dbd430fce5d4b3805758bd97ec5c104b164091c8/cmd/cosign/cli/attach/attestation.go#L39)._x000D_
top_3_comments_text: dlorenc: Makes sense, are there any tools to generate those bundles? Should download also result in a bundle in the case where there are multiple? | TomHennen: I don't believe any public tools are currently creating them at the moment (we do have some internal tooling that will use this feature). It turns out the bundles are typically just multiple attestations separated by `\n` so they can be created pretty easily, and `download` produces them implicitly (at least on *nix systems) if you just send the results to a file, e.g. `cosign download attestation us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/project/repo/image > bundle.intoto.jsonl` | developer-guy: it makes sense to me, I'd love to help

TomHennen: Thanks @Dentrax and @developer-guy, I left a comment on the PR. Thanks for working on this!

This way, we can both consider attestation files and bundles. ```shell $ cosign attach attestation --attestation <file> --bundle <bundle> ``` PTAL @dlorenc @Dentrax
TomHennen: I'm not sure having a separate flag for handling bundles is a great idea. My thinking is that often users of `attach` won't know if the file they have is a bundle with multiple attestations or not. Consider a vulnerability scanner that issues an in-toto attestation. 1. User runs the scanner 2. Scanner produces a single attestation with predicateType A 3. Scanner emits the attestation in <FILE> 4. User runs `cosign attach attestation --attestation <FILE> Later someone develops a new predicate type (B) for vulnerability scan results. Existing vulnerability scanners want to support this new type but don't want to break anyone that's using the old type (A). With implicit bundle support they can do that easily: 1. User runs the scanner 2. Scanner produces attestation with predicateType A, and another with predicateType B 3. Scanner emits both attestations (using a bundle) in <FILE> 4. User runs `cosign attach attestation --attestation <FILE> 5. Downstream users that need type A or B can easily find it. Without implicit bundle support that won't be possible.

title: Rename --k8s-keychain flag
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
The `--k8s-keychain` flag (e.g., in [`cosign sign`](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_sign.md)) is_x000D_
_x000D_
> `whether to use the kubernetes keychain instead of the default keychain (supports workload identity).`_x000D_
_x000D_
This is a bit of a misnomer, since "the kubernetes keychain" as a term isn't particularly well defined, and because what I believe it means is, "the common set of cloud auth helpers that can be included in Kubernetes (i.e., GCP, AWS, Azure)", and in actuality, the flag enables a number of auth helpers that aren't exactly that set of "kubernetes auth helpers":_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/516cc39f5582f46af9fc5b9081af08dba24441e7/cmd/cosign/cli/options/registry.go#L83-L89_x000D_
_x000D_
Along with GCP, AWS and Azure, this set includes the GHCR auth helper, and with #2007 this keychain will also include an Alibaba helper._x000D_
_x000D_
I propose changing this flag to something like `--workload-identity` (ideas welcome!) or at least improve docs to clarify what it does.

title: Discourage (disallow?) naked `cosign verify` invocations
body_text:
Inspired by https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-python/issues/155_x000D_
_x000D_
`cosign verify` (in keyless mode) without any `--cert-email` provided will succeed when literally anybody has signed an image/blob. This is almost never the right behavior: evil@hacker.com can sign any blob you can._x000D_
_x000D_
Instead, we should require *some* verification policy:_x000D_
_x000D_
- `--cert-email` (*and* `--cert-oidc-provider`; see #1947)_x000D_
- a CUE policy_x000D_
- `--insecure`, which will do the current behavior today (possibly a hidden flag)_x000D_
_x000D_
(Keyfull mode is okay, because you're passing the key material or CA in explicitly)
top_3_comments_text: haydentherapper: +100000 to this. A couple thoughts: * This is a significant breaking change, so we should prepare for issues to be filed. Blog posts/Slack/documentation beforehand is critical. * We do have a gap that needs to be resolved first, that a flag like `certificate-identity` must be added in order to support non-email IDs (SPIFFE and GitHub Actions currently). * There is recent support for checking GitHub Actions identities by multiple flags (https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1626). This could be allowed as an alternative to an identity flag, if all of these flags are set simultaneously, since we should be able to reconstruct the `job_workflow_ref` which is the SAN of the certificate. * I'd prefer no `--insecure` flag. This is going to be a breaking change regardless, so why continue to support risky behavior? * I would also prefer that we don't try to tackle policy as part of this, at least for now. Let's let Cosign handle the "simple" case of one identity, and let a policy engine handle more complex use-cases (Cosign as a library). * On this topic, we could consider small UX improvements such as support for multiple identity flags. I don't think we need to tackle this right now though. Let's get the ball rolling and require `certificate-email` and `certificate-oidc-provider` in the next major Cosign release. To unblock this, we'll need to add an identity flag. title: Digest mismatch when fetching module version v1.9.0
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
When using golang to fetch version 1.9.0 of cosign, the computed digest is not consistent between different environments. This causes portability issues in `go.sum` of projects using cosign:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
verifying github.com/sigstore/cosign@v1.9.0: checksum mismatch_x000D_
	downloaded: h1:hzLtZh62rPrGfPUk3XwG6qHwxI6bLC1S6seYUGRE420=_x000D_
	go.sum:     h1:E1Kkc6I99dNCGfjwU0B7XTJNEpltNi2GUVEQcswY2Ow=_x000D_
_x000D_
SECURITY ERROR_x000D_
This download does NOT match an earlier download recorded in go.sum._x000D_
The bits may have been replaced on the origin server, or an attacker may_x000D_
have intercepted the download attempt._x000D_
```_x000D_
Depending on your environment the hashes may be reversed._x000D_
_x000D_
Here's a simple reproducer:_x000D_
```bash_x000D_
mkdir -p /tmp/test{1,2}/{test,cache,modcache}_x000D_
cd /tmp/test1/test_x000D_
go mod init test1_x000D_
GOCACHE=/tmp/test1/cache GOMODCACHE=/tmp/test1/modcache GOPROXY="direct" go get github.com/sigstore/cosign@v1.9.0_x000D_
cat go.sum_x000D_
_x000D_
cd /tmp/test2/test_x000D_
go mod init test_x000D_
GOCACHE=/tmp/test2/cache GOMODCACHE=/tmp/test2/modcache GOPROXY="https://proxy.golang.org,direct" go get github.com/sigstore/cosign@v1.9.0_x000D_
_x000D_
echo 'ANY OUTPUT BELOW MEANS A PROBLEM:'_x000D_
diff /tmp/test1/test/go.sum /tmp/test2/test/go.sum_x000D_
diff -r /tmp/test1/modcache /tmp/test2/modcache_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The output of the `diff` commands is:_x000D_
```_x000D_

1c1_x000D_
< {"Version":"v1.9.0","Time":"2022-06-03T13:47:07Z"}_x000D_
\ No newline at end of file_x000D_
---_x000D_
> {"Version":"v1.9.0","Time":"2022-06-03T10:54:54Z"}_x000D_
\ No newline at end of file_x000D_
Binary files /tmp/test1/modcache/cache/download/github.com/sigstore/cosign/@v/v1.9.0.zip and /tmp/test2/modcache/cache/download/github.com/sigstore/cosign/@v/v1.9.0.zip differ_x000D_
diff -r /tmp/test1/modcache/cache/download/github.com/sigstore/cosign/@v/v1.9.0.ziphash /tmp/test2/modcache/cache/download/github.com/sigstore/cosign/@v/v1.9.0.ziphash_x000D_

< h1:hzLtZh62rPrGfPUk3XwG6qHwxI6bLC1S6seYUGRE420=_x000D_

title: Are secure timestamps omitted intentionally?
body_text:
**Question**_x000D_
_x000D_
Having a quick look at the signature process I can't see any queries to secure timestamping services. Including a signed timestamp is a critical piece of functionlity for almost any scenario involving digital signatures. _x000D_
_x000D_
There's a citition from the [cosign course on Edx](https://learning.edx.org/course/course-v1:LinuxFoundationX+LFS182x+2T2022/home)_x000D_
_x000D_
> Because these keys persist only long enough for signing to take place, signature verification ensures that the certificate was valid at the time of signing._x000D_
_x000D_
If a signature is valid it's impossible to guarantee that the key wasn't expired at the time of signing without usage of signed timestamps from third party. In other words, if I compromised an expired "keyless" key pair, what prevents me from signing another payload and claiming that the signature is valid?_x000D_
_x000D_
Upload to transparency log can help to reveal cheating with signatures, but at the time of writing there're no checks for consistency of subsequent log entries in transparency log e.g. that an entry is older than a pervious one. _x000D_
_x000D_
So, my questions are:_x000D_
- what is the protection from using expired "keyless" pairs and claiming that signatures are valid?_x000D_
- what is the design rationale for not including signed timestamps into signatures like it's done in MS Authenticode?
top_3_comments_text: dlorenc: > * what is the protection from using expired "keyless" pairs and claiming that signatures are valid? We use the transparency log (Rekor) inclusion proof as a timestamp. It serves the same purpose but has a different API than traditional TSA's. I would like to add support for RFC3161 TSAs in addition. There's some discussion here: https://blog.sigstore.dev/its-ten-o-clock-do-you-know-where-your-private-keys-are-5c869cf53234 | asraa: > consistency of subsequent log entries in transparency log e.g. that an entry is older than a pervious one. Agreed, there is no monitoring that verifies monotonicity of the integrated time in Rekor. Even then, the integrated time in an entry can be mutated in the underlying database. There's also no way of adding an external or third party timestamp in our APIs, with either an RFC 3161 timestamp or other timestamping protocols. I agree that there is room to add this data into Rekor entries in a variety of ways, to allow clients to have some external verification besides trust in Rekor and its database. > what is the protection from using expired "keyless" pairs and claiming that signatures are valid? Right now as Dan mentioned, the protection is coming from using the integrated time of the entry as a proxy for when the signature was created (the sig is part of the entry). See also https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/issues/824, @haydentherapper is moving the timestamper into a separate repo, where we can host a TSA. | asraa: > Upload to transparency log can help to reveal cheating with signatures, but at the time of writing there're no checks for consistency of subsequent log entries in transparency log e.g. that an entry is older than a pervious one. One more addition: Rekor supports an RFC 3161 timestamp type, which means you can upload timestamps on a cron or scheduled job to Rekor for more assurance of its integrated time. That can provide some guarantees that entries are monotonic in relation to those timestamps.

It serves the same purpose but has a different API than traditional TSA's. I would like to add support for RFC3161 TSAs in addition. There's some discussion here: https://blog.sigstore.dev/its-ten-o-clock-do-you-know-where-your-private-keys-are-5c869cf53234
asraa: > consistency of subsequent log entries in transparency log e.g. that an entry is older than a pervious one. Agreed, there is no monitoring that verifies monotonicity of the integrated time in Rekor. Even then, the integrated time in an entry can be mutated in the underlying database. There's also no way of adding an external or third party timestamp in our APIs, with either an RFC 3161 timestamp or other timestamping protocols. I agree that there is room to add this data into Rekor entries in a variety of ways, to allow clients to have some external verification besides trust in Rekor and its database. > what is the protection from using expired "keyless" pairs and claiming that signatures are valid? Right now as Dan mentioned, the protection is coming from using the integrated time of the entry as a proxy for when the signature was created (the sig is part of the entry). See also https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/issues/824, @haydentherapper is moving the timestamper into a separate repo, where we can host a TSA.
asraa: > Upload to transparency log can help to reveal cheating with signatures, but at the time of writing there're no checks for consistency of subsequent log entries in transparency log e.g. that an entry is older than a pervious one. One more addition: Rekor supports an RFC 3161 timestamp type, which means you can upload timestamps on a cron or scheduled job to Rekor for more assurance of its integrated time. That can provide some guarantees that entries are monotonic in relation to those timestamps.
luc-lynx: > the protection is coming from using the integrated time of the entry as a proxy for when the signature was created (the sig is part of the entry) Can you elaborate on that? I'm just trying to understand the security guarantees. Let's assume I rely only on the project tooling without additional code written and additional checks performed on my side - just using cosign sign/sign-blob, cosign verify with support for rekor checks (experimental enabled) and fulcio's "keyless" scheme like it's suggested in various posts, documentation and the EDX course. From my perspective the process can guarantee the following: _the signatures are trusted as long as all the signing keys have never been compromised despite the expiration time_. If any of the signing key pairs used was compromised - I cannot trust the root any longer (seems weird, but I need a revokation mechanism for expired keys), because the only way to stop the attack is to remove trust from the root key. This eliminates the advantages of using fulcio and "keyless" signing scheme (it even makes all the things worse because people will see short expiration times and won't be protecting expired keys properly) and gets us back to the security guarantees similar to static pub/priv key pair. Am I right?
haydentherapper: Walking through the signing and verification flow, focusing on where timestamps are referenced: On signing: 1) Fulcio creates a short-lived certificate, associating an identity with an ephemeral public key 2) The certificate is uploaded to a transparency log along with the signature and artifact hash 3) The log returns a signed bundle which includes the inclusion timestamp and artifact hash, and this is persisted with the certificate and signature (you can also ask the log for a proof of inclusion) On verification: 1) The Fulcio certificate's signature is verified from Sigstore's root of trust (shipped with Cosign), and ignoring time 2) The log presents the inclusion time of the entry, either from the signed bundle or requesting it from the log <-- We'll come back to this step 3) A verifier checks that the inclusion time is before the certificate's expiration time. If so, then the verifier knows that the certificate was valid when the artifact was signed, so we can trust the certificate, and therefore trust the ephemeral public key to verify the artifact signature. Step (2) of verification relies on the log to give you the inclusion time. That time is currently not signed by the log, so it could be mutated by a log operator without detection, which would result in a denial of service effectively, since certificates would not be considered valid. This can be mitigated by uploading signed timestamp entries, and we're also working on solving this with other timestamp formats too.
asraa: > the signatures are trusted as long as all the signing keys have never been compromised despite the expiration time. Note that you are still correct here: the expiration time is about 10 minutes, and a compromised key that re-uses the signing cert and signs during that 10 min window would still validate. Keyless attempts to have a small enough window where compromise is feasible compared to std PKI
luc-lynx: Thank you all for the explanation, now it's clear!
asraa: Closing because all clear!

title: Why is an SBOM attestation predicate wrapped in CosignPredicate?
body_text:
**Question**_x000D_
<!--What are you wondering about? Provide as much detail as you feel is_x000D_
necessary. We'll try and answer within our abilities to do so!-->_x000D_
_x000D_
When Cosign creates an SBOM attestation, the SBOM predicate is wrapped in [CosignPredicate](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/0f017f82d1f6201799548dc1d60dfbe61426e562/specs/COSIGN_PREDICATE_SPEC.md_x000D_
). ([spdx](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/5aa17b98ec2cb16721b314d48d5599df8d4387d9/pkg/cosign/attestation/attestation.go#L244-L246), [cyclonedx](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/5aa17b98ec2cb16721b314d48d5599df8d4387d9/pkg/cosign/attestation/attestation.go#L257-L259))_x000D_
Therefore, SBOM locates under `predicate.Data`._x000D_
_x000D_
The photo below is an example of spdx._x000D_
![sbom_attestation](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1850144/182736647-5e81a1cb-b904-4f60-90e7-0632d8d8e76c.png)_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
This differs from the [in-toto spdx specification](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/blob/bfd304734d26e5a10e16609ca812d605407d24c5/spec/predicates/spdx.md_x000D_
). It defines that the SBOM is located under the `predicate`._x000D_
_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
  // Standard attestation fields:_x000D_
  "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v0.1",_x000D_
  "subject": [{ ... }],_x000D_
_x000D_
  // Predicate:_x000D_
  "predicateType": "https://spdx.dev/Document",_x000D_
  "predicate": {_x000D_
    "SPDXID" : "SPDXRef-DOCUMENT",_x000D_
    "spdxVersion" : "SPDX-2.2",_x000D_
    ..._x000D_
  }_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This difference makes it difficult to tell whether the SBOM is in `predicate` or `predicate.Data`, when we get an SBOM attestation._x000D_
_x000D_
So, why is an SBOM attestation predicate wrapped in CosignPredicate?_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Cosign signing bundles
body_text:
Details of this proposal available in this [Google Doc.](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gucjOA_bGyRjK6TeaOI-X5GIUv8WsPzeMDMkq25Kv4Y/edit#heading=h.we5fqok7jai5)_x000D_
_x000D_
### Summary_x000D_
_x000D_
The current `sign-blob` command and documentation steer the user towards producing two files (raw sig and cert) for each signing operation.  This is not ideal because:_x000D_
_x000D_
- the two files do not contain enough information to enable offline verification._x000D_
- more files to store and pass as arguments is worse from a usability stand point._x000D_
- there is a lack of symmetry with the `cosign sign` command for OCI images which produces just one signing artifact._x000D_
_x000D_
These issues are likely to exacerbate inconsistencies across package manager and language ecosystems as each platform could produce a different combination of sig|cert|bundle.  _x000D_
_x000D_
[Our proposal](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gucjOA_bGyRjK6TeaOI-X5GIUv8WsPzeMDMkq25Kv4Y/edit#heading=h.we5fqok7jai5) produces a default blob signing and verification path that produces just one complete artifact supporting all verification use-cases. _x000D_
_x000D_
At this stage mainly looking for feedback/sanity check. Some details left to be worked out. Very happy to take suggestions for improvements. _x000D_

title: Support docker mirrors as default registry
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, when no registry is provided into the Global Unique Name (GUN), such as `vendor/image:version`, cosign will default the registry do `docker.io` and try to upload/retrieve the signatures when using `cosign verify vendor/image:version` or `cosign sign vendor/image:version`._x000D_
_x000D_
This is very true when using the default "mirror" registry, but can be false when there are extra mirror registries configured on the `docker-daemon.json`._x000D_
_x000D_
Although it would be possible to manually call `cosign sign MIRROR_REGISTRY/vendor/image:version`, when using third-party tools, such as connaisseur, on a cluster where there are mirrors configured, connaisseur will automatically pass the GUN to cosign without the registry, since it was pulled from a mirror that was configured on docker-daemon.json, meaning that "I don't" have control over  the image/GUN provided to cosign, causing it to fail since the image will not exist on the docker.io registry, but rather lives on a private registry._x000D_
_x000D_
The scenario that causes us to not prepend with the registry is that we have several mirrors that the URL change depending on the cluster it lives (I have several EKS clusters running on different countries) and I can re-use the same manifest for all of them just by configuring the mirror to that specific region.

title: How to get the Fulcio root certificate securely in `verify-blob`?
body_text:
First of all, thank you for the great project and everyone involved in it. I'm a maintainer of an [OSS project](https://github.com/terraform-linters/tflint) using cosign to sign release binaries. Our project uses GoReleaser for signing, and we run the following commands on the checksum:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 cosign sign-blob --output-certificate=checksum.txt.pem --output-signature=checksum.txt.keyless.sig checksum.txt_x000D_
```_x000D_
https://github.com/terraform-linters/tflint/blob/e7668cb182999e93a2e79534968d8ad686c14f14/.goreleaser.yml#L26-L37_x000D_
_x000D_
To verify this, we provide a verification example as follows:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign verify-blob --cert checksums.txt.pem --signature checksums.txt.keyless.sig --certificate-github-workflow-repository=terraform-linters/tflint checksums.txt_x000D_
```_x000D_
https://github.com/terraform-linters/tflint/blob/e7668cb182999e93a2e79534968d8ad686c14f14/README.md#verification_x000D_
_x000D_
However, I understand that this way does not verify the `checksum.txt.pem`'s certificate chain against the Fulcio root trust, so it is not sufficient:_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/v1.10.1/cmd/cosign/cli/verify/verify_blob.go#L122-L129_x000D_
_x000D_
To avoid this, I understand that I need to pass the Fulcio root certificate with the `--certificate-chain` option:_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/v1.10.1/cmd/cosign/cli/verify/verify_blob.go#L131-L139_x000D_
_x000D_
Now the question is, how can I get this root certificate securely?_x000D_
_x000D_
I have confirmed that I can get certificates locally using TUF by `cosign initialize`. I can use this to build a certificate chain like this:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign initialize_x000D_
cat ~/.sigstore/root/targets/fulcio_intermediate_v1.crt.pem > fulcio_chained.crt.pem_x000D_
echo >> fulcio_chained.crt.pem_x000D_
cat ~/.sigstore/root/targets/fulcio.crt.pem >> fulcio_chained.crt.pem_x000D_
echo >> fulcio_chained.crt.pem_x000D_
cat ~/.sigstore/root/targets/fulcio_v1.crt.pem >> fulcio_chained.crt.pem_x000D_
_x000D_
cosign verify-blob --cert checksums.txt.pem --cert-chain fulcio_chained.crt.pem --signature checksums.txt.keyless.sig --certificate-github-workflow-repository=terraform-linters/tflint checksums.txt_x000D_
Verified OK_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
But I'm not sure I can trust this local cache. In my opinion, it's safest to also get this root certificate by the TUF client, like `COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 cosign verify-blob`:_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/v1.10.1/cmd/cosign/cli/verify/verify_blob.go#L220-L227_x000D_
_x000D_
What do you think about this? Is there a better way?

I think this was noted in a prior issue, but I can't find it right now. > To avoid this, I understand that I need to pass the Fulcio root certificate with the --certificate-chain option: Correct. > But I'm not sure I can trust this local cache. In my opinion, it's safest to also get this root certificate by the TUF client, like Yes, actually `cosign initialize` performs the same retrieval of the targets `GetRoots()` and `GetIntermediates()` like the code you linked to. This is the code run to `GetRoots()`: https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/blob/dbd7b3ace9d39828d0ee8d0e5b6a73101fe094aa/pkg/fulcioroots/fulcioroots.go#L83-L95 It creates a [new TUF environment ](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/blob/dbd7b3ace9d39828d0ee8d0e5b6a73101fe094aa/pkg/tuf/client.go#L316) and gets the targets by name of the file or usage. This is also what's called when you run [cosign initialize](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/25b4d5e0e648036556b4048e5260018fe23c273a/cmd/cosign/cli/initialize/init.go#L39). Originally I will guess the thought was that by providing only the certificate, it's just a vehicle for providing the public key. I'm fine with changing the behavior, either to mandate a chain be provided or fetch from TUF. | wata727: Thank you for answering my question. > Honestly, by default, if no certificate chain is provided, then we SHOULD verify against the root pool retrieved from GetRoots(). body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
@eddiezane and I stumbled on this today - verify-blob has logic for handling DSSE messages _x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/128f8fbd5f1bed0f7f1069d01c7e33cd52f6c381/cmd/cosign/cli/verify/verify_blob.go#L234-L237_x000D_
_x000D_
but when this is combined with COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL, it fails:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
$ cat test.json.sig _x000D_
{"payloadType":"application/vnd.in-toto+json","payload":"eyJfdHlwZSI6Imh0dHBzOi8vaW4tdG90by5pby9TdGF0ZW1lbnQvdjAuMSIsInByZWRpY2F0ZVR5cGUiOiIiLCJzdWJqZWN0IjpbeyJuYW1lIjoiIiwiZGlnZXN0Ijp7InNoYTI1NiI6IjVmMzY0OTgwZjc0NDAwZjg3NzNmODJjZjU4ZWM3ODQ0YTExZDI3Y2YifX1dLCJwcmVkaWNhdGUiOnsibmFtZSI6InVuaXQtdGVzdC0xIiwic3RhdHVzIjoic3VjY2VzcyJ9fQ==","signatures":[{"keyid":"","sig":"MEUCIEha6COOH9fAeqZE36P2nlpmT5dmN/DQdi6ffhdEI5s1AiEAlVTKIYxPAQLxbTUBjOIdFJLzkLf9wgSGH2VuTdx4k9U="}]}_x000D_
_x000D_
$ COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 cosign verify-blob --signature test.json.sig test.json.sig --cert=<(rekor-cli get --log-index 3121421 --format json | jq -r .Body.IntotoObj.publicKey | base64 -d)_x000D_
Error: verifying blob [test.json.sig]: searching log query: [POST /api/v1/log/entries/retrieve][400] searchLogQueryBadRequest  &{Code:400 Message:verifying signature: failed to verify signature: %!w(<nil>)}_x000D_
main.go:62: error during command execution: verifying blob [test.json.sig]: searching log query: [POST /api/v1/log/entries/retrieve][400] searchLogQueryBadRequest  &{Code:400 Message:verifying signature: failed to verify signature: %!w(<nil>)}_x000D_
_x000D_
$ cosign verify-blob --signature test.json.sig test.json.sig --cert=<(rekor-cli get --log-index 3121421 --format json | jq -r .Body.IntotoObj.publicKey | base64 -d)_x000D_
Verified OK_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
We think the root cause is verify-blob is expecting a blob + signature (because by default it's not expecting raw bytes, not a DSSE envelope), so when it tries to look up the rekor entry it fails because the check to whether to lookup by `HashedRekord` or `Intoto` depends on whether a signature is present (it assumes a signature for DSSE is not needed because it's in the message itself):_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/128f8fbd5f1bed0f7f1069d01c7e33cd52f6c381/pkg/cosign/tlog.go#L289-L303_x000D_
_x000D_
however, verify-blob requires --signature, which means you can't query by intoto:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ cosign verify-blob test.json.sig --cert=<(rekor-cli get --log-index 3121421 --format json | jq -r .Body.IntotoObj.publicKey | base64 -d) _x000D_
Error: verifying blob [test.json.sig]: missing flag '--signature'_x000D_
main.go:62: error during command execution: verifying blob [test.json.sig]: missing flag '--signature'_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
We can't use verify-attestation, since that is assuming there's an OCI image (I'm just trying to verify a raw DSSE envelope signed by via keyless signing)._x000D_
_x000D_
One thing that was a bit surprising was that verify-blob had any kind of special casing for DSSE at all. Maybe it would be worth breaking this up into a separate verify-dsse subcommand, or let verify-attestation act on direct messages instead of requiring OCI?_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Proposal: Command and format for signing in-toto attestations with DSSE
body_text:
**Summary**_x000D_
Proposal for a way to easily sign in-toto attestations and optionally upload them to Rekor. After a successful signing the result should be capture in a file on the local filesystem. This is very similar to this issue https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2131 for signing blobs. What I see different is that we would like to capture not just the payload hash, but the entire payload (DSSE envelope) together with the cert, chain and optionally signed timestamp etc. from Rekor._x000D_
This format could also serve as the payload type for APIs, so we can standardize on how to persist and query for attestations._x000D_
_x000D_
**Motivation** _x000D_
The are some initiatives for creating in-toto attestations in DSSE envelopes, and uploading them to Rekor._x000D_
* SLSA GitHub Generator https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator _x000D_
* SLSA build provenance for npm packages https://github.com/npm/rfcs/pull/626_x000D_
* With more package managers looking into signing packages with Sigstore, one could hope that next step would be to also produce provenance attestations, so similar problem would need to be solved again._x000D_
_x000D_
The SLSA GitHub Generator only uploads the in-toto attestation as a build artifact, the Rekor entry is searched for from the ledger during verification. The certificate is stored in the DSSE envelope, as proposed here https://github.com/secure-systems-lab/dsse/issues/42. Having them stored together in a defined format could simplify for clients, as they can perform offline verification (given that they have the public key for Rekor). _x000D_
The build provenances for npm will be uploaded to the package registry, so they can be downloaded by the CLI during install to perform an offline verification. So some way of transfer and receive those together is needed. _x000D_
_x000D_
**Description**_x000D_
Proposed is a JSON schema for capturing a DSSE envelope, certificate and chain, and optionally a Rekor entry. As there can be private artifacts, the Rekor entry is optional. A proposal to start the discussion:_x000D_
_x000D_
```JSON_x000D_
{_x000D_
  "mediaType": "application/vnd.sigstore.attestation-manifest.v1+json",_x000D_
  "attestationType": "attestation/dsse",_x000D_
  "attestation": {_x000D_
    "payloadType": "application/vnd.in-toto+json",_x000D_
    "payload": "B64(STRING)",_x000D_
    "signatures": [_x000D_
      {_x000D_
        "keyid": "",_x000D_
        "sig": "B64(SIGNATURE)"_x000D_
      }_x000D_
    ]_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  "certificate": "PEM-encoded X.509",_x000D_
  "certificateChain": "Array of PEM-encoded X.509 certificates",_x000D_
  "signedEntryTimestamp": "B64(SIGNATURE)",_x000D_
  "integratedTime": "1658759758",_x000D_
  "logIndex": 1234,_x000D_
  "logID": "a374bd6e23dda81396b1285eca20f99326d458505a4a80027a54faa30860eea2"_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Analogue to [this](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gucjOA_bGyRjK6TeaOI-X5GIUv8WsPzeMDMkq25Kv4Y/edit?disco=AAAAeC1DTMs) discussion, the information captured from Rekor is enough to verify the signed timestamp. _x000D_
_x000D_
The reason for having the `attestationType` being specified in the document is that we want to be forward compatible with other envelopes, such as COSE which Rekor supports. This would indicate that the `attestation` schema is actually depending on the value of `attestationType`. _x000D_
_x000D_
I think it's most important to try to settle on a schema first, any API design around this can be thought of in the future.

title: [Bug] Incorrect Verification: Verification succeeds using an expired certificate with offline verification
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
This is a bug about Cosign verification flow. When experimental mode is turned OFF (in "offline verification": we still use bundles), Cosign validates a signature successfully despite the fact that the certificate is expired. This occurs when TLOG upload is bypassed, or the offline bundle is removed. This is because without experimental mode, it has no access to make a network call._x000D_
_x000D_
So, for example, I can bypass TLOG upload, and allow successful verification. I can re-use an old, expired cert, and pass verification, and not TLOG upload. **This is ESPECIALLY the case if I have clients who are only relying on offline bundles (so they turn off COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL). Therefore, I can trick clients who were expecting to use cosign with offline verification.**_x000D_
_x000D_
In other standards, you will fail:_x000D_
* https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2632: `Some of the many places where signature and certificate checking_x000D_
   might fail include:[...]   - the certificate is expired`_x000D_
* In https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-6.1.3, processing certificates requires checking that the certificate is valid._x000D_
* https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5750#section-5: Describes using a reliable time for a certificate validity check_x000D_
_x000D_
**Version**_x000D_
_x000D_
At head, and all versions._x000D_
_x000D_
**Proposed Fix**_x000D_
Exit code 1 in this case. Signatures should only be valid if the certificate is expired OR a timestamp is fetched/provided proving that the signature was generated during the validity window. _x000D_
_x000D_
The output states_x000D_
```_x000D_
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:_x000D_
- The cosign claims were validated_x000D_
- The signatures were verified against the specified public key_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Are the signatures really verified against the certificate? **The certificate is expired.** If a certificate is REVOKED in traditional systems, would you still pass signature validation? _x000D_
_x000D_
_Long term:_ _x000D_
To me, this issue points to a flaw that cosign's validation flow allows signature to be passing UNLESS something like a timestamp has access to be checked, rather than a better, way more secure flow: a signature should be failing until the requirements are satisfied._x000D_
_x000D_
cc @znewman01 @codysoyland @haydentherapper and others who may be interested in security issues._x000D_
_x000D_

title: Cosign should retry Fulcio and Rekor RPCs
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
@vaikas mentioned to me that cosign commands occasionally fail due to an unexpected error either from the network or Sigstore backends.  These errors typically will come at the very end of a CI job.  To avoid failing expensive long running jobs with a transient cosign error we should retry failed Sigstore calls. _x000D_
_x000D_
We should do this in all Sigstore clients. _x000D_
_x000D_
Ideally this would be implemented with configurable exponential backoff and timeout. _x000D_
_x000D_

all versions_x000D_

title: signature revokation support or approach
body_text:
**Question**_x000D_
_x000D_
Is signature revocation supported in "cosign"?_x000D_
_x000D_
if yes, how to achieve that?
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: Revocation is a notoriously tricky problem. In general, at signature verification time, the verifier needs to fetch an up-to-date list of the things that have been revoked (keys, identities, etc.) and check that the signature is still valid. There are a number of approaches here and it's still [an area of active research](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?as_ylo=2021&q=certificate+revocation). In Sigstore, our philosophy is broadly: ["revoke artifacts, not keys"](https://blog.sigstore.dev/how-to-sign-a-release-of-oss-e96ee94286fc). The idea is that *identities* are long-lived (like your Gmail account); we generally don't want to burn those to the ground every time a signature needs to be revoked. If we use a new key pair for each signature, then we can revoke specific artifacts from a signer without revoking everything that signer has ever signed. (In some cases, you *do* want to revoke everything from a particular signer. That's supported by removing the identity from your list of trusted identities, but it's a *different* operation.) How you achieve this depends on how you're doing verification. We have a [blog post](https://blog.sigstore.dev/dont-panic-a-playbook-for-handling-account-compromise-with-sigstore-ee299dca5144) that gives some specific examples for a homemade verification system (which makes the mechanics clearer). But you could achieve the same thing with [sigstore/policy-controller](https://github.com/sigstore/policy-controller) or [Kyverno](https://blog.sigstore.dev/how-to-verify-container-images-with-kyverno-using-kms-cosign-and-workload-identity-1e07d2b85061). Does that make sense? If you can share the scenario in which you're signing/verifying artifacts, we may be able to provide more specific advice. | haydentherapper: Revocation is hard - How do you build such a list? How do you authorize who can upload a revoked artifact to a public list for Sigstore? How should a client poll for updates to a list? Where does a client store this list? How do you prevent this list from growing too large? Echoing @znewman01, I would try to solve this through a verification policy rather than design a revocation mechanism. Specify what identities you trust for which artifacts for example, and update that mapping if an identity needs to be "revoked". | rajpratik71: A similar approach which the "Notary v1" or "docker trust" command does to sign and revoke the signature of an artifact tag, can be used/implemented to achieve a bit level of signature revocation.

Based on the [`docker trust` docs](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/trust_revoke/), it does something pretty analgous to `cosign clean`. I have gone through the approaches provided by [sigstore/policy-controller](https://github.com/sigstore/policy-controller) or [Kyverno](https://blog.sigstore.dev/how-to-verify-container-images-with-kyverno-using-kms-cosign-and-workload-identity-1e07d2b85061) which are fine for K8S based environment. If you have more sophisticated infrastructure, you'll need to use a policy engine there. A couple of caveats: - make sure to refer to images by *digest* (not *tag*) once you've resolved the image, since the tags are mutable (even on an immutable registry, it's possible for an attacker to change the tag). - make sure when you call `cosign verify` you're passing either a key (`--key foo.pub`) or identity (`--certificate-email me@example.com --certificate-oidc-issuer https://accounts.google.com` (see https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2056 for context) Something like the following should work (stick hashes of revoke artifacts in `$BAD_DIGESTS_FILE`) ``` BAD_DIGESTS_FILE=/tmp/bad-digests REPO=gcr.io/projectsigstore/cosign EMAIL=keyless@projectsigstore.iam.gserviceaccount.com ISSUER=https://accounts.google.com TAG=v1.9.0 DIGEST=$(crane digest $REPO:$TAG) grep $DIGEST $BAD_DIGESTS_FILE && exit 1 cosign verify $REPO@$DIGEST \ --certificate-email $EMAIL \ --certificate-oidc-issuer $ISSUER if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then docker run $REPO@$DIGEST else echo "Bad signature!" fi ``` *Edit: added revocation*

But for a CLI based environment like "docker" or "other CLI" or even in "compose" environments, is there any way to achieve it and enforce it by default on system level through plugins in these environments ? or similar thing

But I'd argue that this is really outside the scope of what Docker on its own is meant for—Docker just runs the things you hand it. Making sure that those things are legitimate is the job of whoever's handing Docker the images in the first place.

title: Add `cosign inspect` command.
body_text:
Related to [Sigstore clients should require a provided identity](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1o8_bXIygufgiohJGlmBzqF4_BnXCTfgh4ILgJFJxYRs/edit?resourcekey=0-YEar3v67uoT31kj83dCVvA)._x000D_
_x000D_
Right now, if you want to poke around at a signature/cert, the easiest way to do that is to run `cosign verify`. This is a little dangerous: commands that make it easy to verify artifacts just so you can pretty-print them often lead to patterns like "verify that this artifact was signed, but not *who* signed it."_x000D_
_x000D_
The above doc proposes dropping support in `cosign verify` for this purpose. We want to replace it with a `cosign inspect` command. This will probably look similar to `cosign verify` or `cosign verify-blob` *but* with all of the "predicates" removed (e.g. `--certificate-email`). It should print human-readable output about the certificate/etc. that were passed.
