title: `verify-blob` function should be implemented consistently with verify image function
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
`verify-blob` is now implemented in "cmd/cosign/cli/verify" package, but this is inconsistent with `verify`._x000D_
The core functions of `verify` such as `VerifyImageSignature()` are implemented in "pkg/cosign", and it is easy for developers to invoke cosign's verification function from their own golang projects._x000D_
However, `verify-blob` does not have this type of implementation, and developers need to call `VerifyBlobCmd()` directly. This function requires some arguments that are filepath, and this makes it hard for developers to invoke verify-blob functions from some environment such as read-only container. _x000D_
_x000D_
The core functions of `verify-blob` should be inside "pkg/cosign" as well as verify image functions, and the functions should accept non-filepath arguments._x000D_
(`VerifyBlobCmd()` will be just a wrapper which calls the core func in "pkg/cosign" in the new implementation.)_x000D_
_x000D_
#### Example_x000D_
For example, something like below in "pkg/cosign" is what I am proposing in this issue._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
func VerifyBlobSignature(ctx context.Context, blobBytes, sigBytes []byte, co *CheckOpts)_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
# reference func in pkg/cosign/verify.go_x000D_
func VerifyImageSignature(ctx context.Context, sig oci.Signature, h v1.Hash, co *CheckOpts)_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_

title: FR: offline mode
body_text:
`COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL` was introduced AFAICT for two reasons:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. The Sigstore *idea*, *interface*, and *implementation* were still experimental_x000D_
2. The Sigstore *infrastructure* wasn't reliable/didn't have guarantees._x000D_
_x000D_
So to start, anything that touched Sigstore infrastructure (TUF roots, Fulcio, Rekor) was gated: users needed to set `COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1` to use them._x000D_
_x000D_
Over time, we've blurred the line a little; without turning on experimental mode:_x000D_
_x000D_
- You can pass a Rekor bundle and cosign will check it._x000D_
- To do that, you need the Rekor public key, which you get via TUF (this goes over the network!)_x000D_
- Similarly, you can provide a cert signed by Fulcio, and cosign will check it against Fulcio's key_x000D_
-  It gets that key via TUF_x000D_
_x000D_
There's a question about "what is the point of `cosign verify-blob` without `COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL` but with a provided certificate?"_x000D_
_x000D_
I don't want to answer that, at least not here. It's hopefully going to be an obsolete question soon: we're relatively comfortable with the idea of Sigstore, and we're targeting general availability (GA) for the infrastrcucture soon: https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/issues/766 and https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/issues/1005 . **But**, at least some folks have been deliberately not providing this flag to indicate "don't try to hit the network." That's *sort-of* what it does right now: "I don't try to query Rekor/Fulcio, but I *know* about them, and also I'll get their keys via TUF."_x000D_
_x000D_
That suggests to me that, post-dropping-`COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL`, there should be some mechanism to verify offline. Maybe a `--offline` flag, or even a `verify-offline` command (which is nice because now we can *only* show users the relevant flags). If we do that, we probably want to have some requirement on how out-of-date your TUF roots can be (maybe user-configurable?) and instructions on how to grab them from `cosign initialize`.
top_3_comments_text: haydentherapper: +1 to an offline flag! Here's a copy paste of a comment I left on a doc when we were looking into the Cosign CVE: With no flag, I'd propose the behavior be: * Default to fetching from Rekor without any flags * To avoid a call to Rekor, either --- provide a bundle --- add a flag explicitly opting out of the rekor call | znewman01: +1 to that as the default behavior. Then, the additional changes for an offline mode: - use cached TUF state (after checking their age), which gives you Rekor/Fulcio root certs - fail the command immediately if the bundle or opt-out flag isn't provided - we never hit Fulcio in verification anyway AFAICT (though maybe eventually we should check the CT log by default unless an SCT is provided embedded in the cert) I think that covers it? | znewman01: Additional note: we need to give more guidance about offline settings, especially w/r/t TUF (do you mirror it? do you risk stale root certs?). I think this documentation would be really valuable.

haydentherapper: @asraa's design doc for the Sigstore TUF client also mentioned supporting offline TUF. IIRC it was configurable how to handle expired metadata.
vaikas: this may be relevant for the discussion here too: https://github.com/theupdateframework/go-tuf/pull/397

jku: For reference, I''ve been trying to figure out a good options for sigstore-python (mostly in context of TUF): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1IEVxgCsmLJNiAwdTFQ4aMvmGHJikmI_iOEHGpt8fIe8 (comments welcome) My conclusions so far: * an explicit `--offline` mode in a verifying sigstore client should still preferably use cached TUF metadata to verify the trust root that it has cached (even if this is not strictly an operation TUF spec defines). title: Data race in FetchSignaturesForReference
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--Tell us about the bug. What went wrong? How can we reproduce it? What should the correct behavior be?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
For each fetched signature, a new goroutine is spawned [here](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/pkg/cosign/fetch.go#L87). Each of these goroutines use the same `err error` variable, originally declared [here](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/pkg/cosign/fetch.go#L64)._x000D_
_x000D_
To make it a bit easier to read, I will copy and paste the code below:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
g.Go(func() error {_x000D_
	signatures[i].Payload, err = sig.Payload()_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		return err_x000D_
	}_x000D_
	signatures[i].Base64Signature, err = sig.Base64Signature()_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		return err_x000D_
	}_x000D_
	signatures[i].Cert, err = sig.Cert()_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		return err_x000D_
	}_x000D_
	signatures[i].Chain, err = sig.Chain()_x000D_
	if err != nil {_x000D_
		return err_x000D_
	}_x000D_
	signatures[i].Bundle, err = sig.Bundle()_x000D_
	return err_x000D_
})_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
We can see that we always use the same `err` in each goroutine, as `=` is used. This can lead to a race condition where errors are never propagated. For example, say we have two signatures, so two goroutines. It is possible that something like `signatures[i].Payload, err = sig.Payload()` is called and returns an error for one goroutine, but before it checks `if err != nil`, we context switch to the other goroutine which gives us `err = nil` in `signatures[i].Payload, err = sig.Payload()`. Then, we will never catch the error in either goroutine._x000D_
_x000D_
**Version**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What version are you using? e.g. `cosign version`..._x000D_
-->_x000D_
I am using v1.12.1, but from what I can tell, this has been around since [this PR](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/699), which has been around since v1.2.1.

title: RFE: Allow verifying CN when verifying using certificates
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
I have described how we are trying to use Cosign [here](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1554#issuecomment-1256109541), but in short, we provision identity certificates to all services and want to use those for signing and verification. So far, I've been able to sign using the cert and verify using kyverno (#1554: bug for verification usign cosign CLI)._x000D_
_x000D_
Given that all certificates issued using the Root CA will be valid when verifying using the root CA, we want to limit the servicePrincipal/userPrincipals whose signatures are trusted. It is similar to what is described in the "Self-managed keys in identity-based code signing certificate with auditability" section in [this blog post](https://blog.sigstore.dev/adopting-sigstore-incrementally-1b56a69b8c15)._x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, `cosign verify` command already has a bunch of `--certitificate-*` attributes, presumably intending to verify different attributes about the identity when using OIDC token. But the ask here to extend that to allow verifying `CN` for self managed certificates. Although, it would be better to support fields under `X509v3 Subject Alternative Name` as a more general verification. _x000D_
_x000D_

before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_

title: [bug] verify-blob & rekor shards: search all shards for proposed entries
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/fluxcd/source-controller/issues/899#issuecomment-1261295343_x000D_
_x000D_
After rekor sharded, the current Rekor tree is moved to a new one. _x000D_
_x000D_
When verifying blobs, we search the Rekor log proposed entries:_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/727e3e1d4af2856126f67c014d5bd2cf4b29a94a/pkg/cosign/tlog.go#L392_x000D_
_x000D_
and expect that exactly **one** entry was retrieved._x000D_
_x000D_
Rekor CURRENTLY only searches the **CURRENT** tree for an entry, and will fail if the leaf is not present on the current log. That is causing the flux verify-blob failure after the shard rotation:_x000D_
```_x000D_
could not find entry in tlog: signature not found in transparency logError: verifying blob [./checksums.txt]: signature not found in transparency log_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The entry did not exist on the current log._x000D_
_x000D_
As a fix (TBD), rekor will search ALL previous shards and may return more than one search entry. Because of this, the following changes need to happen in cosign:_x000D_
1. Allow multiple entries returned from [SearchLogQuery](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/727e3e1d4af2856126f67c014d5bd2cf4b29a94a/pkg/cosign/tlog.go#L409)_x000D_
2. In the cosign case, we need to start using a function like `tlogFindEarliestEntry` to replace https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/727e3e1d4af2856126f67c014d5bd2cf4b29a94a/cmd/cosign/cli/verify/verify_blob.go#L410: the earliest entry with the earliest integrated time will always suffice for expiration checks._x000D_
3. In the container case, [these](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/727e3e1d4af2856126f67c014d5bd2cf4b29a94a/pkg/cosign/verify.go#L358-L384) funcs also need to be fixed, again, to handle multiple return entries, and selecting the earliest one for the certificate validation._x000D_
_x000D_
Note: old clients MAY be OK after the rekor fix: this will only affect users who are verifying blobs (or online lookups for containers) with cosign AND there were duplicate uploads on multiple shards. However, if there were re-uploads or duplicate entries across shards, old clients will break if rekor responds with multiple entries._x000D_
_x000D_
cc @haydentherapper @bobcallaway @priyawadhwa @lukehinds @stefanprodan _x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
**Version**_x000D_

title: Verify the binary downloads when installing from .deb (or any other binary release)
body_text:
How can we verify the binary downloads when installing from .deb?_x000D_
_x000D_
Can the downloads be verified with openssl or gpg?_x000D_
_x000D_
It's kind of an chicken and egg problem if you use `cosign` to sign blobs, you assume there is a `cosign` version already on the system, but in my case it is not.
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: If I understand correctly, you're saying: why should I trust the .deb files (and other release artifacts) coming from the Cosign repository on GitHub itself. This is a pretty interesting question, glad you asked it :) I can think of three broad approaches: 1. Provide alternate signatures (e.g., using GPG). 2. Provide instructions for performing Cosign verification manually. There's nothing magic about Sigstore, and you can cobble together everything it does from openssl (ex. [sigstore the bash way](https://gist.github.com/bobcallaway/e669534a9591c802b64c84603323c2c0)). 3. Distribute Cosign over some existing secure channel. In some sense, if you're downloading over TLS, you're already doing this. But this could also refer to downloading Cosign from the official Ubuntu repositories, where it will be signed. IMO (1) and (2) are actually misleading: if you don't have Cosign on your system, you probably don't already have the keys used to sign the Cosign releases on your system. So even if you could use GPG to verify, if you're just pulling the GPG key from the same place you're downloading Cosign you're not really gaining any security since an attacker who could replace the Cosign binary could also replace the purported signing key. You have to take a leap of faith at some point, and it's nice to do (3) and at least tie your trust in Cosign back to something *else* you're already trusting. You might be able to do something convoluted that looks something like [diverse double compiling](https://dwheeler.com/trusting-trust/). You as a client download Cosign and an alternate Sigstore implementation from another organization, and use them to verify each others' signatures. But the problem of "what keys should you check the signatures against" is left unanswered still. You could also try to rebuild the .debs yourself from source and see if they match ([reproducible builds](https://reproducible-builds.org/)). But this just kicks the question up one level: how do you know the source is legitimate? I suppose what I'm saying is that I'm somewhat nihilistic about this whole process and I recommend you just consider the initial Cosign download to be the root of trust for the system. title: Feature: Provide an easier way to retrieve SBOM from In-Toto attestation
body_text:
Since https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1756 cosign issues a warning when using `cosign attach sbom` and `cosign download sbom`, heavily encouraging users to use `cosign attest` and `cosign download attestation` instead:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
WARNING: Downloading SBOMs this way does not ensure its authenticity. If you want to ensure a tamper-proof SBOM, download it using 'cosign download attestation <image uri>' or verify its signature._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
While I don't really like this change, because all our sboms are signed and there is no need to scare the users like that, we are trying to migrate to use said attestations._x000D_
_x000D_
Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be an easy way to retrieve the original SBOM document from an attestation. The `cosign download sbom` could be used to retrieve the original SBOM (and nothing else), but this is a lot harder when using attestations: _x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub --type cyclonedx my-registry/my-image:1.0.0 | jq '.payload | @base64d | fromjson | .predicate.Data'_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This is the easiest way I could come up. This also requires the user to have additional tools available (`jq` in this case)._x000D_
_x000D_
I think there should be a command to retrieve the original SBOM (producing the exact same output) as it is already possible with `cosign download sbom`. Currently, SBOMs attached as attestation-predicates feel like second-class citizens.

This would be consistent with the rest of the CLI commands. When using this flag, the output of the two commands below should be almost the same: ``` cosign verify-attestation ... --decode ``` ``` cosign verify-attestation ... | jq '.payload | @base64d | fromjson | .predicate' ``` The description suggests the `jq` expression to end in `.predicate.Data` but that won't work with all attestation types I'm aware of. They can be retrieved like this: ``` cosign verify-attestation quay.io/lucarval/festoji:latest \ --type spdx \ --certificate-github-workflow-repository lcarva/festoji \ --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/lcarva/festoji/.github/workflows/package.yaml@refs/heads/master' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' cosign verify-attestation quay.io/lucarval/festoji:latest \ --type slsaprovenance \ --certificate-github-workflow-repository lcarva/festoji \ --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/.github/workflows/generator_container_slsa3.yml@refs/tags/v1.7.0' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' ``` Neither one of those would work with the suggested `.predicate.Data` expression. @ChristianCiach, is using `.predicate` instead of `.predicate.Data` a problem for your use case?
ChristianCiach: @lcarva First of all, thank you! > @ChristianCiach, is using `.predicate` instead of `.predicate.Data` a problem for your use case? It is my understanding that `.predicate` is now correct in *all* cases, since the nesting under `.Data` was mistake that has been fixed in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2718
ChristianCiach: It just occurred to me that my proposed solution (`--decode` to decode the payload and concat the resulting documents) may be a bit too naive. I am not an expert when it comes to the in-toto format, but as far as I understand it, there can be multiple predicates for the same `type`. For example, when you do `cosign verify-attestation quay.io/lucarval/festoji:latest --type spdx`, the output may contain multiple spdx-documents. In https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2307#issuecomment-1415670359 I proposed to just concat the JSON documents, using one line for each document (see `jsonl` format). This works nicely if the decoded payload is actually JSON, but it is my understanding that the decoded payload can be everything, including binary blobs. Of course, concatting binary output is obviously a bad idea.. So what should be do? Options: * Only support `--decode` for JSON-like payloads. This also means that we have to remove any linebreaks from the decoded payload. This seems too specialized. I actually don't like that. * Change `--decode` to `--decode-first` or maybe even `--decode=0` (or `--decode=1` and so on) to only decode a single payload and only print this to stdout. I think I prefer this option. **Edit:** * Or just crash with an error if there is more than one document for the given `--type`.
lcarva: Good points! I have a suggestion that might help. Given that a certain predicate type is expected to have a certain structure, it would be very unusual to have a mix of data types when filtering by a particular predicate type. And that, AFAICT, it's not possible to use `cosign verify-attestation` to handle more than one predicate type in the same command execution. And that we mostly care about JSON data for this particular feature. And that multiple JSON documents can be easily represented with JSONL. (One JSON document per line.) Then, let's introduce a new output type called `json-predicate` (or `decoded-json`) to trigger the behavior we get today with `jq '.payload | @base64d | fromjson | .predicate'` If someone uses `--output=json-predicate` with a predicate that is not in JSON format, then an error is expected. In the future, we could add support for things like `xml-predicate`, for example. Thoughts?
ChristianCiach: That would be perfectly fine for me, since I am only interested in cyclonedx-json predicates. That being said, I don't feel it is particularly smart to specialise in specific predicate types. Your solution seems a bit too custom-tailored to my specific use-case. *That* being said, cosign *already is* specialised for specific predicate types (since there is special support for certain `--type` values). Speaking of `--type`, doesn't it make `--output=json-predicate` redundant? If I specify `--type cyclonedx`, then "json" should be implied, right? It doesn't make sense to specify any different `--output` format if json is already guaranteed by the given `--type`.
ChristianCiach: It looks like I've underestimated the complexity of this feature request. I am perfectly comfortable with continuing to work out the details before we implement some solution that turns out to be a bad idea.
lcarva: It also seems like my assumption is incorrect. CycloneDX appears to [use the same predicate type](https://cyclonedx.org/specification/overview/#recognized-predicate-type) for both JSON and XML. So my suggestion may be naive. It also means that inferring the data format from the predicate type is not a viable solution. To be fair, I do not know of many instances where the predicate is not JSON. My perception is that this is the pseudo-standard format for predicates, but admittedly I don't have a large sample size to give this statement any merit. But! My suggestion is not specifically targeting your use case; it's also targeting mine. Having to use `jq` is not the best user experience. Having said all that, I still think my suggestion is reasonable and should work for most cases. That's ok because it's optional - the behavior is not being imposed on anyone. We can always improve it over time as other use cases become clearer. I would be interested in also hearing what others think in case @ChristianCiach and I just happen to have a narrow view of the problem.
ChristianCiach: Thanks for your insight. Maybe it's wise to just do nothing for now. When cosign releases its next version and users are facing the deprecation warnings for the `sbom` attachments, I expect we will see more users asking for ways to produce the same output as `cosign download sbom` did before.
ChaosInTheCRD: Hey all, great to see that this issue is still being crunched through in my absence! I am pretty interested in how this issue shapes up looking towards a proposed implementation. I will probably at some point be looking to do similar in the [witness](https://github.com/testifysec/witness) project! Everything you have both discussed is very valid and I think it's important to consider as close to every possible edge case before implementing something. I do think however that the biggest use case for a feature like this is the "I am learning / debugging and I just want to view the predicate". If that can be done without creating situations where people feel upon using it that it is dysfunctional due to a lack of support of their specific scenario, I think it would be a worthwhile feature 😄

title: Feat: option for online tlog verification of containers/blobs
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Right now, all containers use offline verification by default, and only perform online verification as a fallback mechanism. This is because offline Rekor bundles are stored along in the OCI registry._x000D_
_x000D_
Proposal: Expose an option (default off) to perform online verification against Rekor. By doing this paranoid users can enable online verification, and we can also more easily detect when Rekor is performing incorrectly in testing and probers! The verification outage due to sharding Rekor (https://github.com/sigstore/public-good-instance/pull/871) would have been detected too!_x000D_
_x000D_
This does NOT include verification against some current state: this is just to dictate whether we are using the proof online/offline. For full paranoia, we would require some check against the state of Rekor to some trusted state._x000D_
_x000D_
cc @haydentherapper @priyawadhwa
top_3_comments_text: haydentherapper: Small nit, I know I’ve been calling this paranoid mode, but we should probably call it something more enticing publicly, like “stronger verification” or something. | asraa: I'd probably expose this an option for `VerifyOpts` like `OnlineLogVerify` actually: `RekorOptions` makes more sense! edit: actually i don't know. now I'm thinking `CheckOpts`. | haydentherapper: Another question, should we mandate that you provide a previous checkpoint for the consistency proof? I think yes, otherwise there’s not much point to the online lookup.
all_comments_text:
haydentherapper: Small nit, I know I’ve been calling this paranoid mode, but we should probably call it something more enticing publicly, like “stronger verification” or something.
asraa: I'd probably expose this an option for `VerifyOpts` like `OnlineLogVerify` actually: `RekorOptions` makes more sense! edit: actually i don't know. now I'm thinking `CheckOpts`.
haydentherapper: Another question, should we mandate that you provide a previous checkpoint for the consistency proof? I think yes, otherwise there’s not much point to the online lookup.
haydentherapper: I don’t know if we need to prioritize this before there’s support for gossiping. I would like this mode to provide the strongest assurances against a malicious log.
asraa: > I think yes, otherwise there’s not much point to the online lookup. Part of it is to make sure Rekor isn't misbehaving: Rekor serves you an offline proof, and then gets compromised and the log is rotated, if you were part of the compromise you would fail now, rather than rely on your old bundled proof.
asraa: Honestly, part of my motivation is that no one detected the Rekor outage in staging because no one HAD the option of using Rekor online for containers!
haydentherapper: So maybe two phases for this? One to add a flag just to say “online lookup”, and one to also gossip. I think this also fits in nicely with the required work around removing the experimental flag.
asraa: > One to add a flag just to say “online lookup”, That's the current scope! Feel free to add a follow-up issue for the second. And yeah: I think if the experimental flag goes away, this helps dictate when users are doing verification online & offline
asraa: Added a description about that in the issue of non-goal and that it would require state checking for full paranoia mode.
znewman01: Would it be possible to fold this into https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2466 ? IIUC the proposals there capture it (The gossip stuff isn't tracked there though, but I think that should be a separate issue anyway.)
haydentherapper: https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2466 captures the necessity for an online lookup flag, I've renamed the issue to reflect this. I think we should leave this open for now and have 2466 as a larger tracking issue. I'll open an issue on what's necessary to monitor for consistency and detect split-view attacks once Rekor has support for gossiping.

title: Allow using a TSA instead of Rekor to validate certs
body_text:
Right now, cosign assumes that every Fulcio cert has an associated entry in Rekor. The time that the entry was added to Rekor is used to verify that the signature happened during the cert's validity period._x000D_
_x000D_
We can get the same guarantee with a TSA. We'll need to refactor cosign to allow using a TSA instead of Rekor. We'll also want to store this TSA in the bundle so offline verification still works._x000D_
_x000D_
It would be nice to give users the option to choose between Rekor or the TSA!
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: CC @haydentherapper I know you've talked about this before, I thought there was somewhere this was being tracked but I can't find it. | haydentherapper: This came up in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2194, when discussing how to handle expired certificates. Either a Rekor entry or a signed timestamp should suffice as a countersignature over time. A TSA doesn't offer public auditability however, so it's not exactly equivalent to a Rekor entry. A verifier may want both a timestamp and Rekor entry - The timestamp to provide a third-party assertion over time, and the Rekor entry to provide an auditable record. I've been working on spinning up a timestamp authority - https://github.com/sigstore/timestamp-authority. Sigstore will deploy one, and any other interested community members can spin up their own TSA too. Support for timestamps within Rekor entries, to provide immutable timestamps and replace the integrated time, is something that @cdris is working on! Ceri will be sharing a doc with the community shortly about how we can currently verify entries with a TSA, propose how to include timestamps in Rekor entries, and where we want to go from there. The bundle that's been proposed does have support for RFC3161 timestamps, as we plan to add them into Rekor entries in the near future. We don't have an open issue yet - Related is a discussion on Roughtime (https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/issues/831), but @cdris will open an issue in Rekor soon. cc @asraa also | asraa: > It would be nice to give users the option to choose between Rekor or the TSA! We can start with an env var for trusting a TSA root CA, but we also need a plan for inserting a TSA root CA into TUF. Just FYI: if Sigstore deploys one, no problem, but as we do this work I'll track changes we'll need fro mthe TUF side.

title: Fix Counter-Signing demo in README
body_text:
Right now, the counter-signing demo has you sign an image, then sign the signature as follows:_x000D_
_x000D_
```shell_x000D_
$ crane tag $(cosign triangulate dlorenc/demo) mysignature_x000D_
2021/02/15 20:22:55 dlorenc/demo:mysignature: digest: sha256:71f70e5d29bde87f988740665257c35b1c6f52dafa20fab4ba16b3b1f4c6ba0e size: 556_x000D_
$ cosign sign --key cosign.key -a sig=counter dlorenc/demo:mysignature_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
However, this signs the signature by tag (see #2047), opening you up to race conditions._x000D_
_x000D_
The ideal workflow would be:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. (party A) cosign sign the image_x000D_
2. (party B) cosign triangulate to get the signature_x000D_
3. (party B) crane digest to get the digest of the signature_x000D_
4. (party B) cosign verify the signature by digest_x000D_
5. (party B) cosign sign the signature *by digest*_x000D_
_x000D_
However, (4) is a pain right now AFAICT; the `--signature` parameter doesn't accept OCI references._x000D_
_x000D_
```shell_x000D_
# Party A_x000D_
IMAGE_NAME=$(uuidgen | head -c 8)_x000D_
IMAGE_REPO=ttl.sh/$IMAGE_NAME_x000D_
IMAGE_URL=$IMAGE_REPO:10m_x000D_
IMAGE_URL_DIGEST=$(cosign upload blob -f /dev/null $IMAGE_URL)_x000D_
cosign sign --key cosign.key $IMAGE_URL_DIGEST_x000D_
_x000D_
# Party B_x000D_
cosign verify $IMAGE_URL  # works!_x000D_
_x000D_
SIG_URL=$(cosign triangulate $IMAGE_URL)_x000D_
SIG_DIGEST=$(crane digest $SIG_URL)_x000D_
SIG_URL_DIGEST=$IMAGE_REPO@$SIG_DIGEST_x000D_
cosign verify $IMAGE_URL  --signature $SIG_URL_DIGEST  # doesn't work :'( _x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
You can get around this, but not easily.

body_text:
It seems that cosign login doesn't support private registry on Google Container Registry._x000D_
_x000D_
I got "Error: registries must be valid RFC 3986 URI authorities: https://gcr.io/my-project-id" error while I was running the following scripts to login to my gcr registry._x000D_
_x000D_
```gcr-login.sh_x000D_
#!/usr/bin/env bash_x000D_
_x000D_
set -euo pipefail_x000D_
_x000D_
docker-credential-gcr config --token-source="env" > /dev/null 2>&1 && docker-credential-gcr configure-docker > /dev/null 2>&1_x000D_
TOKEN=$(echo "gcr.io" | docker-credential-gcr get | jq -r .Secret)_x000D_
_x000D_
echo "Docker login gcr.io/${GCP_PROJECT_ID}"_x000D_
cosign login -u oauth2accesstoken -p "${TOKEN}" "https://gcr.io/${GCP_PROJECT_ID}"_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Any ideas how to login to gcr?_x000D_

title: Require embedded SCT on verification by default
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, SCT verification happens on:_x000D_
* Signing, either by checking an embedded SCT (public good Fulcio) or a detached SCT returned in a header. It's skipped if an insecure flag is provided_x000D_
* Verification, if either the `enforce-sct` flag is set or if an embedded SCT is present._x000D_
_x000D_
Signing is good - Always check, unless you explicitly provide an insecure flag. However, for verification, you must present a flag to require the check, which is not ideal - This was added because previously issued certificates did not include an embedded SCT and the Cosign metadata did not include a way to persist the detached SCT._x000D_
_x000D_
I propose:_x000D_
1. We require that an SCT be embedded or explicitly provided for the detached case. For the detached case, we could either add new annotation metadata, or simply require it be passed by flag. Given the detached case is only for private deployments, I would probably go with flag for now._x000D_
1. We remove the `enforce-sct` flag and leverage an `insecure` flag to skip the check on verification._x000D_
_x000D_
This would be a part of Cosign 2.0, since it's a breaking change._x000D_
_x000D_
Code:_x000D_
* https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/d795dcb4ca44472896fec39b6ece4bafaee28f58/pkg/cosign/verify.go#L204-L215_x000D_
* https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/d795dcb4ca44472896fec39b6ece4bafaee28f58/cmd/cosign/cli/options/certificate.go#L77

title: Env variables are not taken into account when Azure user is signed in
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
When trying out signing with a key from Azure Key Vault it doesn't seem that the env variables are taken into account as described in the https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/kms_support#azure-key-vault. What happened was that I was signed in with a user account on the console and have also set the environment variables. The user account had permissions on the registry while the service principal that was set in the env variables had permissions on the Key Vault. It seems though that the code used the user account credentials to sign into Key Vault instead the credentials from the environment variables. _x000D_
_x000D_
Would be good to clarify and document what is the intended flow here._x000D_

title: Signing gitlab CI attestation with cosign
body_text:
Gitlab has recently started generating [attestations for build artifacts](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/runners/configure_runners.html#artifact-attestation). The attestation format is the standard intoto-attestation format._x000D_
_x000D_
I was hoping to sign the attestation and attach it to my docker image, using the command_x000D_
_x000D_
`cosign attest --predicate `gitlab-attestation.json` --key cosign.key my-registry/project`_x000D_
_x000D_
While this works, this seems to wrap another layer over the `gitlab-attestation.json`, because this `attest` command expects a predicate rather than a fully formed attestation._x000D_
_x000D_
Is there any way that I can sign and attach my fully formed gitlab attestation to my docker image, without having to extract only the predicate out from my `gitlab-attestation.json`?_x000D_
_x000D_
sample of the gitlab attestation format can be found in the [gitlab docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/runners/configure_runners.html#attestation-format)

znewman01: I don't completely understand how this is meant to be used. What I'd like to see happen is this: GitLab generates *and signs* (as GitLab) a Statement; you can then attach it to a container image with `cosign attach attestation`. This roughly means "I, GitLab, built these artifacts with this job;" anybody can verify this and trace back to find the workflow used. I believe [this issue](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/-/issues/29063) tracks implementing such a thing. The other common pattern is to take a *predicate* and use it to `cosign attest` to a particular container image. This means "I, Developer Foo, assert that this predicate is true about this container image." Instead, GitLab seems to be generating a Statement but not signing it. Then, somebody else is supposed to sign it. I guess this should be interpreted to mean "I, Developer Foo, grabbed this from GitLab and on GitLab was associated with these artifacts." For `cosign attest`, you provide an `<image URI>` argument separately from the predicate; that's the subject of the attestation. If Cosign let you provide the "subject" separately, it might conflict with the "image URI"! That doesn't make sense, so it's disallowed. You could imagine allowing a full "Statement" object to be passed, but then Cosign would just manually check that every field in the provenance object was correct (`_type`, `subject`, `predicateType`) so to my mind it may as well just create the provenance object itself. Maybe this is a worthwhile use case, though? Given that the GitLab Statement includes the `subject` field, maybe the workflow that *really* makes sense is: 1. GitLab generates a Statement 2. You download the statement and sign it, which means basically "I, Developer Foo, got this statement from GitLab." 3. Use `cosign attach attestation` to upload the signed statement. CC @SantiagoTorres who may have thoughts ------------------------------------------ Regarding the invalid format: see https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/-/issues/29246

I see that [in-here](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/-/issues/29063#note_1146301446) the consensus is around providing a way for gitlab to use a key, rather than managing the envelope. Personally, I would like for us to have a way to say "this gitlab instance attests this provenance". Who attaches it may just be a workflow problem (i.e., do you want to decide where to stick it and where? should that be configurable?). This also does make sense when considering we are fully trusting gitlab to provide the information about the provenance bits...

title: Support fetching a Fulcio certificate with a managed key
body_text:

_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, if you provide a key, this implies that you don't want to use Fulcio. Even if you specify `COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL`, the presence of the key flag will take priority. _x000D_
_x000D_
As per https://blog.sigstore.dev/adopting-sigstore-incrementally-1b56a69b8c15, one of the incremental options was to provide a key, but still get a code signing certificate and upload to the transparency log. This is currently not supported. The simplest way I can think of to implement this is to simply add another flag, something like `issue-certificate`, that will fetch a certificate and include it when uploading to the log and creating the OCI annotations._x000D_
_x000D_
In combination with https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2397, the incremental approaches would then look like:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. (Currently supported) Sign with self managed keys - `cosign import-key-pair --key key.pem`, and `cosign sign --key cosign.key artifact-path`_x000D_
2. (Supported using rekor-cli) Sign with self managed keys with auditability - `cosign sign --key cosign.key --tlog-upload artifact-path`_x000D_
3. NEW - Self-managed keys in code signing certs with auditability - `cosign sign --key cosign.key --tlog-upload --issue-certificate artifact-path`_x000D_
_x000D_

haydentherapper: The existing flags all serve other purposes, for example the one you linked is for fetching the OIDC token. This request is for changing the behavior of [this function](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/cmd/cosign/cli/sign/sign.go#L500), called from sign CLIs like [this](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/cmd/cosign/cli/sign/sign_blob.go#L62). I would recommend the following changes: * Add a boolean flag, `--issue-certificate`, default of `false`, for each of the sign CLI commands * Add a `IssueCertificate` boolean to `KeyOpts` ([code](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/cmd/cosign/cli/options/key.go#L20)). This value will get passed to `SignerFromKeyOpts` automatically. Set this value for each CLI command. * Change `SignerFromKeyOpts` ([code](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/cmd/cosign/cli/sign/sign.go#L500)) to read that value - If it's set, call [`keylessSigner`](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/cmd/cosign/cli/sign/sign.go#L511). * In `keylessSigner`, you'll see where the [Fulcio signers](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/cmd/cosign/cli/sign/sign.go#L483-L490) are called. title: Countersigning support for attestations
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, neither blobs or OCIs support countersigning DSSE envelopes, e.g. appending a signature to a known DSSE envelope, or verifying a DSSE envelope with more than one signature._x000D_
_x000D_
For verification, verifying DSSE envelopes comes with a (t, n) protocol. As in, the client choose to decide that t of the n signatures should be verified._x000D_
_x000D_
It would be nice to start with generating countersignatures, but this would require changing the UX of both OCI and blob attestations signing. Both of hthese take a `--predicate`, and countersigning would require taking in the envelope and appending the signature. Adding a flag would probably be the easiest `--envelope` and make it clear that this is a countersign operation._x000D_

title: Multiple concurrent invocations of the attest command can result in lost attestations
body_text:
Running `cosign attest <image>` (almost) concurrently can have the side effect that attestations written to the container registry previously are overridden by later invocations:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. `cosign attest` no 1 reads existing attestations_x000D_
2. `cosign attest` no 2 reads existing attestations_x000D_
3. `cosign attest` no 1 writes attestations with new attestation1_x000D_
4. `cosign attest` no 2 writes attestations with new attestation2 and the effect that attestation1 is lost

title: Add conformance testing
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Hey Cosign folks! Recently, @woodruffw and I have been working on a conformance testing suite for Sigstore clients. At the moment, it just does a basic sign/verify test along the happy path, but we'll be focusing on building out coverage in the coming weeks. The test suite is exposed via a GitHub Action which can be found [here](https://github.com/trailofbits/sigstore-conformance)._x000D_
_x000D_
At this point, we want to get the test suite running against a few clients to begin dogfooding and check that our assumptions around the CLI design of clients other than `sigstore-python` are reasonable._x000D_
_x000D_
The way this works is that we've designed a [CLI protocol](https://github.com/trailofbits/sigstore-conformance/blob/main/docs/cli_protocol.md), which is essentially a set of flags that the client needs to support in order to be conformance tested. Every client's flags differ slightly so, generally speaking, it's required to write some kind of wrapper script to convert the flags described in that document to those that the client understands. For Cosign, that means that there's going to need to be a wrapper program somewhere called `cosign-conformance` that takes those flags and then invokes `cosign` under the hood. You can take a look at this PR for `sigstore-python` to get an idea of what I mean: https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-python/pull/298._x000D_
_x000D_
If you're happy for Cosign to be included in this, I'd be happy to make a PR to get things going._x000D_
_x000D_
CC: @di
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: Hey @tetsuo-cpp ! This is great—but I'd actually prefer to do the testing at a slightly lower level. For instance, in https://github.com/sigstore/protobuf-specs/pull/5 there's an `Input` protobuf message, which would capture the input to a `Verify()` function. (We could do the same thing for signing.) Clients don't necessarily need to make this the primary interface to their `Verify()` functions, but it should be pretty trivial to parse stuff out of the protobufs and pass it in. We've been imagining a suite of test vectors specified in the form of these protos. This has a few advantages IMO: it avoids shelling out (and should be faster), and is much easier to write a test harness for. It *doesn't* test the CLI interface directly, but I think that's a good thing—we're going to be able to exercise much more interesting paths via the library interface. WDYT? I am open to discussion here if you feel strongly that CLI-level testing is better, or that there's a place for both. **Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
@znewman01 @haydentherapper these are coming up in my refactor, and I want to enumerate them and we can close this out when we know we have testing coverage for these cases._x000D_
_x000D_
@priyawadhwa @hectorj2f _x000D_
_x000D_
We currently have the following options available to users:_x000D_
* Offline_x000D_
* TSA bundle_x000D_
* (Rekor) bundle_x000D_
* Key_x000D_
* Cert_x000D_
* RekorClient_x000D_
* TSAClient_x000D_
* SkipTlogVerify_x000D_
_x000D_
I was hoping it'd be clear what the behavior was in the document, but let's just spec it out here instead._x000D_
_x000D_
Proposal:_x000D_
* Rename SkipTlogVerify to RequireTlogVerify (default on)_x000D_
* Remove the CheckOpt for TSAClient. It's not used for verification, and only used as a toggle for whether we should verify against the TSA._x000D_
_x000D_
This will make the flow as such:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. If a certificate is provided, verify it's chain up to the trust roots. Verify other properties designed from CheckOpts (issuer etc)_x000D_
2. Verify the cryptographic signature._x000D_
3. Check any claims because now we can decode the payload._x000D_
4. Rekor. _x000D_
  a.. [offline] If a (Rekor) bundle is provided, verify it. If fails, exit. If succeeds, extract tlogVerificationTime._x000D_
  b. If we requireTlogVerification and a bundle wasn't present:_x000D_
     i. If we are offline, fail because we didn't have a bundle._x000D_
    ii. We are now definitely online (not offline) and a bundle wasn't provided and we required tlog verification, so perform online Rekor verification. Extract tlogVerificationTime._x000D_
5. TSA:_x000D_
  a. [offline] If a TSA bundle is present, verify it. If fails, exit. If succeeds, extract tsaVerificationTime. (Not that I did NOT say `if TSAClient was set @hectorj2f -- the TSAClient is NOT used in `VerifyTSABundle` anyway)_x000D_
6. Check the certificate verification time against the tlogVerificationTime (if present) and the tsaVerificationTime (if present). Ensure that at least one was checked to ensure signature validity (in case we didn't have a TSA bundle, didnt have a rekor bundle, and didnt require rekor validation)._x000D_
_x000D_
Thoughts? We don't get to force online rekor proofs if a rekor bundle is present, but such is life._x000D_
_x000D_

If I'm allowed to dream big: -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- My overall philosophy here is to *have flags to specify really clearly* what's going on, and then *set sensible defaults* so most people don't have to think about them. title: Generated PEM labels should say "SIGSTORE" rather than "COSIGN"
body_text:
```shell_x000D_
$ cd $(mktemp -d) && COSIGN_PASSWORD="" cosign generate-key-pair && head -n 1 cosign.key_x000D_
-----BEGIN ENCRYPTED COSIGN PRIVATE KEY-----_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This means that any Sigstore client implementation must:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Accept the "COSIGN PRIVATE KEY" format, or else they won't be able to use Cosign keys_x000D_
2. Generate keys with "COSIGN PRIVATE KEY", or else Cosign won't be able to understand those keys. This is a little weird if the client has nothing to do with cosign._x000D_
_x000D_
I'd prefer "BEGIN ENCRYPTED SIGSTORE PRIVATE KEY" if this is going to be a shared format. (That's what sigstore-rs emits.)_x000D_
_x000D_
I propose that Cosign:_x000D_
_x000D_
- *Immediately* start accepting "SIGSTORE" keys (in addition to "COSIGN" keys)_x000D_
- *Eventually* start emitting "SIGSTORE" keys._x000D_
   - I think we could definitely do this right away if we get it in before 2.0 (https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2376)_x000D_
   - Otherwise, we *may* want to transition the behavior subject to a deprecation period (as in [Proposal: Cosign Versioning](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1urWUPhtzXKWqL9CoaEw4Z35v5IDl9yrTRQ40XlYekOo/edit#heading=h.r9yrcczhn25h)). I can see an argument for skipping deprecation too._x000D_
 - *Very* long-term could stop accepting "COSIGN" public keys, probably doesn't need to do this though._x000D_
 - We could consider an option to emit "COSIGN" keys for backwards compat._x000D_
_x000D_
Other Sigstore clients:_x000D_
_x000D_
- MUST emit "SIGSTORE" keys by default_x000D_
- SHOULD accept "COSIGN" keys_x000D_
- MAY have an option to emit "COSIGN" keys_x000D_
_x000D_
Context: https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-rs/pull/165

title: "Chain" for verification is confusingly named

title: Custom Annotation Support for Attestations
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
Currently, when using `cosign download attestation`, every attestation attached to the artifact is returned, which forces additional parsing to take place client-side using tools like `jq` to decode and filter out only the desired attestation (based on `predicateType`, for example).  Adding support for annotations on artifact layers would achieve a few things:_x000D_
1. It would make retrieval of the desired attestation using the `cosign` CLI trivial (`cosign download attestation --annotation foo=bar <image>`)_x000D_
2. Verifying a particular attestation would also be trivial with `cosign verify-attestation --annotation <image>`_x000D_
3. It would have the side effect of making the annotations visible as part of what gets returned by the `v2` registry API, which means any language with basic support for making requests would be able to locate the desired attestation (albeit without attestation verification via `cosign verify-attestatation`)_x000D_
_x000D_
This idea had been brought up before in #1773 and a PR was opened for it in #1934.  That PR was ultimately closed [due to concerns](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1934#issuecomment-1152762144) over how the annotation itself could be verified as part of the payload.  I had [suggested](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1934#issuecomment-1294279234) that perhaps the annotation is specified in both the manifest for the layer and in the payload itself.  In this way, the annotation could be used to filter the desired layer without the need to download all attestations and decode them using an external tool like `jq`, and the `verify-attestation` would be performed by first validating the payload signature and then making sure the user-provided `--annotation` value matched the annotation in the signed payload._x000D_
_x000D_
I'd be willing to contribute a PR to try to provide this, if it sounds like a good idea.

title: document key roation and a way to find a key without being vulnerable to a third party
body_text:
Currently the README.md neither suggests how someone can get the key for verification of signatures without being vulnerable to a third party nor will there be a way to rotate the key to ensure one can reduce the risk of the key having been compromised or recover from it._x000D_
_x000D_
Is that correct, or did I miss something?_x000D_
_x000D_
There are two well known ways to solve this: TUF and Web of Trust. And a way that is not realistic, which is always obtaining the rotated key in person. A widely observed log for the public keys can help less widely observed projects but has the same problem itself again. There are other implementations of the same concepts._x000D_
Are there any noteworthy other concepts to solve this?_x000D_
_x000D_
Obtaining a fingerprint or similar of the public key in person from the owner is simply unrealistic. While it happens that people do this, it that needs to last for multiple decades (from my experience of projects where people use GPG Web of Trust), but key rotation needs to happen perhaps more often than yearly. The tools we use should also strive to automatically do this, e.g. before doing a signature, or where people desire harder compartmentalization prompt the user for a rotated key and refuse to sign until then._x000D_
_x000D_
TUF solves this by signing rotated keys with previous ones creating a chain of them. Then if you managed the expense of obtaining a fingerprint or similar of the key in person from the owner, you do not need to do that again on rotation, but instead follow the chain of key rotations._x000D_
The issue for TUF integration was closed: https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/86_x000D_
Should that be reopened?_x000D_
_x000D_
Web of Trust as known from OpenPGP solves this by obtaining a personal public key in person from someone you know, signing and publishing a statement that you did do so. To get to a public key for someone you did not meet you'd then follow this web constructed by these statements to the one you need. If someone rotates their key you do the previous again. AFAIK there is currently no implementation of a Web of Trust that has good usability and I'll omit a list of potential solutions for that here. Though it still manages to do better than only obtaining a key from some website._x000D_
_x000D_
As cosign supports creating keys, is it in scope to support key rotation?
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: > The tools we use should also strive to automatically do this, e.g. before doing a signature, or where people desire harder compartmentalization prompt the user for a rotated key and refuse to sign until then. I want to echo this sentiment: we don't want users to be doing this themselves. But I think Cosign is the wrong tool for key management. I'll quote myself from https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/677 : > I view key compromise as largely external to the Sigstore project. Sigstore aims to provide a secure mapping from signatures to identities ("artifact X was signed by [user@example.com](mailto:user@example.com) at time T"). Revocation seems to be more about whether (and when) you should trust a particular key/identity. > > Any use of Sigstore needs to answer questions of that form ("whom should I trust?") for itself. The (currently draft) blog post [Signatus, ergo Securus?](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1GpsZei4CV8MKUKWRW2KQYB2Ia5Uwow7x0Te8Q37piFM/edit) (you may need to join [sigstore-dev@googlegroups.com](mailto:sigstore-dev@googlegroups.com) for access) describes potential policies of that form in a few contexts (package repositories, internal to an organization). But that's the level at which to handle revocation. So if you use [TUF](https://theupdateframework.com/) (as recommended in that post), you should use TUF's support for revocation. If you hard-code a key/identity for verification, you need to support revocation at the point of hard-coding ([Don't Panic](https://blog.sigstore.dev/dont-panic-a-playbook-for-handling-account-compromise-with-sigstore-ee299dca5144) walks through an example of what that might look like). These all follow the broad philosophy of ["revoke artifacts, not keys"](https://blog.sigstore.dev/how-to-sign-a-release-of-oss-e96ee94286fc). > > Now, just because this is external to Sigstore doesn't mean that the Sigstore project should stay silent here, so I'm not going to recommend closing this issue quite yet. But I think this is going to fall under the bucket of "advice for adding Sigstore to your setting" and not "documentation about Sigstore itself." I think everything I said about key compromise or revocation applies similarly to rotation, and in fact I'm somewhat inclined to close this issue as a duplicate and concentrate conversation on this issue over to #677 unless you think there's something different here. > The issue for TUF integration was closed: https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/86 > Should that be reopened? It's a good question. IMO I want to scope down what cosign actually does *itself*, and the answer might instead be to add Sigstore support to TUF, as proposed in this [TAP](https://github.com/theupdateframework/taps/pull/141). This makes more sense as a direction to me: you can sign things using a Sigstore/Fulcio identity, and your TUF client would check that and check that signatures were in Rekor. | JanZerebecki: Makes sense to deal with it in #677 , my searches didn't find that. Thank you. > IMO I want to scope down what cosign actually does itself Then we probably want to discourage people from generating keys with cosign, but instead add how get a key elsewhere in the README.md . | znewman01: > Then we probably want to discourage people from generating keys with cosign, but instead add how get a key elsewhere in the README.md . I don't think that follows. Plenty of tools allow generating keys but don't prescribe a complete solution for distributing them (`ssh-keygen`, for one).

@asraa Would it be possible for cosign to be modified to allow it to attest multiple images with a single predicate?_x000D_
_x000D_
For knative, I build multiple images with ko but I need to attach a single attestation to all the images that I build._x000D_
```sh_x000D_
# Before calling sign_release, we do ko resolve first and get a bunch of yaml files with images built by ko. Then we read all those files and pull out the images and store them in a single file called imagerefs.txt_x000D_
_x000D_
function sign_release() {_x000D_
  ID_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-identity-token --audiences=sigstore \_x000D_
    --include-email \_x000D_
    --impersonate-service-account="${SIGNING_IDENTITY}")_x000D_
  echo "Signing Images with the identity ${SIGNING_IDENTITY}"_x000D_
  ## Sign the images with cosign_x000D_
  if [[ -f "imagerefs.txt" ]]; then_x000D_
      COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 cosign sign $(cat imagerefs.txt) --recursive --identity-token="${ID_TOKEN}"_x000D_
      if  [ -n "${ATTEST_IMAGES:-}" ]; then # Temporary Feature Gate_x000D_
        provenance-generator --clone-log=/logs/clone.json \_x000D_
          --image-refs=imagerefs.txt --output=attestation.json_x000D_
        COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 cosign attest $(cat imagerefs.txt) --recursive --identity-token="${ID_TOKEN}" \_x000D_
          --predicate=attestation.json --type=slsaprovenance_x000D_
      fi_x000D_
  fi_x000D_

title: Hash algorithm defaults to SHA256 when verifying with a certificate
body_text:
**Question**_x000D_
When verifying a signature using a certificate and certificate chain the hash algorithm is hard coded as SHA256 [here](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/72dac4d760825f1fe7161e48c93d23bd7ec842a1/pkg/cosign/verify.go#L191). According to verify command help a  _signature-digest-algorithm_ flag could be specified. Do this flag only makes sense when verifying with public key or it is a lapse?_x000D_

title: Inappropriate printing to STDOUT
body_text:
Generally, in Cosign we try to make STDOUT have the *output* of the command: the (often machine-readable) result of execution. We put status messages, errors, etc. on STDERR._x000D_
_x000D_
This is a common convention for CLI tools and a nice thing to do for scriptability._x000D_
_x000D_
However, we're pretty sloppy sometimes._x000D_
_x000D_
---------------------------------------------------------------------_x000D_
 _x000D_
I'm looking mostly at:_x000D_
_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/fa8a799784cafb0779849e69cb939c8dc6132a5e/pkg/cosign/tlog.go#L170_x000D_
-  https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/381ba64a577505d378b49482ee34d39eeab6ea50/cmd/cosign/cli/pivcli/commands.go#L152_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/381ba64a577505d378b49482ee34d39eeab6ea50/cmd/cosign/cli/initialize/init.go#L52_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/d720f040bf493861c1ea8280f462c14e705990e0/cmd/cosign/cli/sign/sign.go#L250_x000D_
_x000D_
But even some of the ones that are actually correct just work by spitting out to STDOUT in the middle of command execution:_x000D_
 - https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/381ba64a577505d378b49482ee34d39eeab6ea50/cmd/cosign/cli/pivcli/commands.go#L265_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/d720f040bf493861c1ea8280f462c14e705990e0/cmd/cosign/cli/tree.go#L152_x000D_
_x000D_
-------------------------------------------------------------------_x000D_
_x000D_
My proposal is the following:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Have the CLI top-level entry point *print* the output of the command. That is, something like [`SaveCmd`](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/30bf1c09c6fde849245648ff294725d86094fe28/cmd/cosign/cli/save.go#L50) would be implemented as a function with a return value, and then we'd hook into Cobra to print the output (if we need to stream output, we could use channels or something)._x000D_
1. Ban (using [Forbidigo](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/381ba64a577505d378b49482ee34d39eeab6ea50/.golangci.yml#L38)) any calls to `fmt.Print{f,ln}` in the Cosign codebase._x000D_
1. Implement a "Cosign output" package. Instead of `fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "warning: foo")` directly, Cosign code would call `Warn()`. Same for any other common output patterns. (That is, calling code can assign *semantics* to its output which helps make sure it goes to the right place)._x000D_
1. Ban (most) other `fmt.*` calls (we can keep `fmt.Sprint*`)._x000D_
_x000D_
This has a number of benefits:_x000D_
_x000D_
- Supporting multiple formats easily and consistently (you could pass `--format=jsonl` or `--format=csv`) without requiring support from every command_x000D_
- Testability: parsing STDOUT is hard. Right now that's part of the reason that the `cmd/` directory is under-tested._x000D_
- Enforce consistent output: of course, this fixes the STDOUT/STDERR thing. But it also starts to unify the output across the whole tool. If we wanted to start putting all STDERR output in red, we could do that in one place easily. If we want to "tee" all output to a log file, we can do that.

title: Encourage signing OCI artifacts that *you* produced, not that the registry gives you
body_text:
A common workflow is:_x000D_
_x000D_
```shell_x000D_
$ ko build --image-refs /tmp/refs_x000D_
$ cat /tmp/refs | xargs cosign sign_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This is *almost good*: it avoids signing tags (https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2047). But unfortunately those image refs are computed *after* a roundtrip to the registry, meaning that you (1) built something, (2) sent it to a third party, and (3) signed something that the third party sent back to you. (Same is true for `docker build`.)_x000D_
_x000D_
Ideally, you'd sign something that you built directly. But OCI makes this hard! You don't know the hash of the thing you're signing until you upload it (unless you [use layouts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TJVoFKTm9I0))._x000D_
_x000D_
We need to do a few things here:_x000D_
_x000D_
- [ ] Docs and education: make sure folks understand that, mostly for the OCI use case._x000D_
- [ ] Try to get upstream tools to *not* have this problem, by producing OCI layouts: track bugs against ko (https://github.com/ko-build/ko/issues/357) etc._x000D_
- [ ] [`cosign` payloads](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/specs/SIGNATURE_SPEC.md#payloads) contain a "docker-reference" field which has something like `gcr.io/foo:latest`; this payload changes when moving an image from `localhost` to `gcr.io`. We should allow users to set this as the ultimate target? Or maybe *not* have the docker-reference at all, I'm not sure._x000D_
- [ ] Making `cosign sign` of layouts idiomatic (I don't know all the details here)_x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Feature: attach+sign or download+verify an SBOM in one command (to avoid currently unavoidable warning)
body_text:
For context please see:_x000D_
_x000D_
* https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2307#issuecomment-1267061747_x000D_
* https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2526#issuecomment-1343327329_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, when using `cosign attach sbom ...` or `cosign download sbom ...` cosign will show unavoidable warnings like these:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
WARNING: Attaching SBOMs this way does not sign them._x000D_
 If you want to sign them, use 'cosign attest --predicate /builds/<REDACTED>_4.5.1-0_spdx.json --key <key path>' or 'cosign sign --key <key path> --attachment sbom <image uri>'._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
WARNING: Downloading SBOMs this way does not ensure its authenticity. If you want to ensure a tamper-proof SBOM, download it using 'cosign download attestation <image uri>' or verify its signature._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
I think these warnings unnecessarily scare the user. _x000D_
_x000D_
I believe warnings should only be used when something went wrong or when the user did something in a non-optimal way. In other words: Warnings should be avoidable, which is not the case here._x000D_
_x000D_
Using in-toto attestations is currently not a viable replacement as described in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2307._x000D_
_x000D_
I am *not* saying these warnings are wrong! But I think they should be *avoidable* by doing something better than the user is currently able to do._x000D_
_x000D_
Currently, a user has to execute two commands to attach+sign or download+verify an SBOM, and the warning emitted after the first command is unavoidable:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign attach sbom --type <image-url> --sbom <sbom-file> <image-url>_x000D_
cosign sign --attachment sbom --key <private-key> <image-url>_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign download sbom <image-url>_x000D_
cosign verify --attachment sbom --key <public-key> <image-url>_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
**Proposal**_x000D_
_x000D_
To avoid these warnings, I propose to extend the commands `cosign attach sbom` and `cosign download sbom` with a `--key` parameter that takes a private- or public-key respectively. This way, `cosign attach sbom --key` could automatically sign the attached sbom artifact in the same invocation, so there is no reason for the warning anymore. In the same way, `cosign download sbom --key` could verify the sbom before outputting it. When omitting the `--key` parameter, cosign should emit the warnings just as it does right now._x000D_
_x000D_
By implementing this proposal, the command-pairs above will effectively be merged into:_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign attach sbom --type <image-url> --sbom <sbom-file> --key <private-key> <image-url>_x000D_
```_x000D_
and_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign download sbom --key <public-key> <image-url>_x000D_
```

title: Support signing multiple blobs, producing a single bundle which may verify any of them
body_text:
Implementing cosign in the [Pulumi/Pulumi](https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/releases/tag/v3.50.0) repository shows how much noise it adds to releases, doubling the number of assets published._x000D_
_x000D_
Additionally, if we were to publish these assets to an OCI Registry, we would have to upload at least 6 additional blobs to represent the signatures for the combinations of OS and architecture._x000D_
_x000D_
It would be an ergonomic improvement if cosign supported signing an unordered set of `hashedrekords` in a single operation, and it would reduce the number of operations performed against rekor, fulcio, et al._x000D_
_x000D_
This would also help in workflows that are file-oriented:_x000D_
_x000D_
* Signing individual files produced by one CI step and verifying them on downloading in another, e.g.: when using GitHub Actions `@actions/download-artifact` and `@actions/upload-artifact`. Adding a step to tar/untar defeats the optimizations done to enable fast file transfers without intermediate copies on disk._x000D_
_x000D_
* Signing multiple blobs within an OCI Artifact Manifest. This is useful in scenarios where the artifact manifest or even the OCI registry may be controlled by one party but one or more blob(s) are authored by another. Consider the scenario of a package manager: 1..N blobs may be produced by a package author, producing 1..N signatures, which are then uploaded via an API to the package manager, which distributes those back by inserting them into an OCI Registry._x000D_
_x000D_
The second point is significant: some or all **blobs** would be signed by one party, the **manifest** would be signed by a different party. In fact, blobs could be signed by multiple parties depending on origination as part of a composite "package". (Think: CNAB Bundle or Homebrew package.) Limitations of the referrers API and OCI specification may require a client to download O(n/2) signatures on average to find the right signature for a given blob._x000D_
_x000D_
If, however, a single bundle could be used to verify multiple blobs, only a single signature would be necessary, greatly reducing the overhead.

title: FR: BYO PKI Revocation: CA-issued cert
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
In a Bring your Own PKI scenario, a user may want to specify a CRL file ( in addition to a fullchain file ) that can be used to check if the certificate embedded in a signature artifact has been revoked. This could be done by passing in a `--crl` switch or environment variable? Something like the following:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 \_x000D_
SIGSTORE_ROOT_FILE=./your/fullchain.pem \_x000D_
cosign verify --rekor-url="" --crl ./your/crl.pem repo/someImage:someTag _x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
My target scenario assumes the CA ( and intermediate CAs ) are trusted; but the signing key/cert is revoked; in which case a --crl type of option which allows a user to opt into that CRL aware behavior could act accordingly. With a correct CA chain & current CRL, they should then be able to dis-trust the signing certificate that is baked into an existing signature artifact._x000D_
_x000D_
In thinking of this a OpenSSL primitives perspective, we'd be 1) create the store with CA certs, 2) add crls to the store 3) create the certificate context from the cert stored on the artifact 4) see the certificate context fail to validate due to the CRL._x000D_
_x000D_
Since its a Bring Your Own PKI situation, questions about the distribution / maintenance of CRL files is outside of the scope of cosign._x000D_
_x000D_
This concept builds off of workflows noted in #1554

That said, there's still a bandwidth problem and potentially storage as well (if the local client caches the CRL), which makes OCSP _in general_ more suited to this use case. Sadly, WebPKI seems to mostly be walking away from OCSP, which might make support for it in the future harder to advocate for. > * CRLs grow indefinitely. Are you going to support the standard PKCS#7 CRLs? Or do you want to support the bloom filter based [CRLite](https://github.com/mozilla/crlite)? You'll find more Golang library support for PKCS#7 CRLs, but that comes with all of the typical baggage. As I mentioned above, CRLs can, yes, grow to an unbounded size _if_ unlimited issuance within a standard validity period occurs... But they'll naturally be pruned once revoked certs expire assuming compliance with RFC 5280. If short-lived, post-expiry revocation is to be supported, then they will indeed grow.
haydentherapper: > how would cosign differentiate a long-lived PKI issuer from a short-lived one? To verify a short-lived certificate, a signed timestamp over the artifact signature needs to be presented and verified, and that timestamp's time is used to verify the certificate. This can also be done for a long-lived certificate, but the tooling doesn't mandate it by default if the system time can verify the certificate (note that [sigstore-go](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go) allows developers to create verification policies that can require signed timestamps, which Cosign is actively starting to integrate with). There's another issue on this repo that discusses the idea of having a separate API for non-Fulcio certificates, for bring-your-own PKI use cases. I very much like this idea, as it lets us keep the most commonly used API for Sigstore lean (for verifying certificates conforming to the Fulcio certificate profile), while expanding the other API for use cases such as this. On my point about RFC 5280 compliance, I bring this up because we don't want to say we conform to _all_ of RFC 5280. I don't expect us to deviate against it because of our reliance on Go's x509 library (though even then, it is a subset of RFC 5280 primarily for TLS certificates, which we've dealt with before when we wanted to use a non-URI/DNS/email SAN), but I don't expect us to implement support for every part of the RFC, at least in the core API. I'm open to a proposal for adding support for CRLs if someone wants to design and implement it, though I'd be even more open to it if it were a part of the Cosign refactor around sigstore-go's APIs where we have a separate API for handling these non-Sigstore-spec use cases.

title: Support custom error messages when evaluating Rego policies
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
At the moment, cosign Rego policies are expecting a specific template and the result is evaluated as a boolean to determine if the policy is satisfied or not. The current template is detailed below:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
package sigstore_x000D_
_x000D_
default isCompliant = false_x000D_
isCompliant {_x000D_
_x000D_
# Rego logic goes here; must evaluate to true for policy to pass_x000D_
_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
`Cosign` should support custom error messages when any Rego policy evals to `false`. To do so, I propose to support the following Rego module template:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
package sigstore_x000D_
_x000D_
isComplaint[response] {_x000D_
   result := ( ... Rego logic evaluated here to a boolean ....) _x000D_
   _x000D_
   errorMsg := "Your custom error message..."_x000D_
   response :={_x000D_
	"result" : result,_x000D_
	"errors" : errorMsg,_x000D_
  }_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
With this new template, the value store in `result` will determine if the logic evaluated is complaint. If `result` evals to `false` then the cosign source code will return the content of `errorMsg`. _x000D_
_x000D_
Note that the result evaluation within cosign will be able to handle both templates the old (legacy) and the new proposed here. _x000D_
_x000D_
Other alternatives have been discarded due to the complexity to ensure a proper handling of the Rego.ResultSet without increasing the complexity of the current user experience.

title: Cannot verify PredicateType `cyclonedx` generated with previous versions of cosign, or vice versa.
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
The predicate URL for cyclonedx was changed here:_x000D_
https://github.com/in-toto/in-toto-golang/commit/86e515c6e15f0d9bc2cc9cb8253165f8176f6ce6_x000D_
_x000D_
And the CLI options allow for convenience fields (in this case `cyclonedx`) which are keyed off of here:_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/cmd/cosign/cli/options/predicate.go#L40_x000D_
_x000D_
So, depending on when your cosign was built, you're going to get `cyclonedx` URI mapping to either:_x000D_
`https://cyclonedx.org/schema` or `https://cyclonedx.org/bom`_x000D_
_x000D_
And then when handling attestation here, the predicate URI has now changed from `schema` to `bom`, it will not be considered valid:_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/pkg/policy/attestation.go#L75_x000D_
_x000D_
So, if you attest with say cosign 1.13.1 using `--type=cyclonedx` but use the head (soon to be v2) with the `--type=cyclonedx` it will fail, and vice versa._x000D_
_x000D_
You can of course use the full URL, but one could argue that it dilutes the value of the convenience types._x000D_
_x000D_
**Version**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What version are you using? e.g. `cosign version`..._x000D_
-->_x000D_

title: Predicate URIs aren't RFC 3986 compliant
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--Tell us about the bug. What went wrong? How can we reproduce it? What should the correct behavior be?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
[In-toto spec says](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/blob/main/spec/field_types.md#TypeURI) that predicate URIs should be [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-3) compliant, which means that we should include a scheme (i.e. `https://` in the URIs we're producing._x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/04fb9c0a5bdebf7580d772dfd3e439ae66ac2b8a/pkg/cosign/attestation/attestation.go#L31-L37_x000D_
_x000D_
The change to add the scheme seems simple enough, but could be construed as a breaking change if clients are switching on these values, so not sure if we need to take extra steps to change this. Thoughts? 👀 _x000D_
_x000D_
**Version**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What version are you using? e.g. `cosign version`..._x000D_
-->_x000D_

_x000D_

_x000D_
**Motivation**_x000D_
_x000D_
Encourge the end users to use Wolfi/Chainguard images and spray the aweraness of those images around with the community._x000D_
_x000D_
**Algorithm**_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Implement new subcommand_x000D_
2. Aggregate all image indexes from _sources__x000D_
3. Traverse entire Dockerfile_x000D_
3.1. Check if _current_ image is exist on source_x000D_
3.1.1. Check if image version/digest pinned_x000D_
3.1.1.1. Check If specific tag exist on _source__x000D_
3.1.1.2. Continue if not exist_x000D_
3.2. Replace the image_x000D_
3.3. Otherwise, keep it as-is_x000D_
4. Write new Dockerfile_x000D_
_x000D_
**Source of Truth**_x000D_
_x000D_
To get all available chainguard images, we need some _source of truth_:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. [Makefile](https://github.com/wolfi-dev/os/blob/main/Makefile) of Wolfi_x000D_
2. [chainguard-images](https://github.com/chainguard-images/images/tree/main/images) repo_x000D_
3. Any other way?_x000D_
_x000D_
**Related Work**_x000D_
_x000D_
The idea is similar to [PR: dockerfile/resolve](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/1120), the command actually _rewrites_ all the images to pin their digest. /cc @developer-guy_x000D_
_x000D_
**Open Questions**_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Does it make sense in overall?_x000D_
2. What if image pinned with its version/digest and that specific version of package is not exist on _source_? Should we respect only `latest` tags for this concern? _x000D_
3. Is cosign right place to implement this? (Since its already widely adopted by open-source projecs) Would [wolfictl](https://github.com/wolfi-dev/wolfictl) be more suitable?_x000D_
_x000D_
Waiting your thoughts!
