title: Feature: Support "keyless" verification non-Fulcio certificate authorities
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently we have some support for signing with x509 certificates using haven't come from a Fulcio CA and and don't chain up to a TUF root. For example_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign sign --certificate cert.pem --key key.pem --certificate-chain bundle.pem example.com/foo@sha256:....._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
> Aside: the key format needs to be cosign's format to make this work so you often need to run e.g `cosign import-key-pair` to make that the case_x000D_
_x000D_
The current invocation to verify this kind of signature is a little inconvenient as you need to specify the leaf certificate like so:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign verify --certificate cert.pem --certificate-chain bundle.pem example.com/foo@sha256:...._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This means grabbing that leaf certificate off the OCI manifest or from the Rekor bundle or something.  Would be great to be able to do the same kind of invocation as Fulcio's verification like_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign verify --certificate-chain bundle.pem --certificate-identity foo@example.com --certificate-oidc-issuer https://id.example.com example.com/foo@sha256:....._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This convenient keyless verification would be awesome for folks using a custom CA, provided they're using certificates in a similar shape that Fulcio does (Efforts to standardize these extensions like https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/pull/945 would make it easy for folks to create a CA that does this)_x000D_

title: Improved CLI UX for verifying online/offline for {TSA,Rekor,Fulcio}
body_text:
I think these are all fine as incremental improvements. If I'm allowed to dream big:_x000D_
_x000D_
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------_x000D_
_x000D_
My overall philosophy here is to *have flags to specify really clearly* what's going on, and then *set sensible defaults* so most people don't have to think about them. I think "boolean" is the wrong type for many of these flags, which can interact in complicated ways._x000D_
_x000D_
So here's a proposal:_x000D_
_x000D_
- Flags_x000D_
  - What Sigstore infra to use?_x000D_
    - Where do the keys come from?:_x000D_
      - `--tuf-root=URL` (default: Sigstore public good)_x000D_
      - `--fulcio-root` (replaces `--certificate-chain`; default: comes from TUF root)_x000D_
      - `--rekor-root` (default: comes from TUF root)_x000D_
      - `--ct-log-root` (default: comes from TUF root)_x000D_
    - `--rekor-url=URL`, `--fulcio-url=URL`, `--tsa-url=URL` (defaults: URLs provided from the TUF root)_x000D_
  - How should Cosign actually verify?_x000D_
    - `--rekor-verification={offline,fallback,online,insecure}` (default `fallback`)_x000D_
    - `--sct-verification={offline,fallback,online,insecure}` (default `fallback`; replaces `--enforce-sct` flag)_x000D_
    - `--tsa-verification={offline,fallback,online}` (default `fallback`)_x000D_
  - Verification material:_x000D_
    - `DATA` (positional): file name for `verify-blob`, `gcr.io/foo:latest` for `verify`_x000D_
    - `--bundle` (the new bundle format)_x000D_
       - Can replace all of these:_x000D_
         - `--rekor-bundle=FILE`_x000D_
         - `--certificate=FILE`_x000D_
         - `--signature=FILE`_x000D_
      - For *OCI only*, default is fallback to fetching from OCI._x000D_
    - `--offline` flag doesn't affect fetching verification material from OCI registry!_x000D_
  - Identity flags: _x000D_
    - Require one of:_x000D_
      - `--certificate-issuer` AND `--certificate-identity` (optionally: also `--certificate-github-*`)_x000D_
      - `--key`_x000D_
      - `--sk` (and optional `--slot`, which should be renamed to `--sk-slot`)_x000D_
  - `--offline`: force all of the flags above to `offline` (except probably fetching the image from the OCI registry)_x000D_
- If anything is *explicitly* provided (e.g., via a flag) and doesn't validate, fail._x000D_
- If anything is *implicitly* provided (e.g., via a "fallback", or via the bundle) and doesn't validate, warn ("found TSA in the Cosign annotation but it fails")._x000D_
_x000D_
I believe this accomplishes the following goals:_x000D_
_x000D_
- Doesn't exhibit "adding more information makes verification fail" behavior for implicit _x000D_
- Only makes necessary network calls_x000D_
_x000D_
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------_x000D_
_x000D_
One point I'd like to respond to:_x000D_
_x000D_
> > > Check the certificate verification time against the tlogVerificationTime (if present) and the tsaVerificationTime. Ensure that at least one was checked to ensure signature validity._x000D_
> > _x000D_
> > What do we do if one fails? Print a warning? I think we should require that both succeed, and if there's pushback, add policy flags to dictate which you trust (also solvable via delegations in the future)_x000D_
>_x000D_
> Agree, this checks both, and requires at least one to have been checked (just in case no TSA is provided, and no bundle was provided)_x000D_
_x000D_
(Related also to "Remove the CheckOpt for TSAClient. It's not used for verification, and only used as a toggle for whether we should verify against the TSA.")_x000D_
_x000D_
I'd like folks to be more explicit about what they're expecting here (with a reasonable default). This strikes me as a potential source of confusion._x000D_
_x000D_
_Originally posted by @znewman01 in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2466#issuecomment-1320213278__x000D_

title: PCKS11 tokens are opened with read/write sessions, even for enlisting keys and signing
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
I am trying to get our own SignPath PKCS#11 module to work with cosign. It is a "write-protected token" (`C_OpenSession()` immediately returns `CKR_TOKEN_WRITE_PROTECTED` in case of `CKF_RW_SESSION`) because the PKCS#11 interface basically only allows signing, all management (modifications) happens within the "back end". Still an authenticated session is required._x000D_
_x000D_
We had the same issue with the original pkcs11-tool (see their issue [2812](https://github.com/OpenSC/OpenSC/issues/2182)). _x000D_
_x000D_
Cosign uses the `pkcs11.CKF_RW_SESSION` flag in its `GetKeysInfo` function at https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/27bb6ad4c60abd79ad126380d19f99241e08edda/cmd/cosign/cli/pkcs11cli/commands.go#L129_x000D_

As soon as you confirmed fixing this problem, I'd be happy to open an issue in their project also._x000D_
_x000D_
In both cases (enlisting and signing), a RW session is not required (only for creating keys it would be) and prevents cosign from being used with an read-only token. Please change the behavior to using a read-only session._x000D_

title: Supporting buildkit's SBOMs / attestations
body_text:
**Question**_x000D_
_x000D_
Docker's buildkit and buildx can produce SBOMs and Provenance attestations when it builds an image using a Dockerfile (that's good!). They emit this information in a format that's different from cosign's format, described here: https://github.com/moby/buildkit/tree/master/docs/attestations_x000D_
_x000D_
TL;DR: attestations are included in an image index manifest alongside the image(s) that are built, with the descriptor having a `platform` of `unknown` and `annotations` describing the image they're referring to, and how. These descriptors point to an OCI image manifest with `layers` pointing to blobs ([SBOM example](https://github.com/moby/buildkit/blob/master/docs/attestations/sbom.md#output), [more examples](https://github.com/moby/buildkit/blob/master/docs/attestations/attestation-storage.md#examples))._x000D_
_x000D_
This means that attestations can't be attached to existing images in this format without modifying the digest of the manifest, and attestations aren't signed as described in those links above. Signing might be coming in a future release, I have no idea._x000D_
_x000D_
I don't think `cosign` or related tooling should _produce_ attestations in this way, but maybe it'd be worth teaching `cosign` and policy-controller, etc., how to _discover_ these attestations, and make decisions based on them, in addition to understanding `cosign`'s externally-attached signed attestations.

title: Sugar for common GitHub Actions (and other CI/CD workflows)
body_text:
(This is written about GitHub so we have a specific example, but applies to all future CI/CD providers!)_x000D_
_x000D_
Right now, you need to deal with a menagerie of flags to verify GitHub actions workflows (`cosign verify-blob`):_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
      --certificate-github-workflow-name string                                                  contains the workflow claim from the GitHub OIDC Identity token that contains the name of the executed workflow._x000D_
      --certificate-github-workflow-ref string                                                   contains the ref claim from the GitHub OIDC Identity token that contains the git ref that the workflow run was based upon._x000D_
      --certificate-github-workflow-repository string                                            contains the repository claim from the GitHub OIDC Identity token that contains the repository that the workflow run was based upon_x000D_
      --certificate-github-workflow-sha string                                                   contains the sha claim from the GitHub OIDC Identity token that contains the commit SHA that the workflow run was based upon._x000D_
      --certificate-github-workflow-trigger string                                               contains the event_name claim from the GitHub OIDC Identity token that contains the name of the event that triggered the workflow run_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
We've talked about simplifying this (CC @haydentherapper) by splitting into specific `verify-github` subcommands. This helps a bit, but still requires values for many (all?) of these fields. That's required for full power for sure._x000D_
_x000D_
But @sudo-bmitch points out that there's a really common query we can optimize for: did this signature come from a workflow in "its" GitHub repository? This would boil down to something like *just* `--certificate-github-workflow-repository`._x000D_
_x000D_
Need to be careful here but I think if we're clear about what it's checking, we can make this common use case really nice! Let's think through this if we're building a `verify-github` command._x000D_

title: Support non-Sigstore TSAs
body_text:
The [sigstore TSA](https://github.com/sigstore/timestamp-authority/) implements an API to fetch timestamps, as does any other public TSA. Every API uses different paths to request timestamps, but all should conform to the same API structure, accepting timestamp queries and returning timestamp responses. We should support providing a path (`timestamp-url`) not to the sigstore TSA instance, but instead to the complete path to fetch a TSR (e.g. `<sigstoretsapath.com>/api/v1/timestamp`, or `https://freetsa.org/tsr`, or `http://timestamp.digicert.com`)_x000D_
_x000D_
This means using a different TSA client than the sigstore TSA client, which is only useful for fetching timestamps from a service that has the same API paths as the sigstore TSA._x000D_
_x000D_
**Ignore everything below, left as an unnecessary alternative**_x000D_
_x000D_
For users that want to leverage a TSA that uses a different API than the [sigstore TSA](https://github.com/sigstore/timestamp-authority/), we should support attaching a signed timestamp after artifact signing. _x000D_
_x000D_
For container signing, UX would look something like:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. User signs container with Cosign_x000D_
2. User fetches signature from OCI annotation_x000D_
3. User crafts a timestamp query, for example using openssl (where `--data` should be the signature)_x000D_
4. User requests a timestamp from their trusted TSA, for example [FreeTSA](https://www.freetsa.org/index_en.php#tcp)_x000D_
5. User attaches the signed timestamp to OCI_x000D_
_x000D_
Verification with a signed timestamp should then work without any modification, but this should be confirmed._x000D_
_x000D_
For blob signing, during verification, simply pass the signed timestamp you fetched from a trusted TSA after signing with `--rfc3161-timestamp`. The one caveat is it must be crafted as a [struct]https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/a84600e3f403c16e3cfc4bcf90a483bd34392a69/pkg/cosign/bundle/tsa.go#L18-L24). I propose we be more lax in accepting a raw or base64 encoded TSR in addition to the struct (I don't think we should add a command to convert a TSR into this struct)

title: Improvements to verification for private repositories without log upload

**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
_x000D_
I received some feedback that it's unexpected you need to explicitly opt out of tlog verification for a container hosted on a private repository when you don't have to explicitly opt out for upload during signing. I'm not sure there is a good way to improve this, but filing this issue so we can discuss more._x000D_
_x000D_
Some ideas:_x000D_
* Alias the `insecure-tlog-skip` flag to something like `private-repository` which would result in the same behavior. I don't really love this though because it is technically "insecure" to skip uploading to a tlog for private artifacts, you aren't getting the auditability Sigstore recommends._x000D_
* Detect if the artifact is private during verification, and skip tlog verification if so. However, we then miss the case of an upload occurring on signing. We could require the user to set a flag to force tlog verification, but this isn't secure by default. _x000D_
* Do nothing, and just document this.

title: Deprecate `--attachment sbom` commands
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
There are two ways to sign an SBOM and connect it an image._x000D_
_x000D_
The first option relies on `cosign attach sbom` to push the SBOM to the OCI registry and connect it to the image. Then, the user must use `cosign sign --attachment sbom` to sign the SBOM image attached to the underlying image. NOTE: this is a new `.sig` image for the SBOM image itself. The verification is also a two step process. 1) `cosign verify --attachment sbom`; then B) `cosign download ...` . Given that these commands take the digest of the underlying image and not the digest of the SBOM image, the verification process is susceptible to TOCTOU attacks._x000D_
_x000D_
The second option adds a new layer to the `.att` image which includes the signed SBOM data. This is done via `cosign attest --type ...`. It can be verified in one step via `cosign verify-attestation type ... `. It is also a more generic approach since it can also be used to verify SLSA Provenance and other attestations types._x000D_
_x000D_
As a user, it is confusing that both options are available. It is also not obvious, at first, which option is better._x000D_
_x000D_
Let's deprecate the `--attachment` parameter of `cosign sign` and `cosign attest` according to the deprecation [guidelines](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/VERSIONING.md#deprecation).

Print a deprecation messaged to stderr whenever the `--attachment` flag is passed. We should mention that the `cosign attest` command should be used instead. 2. Remove the flag in 6 months :) | ChristianCiach: I am confused about this proposal. Do you want to effectively deprecate the `.sbom` artifacts in favor of the `.att` artifacts? We currently prefer to use SBOMs over attestations because attestations are too hard to work with: * https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2307 I agree that the current two-step process of uploading and signing, or downloading and verifying an SBOM is cumbersome and also produces unavoidable warnings. That's why I've created this issue a while ago: * https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2528 If cosign decides to deprecate and eventually remove SBOMs in favor of attestations, I would be fine with that, because we are currently struggling to decide which attachment type we should use for our SBOMs. We are currently using `.sbom` for the sole reason that these are easily retrieved by using `cosign download sbom`. Before making attestations the only option, **please** solve https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2307 before doing so. | lcarva: @ChristianCiach, I just realized the main downside of using attachments. The connection between the attachment (SBOM) and the underlying image is done via tag convention, i.e. `:sha256-<digest>.sbom`. If image A has SBOM A', and image B has SBOM B', someone with registry access can swap the relationship so image A has SBOM B', and vice-versa. Contrast this with attestations. An attestation contains the data and the subject in a signed envelope. Swapping SBOMs requires re-signing the envelope. The relationship between an attestation and an image is signed. For this reason, and the possibility of TOCTOU attacks (mentioned in the description), I am convinced that the attachments approach should be deprecated ASAP. This does provide a stronger connection between the SBOM and the underlying image. Of course, this is highly dependent on the SBOM format itself, and requires custom verification.

If image A has SBOM A', and image B has SBOM B', someone with registry access can swap the relationship so image A has SBOM B', and vice-versa. Contrast this with attestations. An attestation contains the data and the subject in a signed envelope. Swapping SBOMs requires re-signing the envelope. The relationship between an attestation and an image is signed. For this reason, and the possibility of TOCTOU attacks (mentioned in the description), I am convinced that the attachments approach should be deprecated ASAP. UPDATE: The SBOM itself does mention which image it describes. For CycloneDX, this is found under `.metadata.component`. This does provide a stronger connection between the SBOM and the underlying image. Of course, this is highly dependent on the SBOM format itself, and requires custom verification.
ChristianCiach: It's a bit sad to see that the `sbom` commands have been deprecated while the consumption of attestations (like extracting the SBOM from an attestion) is still so cumbersome and needs external tooling, as described in my previous comment.
ChristianCiach: Seeing that SBOM attachments will be removed soon, I want to point out that it's still not possible to push SBOM **attestations** as an OCI compliant artifact, because https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1397 only added (still experimental) support for pushing signatures and SBOM attachments as OCI artifacts, but not attestations. This makes it currently impossible to push attestations to https://zotregistry.dev See related issue: * https://github.com/project-zot/zot/issues/724#issuecomment-1796510901
haydentherapper: Hey @ChristianCiach, happy to revisit this. Reviewing this issue, I think both approaches are not ideal - SBOM signatures as separate artifacts have the TOCTOU concerns @lcarva brought up, while attestations as signatures are more heavyweight. Are there efforts to standardize signed SBOMs that we could implement? Something like [SBOMit](https://sbomit.dev)? Or can we design detached signatures in such a way to mitigate TOCTOU concerns? I'm not very familiar with this space. @lumjjb did you have thoughts on this, detached SBOM sigs vs attestations over SBOMs vs something more standardized?
ChristianCiach: I think attestations are the way to go. There is nothing wrong with using attestations for SBOM purposes, IMHO. The only thing missing in Cosign is the support for the OCI 1.1 Referrers-API to store attestations. Related issue: * https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1397 Or, at the very least, Cosign should support using OCI compliant media-types instead of the proprietary Docker media-types.
lumjjb: Attestations for an SBOM is good to be able to be able to provide integrity and provenance for an SBOM, as well as an optional effect of attaching it to a subject. I believe SBOMs should still be their own blobs (i.e. not an embedded predicate), since they are meant to be composable by bundling SBOM files together, and they reference each other by their file hash, and they can become very large (we've seen 500MB+ SBOMs). +1 to OCI 1.1 referrers api, that's what we're implementing as well for [GUAC](https://github.com/guacsec/guac) OCI collector.
crispysipper: can we hold off deprecating `--attachment sbom` and the like until this is addressed: https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2307 we use declarative cluster policies to verify presence of a CycloneDX sbom attached to images in order for them to deploy, and trying to validate that requirement against an in-toto `.att` artifact is painful as hell.

title: Verify local image with Cosign
body_text:
**Question**_x000D_
Hi,_x000D_
I want to pull an image from a repo, and verify my locally pulled image in my local docker cache, NOT directly against the public repo. _x000D_
_x000D_
Is that possible? I can't identify a CLI option to enable this?
top_3_comments_text: znewman01: A workflow like the following should accomplish much the same: ``` $ IMAGE=$(docker image inspect cgr.dev/chainguard/static -f '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}') $ cosign verify $IMAGE --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/chainguard-images/images/.github/workflows/release.yaml@refs/heads/main' --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' ``` Part of the issue is that pulling the image [causes the digest to change](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45533005/why-digests-are-different-depend-on-registry), so you can't really verify the signatures against the local image. | captainfalcon23: Reading through that link, it seems that only images which use a v1 manifest will cause the digest to change. What if there is a scenario where someone is performing a man-in-the-middle attack? By verifying the locally downloaded image, we can be sure that the image we downloaded is exactly the same as the image in the repo, and the exact image we were intended to download. It's not too dissimilar to having yum use a GPG key to verify a package _after_ it has been downloaded. | znewman01: > Reading through that link, it seems that only images which use a v1 manifest will cause the digest to change. Lots of popular registries/images are still using v1 manifests: ``` $ docker pull alpine $ docker image inspect alpine -f 'local={{.Id}} repo={{index .RepoDigests 0}}' local=sha256:d74e625d91152966d38fe8a62c60daadb96d4b94c1a366de01fab5f334806239 repo=alpine@sha256:ff6bdca1701f3a8a67e328815ff2346b0e4067d32ec36b7992c1fdc001dc851 ``` In general, your local Docker daemon functions quite different from a registry; most of the tricks Cosign uses to, e.g., store signatures require the full registry API. I'm personally optimistic that most of the standardization work in OCI will move us in the direction of enabling Cosign-like workflows directly on your local Docker (or Podman) daemon but that will take some time. > What if there is a scenario where someone is performing a man-in-the-middle attack? By verifying the locally downloaded image, we can be sure that the image we downloaded is exactly the same as the image in the repo, and the exact image we were intended to download. Docker digests help with that: if you pull by digest, you get integrity checking during download. So the workflow: 1. resolve digest 2. check signature 3. pull by digest will handle MITM attacks. > It's not too dissimilar to having yum use a GPG key to verify a package after it has been downloaded. But isn't it better not to download the bad package in the first place? You can verify a signature over an artifact digest, and only then download the artifact. If the digest doesn't match (due to MITM or some other condition), you can reject the artifact during download. This is how [The Update Framework](https://theupdateframework.io) (TUF) handles this issue and it has a couple nice side-effects: one is that if an image pull completes successfully, we know that the signature was verified. So you don't have to figure out which local images are/are not trusted. --------------------------------------------------------------- To be clear, we've left this issue open because we agree with you that there should be better workflows for local Docker images with Cosign. Don't interpret my arguing as trying to defend the status quo, just explaining why we haven't (1) prioritized this workflow (there are passable workarounds, and in a Kubernetes context, which has been a big focus thus far, a registry-centric verification flow works) and (2) why it's not a straightforward matter to implement. Unfortunately we've got to work with the reality of how Docker is implemented, and if we recommend a workflow that doesn't work a large portion of the time that's worse than nothing IMO. We're hopeful that future work in OCI will make the situation a little better: https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2516 CCing my resident OCI experts to see if they have any ideas for how to make this better: @sudo-bmitch @jdolitsky @imjasonh

**Description**_x000D_

top_3_comments_text: znewman01: I think my preference here is to make opt-in explicit with a unique `--accept-terms` flag. It seems somewhat wrong that non-interactive clients don't actually accept the terms (similarly for `--yes`). That said, it's a little user-hostile so I'd be happier if we introduce a local Cosign state first so you could accept the terms permanently. | haydentherapper: Chatted with Zack about this, summary of a few ideas from the chat: * Each prompt should be "pre-answerable" using a unique CLI flag (`--accept-terms`, `--allow-private-container-upload`) * We should have a Cosign config file which lets you define the values for each flag. Hopefully should be easy to add, mapping a flag to an env var to a config value * We should rename `--yes` to something like `--accept-defaults`. It should be very clearly documented what this does (skips all prompts, push for private containers, may in the future permit other behavior unexpectedly) * The default value for the ToS prompt should be no, forcing explicit consent (note that it currently is) Shouldn't have to worry about deprecations for any of these changes. We'll alias `--yes` and remove it later, but no need to prioritize that. | favonia: > * We should rename `--yes` to something like `--accept-defaults`. title: verify/-blob should provide more guidance in identity assertions
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
With cosign 2, when verifying a signature in the transparency logs, an OIDC issuer and subject must be matched, but there's very little guidance as to what the options are.  The error messages just specify that the options are needed, and even when using `--verbose` with the `-regexp` variants, we can't see what was actually matched._x000D_
_x000D_
So when people do "the easy thing", they'll find that the easiest thing is to use:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
cosign verify-blob --certificate-identity-regexp=.+ --certificate-oidc-issuer-regexp=.+ [...]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
which is counterproductive._x000D_
_x000D_
My operating model here is that the first time people encounter this is when they've downloaded artifacts from safe locations and they're trying to ensure that future downloads, perhaps inside CI systems, as also safely downloaded.  So if someone does not yet know what identity they _should_ validate, then the data they see before them is reasonable to present as suggestions, together with "if this is reasonable and accurate" caveats._x000D_
_x000D_
Thus if neither option is given, then instead of complaining about first one being missing, then the other, they should be complained about together, plus seeing the actual data which can be matched against.  Or if #2210 is implemented, then people can be pointed to that command._x000D_
_x000D_
Further, if the repository information truly is deprecated, so that the only fully supported option is to match against URLs, then the help text should warn against regexp metacharacters and present escape command-line options (or reconsider if perhaps the ability to match against a repo name is important, for safe usage)._x000D_
_x000D_
I am not a cosign expert, but am more aware of the problem space and terminology than 95% of developers, and it took me far too long to get to an invocation of:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
cosign verify-blob \_x000D_
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \_x000D_
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github\.com/goreleaser/goreleaser-pro-internal/\.github/.+' \ _x000D_
  --signature checksums.txt.sig --cert checksums.txt.pem \_x000D_
  checksums.txt_x000D_
```_x000D_

title: verify should support code forges for more robust assertions
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Asking end-users to construct regular expressions to match against a URL for the full spec of a release of a project, while allowing the project to issue new releases, or switch branch names, or whatever else, is asking for verification mistakes._x000D_
_x000D_
If the UX for verifying signatures is to use `cosign`, then cosign should probably reconsider the OID deprecation of the GitHub attributes and provide a UX around verifying identities._x000D_
_x000D_
(I'm being careful around "forge" as a shorthand for "code hosting repository", because `--issuer-forge` sounds like forge in the sense of "forgery", so I'm using `codeforge` here to provide the limited service agnosticism.)_x000D_
_x000D_
So instead of:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
cosign verify-blob \_x000D_
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \_x000D_
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github\.com/goreleaser/goreleaser-pro-internal/\.github/.+' \_x000D_
  [...]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
cosign might consider:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
cosign verify-blob --issuer-codeforge github:goreleaser/goreleaser-pro-internal [...]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
and then maintain an internal mapping of forge names to OIDC issuers, and which attributes make sense to use by default.  The self-hosted options can still be supported by explicit `--certificate-oidc-issuer` and probably _should not be supported by the simplified UX_, since the whole model here is that we're encouraging people to trust OIDC for claims from a well-run code forge.

title: New tlog & sct insecure CLI options - are they really insecure ?
body_text:
Hello,_x000D_
_x000D_
Throughout cosign version 1.x.x it was possible to verify images by just providing a public key file and an image reference alone, without integration with transparency log (which was experimental, if i'm not mistaken)_x000D_
_x000D_
With 2.0.0, transparency log verification enforcement is on by default and, in order to opt out, we have to use the flag `insecure-ignore-tlog`._x000D_
_x000D_
About that *insecure* part there: If one did not rely on a transparency log up to this point (as it was an experimental feature), is this practice necessarily considered "insecure" from this point? Checks backed by a transparency log adds security, but does it deem working without it as totally bad practice?_x000D_
_x000D_
Otherwise, this option could just be named as `--ignore-tlog`?_x000D_
Same goes for `insecure-ignore-sct` I suppose._x000D_
_x000D_
Also, when running with these flags, the program outputs:_x000D_
```_x000D_
**Warning** Skipping tlog verification is an insecure practice that lacks of transparency and auditability verification for the signature._x000D_
```_x000D_
Maybe, word it like:_x000D_
```_x000D_
**Warning**, Skipping tlog - signature will not be checked against public transparency logs_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Thanks

```_x000D_

i.e. it should be like this:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
if c.KeyRef == "" && c.CertRef == "" {_x000D_

		return err_x000D_
	}_x000D_
}_x000D_

_x000D_

release cosign v2_x000D_

title: Better docs about ambient credential detection
body_text:
**Problem**_x000D_
_x000D_
The current OIDC device flow prints out a URL to complete OIDC and then waits for the OIDC token. However, this is not compatible with how GitHub Actions logging is buffered, as the printed URL may not be visible until the 300-second timeout if the Actions log is opened too early or too late._x000D_
_x000D_
**Proposed Solution**_x000D_
_x000D_
I wonder if we can split the flow into two commands. One command would print out the URL, while the other command would wait for the token. This approach has the added benefit of easily allowing the printed URL to be redirected to other devices, via a notification service, so that the user doesn't have to actively wait for the GitHub Actions to reach the Cosign step. The method for communicating the necessary information to continue the OIDC protocol (if any) needs some thinking, but it could be an environment variable, a command-line argument, or a file, and GitHub Actions can handle any of these. I'd prefer to leave the details of how to implement this information-passing part to those who are more familiar with the OIDC protocol.

top_3_comments_text: haydentherapper: `cosign verify --certificate-chain bundle.pem --certificate cert.pem <IMAGE>` is currently broken as noted in #2632. Also note that if the certificate you've provided doesn't conform to Fulcio's certificate profile, where an identity is included in it, the command will fail. To work around this, you can do your own verification of the certificate using the chain and extract the public key to use with `cosign verify --key key.pem <IMAGE>`. You can use step's CLI https://smallstep.com/docs/step-cli/reference/certificate/key to do so. | lmussier: > Also note that if the certificate you've provided doesn't conform to Fulcio's certificate profile, where an identity is included in it, the command will fail. > And this will the case even when #2632 will be fixed? | haydentherapper: Correct. With Cosign 2.0, we swung the pendulum more towards identity verification. We will need to think through how to do byo-pki without impacting the required checks for identity.

To work around this, you can do your own verification of the certificate using the chain and extract the public key to use with `cosign verify --key key.pem <IMAGE>`. title: Storing VAULT_TOKEN as environment variable - security concern?
body_text:
I've been looking into use Cosign with Hashicorp Vault to avoid generating & storing keys locally or as Kubernetes secrets. Whilst digging into this, I've become aware that I would need to store the token for Vault as an environment variable "VAULT_TOKEN", as detailed [here](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/kms_support/#hashicorp-vault)._x000D_
_x000D_
From previous research and conversation with colleagues, it is my understanding that storing secrets in environment variables is not considered to be a secure practice, given that there are situations whereby logs and traces could include them, or they could be exposed via container inspection commands etc._x000D_
_x000D_
Kubernetes offers the alternative to mount secrets as permissioned files, so I was wondering of Cosign would be able to handle this? I've seen the Vault CLI (and Terraform) can use a token from `~/.vault-token` as documented [here](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/commands#token-helper)._x000D_
_x000D_
Or perhaps my security concerns aren't valid - happy to hear why not if that's the case._x000D_
_x000D_
Thanks!_x000D_
_x000D_
Matt

title: Environment variable ID token detection
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
I'd like to propose adding environment variable OIDC token detection for cosign._x000D_
_x000D_
Main use case is to support [GitLab CI OIDC tokens](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/secrets/id_token_authentication.html) - see https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/pull/983 for more details._x000D_
_x000D_
## Proposal_x000D_
_x000D_
Today, users can already use arbitrary OIDC tokens by using the `--identity-token` flag._x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
cosign sign --identity-token=${TOKEN} ..._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
To make this easier, I want to allow cosign to detect a token from environment variables._x000D_
To help avoid collisions with existing token variables, we should use a prefixed value such as `SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN`._x000D_
_x000D_
This could also be used to allow other CI providers to hook in without needing additional changes to cosign (though I'm still in support for allowing custom providers per host)._x000D_
_x000D_
Example: GitLab_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
build:_x000D_
  stage: build_x000D_
  id_tokens:_x000D_
    SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN:_x000D_
      aud: sigstore_x000D_
  script:_x000D_
     - cosign sign registry.gitlab.com/my-image_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
I'm happy to implement this._x000D_
_x000D_
Previous GitLab related issues:_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/2697_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/1254

In your case, `data.signature.allow` is a string with an error message. ```rego package signature allow[msg]{ input.type == "twistlockquality" result := less_than(input.stage_properties.scan_results.vulnerabilityDistribution.critical) msg := sprintf( "FAILED - twistlockquality, REASON: Found %v criticals", [input.stage_properties.scan_results.vulnerabilityDistribution.critical], ) result != true } ... ``` I suggest changing it to something like this: ```rego package signature allow { input.type == "twistlockquality" less_than(input.stage_properties.scan_results.vulnerabilityDistribution.critical) } ... ``` It looks like you're trying to pass an error message if the rule does fail, is that correct? title: `cosign copy` should have an option to create a "copy attestation"
body_text:
A user in Slack has a use case that looks like the following:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. There's an upstream image we depend on (`alpine:latest`) with no signatures._x000D_
2. We want to verify the images we use. Obviously if there's no upstream signatures, we can't use those._x000D_
3. So we want to sign the images when copying to a private repo to note "hey, I got this from hub.docker.com/alpine:latest at time T"_x000D_
_x000D_
This used to be possible via:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign copy upstream:latest private-repo_x000D_
cosign sign private-repo:latest_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
But now that we don't allow signing by tag (#2047) it's trickier, you need to:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
DIGEST=$(crane resolve upstream:latest)_x000D_
cosign copy upstream@$DIGEST private-repo_x000D_
cosign sign private-repo@$DIGEST_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This is a little safer in case "private-repo" is malicious._x000D_
_x000D_
But it's annoying to do. Also, semantically, the signature here means "I copied this." We could have the user `cosign attach attestation` instead that basically says "I copied this from <upstream>:<tag> at time T". If this becomes a common pattern, we could build that into `cosign copy`!_x000D_
_x000D_
(This hints at a general need for "common attestation patterns" with sugar support in Cosign.)

title: Is `cosign verify --key https://...` a foot-gun?
body_text:
Added in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/issues/247 to support a use case like:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
cosign verify \_x000D_
    --url https://raw.githubusercontent.com/image-publishing-org/project-repo/$RELEASE_TAG/cosign.pub \_x000D_
    gcr.io/image/to/verify:$RELEASE_TAG_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This seems to get used in a few places:_x000D_
_x000D_
- Misc. places in our docs._x000D_
- [Distributing keys for SUSE's signed images](https://codeengineered.com/blog/2022/bci-verify-cosign/)_x000D_
- [Distributing keys for Istio's signed images](https://istio.io/latest/docs/ops/best-practices/image-signing-validation/)_x000D_
_x000D_
We could:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Leave it._x000D_
2. Rip out `--key https://` with the logic that you can just pass `--key <(curl ...)`_x000D_
3. Require that HTTP-fetched keys also have a `--fingerprint` flag passed. This would support the "easy one-liner in our docs on image verification" use case._x000D_
_x000D_
The argument against (3) is that it doesn't support any notion of rotation (a BYO PKI situation would be a little better). The argument against (2)/(3) is that it's kinda security theater: if we're worried so much about https://istio.io/misc/istio-key.pub being compromised, why couldn't the attacker also modify https://istio.io/latest/docs/ops/best-practices/image-signing-validation/ ?
top_3_comments_text: sigwinch28: I think another argument here is that any form of key verification the user wants to perform is inherently racy with the use of the `--url` flag with the current form of the `verify` command. Since the `verify` command doesn't output either the public key or its fingerprint there is a race condition between running `verify` and the user fetching the key out of band to verify it somehow. Something like `curl ... -o key.pub; run-some-verification-steps key.pub; cosign verify --key key.pub` would avoid the race condition.

title: Support for signing and verifying items in IPFS
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
IPFS (InterPlanetary FileSystem, https://ipfs.tech/) provides a public, content-addressable filesystem._x000D_
_x000D_
IPFS files can be address via `ipfs://[hashcode]` where `hashcode` is the immutable hash of the file (technically, it's a Merkle tree of hashes where `hashcode` is the root)._x000D_
_x000D_
Thus, the bytes at a given `hashcode` will either not exist or will be the same everywhere, to everyone, for all time._x000D_
_x000D_
Signing an IPFS url/contents will provide a mechanism for signing and verifying the signature of an immutable item._x000D_
_x000D_
So... what can be immutable? An SBOM. Other build artifacts (e.g., [OmniBOR](https://omnibor.dev) receipts.)_x000D_
_x000D_
Adding IPFS signing and verification capabilities to cosign will allow for signing public SBOMs and other artifacts_x000D_
stored in IPFS._x000D_
_x000D_

title: cosign sign: the error message of passing mis-ordered CA chain is not clear (misleading).
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
I met this error when trying `cosign sign`. _x000D_
```_x000D_
$ COSIGN_PASSWORD="" ./cosign sign --upload=true --tlog-upload=false --certificate-chain staging_ca_bundle.pem --key import-cosign.key --cert cert --timestamp-server-url https://tsa.enforce.dev/api/v1/timestamp haskell@sha256:f33e8cb119fd5b436c39a3f45000bf732bce8e2ac71553ac5d307c10d01418ba_x000D_
_x000D_
Error: signing [haskell@sha256:f33e8cb119fd5b436c39a3f45000bf732bce8e2ac71553ac5d307c10d01418ba]: getting signer: unable to validate certificate chain: cert verification failed: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. Check your TUF root (see cosign initialize) or set a custom root with env var SIGSTORE_ROOT_FILE_x000D_
main.go:74: error during command execution: signing [haskell@sha256:f33e8cb119fd5b436c39a3f45000bf732bce8e2ac71553ac5d307c10d01418ba]: getting signer: unable to validate certificate chain: cert verification failed: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. Check your TUF root (see cosign initialize) or set a custom root with env var SIGSTORE_ROOT_FILE_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
The root cause is that I did not permutate the CA cert chain following the instruction:_x000D_
```_x000D_
$ ./cosign sign --help | grep root                                                                                                    _x000D_
      --certificate-chain string                                                                 path to a list of CA X.509 certificates in PEM format which will be needed when building the certificate chain for the signing certificate. Must start with the parent intermediate CA certificate of the signing certificate and end with the root certificate. Included in the OCI Signature_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
`staging_ca_bundle.pem` includes 13 self-signed root CA certs for different environments. There is no intermediate CA. The code signing cert is directly signed by one of the root CAs and that CA cert is in the second place in `staging_ca_bundle.pem` (1 cert above and 11 certs below). After I delete other root CA certs or put that cert to the bottom, it works._x000D_
_x000D_
The error message is a little bit misleading because `cosign sign` does not load `SIGSTORE_ROOT_FILE` anywhere (only loaded in `cosign verify`)._x000D_
_x000D_
More info: https://sigstore.slack.com/archives/C01PZKDL4DP/p1682632649714239_x000D_
_x000D_

title: 'cosign sign' fails with JFrog Artifactory docker registry due to 403 response on non-existing tag
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
We observe the `cosign sign` started to fail with the Artifactory Registry from commit https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/commit/17cc13812d8a7bfbb068ffc10fdbbdb3a9416f11 / https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2929.  The `cosign` clients sends a GET request with a tag derived from the digest but with `:` changed to `-` and `.sig` append, such as:_x000D_
`GET https://docker.xyz.com:4443/v2/dmitris777/scratch-3047c035/manifests/sha256-766b3e7864fcccb18ca4bd0d3a396c8ee16da4fe5b321ccbae79bec32c95139f.sig`_x000D_
It does so to check if there is a signature image already or not, expecting the "regular" 404 (Not Found) if there is no such tag.  Unfortunately, some Docker Registries such as JFrog Artifactory apparently return 403 (Forbidden) instead of 404 for the `/v2/<image>/manifests/<reference>` when `<reference>` is a non-existing tag:_x000D_
```bash_x000D_
$ curl -v -i -H “$acc” -H “$host” -H “$jwt” https://docker.xyz.com:4443/v2/dmitris777/scratch-3047c035/manifests/xyznosuch_x000D_
< HTTP/1.1 403_x000D_
{“errors”:[{“code”:“UNAUTHORIZED”,“message”:“The client does not have permission for manifest: Download request for repo:path ‘docker-ouroath-cache:dmitris777/scratch-3047c035/xyznosuch/list.manifest.json’ is forbidden for user: ‘token:dockerwrite’.“,”detail”:{“manifest”:“dmitris777/scratch-3047c035"}}]}_x000D_
```_x000D_
It may be related to https://jfrog.atlassian.net/browse/RTFACT-13797 "Artifactory return 403 instead of 404 for non-existing artifacts in virtual repositories."_x000D_
_x000D_
<!--What needs to be improved? What should be done? Has there been any related work_x000D_
before? Any relevant links or material?_x000D_
-->_x000D_
The proposed workaround is to treat the 403 response the same way as 404 when checking for existence of the signature image and not do a hard/fatal error in this case.  This is similar to a recent change in https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/pull/1691/files.  When testing with modification in https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2972, I was able to do `cosign sign` (and the subsequent `cosign verify`)._x000D_
_x000D_
/cc @jonjohnsonjr

title: Cosign release verification instructions succeed despite root key having expired
body_text:
I've been going through the [Verifying Cosign Releases](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/installation/#verifying-cosign-releases) section of the cosign install instructions. (I'm looking into the right way to validate an automated install of cosign.)_x000D_
_x000D_
The instructions start with installing TUF and running :_x000D_
```console_x000D_
$ curl -o sigstore-root.json https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sigstore/root-signing/main/ceremony/2022-10-18/repository/5.root.json_x000D_
$ tuf-client init https://tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev sigstore-root.json_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
If I look at `5.root.json` (`sigstore-root.json` after downloading), I see:_x000D_
```json_x000D_
{_x000D_
 "signed": {_x000D_
     "_type": "root",_x000D_
     "spec_version": "1.0",_x000D_
     "version": 5,_x000D_
     "expires": "2023-04-18T18:13:43Z",_x000D_
     "keys": {_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
So it seems to be expired. And looking at the root-signing repo, I can see there are more recent versions which aren't expired: https://github.com/sigstore/root-signing/tree/main/repository/repository_x000D_
_x000D_
When I proceed with the validation instructions using the expired `5.root.json` trust root, everything succeeds — the cosign binary matches the signature, and the signature matches the public key tuf-client produces._x000D_
_x000D_
Shouldn't this have failed though? _x000D_
_x000D_
From the POV of someone who isn't familiar with TUF, it's not clear to me what trust assumptions I'm making when installing go-tuf and using it to fetch the `artifact.pub` public key. My guess is that it should be checking that the key has been signed by the keys in the root, or is derived from the root in some way. But I'd expect that to fail if the root says it's expired._x000D_
_x000D_
I feel like the instructions could describe the security/trust model that the validation follows, as I assume most people won't be familiar with TUF._x000D_
_x000D_
Also, it seems like the trust hinges on trusting that downloading`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sigstore/root-signing/main/ceremony/2022-10-18/repository/5.root.json` does is in fact result in the keys the project expects. Shouldn't there be some kind of external verification of this? Like something to tie it back to your initial signing ceremony livestream for example?

title: Add CLI to override `docker-reference`
body_text:
I proposed a RFC PR to be able to override the `critical.identity.docker-reference` field in the signature to a different container image reference: https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2984_x000D_
_x000D_
I'd like to discuss the feature here with y'all to see if that's a feasible extension to cosign._x000D_
_x000D_
Setting the field is particularly useful when using proxy mirrors like registry.k8s.io (used by upstream Kubernetes), where end-users have no chance to actually assume the underlying registry. This change allows signing images using the mirror/proxy identifier, while validation can then happen without requiring any additional remapping._x000D_
_x000D_
It is necessary not only for proxies, but also for many staging workflows (creating an image signed with the production key, with a production identity, but not publishing it yet and storing it in an internal registry)._x000D_
_x000D_
Refers to https://github.com/containers/image/issues/1952, https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/pull/1166

title: Add Gitpod Provider Interface
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Gitpod is a remote workspace solution that has the ability (still in BETA) to generate JWT tokens to authenticate users within a workspace against external services like Sigstore, Vault or AWS directly._x000D_
_x000D_
Because gitpod can generate these tokens using a command line, and thus does not require a browser to do any auth, it makes sense to create a provider within cosign and gitsign that can automatically call this CLI on the users behalf, thus eliminating the need to do any external auth checks._x000D_
_x000D_
The command line in question is `gp idp token --audience sigstore` and is currently still in BETA, but can be run from any gitpod workspace. The devs are currently working to [add the correct email claims](https://github.com/gitpod-io/gitpod/issues/17530) to the resulting token so that it is compatible with sigstore.

title: add support for mTLS connection to the TSA (timestamp server)
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Currently there is no way to:_x000D_
* pass client TLS certificates when establishing https connection to the timestamp server (TSA)_x000D_
* specify custom CA certificate chain for that connection except the `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` environment variables which have a number of disadvantages such as 1) not having any effect on Darwin or Windows 2) to overwrite instead of extending the system certificate store you normally need to set _both_ `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR`, possibly to some "fake" locations (overwriting instead of extending is necessary if you want to make sure that only custom CA certs can be used for the connection to the TSA)_x000D_
* specify SAN values that the server's certificates must have (SAN validation of the TSA server's TLS certificates)_x000D_
_x000D_
These missing features make it currently impossible to use a TSA server in an environment where every connection must be done using mTLS (for example cloud setup where mTLS is required for authentication and authorisation)._x000D_
_x000D_
Currently we have the `--timestamp-server-url` parameter for `cosign sign`.  _x000D_
We can add additional command-line (or possibly configuration) parameters to add those features. We can borrow some names from the corresponding `curl` parameters:_x000D_
```bash_x000D_
$ curl --help all | egrep 'cert|key'_x000D_
     --cacert <file>      CA certificate to verify peer against_x000D_
-E, --cert <certificate[:password]> Client certificate file and password_x000D_
      --key <key>          Private key file name_x000D_
     --key-type <type>    Private key file type (DER/PEM/ENG)_x000D_
     --pass <phrase>      Pass phrase for the private key_x000D_
```_x000D_
     _x000D_
Some possible new parameter names:     _x000D_
* `--timestamp-server-cacert`_x000D_
* `--timestamp-server-cert`_x000D_
* `--timestamp-server-key`_x000D_
* `--timestamp-server-san`   # for SAN validation of the TSA server's certificates_x000D_
_x000D_
Eventually, for the "full blown" mTLS, it would be good to have a parameter on the server's side to specify the allowed values in the SAN values of the client's TLS certificate._x000D_
_x000D_
References:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. https://www.openssl.org/docs/man1.1.1/man3/SSL_CTX_set_default_verify_paths.html_x000D_
2. https://go.googlesource.com/go/+/refs/heads/master/src/crypto/x509/cert_pool.go#102_x000D_
> _x000D_
```_x000D_
On Unix systems other than macOS the environment variables SSL_CERT_FILE and_x000D_
SSL_CERT_DIR can be used to override the system default locations for the SSL_x000D_
certificate file and SSL certificate files directory, respectively. The_x000D_
latter can be a colon-separated list._x000D_
```_x000D_
3. https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/36093 crypto/x509: load certs from env vars + extra locations_x000D_
4. [Discussion](https://gophers.slack.com/archives/C6CKB7AA2/p1685095252459469?thread_ts=1685051992.319459&cid=C6CKB7AA2) about `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` in #crypto channel of the Gophers slack (highlights that both needs to be set to achieve overwrite of the system roots)_x000D_

title: Does Cosign support sub-keys?
body_text:
**Question**_x000D_
In TLS PKI, it is generally considered best practice to create a root certificate authority (CA), but NOT use that CA to sign individual leaf certificates. Instead, you should create one or more intermediate CAs which are signed by the root CA. Those intermediate CAs should then be used to either create more CAs, or sign individual leaf certificates. This creates a certificate chain (example below)._x000D_
_x000D_
```mermaid_x000D_
  graph TD;_x000D_
      A[root CA]-->B[Intermediate CA 1]_x000D_
      A-->C[Intermediate CA 2]_x000D_
      B-->D[Leaf certificate 1]_x000D_
      B-->E[Leaf certificate 2]_x000D_
      C-->F[Leaf certificate 3]_x000D_
      C-->G[Leaf certificate 4]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This has a number of benefits:_x000D_
_x000D_
- The root CA private key only needs to be used when signing intermediate CAs, then can be kept offline the rest of the time_x000D_
- Individual leaf certificates can have a shorter expiration timeframe (e.g., docs.sigstore.dev is [90 days](https://crt.sh/?id=9033218940)), while the root CA certifcate can have a long expiration timeframe (e.g., [20 years](https://crt.sh/?id=9314791) in the case of Let's Encrypt)_x000D_
-  You only need to trust the root CA public certificate on each device (not each intermediate CA public certificate). Anything signed by that root CA public certificate will be trusted._x000D_
_x000D_
Does cosign have similar functionality?_x000D_
_x000D_
**Potential use case**_x000D_
We want to use a different cosign key for each Jenkins instance we have. However, this would require us to publish multiple cosign public keys. This could be confusing for customers trying to verify our Docker images if we have to specify a specific key for one image, a different key for another, etc..._x000D_
_x000D_
It would be much easier if cosign had the concept of sub-keys. This way, we would only be required to give out one "root" public key, which could then be used to verify images signed by any of that root's sub-keys._x000D_
top_3_comments_text: haydentherapper: Hey, this is already supported by the sigstore infrastructure and actually how the public instance of our CA, Fulcio, is configured. Certificates are issued from an intermediate CA. Note that both the root and intermediate are shipped through our TUF root of trust (see https://github.com/sigstore/root-signing/tree/main/targets for the list of targets), so it doesn't really matter if we were to use a root vs intermediate, as both are a part of our root of trust. I would recommend reading over https://docs.sigstore.dev/security/ to learn more about identity-based signing. You could for example configure a service account for your Jenkins instance, and for each signing, use an identity token for that service account to fetch a certificate from the Fulcio CA. | lmarchione-r7: @haydentherapper - Sorry about the confusing wording. I was specifically wondering about locally-generated cosign keys (e.g., when running `cosign generate-key-pair`), not the certificates that Fulcio uses. | haydentherapper: That’ll be the best way to avoid distributing multiple keys. There’s no support for subkeys without using PKI.

title: COSIGN_REPOSITORY does not allow using a port in the path
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
Getting the error _x000D_
```_x000D_
$COSIGN_REPOSITORY: repository can only contain the characters `abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789_-./`_x000D_
```_x000D_
Our repository has a port in it e.g. `repo-app.datacenter.net:5001`._x000D_
_x000D_
Cosign is able to handle that just fine when it infers the repository from the image name, but when setting the env var `COSIGN_REPOSITORY` it fails. I feel like this might just be a bug with parsing that env var vs using the image path to decide which repository to use._x000D_
_x000D_
**Version**_x000D_
```_x000D_

top_3_comments_text: znewman01: I think this is just a misleading error message and bad docs: ``` $ cosign env | grep COSIGN_REPOSITORY # COSIGN_REPOSITORY can be used to store signatures in an alternate location COSIGN_REPOSITORY= ``` You're supposed to give a full *repository* rather than just the *registry* to COSIGN_REPOSITORY. So ``` $ COSIGN_REPOSITORY=repo-app.datacenter.net:5001/foo cosign sign hub.docker.com/alpine@sha256:... ``` should work, and will sign the `alpine` image on DockerHub but store the signatures in `repo-app.datacenter.net:5001/foo`. I could imagine wanting a shortcut like `$COSIGN_REGISTRY` which would use the *relative* repository name on an alternate registry.

sudo-bmitch: For an artifact, you do not want to use "application/vnd.oci.image.config.v1+json" for the config. That's a sign that this is a container image (though runtimes will throw errors when they see the layer media type). Instead you either need a dedicated config blob with your own type and content, or if you have no separate config, you would use the artifactType field. The one registry that I know you'll want to work with is GitLab who has an allow list on their config mediaType and may do the same for the artifactType.
chaospuppy: So sounds like you're on the money @lcarva, we will still need to set the annotation if we wish to identify which layer contains the desired predicate type, even after reference types are introduced.
sudo-bmitch: Assuming you only have a single layer, you would want to define any annotations useful for filtering on the manifest itself, rather than the layer. Annotations on the manifest are pulled up in the referrers response, allowing you to pick the dsse envelope artifact from a list of artifacts all created for the same image. This is a bit different from the current cosign design where there's one attestation manifest with multiple layers. The goal of the OCI design is to make it easier to add and remove entries, especially when the registry is managing the referrers response.

title: `cosign digest` subcommand to resolve tag to digest
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
A `cosign digest $artifact-reference` subcommand that can resolve an image tag to the digest._x000D_
_x000D_
**Why**_x000D_
_x000D_
Signing (or any other operation) by tag is generally discouraged (ref #2047), as tags can be mutable and change between two different steps in a workflow (eg publish and sign)._x000D_
_x000D_
In most cases, users should try and get an image digest from a previous step, eg directly from the output of their build tool._x000D_
_x000D_
However, there are situations where there is no previous stage that can produce an image digest, and we'd like to resolve a tag to a digest, and only use the digest going forward in a workflow._x000D_
Example: check if there's a signed copy of in image in a private mirror. If not, run processes to generate trust on the image (scanners), and push the signed result into the private mirror for use._x000D_
_x000D_
There are other tools that can do this, eg `crane digest`, but installing an extra tool that isn't otherwise needed seems wasteful._x000D_
`cosign` already partially does this with `cosign triangulate`  (the digest is used as the tag for the signature) and some massaging of the output can turn it into the digest, but it would be nice to to have to do that:_x000D_
_x000D_
```sh_x000D_
$ cosign triangulate $image | tr ':-' '@:' | sed 's/\.sig$//'_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_

title: Observations whilst using Cosign as a Library
body_text:
Cosign initially was created as a binary, and with it's use being quite wide and popular there's been more and more users that have expressed desire to use Cosign in their own coded custom workflows. This is also true of any third-party tooling that wants to integrate with Cosign and use it's functionality but does not want to include the calling of the binary itself. This is where the ability of being able to integrate Cosign as a library would come in handy. There has been previous threads about this, so I won't go any further with it. I just want to outline the current state of play when it comes to using Cosign as a library, so decisions can be made in future about how to make this more streamlined._x000D_
_x000D_
The primary observations were the following:_x000D_
_x000D_
- Due to a lot of functionality being in the `cmd` layer that cannot be bypassed, users have to create all of the config structs in-code with default values and pass them to the `cmd` layer. At the CLI level, this isn't required because Cosign is built with the [`cobra`](https://github.com/spf13/cobra) library which allows for the default setting of values - which isn't possible when using Cosign as a library, so we should probably allow this in future._x000D_
- When specifying registry credentials, it wasn't obvious on how this could be done. With a couple of hours of sifting through older Cosign issues, I saw that there is some code that looks to a local docker creds store but if one wasn't present where the code was being run (in my case a container), you had a number of options through Keychains. We should probably make this easier instead of users having to write the following pieces of code, or at least document it in future for the cases where there are no `.dockerconfig.json` files:_x000D_
_x000D_
```golang_x000D_
// A keychain that is able to return the creds based on the registry url_x000D_
type InMemoryKeyChain struct {  _x000D_
	// An in-memory map of username/passwords_x000D_
	credentials map[string]userCredentials_x000D_
}_x000D_
..._x000D_
    keychain := &InMemoryKeyChain{_x000D_
		credentials: map[string]userCredentials{_x000D_
			req.Source.Cosign.Registry: {_x000D_
				username: req.Source.Username,_x000D_
				password: req.Source.Password,_x000D_
			},_x000D_
		},_x000D_
	}_x000D_
..._x000D_
		Registry: options.RegistryOptions{_x000D_
			AllowInsecure:      false,_x000D_
			KubernetesKeychain: false,_x000D_
			Keychain:           keychain,_x000D_
		},_x000D_
..._x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
- Providing signing key had to be done via an environment variable - which isn't the most secure. In containerised environments this isn't the end of the world as the environment variable could have been set in the code (in my case it was) and so it would not have been visible by any process other than the application itself and it's child-processes. But on longer running applications, where the variable is not set in code, this is probably not ideal. In more library compatible versions of a future Cosign, we should probably allow the option of users being able to just pass the key through as a parameter to the API sign function, how they get the key into code can be of their own concern. But allowing it to be as easy as possible without compriomising on security is probably a wise idea._x000D_
_x000D_
- A similar story to the `COSIGN_PASSWORD` variable. Because it has to be entered by a user that runs the binary, or set as a variable, we should probably make this similar to the signing key point above where we allow it to be passed as a parameter to the function in future API friendly versions of the library._x000D_
_x000D_
All round, the experience actually wasn't that painful. The Keychain took longer than I'd like it to have took, but it still works, and the key and password variable setting isn't the end of the world, but can definitely be made easier and more secure. I think the painful process will be how strike a balance between the `cmd` and `pkg`/`api` layer so that we offer the same functionality across both whilst keeping the same user experience for the `cmd` layer and making the API layer easier. I suspect that we definitely want to allow users to set all of the same flags as I had to in the `cmd` version, but in order to cut the code down, perhaps we set defaults? (like we do in the `cmd` layer using `cobra`) so users don't have to provide all of them._x000D_
_x000D_
As a footnote, we have started to implement custom error types in the `pkg` layer that will be useful when using Cosign as a library so users can write error handling code on their end:_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2673_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2766_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2976_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/3038_x000D_
_x000D_
The reference PR for all of this can be found in the following PR where I implemented Cosign support for the `registry-image-resource` for Concourse: https://github.com/concourse/registry-image-resource/pull/341/files_x000D_
_x000D_
- https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go_x000D_

title: Support the protobuf bundle format in Cosign
body_text:
## Background

Sigstore created a common format in [sigstore/protobuf-specs](https://github.com/sigstore/protobuf-specs/blob/main/protos/sigstore_bundle.proto) for the output from Sigstore clients. sigstore-python, sigstore-java and sigstore-js currently support the bundle format. Golang currently does not support the bundle: sigstore-go is under active development, and Cosign has defined its own format.

## Requirements

- [x] [P0] Output bundle for `cosign sign-blob` or `cosign attest-blob`
- [x] [P0] Read bundle for `cosign verify-blob` or `cosign verify-blob-attestation`
- [x] [P0] Verify conformance with other clients

## Secondary goals

- [x] [P1] Persist bundle in OCI image manifest for `cosign sign`
- [x] [P1] Persist bundle in OCI image manifest for `cosign attest`
- [x] [P1] Read bundle from OCI image manifest for `cosign verify` or `cosign verify-attestation`

## Nice to haves

- [ ] [P2] Separation of utilities in a dedicated package to make it easy to move code to sigstore-go
- [ ] [P2] Support for uploading a bundle to OCI with `cosign attach`

## Resources

* [Bundle specification](https://github.com/sigstore/protobuf-specs/blob/main/protos/sigstore_bundle.proto)
* [Rekor output to protobuf library](https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/blob/main/pkg/tle/tle.go)

Justification for sign-blob being a P0 and sign being a P1 is that OCI handles storage already, so it's less critical to have a new format.

We can also add and replace the sigstore-go dependencies if you wish. - Add `--sigstore-bundle` flag to sign-blob command. This patch is a work in progress, and if you agree with the direction, I could add support for attest-blob and verify, refactor redundant implementations, add tests, etc. Having said that, I'm concerned about the following points at the moment: - Handling of the root certificate - As I was proceeding with this implementation, I noticed https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/3138#discussion_r1275534788. I did some research, but I couldn't figure out a pattern that would actually return anything other than a leaf certificate. - Public key hint - In the current implementation, the `Hint` field is always empty when returning a public key. When I looked at the implementations of sigstore-js, sigstore-python, and sigstore-java, they didn't seem to generate hints either. Is this okay? - According to the [spec](https://github.com/sigstore/protobuf-specs/blob/v0.2.1/protos/sigstore_common.proto#L117-L125), it says "The format of the hint must be agreed upon out of band by the signer and the verifiers" but it is my understanding that there is no consensus across the Sigstore ecosystem yet. - Package interface compatibility - I ended up choosing an interface centered around `sigstore-go/pkg/verify.SignedEntity`, but I'm not sure if this is appropriate. I was assuming that for conformance testing, `verify-bundle` and `sign-bundle` would make use of the new codepaths that implement `--new-bundle-format`, and `verify` and `sign` would use the previous / existing cosign codepaths. However, there are conformance tests that use `--trusted-root` with `verify`, which we did not implement support for in #3796. I think there's a couple of options here: - Go back and implement `--trusted-root` support in cosign, even when you aren't specifying `--new-bundle-format` - Maybe we want to do this anyways? Adding support for specifying a trusted root via CLI should be straightforward. For fetching roots via TUF, I'd recommend we initialize two TUF clients, the new and old one, and merge targets fetched from the old TUF client (which would handle private deployments with the custom metadata) into the `TrustedRoot` struct. title: Support importing GPG keys for signing
body_text:

title: Feature: Certificate Caching
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
We've been running into rate-limits for the public sigstore instance:_x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
unable to sign image: getting signer: getting key from Fulcio: retrieving cert: POST https://fulcio.sigstore.dev/api/v1/signingCert returned 429 Too Many Requests_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
This is somewhat self-inflicted, since we build and publish a bunch of container images in parallel ([sample successful run](https://github.com/chainguard-images/images/actions/runs/5686675901)), but I don't think it's an uncommon issue users will run into._x000D_
_x000D_
For gitsign, we made an optional [credential cache](https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/tree/main/cmd/gitsign-credential-cache) for avoiding multiple calls to Fulcio. This is disabled by default and if enabled gitsign will use the configured local socket to cache certs it fetches in memory for the lifetime of the cert, and reuse the cert for future signing operations until it expires._x000D_
_x000D_
This also has some useful side-benefits like letting users [SSH forward the socket to support remote-signing operations](https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/tree/main/cmd/gitsign-credential-cache#forwarding-cache-over-ssh)._x000D_
_x000D_
Nothing in the cache is actually specific to gitsign - the functionality is exposed over a [simple RPC API](https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/internal/cache/api/api.go). Would it make sense to add credential-cache support to cosign to allow for client-side caching of certs to avoid Fulcio rate limits?_x000D_
_x000D_
(Rekor rate limits would be the next concern - I don't think we publish the default rate limits, so I'm not sure how much of a concern this is in practice though 🤷)_x000D_
_x000D_
cc @jonjohnsonjr

I understand that we need to update the private key's password. So, to implement that: - It requires a `key` path - and flag, `update-password` So, the whole command would be like: ``` cosign generate-key-pair --key cosign.key --update-password=true ``` So, the above command does the following procedure: - First, read the file of the key, then decode the pem format - Secondly, Decrypt the ciphertext using the old password. - Then, we can Encrypt it again, with a new password provided by the user. title: Allow configurable signing algorithms
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
_I've filed similar issues under Cosign and Rekor. I realise there's a lot of overlap in maintainers, but wanted to make sure that we discuss each project that we plan to touch. Apologies if this feels a bit spammy.__x000D_
_x000D_
Hi there! At Trail of Bits, we're looking at potentially implementing part of the [Configurable Crypto Algorithms](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-wF1t6lmJO37BzStbyz8ZkDhNm86HyvKZSaDl7uyHxI) proposal (specifically Phase 1). I wanted to float this idea to each of the relevant Sigstore sub-projects so we can hash out the details in a more concrete way._x000D_
_x000D_
Across the Sigstore stack, we default to using ECDSA for signatures and SHA256 for hashing. There's more detail in the linked proposal but there are a number of motivations for wanting to customise the signatures that are generated, including paving the way for post-quantum signatures. The proposed design includes having a "supported algorithm" registry (perhaps this can go in the Protobuf specs) that outlines enumerates the approved signature/hash algorithm combinations. We specifically don't want to allow arbitrary mixing and matching of signature and hash algorithm to avoid some of the security pitfalls listed in the proposal._x000D_
_x000D_
For Cosign, we want to support this set of approved signing algorithms. This can be as simple as a `--signing-algorithm` flag. As a first pass, we'd like to support ECDSA with SHA256 and SHA384 as well as EdDSA, with ECDSA-SHA256 remaining as the default._x000D_
_x000D_
I believe that in order to change this, we may have to make changes to the [sigstore-go](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go) and [sigstore](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore) libs, but I figured that I'd make the issue here since `cosign` is going to be entrypoint for this functionality.

This function is used in the `cosign import-key-pair` command - [cosign.LoadPrivateKey](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/pkg/cosign/keys.go#L208-L237) - signer/verifier objects: https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/tree/main/pkg/signature here ECDSA is assumed. - [LoadVerifier](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/blob/main/pkg/signature/verifier.go#L42), used on the verify side (e.g. `cosign verify-blob`) to load a verifier for the right algo. | dlorenc: This is awesome! | haydentherapper: For the public instance, the TUF root keys will need to be rotated to PQ keys and the metadata will also need to be re-signed. body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
_x000D_
We are using a cosign container inside our pipeline to sign newly build images. _x000D_
Up until v2.1.1 (public.ecr.aws/bitnami/cosign:2.1.1) this works without problems:_x000D_

[...]_x000D_

}_x000D_

After updating to v2.2.0 (public.ecr.aws/bitnami/cosign:2.2.0) the **Created** timestamp is totally wrong and leads to this:_x000D_

  "Parent": "",_x000D_
  "Comment": "",_x000D_

 [...]_x000D_

}_x000D_

title: cosign save fails with oci artifacts
body_text:
**Description**_x000D_
When using `cosign save` (and additionally `cosign load`) to download and upload images with oci artifacts, `cosign save` does not include the all oci artifacts. _x000D_
_x000D_
`cosign copy` from registry to registry **does** copy the image and all oci artifacts. I'm not sure of a use case for `cosign save` (and additionally `cosign load`) to not include all oci artifacts, so I assume it is bug/error and `cosign save` and `cosign copy` should have the same functionalities. I've tried this with many different images and produced the same result. Please let me know if you need any additional information, troubleshooting, or validation from me!_x000D_
